question:
A retailer runs an Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in eu-west-1. Amazon CloudFront serves the website at a custom domain in a Route 53 public hosted zone. The retailer requires DNS response authentication for validating resolvers and TLS encryption on both the viewer-to-CloudFront and CloudFront-to-ALB connections.

Which configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable DNSSEC signing and publish the delegation signer (DS) record in the parent zone. Attach an ACM certificate from us-east-1 to CloudFront and an ACM certificate from eu-west-1 to the ALB. Require HTTPS from viewers and use an HTTPS-only origin protocol policy.

Enable DNSSEC signing and publish the DS record in the parent zone. Attach an ACM certificate from eu-west-1 to both CloudFront and the ALB. Require HTTPS from viewers and use an HTTPS-only origin protocol policy.

Enable DNSSEC signing and publish the DS record in the parent zone. Attach appropriately located certificates to CloudFront and the ALB. Require HTTPS from viewers, but use HTTP-only for the origin connection.

Enable DNSSEC signing without publishing a DS record in the parent zone. Attach appropriately located certificates to CloudFront and the ALB. Require HTTPS from viewers and use an HTTPS-only origin protocol policy.

explanation.text:
<<1>> meets all three requirements. DNSSEC needs a chain of trust from the parent zone, while TLS separately protects each connection. CloudFront requires its ACM viewer certificate in us-east-1; the ALB certificate belongs in the ALB Region.

<<2>> places the viewer certificate in the wrong Region. <<3>> leaves the CloudFront-to-origin connection unencrypted even though viewers use HTTPS. <<4>> signs the zone without establishing the parent-to-child trust chain.

Treat DNS authenticity and transport encryption as separate controls. DNSSEC does not encrypt DNS responses, and signing helps clients only when their resolver validates the chain. Certificates must also cover the names used on their respective connections.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/dns-configuring-dnssec.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/cnames-and-https-requirements.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/dns-configuring-dnssec-enable-signing.html

question:
A company exposes Python Lambda functions through an Amazon API Gateway REST API. Only IAM principals with permission to invoke the API may call it. The operations team also needs latency traces and service maps for sampled requests across API Gateway, Lambda, and instrumented downstream calls.

Which solution meets both requirements?

options.text: Set method authorization to AWS_IAM, grant scoped execute-api:Invoke permissions, and have callers sign requests with Signature Version 4. Enable active X-Ray tracing on the API stage and Lambda functions, including downstream instrumentation and permissions.
Restrict CORS to the company website and grant callers execute-api:Invoke permissions. Leave method authorization set to NONE and use API Gateway access logs to produce distributed traces.
Require an API key and usage plan for each caller. Enable X-Ray tracing on the API stage and Lambda functions, and use the API key to enforce the caller’s IAM permissions.
Create an API Gateway backend client certificate and distribute it to callers. Enable execution logging in CloudWatch Logs and use the certificate to identify each caller’s IAM role.

explanation.text:
<<1>> combines IAM authorization with distributed tracing. AWS_IAM requires a signed request whose principal is permitted to invoke the relevant API resource. Active tracing samples requests; instrumented services contribute segments to the same trace. Prefer temporary role credentials.

<<2>> fails authentication: CORS governs browser access to responses, and an IAM grant is not enforced by a method configured with authorization NONE. Access logs alone do not create end-to-end traces. <<3>> confuses API keys, which identify usage-plan consumers, with IAM authorization. <<4>> reverses the certificate’s purpose: an API Gateway backend client certificate authenticates API Gateway to a backend, not callers to IAM.

Authentication, authorization, usage limits, and observability are separate concerns. X-Ray sampling does not guarantee a trace for every request.

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/api-gateway-control-access-using-iam-policies-to-invoke-api.html

question:
A company deploys a stateless web application to Amazon EC2 instances by manually running scripts. It wants an automated deployment process that validates a new version before production cutover and can return to the previous version without reinstalling it. The application can run on Elastic Beanstalk, and database changes remain compatible with both application versions.

Which deployment design best meets these requirements?

options.text: Automate deployment to a separate Elastic Beanstalk environment and run the scripts as platform hooks. Test the new environment, swap the environment CNAMEs, and retain the previous environment for a reverse swap if needed.

Automate an Elastic Beanstalk rolling deployment with an additional batch. Terminate the additional instances when the update completes, and redeploy the previous application bundle if production errors occur.
Use CodeBuild to install the new version on one production instance, test it, and then update the remaining instances in place. Reinstall the previous bundle on all instances if errors occur.

Use a Systems Manager Automation runbook to validate the release in staging and then replace the application on every production instance. Run the deployment again with the previous bundle if errors occur.

explanation.text:
<<1>> keeps the old and new versions in separate environments. After testing green, a CNAME swap directs clients toward it; reversing the swap provides rollback without reinstalling blue. Platform hooks can run deployment customization scripts.

<<2>> is a rolling replacement of the existing environment, so returning to the previous release requires redeployment. <<3>> tests a canary but then overwrites the production fleet. <<4>> automates testing and installation, but also overwrites the old production release. All three lack the retained environment required by the stem.

A DNS cutover is not instantaneous for every client. Keep the old environment available while cached records expire and connections drain. Shared data must remain compatible; application rollback does not undo database migrations.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/using-features.CNAMESwap.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/platforms-linux-extend.hooks.html

question:
A company is migrating a Linux application to an EC2 Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones. Its license is bound to a network adapter’s MAC address, and the vendor takes 15 hours to issue a license. The application can use an attached secondary adapter for licensing. New license inventory must be usable without rebuilding the AMI.

The application accepts only database IP addresses. There are no stable database DNS names, but the database replacement workflow publishes the current addresses. New and running application instances must pick up those updates.

Which actions meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Pre-create secondary ENIs in each required Availability Zone and obtain a license for each MAC address. Store the license files in S3. At launch, atomically claim an available ENI and license, attach that ENI in the instance’s AZ, and release it safely when the instance is retired.
Pre-create licensed ENIs and embed their complete license inventory in the application AMI. Require each new instance to select a license only from the files baked into that AMI.
Resolve the database hostnames once during instance bootstrap and write the returned addresses to the application configuration.

Have the database replacement workflow invoke Lambda to update Systems Manager Parameter Store. Retrieve the parameters during bootstrap and through a controlled refresh process that updates running applications.
Create an AMI from a licensed instance and configure Auto Scaling to launch that image. Rely on the AMI to reproduce the original instance’s adapter MAC address.

explanation.text:
Select <<1>> and <<4>>. An ENI retains its attributes, including its MAC address, when reattached to a compatible instance in the same AZ. A prelicensed pool avoids waiting for issuance during scale-out. Parameter Store provides current configuration independently of the AMI; the replacement workflow supplies the updates.

<<2>> ties available license files to an AMI version, violating the requirement to extend inventory without rebuilding images. <<3>> assumes stable DNS names that the scenario does not provide and never refreshes running clients. <<5>> copies the software image, not the original ENI or its MAC identity.

ENI inventory limits scale-out capacity. Claim pairs atomically, preserve the ENI after instance termination, and ensure the application uses that adapter. Parameter Store does not discover database addresses or reconfigure applications by itself.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/using-eni.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html

question:
A web application runs on EC2 instances in private subnets across two Availability Zones behind an internet-facing ALB. Each private subnet routes outbound internet traffic through a NAT instance in its own AZ. Login works, but a server-side request to a map provider fails for about half of page loads.

Requests fail only from one AZ. Its NAT instance is stopped; the application instances are healthy, and route-table and network ACL configurations are otherwise correct. The company wants to restore access and reduce NAT maintenance.

Which solution best addresses the failure?

options.text: Add outbound network ACL rules for the map provider’s addresses and restrict future network ACL changes with IAM policies.
Enable ALB cross-zone load balancing so every server-side request to the map provider uses the healthy AZ’s NAT instance.
Increase the stopped NAT instance’s instance size and retain one manually managed NAT instance per AZ.
Replace the NAT instances with a public zonal NAT gateway in each AZ. Route each private subnet to its same-AZ gateway, and route the gateways’ public subnets to an internet gateway.

explanation.text:
<<4>> repairs the confirmed outbound failure and replaces self-managed instances with AWS-managed NAT gateways. A zonal gateway in each AZ avoids making one AZ’s egress depend on another AZ.

<<1>> changes a control already verified as correct. <<2>> confuses inbound ALB distribution with outbound routing: an application instance uses its subnet route table for the map call. <<3>> does not establish a capacity problem and retains the maintenance and failover burden.

A 50% failure rate alone would not prove a NAT outage; the stopped instance and AZ-specific tests supply the decisive evidence. NAT gateways need correct routing and do not make external providers highly available.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-nat-comparison.html

question:
An internal portal runs on EC2 instances and reads confidential objects from an S3 bucket in the same Region. The instances must access S3 without an internet gateway or NAT device. Object access must be limited to the portal’s IAM role and a designated S3 gateway endpoint, even if another identity later receives an S3 permission grant.

The endpoint is already associated with the portal subnets’ route tables. Which additional configuration meets the access requirements?

options.text: Restrict the endpoint policy to the bucket and allow the endpoint in the bucket policy. Add a network ACL rule that references the S3 managed prefix list to block other instances.
Allow object access when aws:SourceIp matches the portal instances’ private addresses. Use this condition instead of restricting the requesting IAM role.

Grant the portal role the required S3 actions and restrict the endpoint policy to the bucket. Add bucket-policy denies for object requests outside the designated endpoint or from principals other than the portal role, using aws:SourceVpce and aws:PrincipalArn.
Restrict the endpoint policy to the bucket and grant the portal role S3 permissions. Leave the bucket policy unrestricted because the endpoint policy governs every possible path to the bucket.

explanation.text:
<<3>> enforces both the network path and the caller identity. The role supplies permission, the endpoint policy limits requests through that endpoint, and the bucket’s explicit denies prevent access through other paths or principals despite additional grants.

<<1>> uses a prefix list in a network ACL, which is unsupported, and does not reliably enforce the role restriction. <<2>> uses aws:SourceIp for endpoint traffic; aws:VpcSourceIp is the relevant IP condition, and an address is not the required role identity. <<4>> assumes the endpoint policy applies to requests that bypass the endpoint. It does not.

Separate private routing from authorization. An endpoint policy does not independently grant access. Scope resource-policy denies carefully; encrypted objects using SSE-KMS also require the appropriate KMS permissions.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpc-endpoints-s3.html

question:
A company publishes downloadable reports for global customers. It must block report requests whose source IP addresses are geolocated to countries on a company-maintained denylist, while retaining low-latency delivery elsewhere. The same country policy applies to every report. Reports can be stored in a private S3 bucket.

Which solution meets these requirements with the least operational effort?

options.text: Serve the reports from EC2 instances and maintain country IP ranges as deny rules in the instances’ subnet network ACLs.
Use Route 53 geolocation routing to return no record for denied countries. Serve the reports from a publicly accessible S3 website endpoint.
Use Route 53 geoproximity routing to shift denied-country requests to another AWS Region. Serve the same reports from that Region.
Deliver the reports through CloudFront with a country denylist. Use origin access control and a bucket policy that permits origin access only through the distribution.

explanation.text:
<<4>> combines country-level request filtering at CloudFront with global edge delivery. A private S3 origin with origin access control prevents clients from bypassing that distribution to fetch the same reports directly.

<<1>> requires maintaining changing IP ranges and does not provide a global content cache. <<2>> treats DNS answer selection as authorization; a client can bypass the intended DNS answer and reach the public origin. <<3>> changes routing proximity but does not deny report access.

CloudFront geographic restrictions apply to the entire distribution and depend on IP geolocation. They do not prove a user’s residence or identity; unknown locations and proxies require separate consideration when designing a stricter policy.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/georestrictions.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.html

question:
A company runs an application on EC2, S3, and DynamoDB. An external audit firm needs read-only access to evidence of AWS management activity and object- and item-level API activity during the next audit period. The auditor must not receive shared long-term credentials or general access to production data.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use CloudTrail Event history in each Region as the audit record. Let the auditor assume a role with permission to look up events, and rely on Event history to include all object and item operations.

Configure a CloudTrail trail with management events and the required S3 and DynamoDB data events. Retain the logs in a protected S3 bucket. Let the auditor assume a role scoped to those logs, with appropriate cross-account trust and an external ID for the firm’s multi-customer integration.
Enable CloudTrail management events and send S3 delivery notifications through SNS. Treat those notifications as the full record of object and item access and grant the auditor no log-bucket access.
Create an audit IAM role, attach it to the production EC2 instances, and add it to the S3 and DynamoDB resource policies. Ask the auditor to use that role without configuring a trust relationship.

explanation.text:
<<2>> supplies both the evidence and a usable, limited access path. CloudTrail data events must be enabled for the relevant S3 objects and DynamoDB tables. The auditor assumes a trusted role and receives temporary credentials whose permissions cover the log evidence. An external ID addresses the confused-deputy risk for a third party serving multiple customers.

<<1>> relies on Event history, which contains the last 90 days of management events in a Region and does not include the required data events. <<3>> omits data events and confuses delivery notifications with their log contents. <<4>> assigns permissions to resources without allowing the auditor to assume the role; it also fails to establish the required logging.

Configure collection and retention before the audit period. CloudTrail records AWS API activity, not arbitrary application logs, and enabling a trail cannot recreate unrecorded past data events.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/logging-data-events-with-cloudtrail.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_common-scenarios_third-party.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/view-cloudtrail-events.html

question:
A company has a documented patch approval list for its on-premises servers. It wants EC2 instances to follow equivalent operating-system patch rules during an existing weekly maintenance window. The instances can reach Systems Manager and their package repositories. The company wants managed compliance reporting and as little custom orchestration as possible.

Which solution should a solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Use Session Manager to open sessions on the instances during the maintenance window. Have operators run the approved installation commands and record the results manually.
Create matching Patch Manager baselines and use a scheduled Lambda function to discover targets, invoke patch commands, track completion, and implement cutoff and concurrency controls.
Package approved updates with Systems Manager Distributor and create a State Manager association that installs the package whenever it changes, regardless of the maintenance window.

Ensure the instances are Systems Manager managed nodes with SSM Agent and the required IAM permissions. Create matching Patch Manager baselines and register an AWS-RunPatchBaseline task in the maintenance window with appropriate targets and execution controls.

explanation.text:
<<4>> separates patch approval from execution timing. Patch Manager evaluates the configured baseline, while Maintenance Windows schedules the patch task and controls its execution. Managed-node prerequisites and package-repository connectivity are still required.

<<1>> substitutes manual sessions for fleet patch automation and compliance reporting. <<2>> can be engineered to work, but recreates orchestration already available in the maintenance-window service. <<3>> distributes packages without respecting the stated maintenance schedule or providing the same baseline-driven patch workflow.

Translate the on-premises approval policy into supported operating-system baselines; Patch Manager does not automatically import every third-party baseline format. State Manager can participate in patch workflows, so its mere presence is not what makes a design incorrect.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/patch-manager.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/maintenance-windows.html

question:
A financial-data provider processes market feeds in an on-premises Apache Kafka cluster. It wants to forward the output into Kinesis Data Streams and push near-real-time updates to authorized browser clients. Its AWS application already uses API Gateway WebSocket APIs. The primary link between the data center and AWS must avoid the public internet and support predictable network performance.

Which actions form a suitable solution? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Provision redundant Direct Connect connectivity and the required private virtual interfaces and routing between the data center and the AWS VPC.
Run Kafka consumers on EC2 and use the Kinesis Client Library to publish their output records into Kinesis Data Streams.
Run Kafka consumers on an EC2 Auto Scaling group and use the Kinesis Producer Library to publish records into Kinesis Data Streams. Coordinate Kafka consumer groups and handle retries.
Configure a Lambda event-source mapping for the stream. Track authorized WebSocket connection IDs and have the function call the API Gateway Management API PostToConnection operation to send updates.
Create an AppSync GraphQL API and send callbacks to the existing API Gateway WebSocket clients by using the AppSync @connections endpoint.
Use Site-to-Site VPN tunnels over the public internet as the only data-center connection and rely on encryption to provide predictable dedicated-link performance.

explanation.text:
Select <<1>>, <<3>>, and <<4>>. Direct Connect supplies a private network path; redundant connections address link resilience. Kafka consumers become Kinesis producers through KPL. A Lambda event-source mapping reads the stream, and the function sends updates to established WebSocket connections through PostToConnection.

<<2>> reverses the Kinesis libraries: KCL is for consuming stream records, not publishing them. <<5>> assigns API Gateway’s @connections mechanism to AppSync and does not address the existing API. <<6>> encrypts traffic but still uses the public internet, contrary to the primary-path requirement.

The stream event source and the client connection lifecycle are separate. Authorize connections, retain their IDs, grant the sender connection-management permissions, and remove stale IDs. Configure retry and duplicate handling; dedicated connectivity alone does not guarantee application latency.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/Welcome.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/streams/latest/dev/developing-producers-with-kpl.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/with-kinesis.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/apigateway-how-to-call-websocket-api-connections.html

question:
A publisher is building a global news website. Editors frequently update articles, readers post comments, and read traffic greatly exceeds write traffic. The relational database must survive an Availability Zone failure, and public article reads must scale independently of writes. Images must have durable shared storage, and global readers need low-latency delivery.

Which components should the architecture include? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use CloudFront to cache public articles and media. Configure cache lifetimes and invalidation or versioned URLs to meet the publisher’s freshness requirements.
Use an RDS MySQL Multi-AZ DB instance deployment for availability, separate read replicas for suitable read traffic, and S3 for images and other shared media.
Use an RDS MySQL Multi-AZ DB instance deployment and direct article queries to its synchronous standby instance to scale reads.
Use Lambda for article requests and keep the authoritative article and comment records in each execution environment’s temporary storage.
Keep the authoritative media collection on an EBS RAID 0 array attached to one EC2 instance, and serve that instance directly to all readers.

explanation.text:
Select <<1>> and <<2>>. CloudFront reduces repeated origin reads and delivery distance. The RDS primary handles writes; its synchronous standby provides failover, separate asynchronous read replicas serve suitable queries, and S3 stores shared media.

<<3>> confuses the standby in a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment with a readable replica. <<4>> uses temporary execution storage as an authoritative database. <<5>> concentrates media availability in one instance and AZ; striping does not create redundant storage.

Availability, read scaling, durability, and content freshness require different controls. Read replicas can lag, so route reads needing immediate consistency appropriately. Cache public content deliberately and refresh changed articles. The unreadable-standby distinction here applies to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, not every RDS cluster architecture.

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Concepts.MultiAZSingleStandby.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReadRepl.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/Expiration.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/Welcome.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-ephemeral-storage.html

question:
A stateless application runs on 25 EC2 On-Demand Instances across three Availability Zones behind a Network Load Balancer. The fixed fleet is underused off peak and saturates during events. Load tests and usage forecasts establish that at least five instances are needed continuously and up to 30 instances meet forecast peak demand with the required latency. The five-instance baseline and instance configuration are expected to remain stable for three years.

The application is not designed to tolerate Spot interruptions. Which solution best balances performance and cost?

options.text: Use an Auto Scaling group with a minimum of five and maximum of 30 instances, a tested CPU target-tracking policy, and scheduled pre-scaling for known events. Purchase matching three-year Reserved Instances for the five-instance baseline and use On-Demand pricing for excess usage.
Use a fixed fleet of 25 Spot Instances behind the NLB. Enable EBS optimization and rely on the purchase discount to offset peak-period performance degradation.
Use a fixed fleet of 30 Spot Instances behind the NLB. Configure interrupted instances to stop so the full serving capacity remains available until demand falls.
Use an Auto Scaling group with a minimum of 15 and maximum of 25 instances. Purchase three-year Reserved Instances for all 15 baseline instances and use CPU target tracking.

explanation.text:
<<1>> matches the commitment to the measured usage floor and adds capacity when demand rises. Target tracking adjusts the fleet, while scheduled scaling prepares for predictable events. Reserved Instances apply a billing discount to matching usage; they are not a separate type of running server.

<<2>> retains insufficient peak capacity and introduces interruption risk. <<3>> adds peak capacity but cannot promise that interrupted Spot instances continue serving. <<4>> commits to more continuous capacity than required and caps the fleet below the tested peak need.

Use measured latency and headroom to choose scaling targets, warm-up settings, and limits. Average CPU alone cannot prove a safe minimum fleet size. Savings Plans are another commitment model, but are outside the listed alternatives.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-scaling-target-tracking.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ec2-reserved-instances.html

question:
A research company uses IAM Identity Center for its scientists. Each scientist has a centrally managed, unique userNameID attribute and owns the matching prefix in a shared S3 bucket. Scientists must list and access only their own objects. Administrators want one reusable permission set rather than per-scientist access infrastructure. They also need monthly reports of object API access attributable to individual scientists.

Which actions meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Configure Identity Center attributes for access control. In the permission set, scope object actions to the ${aws:PrincipalTag/userNameID} prefix and scope s3:ListBucket separately with an s3:prefix condition. Prevent scientists from modifying the trusted attribute.
Enable S3 Object Lock in Governance mode and use AWS Config resource history as the record of scientists’ GetObject and PutObject requests.

Enable CloudTrail S3 data events for the research bucket, retain the logs in a protected bucket, and query them monthly with Athena. Preserve the identity and session information needed to map requests to scientists.
Create and maintain a separate S3 access point and access policy for each scientist. Use the access-point name as the only identity field in the monthly audit report.
Enable only CloudTrail management events for the bucket and query those logs with Athena to report every object download and upload.

explanation.text:
Select <<1>> and <<3>>. Identity Center passes trusted attributes into role sessions; the permission set uses that value to restrict each session to its own prefix. Bucket listing and object access need separate policy statements. CloudTrail data events capture object API activity, which Athena can query directly from log files in S3.

<<2>> confuses retention and configuration history with authorization and data-access auditing. <<4>> violates the shared-policy operating requirement and an access-point name alone does not identify the scientist who made a request. <<5>> omits the S3 data events required for object operations.

The attribute must be unique, validated, and protected against user modification. Retain reliable session-to-person attribution; a shared assumed-role ARN alone does not distinguish all people using that role.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/abac.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_variables.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/logging-data-events-with-cloudtrail.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/athena/latest/ug/cloudtrail-logs.html

question:
A company runs a provisioned Amazon Redshift cluster. Its disaster recovery objectives for a Region outage are a recovery point objective (RPO) of 24 hours and a recovery time objective (RTO) of 1 hour. Repeated recovery exercises have restored a representative snapshot in the recovery Region and completed client cutover within 40 minutes. The company wants to avoid paying for an always-running recovery cluster.

Which configuration best supports these objectives?

options.text: Take automated snapshots in the primary Region. Start copying the latest snapshot to the recovery Region only after a Region outage is declared.

Enable automated snapshots and cross-Region snapshot copying. Monitor that the latest successfully copied recovery point is less than 24 hours old, and maintain the tested restore-and-cutover runbook and recovery dependencies.
Enable cross-Region synchronous replication between the Redshift cluster and a continuously running standby cluster, then configure automatic DNS failover.
Rely on the default automated snapshots in the primary Region. During an outage, restore those snapshots to a different Availability Zone in that same Region.

explanation.text:
<<2>> places recoverable data outside the failure Region before the incident. Snapshot copy produces backups, not a running cluster. On failure, restore from the destination copy and execute the tested client cutover.

<<1>> depends on an unavailable source Region during the incident. <<3>> describes neither the snapshot-copy feature nor the requested cost model, and Redshift does not provide the claimed synchronous cross-Region standby switch. <<4>> changes Availability Zone within the failed Region and provides no independently stored regional recovery copy.

RPO measures the age of the recoverable data; RTO measures the time to restore service. A schedule alone does not establish either result: monitor completed copies and rehearse restoration, permissions, capacity, networking, and cutover. The one-hour RTO is supported here by scenario-specific tests, not a service guarantee.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/redshift/latest/mgmt/cross-region-snapshot-copy.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/redshift/latest/mgmt/working-with-snapshots.html

question:
A charity expects short, unpredictable bursts of donation-pledge submissions after television advertisements. Each pledge is an independent record identified by a request ID. The website may acknowledge durable receipt immediately and finish validation and storage asynchronously. Payment processing is handled separately. The charity wants to absorb bursts without provisioning its database for every instantaneous peak and to minimize database administration.

Which design best meets these requirements?

options.text: Write every pledge synchronously to DynamoDB and add CloudFront caching for the static website files. Use the cache to absorb bursts of pledge writes.
Queue pledges in SQS and process them into an Oracle database on a single large EC2 instance. Manage database patching, backups, and recovery on that instance.
Write every pledge synchronously to a fixed-size RDS instance with Provisioned IOPS. Add read replicas when the pledge-write rate increases.

Put pledge records in an SQS queue. Scale EC2 workers to process the backlog and write idempotently to DynamoDB with appropriately configured write capacity. Delete each message only after its write succeeds.

explanation.text:
<<4>> decouples arrival rate from processing rate. SQS durably holds accepted work, workers drain the backlog at a sustainable rate, and DynamoDB removes server-level database administration. Use request IDs for idempotency because a standard queue can deliver a message more than once.

<<1>> improves delivery of static files but does not buffer write requests. <<2>> buffers work, yet introduces the database operations and single-instance recovery burden the charity wants to avoid. Hosting databases on EC2 is supported; it is simply a poor fit for these constraints. <<3>> does not buffer bursts, and read replicas do not increase primary write capacity.

A queue shifts work in time; it does not eliminate required throughput. Monitor backlog age, provision sufficient sustained write capacity, and handle repeated failures with retries and a dead-letter queue.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/standard-queues.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/provisioned-capacity-mode.html

question:
A company has 50 AWS accounts with VPCs connected to a shared transit gateway in one Region. Each VPC currently has its own internet egress. The security team requires a single shared egress VPC with managed, rule-based outbound inspection. Workloads must not have an alternate uninspected internet route. The team wants to avoid operating firewall or proxy servers.

Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy a Network Firewall in every workload VPC and centrally distribute policies with Firewall Manager. Retain each VPC’s local NAT gateways and internet egress.

Connect an egress VPC to the transit gateway. Deploy AZ-appropriate Network Firewall endpoints and public NAT gateways there. Route spoke default traffic to the transit gateway and then the egress attachment, and route locally through the firewall, NAT, and internet gateway with symmetric return routing. Remove bypass paths.
Create an Auto Scaling group of proxy EC2 instances in every account. Use each Auto Scaling group as the default-route target in its workload VPC.
Deploy Network Firewall endpoints and NAT gateways in one egress VPC. Set every spoke VPC’s default route directly to a firewall endpoint ID in the egress VPC, bypassing transit-gateway routing.

explanation.text:
<<2>> uses valid next hops at each boundary: spoke route to transit gateway, transit-gateway route to the egress attachment, then local routes through inspection and NAT. The return path must traverse the matching stateful firewall path.

<<1>> is a viable distributed inspection design, but violates the required single shared egress topology. <<3>> adds self-managed servers and an Auto Scaling group is not a route-table target. <<4>> attempts to route directly to an endpoint in another VPC; the transit gateway must connect those routing domains.

Network Firewall inspects traffic and NAT translates addresses; neither replaces the other. Design per-AZ paths, remove bypass routes, test stateful return routing, and size the complete path for actual traffic. Central policy administration alone does not imply centralized egress.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/building-scalable-secure-multi-vpc-network-infrastructure/using-nat-gateway-with-firewall.html

question:
A sports website stores match statistics and votes in an existing RDS MySQL Multi-AZ DB instance deployment. It publishes the same statistical report files to all readers once each day. Published versions are immutable, and users may see the latest daily edition. Report downloads are expected to grow from 10 million to 30 million per event. Voting remains on the existing uncached application API.

Which report-serving design best limits database load and provides durable, low-latency global delivery?

options.text: Add RDS read replicas and generate each report on demand for every download. Run a daily cleanup query on the reporting tables.
Cache query results in ElastiCache and have the application render each download from the cache. Keep the generated report files only in application memory.
Generate the daily reports from a read replica and store versioned files in S3. Serve the files through CloudFront and refresh the daily-edition reference according to the publication schedule.
Copy all source rows to DynamoDB every day and query them for every report request. Delete and recreate the reporting table after each daily publication.

explanation.text:
<<3>> computes each edition once and serves many downloads from durable objects and edge caches. A read replica isolates the report-generation queries from primary writes; S3 retains the published files independently of the application.

<<1>> repeats database and rendering work for identical downloads and provides no edge distribution. <<2>> can reduce database reads but retains application rendering and lacks durable report artifacts and global delivery. <<4>> introduces another serving database and repeated report queries when the requested output is an immutable daily file. DynamoDB itself is durable; its durability is not the issue.

Cache lifetime must match publication semantics. Versioned file URLs let immutable editions remain cached; update the daily-edition reference with a suitable TTL or invalidation. Do not cache vote submission requests as report content.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReadRepl.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/Expiration.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/Welcome.html

question:
A company runs a Node.js application on EC2 instances and on-premises Linux servers. Database credentials are already stored as a SecureString parameter encrypted with a customer managed KMS key. The company wants automated application deployments to both environments. Servers must retrieve the credential over TLS using scoped, temporary AWS credentials, and deployment artifacts must not contain the plaintext secret.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use Elastic Beanstalk to manage both EC2 and on-premises servers. Install SSM Agent on all servers and give the Beanstalk service role permission to read the parameter.
Use CodeDeploy for both environments, but install only SSM Agent on the targets. Configure a CodeDeploy service role and expect that role to provide runtime AWS credentials to every server.

Install CodeDeploy agents and configure a CodeDeploy service role. Use an EC2 instance-profile role and supported, periodically refreshed IAM role-session credentials for registered on-premises targets. Give runtime identities scoped parameter-read and KMS-decrypt permissions and retrieve the secret with the AWS SDK over TLS.
Download the decrypted parameter during the build and package it in the application bundle. Use CodeDeploy agents and temporary target credentials to install that bundle on both environments.

explanation.text:
<<3>> separates deployment orchestration from target authentication and runtime secret access. CodeDeploy supports EC2 and registered on-premises targets. EC2 can use instance-profile credentials; on-premises registration supports refreshed IAM role-session credentials. SecureString values are encrypted with KMS and retrieved with the relevant permissions.

<<1>> assumes Elastic Beanstalk manages on-premises application servers. <<2>> substitutes SSM Agent for the required CodeDeploy agent and mistakes a service role for target credentials. <<4>> puts the plaintext database secret into deployment artifacts, violating the stated custody requirement.

A CodeDeploy service role and an application runtime identity have different responsibilities. The AWS SDK can retrieve parameters without SSM Agent. Protect the returned plaintext in process memory and avoid logging it. Secrets Manager is appropriate when dedicated secret rotation and lifecycle features are required.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/register-on-premises-instance-iam-session-arn.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/secure-string-parameter-kms-encryption.html

question:
A security team observes port scans from one public IPv4 address against internet-facing EC2 instances in several subnets. It needs to deny that source at the subnet boundary immediately. The company also requires baseline protection against common network- and transport-layer DDoS attacks and wants to avoid a paid security subscription unless it is needed for those requirements.

Which approach best meets the requirements?

options.text: Add an inbound network ACL deny rule for the source /32 in each affected subnet’s ACL, with a lower rule number than matching allow rules. Use the automatic AWS Shield Standard protections already included for AWS customers.
Add the source address to an AWS WAF IP set and associate a blocking web ACL with an ALB in front of the application. Use Shield Standard for baseline DDoS protection.
Block the address in each instance’s host firewall and enable GuardDuty and Patch Manager. Use the resulting findings and patch compliance as the DDoS mitigation control.
Add an explicit deny rule to every instance security group and use AWS Config to discard packets that match the denied source.

explanation.text:
<<1>> places an explicit IP deny at the requested subnet boundary. Network ACLs evaluate the lowest-numbered matching rule first. Shield Standard automatically provides baseline protection against common network- and transport-layer DDoS attacks without a paid subscription.

<<2>> filters web requests at the ALB. It does not install the required subnet-boundary deny or block arbitrary port scans against the instances’ public addresses. <<3>> can block traffic at a host, but does not implement the required subnet-boundary control; threat detection and patching are not substitutes for DDoS mitigation. <<4>> proposes security-group deny rules, which do not exist, and treats AWS Config as a packet-filtering service.

Shield Advanced adds capabilities beyond this baseline and may be justified by other requirements. A network ACL deny targets a source address; it is not by itself protection against a distributed attack. Preserve required return-traffic rules because ACLs are stateless.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-network-acls.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/ddos-standard-summary.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/how-aws-waf-works.html

question:
A company is replacing an EC2 application with API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB. It needs a repeatable pipeline that builds and tests the code and gradually shifts API traffic between published Lambda versions. A failed validation or a CloudWatch alarm must trigger rollback. API Gateway must invoke the controlled production version throughout deployment.

Which solution meets these requirements with the least custom deployment logic?

options.text: Define the application with AWS SAM. Use CodePipeline and CodeBuild for orchestration, build, and tests. Configure AutoPublishAlias and a canary or linear DeploymentPreference with hooks and alarms so CodeDeploy shifts traffic through the Lambda alias used by API Gateway.

Define the application with AWS SAM using AutoPublishAlias and an AllAtOnce deployment preference. Use CodePipeline and CodeBuild for build and tests, connect API Gateway to the alias, and configure hooks and alarms for rollback.
Use CodePipeline and CodeBuild, then have a Systems Manager Automation runbook update the Lambda function’s $LATEST code. Invoke $LATEST from API Gateway and treat the update as a gradual deployment.

Publish the application to the Serverless Application Repository and deploy each new version from the repository. Rely on publication alone to create build tests, an alias traffic-shifting policy, and automatic rollback.

explanation.text:
<<1>> joins the pipeline to the mechanism that actually shifts traffic. SAM’s AutoPublishAlias creates the version/alias structure, and DeploymentPreference configures CodeDeploy canary or linear shifting with validation hooks and alarms. API Gateway must invoke the alias for its requests to follow the controlled rollout.

<<2>> supplies versions, an alias and rollback controls, but AllAtOnce shifts all traffic in one step instead of gradually. <<3>> replaces $LATEST without establishing weighted routing between published versions; a runbook could orchestrate a fuller design, but this one does not. <<4>> confuses application packaging and distribution with an implemented CI/CD and rollout policy.

Traffic shifting needs both an old and a new version. Establish the initial alias/version before performing a gradual update, and keep shared data changes compatible with both versions so rollback remains useful.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/serverless-application-model/latest/developerguide/automating-updates-to-serverless-apps.html

question:
A university runs a student portal with AWS Lambda and a Regional Amazon API Gateway REST API. After an SQL injection incident, the application team is fixing unsafe database queries. The security team also needs managed request filtering and a history of changes to the firewall configuration. The portal does not need a content delivery network.

Which solution meets these requirements with the least additional infrastructure?

options.text: Associate an AWS WAF regional web ACL containing SQL injection rules with the REST API stage. Enable AWS Config recording for the supported WAF resources.
Associate an AWS WAF web ACL directly with each Lambda function. Use AWS Firewall Manager to retain the firewall configuration history.
Create a CloudFront distribution in front of the REST API and associate a WAF web ACL with the distribution. Enable AWS Config recording for the supported WAF resources.
Block the attacking IP addresses in the database subnet network ACL. Use VPC Flow Logs to retain the history of the filtering rules.

explanation.text:
Correct: <<1>>. API Gateway REST API stages support direct association with a regional AWS WAF web ACL in the same Region. SQL injection rules inspect requests before they reach the integration. AWS Config records supported resource configurations and their changes.

<<2>> is incorrect because WAF does not associate directly with Lambda functions. Firewall Manager distributes security policies; it does not replace Config configuration history.

<<3>> can provide filtering, but adds a distribution that the scenario does not need. Direct stage association meets the stated requirements with fewer components.

<<4>> filters network traffic by addresses and ports, not SQL syntax. Flow Logs record traffic metadata, not historical rule configurations.

Use WAF as defense in depth. Parameterized queries and appropriate database permissions remain necessary; request filtering cannot guarantee that every injection attempt is blocked.

Official AWS references (checked 2026-09-18):
[WAF integration with REST APIs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/apigateway-control-access-aws-waf.html)
[WAF monitoring tools](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/monitoring_automated_manual.html)

question:
A retailer is launching a mobile photo-sharing application and expects large, unpredictable traffic increases. Users sign in with social identities and upload photos with captions of up to 100 characters. The application retrieves metadata by user ID and photo ID and does not need relational joins. The team wants managed services that minimize server and database capacity administration.

Which architecture best meets these requirements?

options.text: Use Amazon Cognito for sign-in, an Amazon RDS for MySQL instance for metadata, and Amazon EBS volumes attached to application servers for photos. Serve the photos directly from the servers.
Use Amazon Cognito for sign-in, DynamoDB on-demand tables for metadata, and a private S3 bucket for photos. Deliver published photos and static assets through CloudFront with origin access control.
Use an on-premises Active Directory deployment for customer identities, DynamoDB for metadata, and S3 with CloudFront for photos. Build and operate a custom identity integration.
Use Amazon Cognito for sign-in, a provisioned RDS for MySQL deployment for metadata, and S3 with CloudFront for photos. Size and resize the database instances for expected peaks.

explanation.text:
Correct: <<2>>. Cognito supports social sign-in; DynamoDB fits the stated key-based metadata access; S3 stores image objects; and CloudFront caches published content near users. On-demand capacity reduces database throughput administration. Keep the S3 origin private and authorize uploads and private content separately.

<<1>> couples photo availability to application servers and EBS volumes and introduces instance capacity management.

<<3>> adds an identity system and custom integration that this public consumer application does not require.

<<4>> can be a valid application architecture, but the specified provisioned database requires capacity administration without a relational requirement to justify it. RDS is not inherently incapable of storing captions or scaling.

Separate large objects from queryable metadata. Automatic scaling still has quotas and ramp-up behavior: prepare DynamoDB warm throughput and relevant service quotas for a known launch surge.

Official AWS references (checked 2026-09-18):
[Cognito social identity providers](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-user-pools-identity-provider.html)
[DynamoDB on-demand capacity](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/on-demand-capacity-mode.html)
[CloudFront private S3 origins](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.html)

question:
A company serves several HTTPS applications through an Application Load Balancer in us-west-1. The ALB uses public certificates managed by AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). The company is deploying an ALB in each of three additional AWS Regions and will keep the same application hostnames.

What should a solutions architect do before routing users to the new ALBs?

options.text: Create an asymmetric AWS KMS key in each destination Region and use its key ARN as the HTTPS listener certificate.
Create a multi-Region AWS KMS key and associate its replica key ARN with each ALB HTTPS listener.
Request the required certificates in ACM in us-west-1 and associate those certificate ARNs with the ALBs in every destination Region.
Request and validate the required certificates in ACM in each destination Region. Associate each issued certificate with the ALB in that Region and verify HTTPS before shifting traffic.

explanation.text:
Correct: <<4>>. An ALB must use a certificate that exists in the same Region. Request certificates covering the application hostnames in every destination Region, complete validation, and configure and test the HTTPS listeners before changing traffic routing.

<<1>> and <<2>> are incorrect because KMS keys are cryptographic keys, not TLS certificates that an ALB listener can use. Multi-Region KMS replication does not create regional ACM certificates.

<<3>> fails the same-Region requirement: an ACM certificate ARN in us-west-1 cannot be attached directly to an ALB in another Region.

The hostname can stay the same across regional certificates. CloudFront has a different rule: its viewer certificate must be in us-east-1. That global-service exception does not apply to regional ALBs.

Official AWS references (checked 2026-09-18):
[ACM certificate scope](https://aws.amazon.com/certificate-manager/faqs/)

question:
A research organization has 50 AWS accounts, each with a VPC. A central DNS team owns one Route 53 private hosted zone that all of these VPCs must resolve. The team wants to retain the single zone and use direct VPC associations without deploying DNS forwarding infrastructure. Application connectivity is managed separately.

Which configuration meets the requirement?

options.text: In the zone-owning account, authorize each cross-account VPC association. In each VPC-owning account, associate the VPC with the zone. Enable DNS support and DNS hostnames in the participating VPCs.
Peer every VPC with the central VPC and enable DNS resolution over peering. Associate the private hosted zone only with the central VPC.
Create a private hosted zone with the same name in every account. Copy the central zone's name server records into those zones instead of associating the VPCs with the central zone.
Authorize and complete the cross-account VPC associations. Disable DNS support in the participating VPCs so that private queries use the central zone exclusively.

explanation.text:
Correct: <<1>>. Direct cross-account association is a two-party operation: the hosted-zone owner authorizes a specified VPC, then the VPC owner associates it. Both VPC DNS attributes must be enabled. The temporary association authorization can be removed afterward without removing the association.

<<2>> is incorrect because peering alone does not associate the peer VPC with the private hosted zone. Peering DNS options do not share all private hosted-zone records.

<<3>> creates separate zones; copying name server records does not establish the requested association or synchronize records.

<<4>> disables the resolver capability needed for this pattern.

DNS visibility and packet connectivity are separate requirements. Associating a zone does not create routes or security-group permissions. Route 53 Profiles offer another sharing approach, but the question explicitly requires direct associations.

Official AWS references (checked 2026-09-18):
[Cross-account private-zone association](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/hosted-zone-private-associate-vpcs-different-accounts.html)
[Private hosted-zone considerations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/hosted-zone-private-considerations.html)

question:
An Amazon ECS service runs Linux tasks on AWS Fargate in private IPv4 subnets. The task execution role has the required ECR permissions, but image pulls time out. The VPC has no NAT gateway or VPC endpoints. Security policy prohibits public IP addresses on tasks but permits outbound HTTPS through a managed NAT gateway.

Which change restores image pulls from Amazon ECR?

options.text: Enable public IP assignment in the service network configuration and create a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon ECR.

Keep public IP assignment disabled. Create a public NAT gateway with an Elastic IP in a public subnet, route that subnet to an internet gateway, and route the private subnets' default IPv4 traffic to the NAT gateway.
Keep public IP assignment disabled. Create a private NAT gateway in an isolated subnet and route the task subnets' default IPv4 traffic to it for internet access.
Change the Fargate task definition from awsvpc network mode to bridge network mode so that tasks can use the host's internet connection.

explanation.text:
Correct: <<2>>. The task ENI keeps its private address. Its subnet route sends outbound traffic to a public NAT gateway, which uses an Elastic IP and an internet gateway to reach public service endpoints. Return traffic follows the established translation.

<<1>> violates the no-public-IP requirement, and ECR uses interface endpoints, not an ECR gateway endpoint. Public IP assignment also cannot repair missing routes by itself.

<<3>> is incorrect because a private NAT gateway does not provide internet access through an internet gateway.

<<4>> is unsupported: Fargate requires awsvpc networking.

Internet egress is not universally required for ECR pulls. A private alternative for current Fargate Linux platforms uses ECR API and registry interface endpoints plus the S3 gateway endpoint, appropriate DNS/security settings, and endpoints for any additional task dependencies.

Official AWS references (checked 2026-09-18):
[Fargate task networking](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/fargate-task-networking.html)
[ECR VPC endpoint requirements](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECR/latest/userguide/vpc-endpoints.html)
[Public and private NAT gateways](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-nat-gateway.html)

question:
A company uses Systems Manager Patch Manager to maintain a Windows EC2 web fleet. Every service has redundant instances, and either of two patch cohorts can handle the full workload. The company needs recurring installation of approved patches, including required reboots, without taking both cohorts out of service together. An existing automation runbook can verify application health and stop a rollout.

Which approach best meets the requirement?

options.text: Tag instances into two disjoint PatchGroup values and register an approved Windows baseline for each. Schedule AWS-RunPatchBaseline installation in separate maintenance windows, and have the runbook allow the second cohort only after the first is healthy. Set appropriate concurrency and error limits.
Place all instances in one patch group. Run AWS-RunPatchBaseline with Install and RebootIfNeeded on every target concurrently in a single maintenance window.
Create two patch groups with different baselines. Schedule both groups to install and reboot at the same time; rely on the different baseline IDs to serialize execution.
Run AWS-RunPatchBaseline with Scan for all instances on a recurring schedule. Treat a successful scan as confirmation that the approved patches have been installed.

explanation.text:
Correct: <<1>>. Patch groups select the applicable baseline; maintenance windows schedule the work; and the health gate prevents the next cohort from starting while the first remains unavailable. Concurrency and error controls limit rollout impact within a cohort.

<<2>> allows the entire fleet to reboot together. A single window can support a safe rolling design, but this option explicitly runs all targets concurrently.

<<3>> is incorrect because distinct baselines do not serialize tasks. Simultaneous schedules can disrupt both cohorts.

<<4>> evaluates patch compliance but does not install patches. Use Install and an appropriate reboot policy to complete patching.

Non-overlapping scheduled windows alone are not proof of application recovery: an earlier execution can overrun or leave unhealthy services. Patch policies in Quick Setup are a current alternative; this scenario uses an existing patch-group workflow.

Official AWS references (checked 2026-09-18):
[Patch groups](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/patch-manager-patch-groups.html)
[AWS-RunPatchBaseline](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/patch-manager-aws-runpatchbaseline.html)

question:
A delivery company runs an EC2 application and an RDS for MySQL DB instance in one AWS Region. It needs a lower-cost alternative to a pilot-light deployment for regional disaster recovery, with an RPO of 15 minutes and an RTO under 3 hours. Restore exercises using a supported destination Region have met both targets. Application infrastructure is reproducible from templates. The company also exports selected records as Parquet files to a controlled S3 bucket and must discover sensitive data in those exports.

Which solution meets the requirements with the lowest ongoing recovery-environment cost?

options.text: Copy a daily RDS snapshot to the recovery Region and use that snapshot as the only database recovery source. Run Amazon Macie discovery jobs against the S3 exports.

Enable RDS automated backups and cross-Region automated-backup replication. Restore to an available recovery point and recreate the application during recovery. Run Macie discovery jobs on the S3 exports and route findings to a separate remediation workflow.
Keep an RDS cross-Region read replica and a running EC2 fleet in the recovery Region. Use AWS Shield to discover sensitive data in the database and S3 exports.
Enable a Multi-AZ RDS deployment in the source Region and use it as the regional disaster-recovery copy. Run Macie directly against RDS-managed automated backups.

explanation.text:
Correct: <<2>>. Backup and restore avoids a continuously running recovery application and database. RDS can replicate automated snapshots and transaction logs to a supported destination Region; recovery uses the destination's available restore points. Macie analyzes the exported, supported S3 objects, and a separate workflow handles remediation.

<<1>> leaves up to a day of database changes outside the recovery copy, exceeding the 15-minute RPO.

<<3>> incurs the standby cost the company is trying to avoid. Shield mitigates DDoS attacks; it does not classify sensitive records.

<<4>> protects against some in-Region failures, not loss of that Region. Macie does not inspect RDS-managed backups in place.

RPO measures data loss; RTO includes database restore, application deployment, and cutover. Monitor the destination recovery point and repeat recovery exercises as data volume changes. The tested targets are workload evidence, not an AWS restore-time guarantee.

Official AWS references (checked 2026-09-18):
[RDS point-in-time recovery](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_PIT.html)
[Cross-Region automated backups](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReplicateBackups.html)
[Macie supported data](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/macie/latest/user/discovery-supported-storage.html)

question:
A document-processing portal runs on one EC2 instance and stores uploaded files on attached EBS volumes. Upload bursts delay responses while the same instance performs lengthy verification jobs. Files must remain available when workers are replaced, and the company needs a copy of uploads in another Region for recovery. Jobs can run asynchronously and safely retry.

Which redesign provides scalable storage and resilient processing?

options.text: Store uploads in S3 with cross-Region replication. Queue object references in SQS and process them with an EC2 Auto Scaling group spanning multiple Availability Zones. Scale workers using queue backlog per instance and keep templates to recreate regional infrastructure.
Store uploads on a larger Provisioned IOPS EBS volume attached to the original instance. Publish jobs to an SNS topic subscribed by every worker and scale workers using the number of notifications.
Store uploads on each worker's local EBS volume. Use SQS and an Auto Scaling group across Availability Zones, and delete each local volume when its worker is replaced.
Store uploads in S3 with cross-Region replication. Invoke one fixed EC2 processing instance synchronously for every upload and retain that instance during demand spikes.

explanation.text:
Correct: <<1>>. S3 separates durable files from worker lifecycles, SQS buffers bursts, and a multi-AZ worker group processes independent jobs. Backlog per worker is a useful scaling metric because required capacity depends on both queued work and processing rate.

<<2>> retains the single-instance storage dependency. SNS fan-out sends work to subscribers; by itself it is not the competing-consumer queue described here.

<<3>> improves compute elasticity but loses durable uploads when the worker volumes are deleted and does not create the required regional copy.

<<4>> fixes storage but preserves the synchronous single-worker bottleneck.

Make workers idempotent, configure visibility timeouts and failure handling, and protect work during scale-in. S3 replication is asynchronous and does not replicate SQS messages or application state; a regional recovery runbook must account for those separately.

Official AWS references (checked 2026-09-18):
[SQS-based Auto Scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-using-sqs-queue.html)
[S3 object replication](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/replication.html)

question:
A clinic runs Windows applications on EC2. Security policy requires scheduled installation of approved operating-system patches and notification whenever a running instance uses an AMI outside an approved list. Developers must still be able to launch an unapproved AMI for investigation. All instances meet Systems Manager managed-node prerequisites.

Which actions meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Attach an IAM policy that denies RunInstances when the requested AMI is not on the approved list.
Enable GuardDuty and use its threat findings as the authoritative record of missing operating-system patches and unapproved AMIs.
Schedule AWS-RunPatchBaseline with Scan for all Windows instances. Treat a successful scan and its compliance report as evidence that all approved updates have been installed.
Define approved patches in a Systems Manager Patch Manager baseline and schedule AWS-RunPatchBaseline with Install, an appropriate reboot policy, and compliance reporting.
Record EC2 instances in AWS Config and configure the approved-amis-by-id managed rule. Route NON_COMPLIANT compliance-change events through EventBridge to an SNS topic.

explanation.text:
Correct: <<4>> and <<5>>. Patch Manager defines and installs approved updates on managed nodes. AWS Config evaluates running instances against the AMI list, and EventBridge routes compliance changes to the notification target. This is a detective control, so it does not prevent a launch.

<<1>> is a preventive control and conflicts with the requirement to permit investigation instances.

<<2>> is incorrect because GuardDuty threat detection does not replace the patch installation workflow or the specified AMI allow-list evaluation.

<<3>> checks patch compliance but does not install updates. A successful Scan execution does not establish that the machine is patched; installation and any required reboot remain separate actions.

<<4>> requires an execution schedule as well as a baseline: approval rules alone do not install patches. <<5>> requires Config resource recording and permissions for the EventBridge-to-SNS delivery. Distinguish patch compliance, image compliance, and threat detection when selecting controls.

Official AWS references (checked 2026-09-18):
[AWS-RunPatchBaseline](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/patch-manager-aws-runpatchbaseline.html)
[Approved AMI rule](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/approved-amis-by-id.html)
[Config events in EventBridge](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/monitor-config-with-cloudwatchevents.html)

question:
A company runs a public web application on EC2 and wants to improve resilience to network floods and HTTP request floods. Its budget permits CloudFront, AWS WAF, and capacity scaling but not a Shield Advanced subscription.

Which actions directly improve DDoS resilience? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Place CloudFront in front of the application, cache suitable content, restrict direct origin access, and monitor demand with CloudWatch to support controlled Auto Scaling.
Move all application files from EBS to S3 and schedule operating-system patching. Use these changes as the primary protection against request floods.
Distribute allowed HTTP traffic through an Application Load Balancer to a multi-AZ fleet. Associate a WAF web ACL with tested filtering and rate-based rules.
Attach additional network interfaces to each EC2 instance and rely on the extra interfaces to filter malicious requests before they reach the application.
Purchase EC2 Reserved Instances for the existing fleet and rely on the reservation to increase each instance's network capacity during attacks.

explanation.text:
Correct: <<1>> and <<3>>. CloudFront moves request handling to the edge and reduces origin load through caching. WAF filters application-layer requests, while an ALB and a multi-AZ fleet distribute permitted work. Restrict origin access so attackers cannot simply bypass the edge.

<<2>> may improve storage and patch hygiene, but neither change directly filters or absorbs a request flood.

<<4>> does not provide a malicious-request classifier or make instance bandwidth unlimited; network limits still depend on the instance configuration.

<<5>> changes the billing model, not the performance of an otherwise identical instance.

Shield Standard provides automatic baseline protection without a Shield Advanced subscription. WAF rules and application capacity still need tuning. Scaling improves availability but can increase costs and cannot be treated as unlimited attack absorption.

Official AWS references (checked 2026-09-18):
[CloudFront DDoS resilience](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-best-practices-ddos-resiliency/cloudfront.html)
[AWS DDoS mitigation techniques](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-best-practices-ddos-resiliency/mitigation-techniques.html)

question:
A company runs Amazon EKS on EC2 and an RDS for MySQL database. Its steady compute usage will continue for at least a year, but node families and Regions may change. Additional batch workers can tolerate Spot interruptions. Planned sales events temporarily increase database write demand, and tested vertical resizing fits an allowed maintenance window. The database team has selected an eligible Reserved DB Instance offering for its steady usage.

Which purchasing and scaling strategy best reduces costs while meeting these constraints?

options.text: Cover measured baseline EC2 usage with a Compute Savings Plan and run eligible burst workers on diversified Spot capacity. Purchase the selected RDS reservation for baseline usage and schedule tested database resizing for events.
Cover baseline EC2 usage with an EC2 Instance Savings Plan tied to one family and Region. Run all burst workers On-Demand and keep the database sized for the largest event throughout the year.
Cover baseline EC2 usage with a Compute Savings Plan and use On-Demand Capacity Reservations for every burst. Add RDS read replicas to increase the primary database's write capacity.
Use Standard EC2 Reserved Instances for baseline usage and Dedicated Instances for bursts. Purchase the selected RDS reservation and rely on it to increase database capacity automatically.

explanation.text:
Correct: <<1>>. Compute Savings Plans preserve discount flexibility across EC2 families and Regions. Spot suits interruptible batch bursts, while the reservation covers eligible steady RDS usage and explicit resizing supplies temporary capacity.

<<2>> limits discount flexibility and pays for non-interruptible burst capacity and peak database sizing when those tradeoffs are unnecessary here. EC2 Instance Savings Plans can offer deeper discounts when their narrower scope fits.

<<3>> confuses capacity assurance with discounted burst pricing. Read replicas scale reads; they do not add write capacity to the primary.

<<4>> adds dedicated-tenancy costs without a stated requirement. An RDS reservation is a billing benefit, not a scaling instruction.

Commit only to sustained eligible usage. RDS MySQL reservation size flexibility is limited to eligible configurations within the same family and Region; extra normalized capacity may remain On-Demand. Spot availability and interruption handling still require design. This selects among the stated strategies, not a universal cheapest configuration.

Official AWS references (checked 2026-09-18):
[Savings Plans types](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/savingsplans/latest/userguide/plan-types.html)
[Spot Instances](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/using-spot-instances.html)
[RDS Reserved DB Instances](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_WorkingWithReservedDBInstances.html)

question:
A company manages Ubuntu EC2 instances in development, test, and production using an existing Systems Manager Patch Manager workflow. Each environment has its own approved patch baseline. A security update must be installed in development and test now, but production must remain unchanged until application testing succeeds. All instances are managed nodes.

Which approach meets these requirements with the least custom administration?

options.text: Tag instances by environment and operating system. Maintain separate shell scripts that implement package approval, installation, reboot handling, and compliance reporting for each environment.
Tag every Ubuntu instance with the same PatchGroup value. Register the development baseline for that group and run AWS-RunPatchBaseline with Install against all Ubuntu instances.

Assign distinct PatchGroup values for each environment and register the appropriate Ubuntu baseline for each. Run AWS-RunPatchBaseline with Install only for development and test targets. Review compliance and application tests before approving and targeting production.

Create one nightly maintenance window targeting every Ubuntu instance. Use the production baseline for the whole fleet and install its approved patches in every environment before reviewing test results.

explanation.text:
Correct: <<3>>. Environment-specific patch groups map nodes to the right baseline. Explicitly targeting only development and test controls which instances receive the current installation. After successful testing, update production approval as required and run a separately targeted installation.

<<1>> can implement the workflow but recreates capabilities already supplied by Patch Manager.

<<2>> discards the environment boundary and targets production along with nonproduction nodes. Different environment baselines cannot be selected by a shared Ubuntu-only group value.

<<4>> has a schedule but lacks the required staged approval and separate baseline selection. Maintenance windows are useful when paired with correct targets and tasks.

The operating system determines a compatible baseline; environment determines approval and rollout timing. Patch-group tags can use PatchGroup or Patch Group, and a node belongs to one group. Current Quick Setup patch policies provide another managed approach and do not use patch groups.

Official AWS references (checked 2026-09-18):
[Patch groups and baseline selection](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/patch-manager-patch-groups.html)
[Quick Setup patch policies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/patch-manager-policies.html)

question:
A global mobile marketplace runs regional APIs and needs low-latency access to order-event metadata. Each event has a globally unique ID and is written in one Region. Users in other Regions may see a short replication delay. Payment settlement uses a separate authoritative system; this metadata store does not require cross-Region atomic transactions. The team wants local reads and writes without operating a custom replication service.

Which design best meets these requirements?

options.text: Create independent DynamoDB tables in each Region and use custom Lambda consumers to copy writes, handle retries, and prevent replication loops.
Create a DynamoDB global table with multi-Region eventual consistency and replicas in the required supported Regions. Have each API read and write its local replica.
Use CloudFormation StackSets to create identical DynamoDB tables in each Region and rely on StackSets to synchronize the data written to those tables.
Write metadata as objects to S3 buckets and configure cross-Region replication. Replace key-based database operations with object listings and custom metadata indexes.

explanation.text:
Correct: <<2>>. DynamoDB global tables provide managed multi-active replication, allowing the regional APIs to use local replicas. The stated tolerance for replication delay and single-Region ownership of each event fit multi-Region eventual consistency (MREC).

<<1>> can be built, but adds the replication, failure-handling, and loop-prevention code the team wants to avoid.

<<3>> synchronizes infrastructure deployment, not application records written into the tables.

<<4>> replicates objects but adds custom indexing to reproduce the stated database access pattern.

Do not infer cross-Region transactional guarantees from multi-Region replication. MREC can expose writes at different times in different Regions and requires conflict-aware design when multiple Regions modify the same item. DynamoDB also offers multi-Region strong consistency with its own supported configurations; choose the mode from the actual consistency requirements.

Official AWS references (checked 2026-09-18):
[DynamoDB global tables](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/GlobalTables.html)
[Global-table replication and transactions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/globaltables-CoreConcepts.html)

question:
A company operates 200 Windows and Linux EC2 instances managed by Systems Manager.
