A monthly operations report must include guest memory utilization, filesystem free space, and analysis of application log messages. The report results must be written to an S3 bucket. The team wants to reuse managed collection and query services.

Which solution meets the requirements with the least custom telemetry code?

options.text: Use Systems Manager to install and configure the unified CloudWatch agent. Send guest metrics to CloudWatch Metrics and log files to CloudWatch Logs. Schedule metric retrieval and Logs Insights queries, then write the completed query results and report to S3.
Enable EC2 detailed monitoring and query its default metrics for guest memory utilization and filesystem free space. Use those metric results as the application log analysis and save them to S3.
Keep only SSM Agent installed and assume it automatically streams all application logs and guest metrics to CloudWatch. Run Logs Insights queries and save the results to S3.

Configure VPC Traffic Mirroring for each instance and analyze the mirrored packets to obtain local memory utilization, filesystem free space, and all application log messages. Save the analysis to S3.

explanation.text:
Correct: <<1>>. The unified CloudWatch agent collects guest operating-system metrics and configured log files on Windows and Linux. Metrics and logs have distinct destinations and query interfaces; the scheduled workflow must retrieve the results and explicitly persist the report in S3.

<<2>> increases the frequency of supported EC2 metrics but does not add arbitrary guest memory, filesystem, or log-message collection.

<<3>> confuses management with telemetry collection. SSM Agent can install and manage the CloudWatch agent, but its presence alone does not publish all of those signals.

<<4>> observes network packets, not internal operating-system counters or every local log file.

Logs Insights queries log events; use metric APIs for time-series utilization. Writing a report to S3 is a separate step from querying logs, and guest metrics collected by the agent can incur custom-metric charges.

Official AWS references (checked 2026-09-18):
[Unified CloudWatch agent](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/Install-CloudWatch-Agent.html)
[Retrieve Logs Insights results](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatchLogs/latest/APIReference/API_GetQueryResults.html)

question:
A company makes pet collars that submit authenticated HTTPS measurements every second. Its portal must show recent biometric trends within seconds and support independent consumers that can replay at least 24 hours of measurements. Analysts also need a durable archive for historical SQL analysis.

Which architecture best meets these requirements?

options.text: Accept uploads through an HTTPS API and store them in S3. Run a scheduled daily batch job and refresh all portal measurements from its output.

Use an authenticated HTTPS API to write measurements to Kinesis Data Streams with at least 24 hours of retention. Use a streaming consumer such as Managed Service for Apache Flink to compute live results for the portal, and deliver records to S3 for historical analysis with Redshift.
Use an authenticated HTTPS API to put measurements on one SQS queue. Have independent analytics consumers compete for messages and delete each message after the first consumer processes it.
Use an authenticated HTTPS API to overwrite one current-value item per collar in DynamoDB. Build every historical report and replay consumer from those current-value items.

explanation.text:
Correct: <<2>>. A retained stream separates ingestion from processing and lets independent consumers read and replay records. A streaming processor computes live trends; a separate serving path exposes those results to the portal. S3 retains historical data that Redshift can load or query for analysis.

<<1>> supports an archive but a daily batch refresh does not meet the seconds-level display requirement.

<<3>> uses competing consumers: deleting a queue message after one consumer finishes does not provide every independent consumer with a replayable history. SQS can participate in other valid designs, but this configuration misses the requirement.

<<4>> discards prior measurements by overwriting them, so it cannot support the required replay and historical reports.

A stream is a transport and retention service, not the analytics calculation or dashboard. Configure retention, throughput, consumer failure handling, and idempotency explicitly; retained records can be processed more than once.

Official AWS references (checked 2026-09-18):
[Processing Kinesis records](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/with-kinesis.html)
[Kinesis retention and consumers](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/streams/latest/dev/key-concepts.html)
[Managed Flink processing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/managed-flink/latest/java/how-it-works.html)
[Redshift Spectrum](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/redshift/latest/dg/c-using-spectrum.html)

question:
A company operates several VPCs in one account. Required VPC peering routes and security-group rules already allow approved applications to connect to a central EC2 database server using its private IPv4 address. The database has no public address. The applications must resolve database.internal.example.com, while internet DNS clients must not receive that private record.

Which Route 53 configuration meets the requirement?

options.text: Create a public hosted zone for internal.example.com and add an A record pointing to the database private address. Enable both VPC DNS attributes.
Create a private hosted zone associated with the application VPCs and add the A record. Set enableDnsHostnames to true and enableDnsSupport to false.
Create a private hosted zone associated only with the database VPC and add the A record. Rely on VPC peering alone to make that private zone visible to every application VPC.

Create a private hosted zone for internal.example.com, associate it with the database and application VPCs, and create the database A record pointing to the private address. Set enableDnsHostnames and enableDnsSupport to true.

explanation.text:
Correct: <<4>>. A private hosted zone supplies records to associated VPCs through the VPC resolver. Both required DNS attributes must be enabled. An A record maps the database name to its private IPv4 address.

<<1>> publishes the DNS record publicly. A private IP address in a public zone does not make that zone private, even though the address itself is not publicly routable.

<<2>> disables DNS support required for this resolution path.

<<3>> is incorrect because peering does not automatically share private hosted-zone associations.

DNS visibility does not grant network access. The stem separately supplies the routes, security rules, and absence of a public database address. In a cross-account design, direct associations also require authorization by the hosted-zone owner.

Official AWS references (checked 2026-09-18):
[Private hosted-zone behavior](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/hosted-zone-private-considerations.html)
[Cross-account association](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/hosted-zone-private-associate-vpcs-different-accounts.html)

question:
A company is migrating a Windows Server and IIS application with a MySQL database to AWS. It must run in one Region across at least two Availability Zones. The team cannot containerize or rewrite the application. The load balancer must route /catalog/* and /checkout/* to separate target groups, and the web tier must scale with demand.

Tests have validated Aurora MySQL compatibility and performance. Database resources must remain usable if their CloudFormation stack is deleted; required networking and secrets are in a separate retained stack.

Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy Windows EC2 instances across two AZs behind a Network Load Balancer. Configure NLB listener rules to select target groups by HTTP path, and retain a Multi-AZ RDS database.

Deploy Windows EC2 Auto Scaling capacity across two AZs behind an ALB with path-based rules and a Route 53 alias. Deploy an Aurora MySQL writer and reader in different AZs, and set DeletionPolicy: Retain on the DB cluster and DB instances.
Deploy Windows Auto Scaling capacity and an ALB in each of two Regions. Use Aurora Global Database, Route 53 latency routing, and Retain policies for the database resources.
Containerize the application on ECS behind an ALB and deploy a Multi-AZ database. Set DeletionPolicy: Snapshot so that the live database remains after stack deletion.

explanation.text:
Correct: <<2>>. ALB path conditions supply the required request routing. Windows EC2 supports the unchanged application, and Auto Scaling across AZs provides elastic web capacity. Retain on both the Aurora cluster and its instances preserves those resources when the stack is deleted.

<<1>> fails because an NLB does not evaluate HTTP path conditions.

<<3>> violates the single-Region constraint, even though it could be a valid design for a different recovery requirement.

<<4>> requires prohibited containerization. Snapshot creates a recovery artifact and deletes the resource; it does not retain a running database.

Retention applies per resource and retained resources continue to incur charges. Dependencies must survive too, as specified here. DeletionPolicy does not control an update that replaces a resource; use the separate replacement policy where required. Aurora is justified by the stated compatibility tests, not by an assumed user-count threshold.

Official AWS references (checked 2026-09-18):
[ALB rule conditions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/rule-condition-types.html)
[CloudFormation DeletionPolicy](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/TemplateReference/aws-attribute-deletionpolicy.html)

question:
A company wants three million mobile users to share preferences across devices. Each user has one 4 KB preference document accessed by user ID, with no relational queries. Users sign in through social identity providers. The mobile application must access its user's preferences without embedded long-term AWS credentials, and the company wants minimal infrastructure administration.

Which design best meets these requirements?

options.text: Store each document in S3 and its object key in DynamoDB. Give the authenticated mobile role unrestricted read and write permissions to the table and bucket so the application can enforce user isolation.

Store one item per user in DynamoDB. Use a Cognito identity pool with social federation to obtain temporary role credentials, and restrict permitted DynamoDB operations with a LeadingKeys condition tied to the authenticated user's identity.
Store preferences in an RDS MySQL database behind a custom EC2 authentication service. Operate and scale the service and database to support the user population.
Store preferences in an RDS MySQL database with read replicas. Embed a shared database username and password in the mobile application and have clients enforce row ownership.

explanation.text:
Correct: <<2>>. A small key-addressed document fits a DynamoDB item. Cognito identity pools exchange supported identity tokens for temporary AWS credentials. An IAM policy restricts the allowed actions and partition keys so each identity accesses only its own preferences.

<<1>> adds an unnecessary object lookup and, more seriously, relies on untrusted client code to enforce access isolation. S3 plus metadata can be valid for larger objects, but broad permissions are not a security boundary.

<<3>> can implement secure access, yet adds custom authentication infrastructure and relational database administration for a key-value workload. RDS is not inherently unable to store preferences.

<<4>> distributes reusable credentials and trusts client-side checks; read replicas also do not accept preference writes.

Authentication identifies the user; IAM authorization restricts the data the resulting role session may access. Use a stable identity mapping across devices, scoped actions, and a ForAllValues condition for dynamodb:LeadingKeys. Do not allow unrestricted scans through another policy.

Official AWS references (checked 2026-09-18):
[Cognito identity pools](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-identity.html)
[DynamoDB fine-grained access](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/specifying-conditions.html)

question:
A bank runs a web application across two Availability Zones. Its TLS private key must be generated inside a company-controlled CloudHSM cluster and must never be exportable to a web server. The architecture must remain available after losing one AZ. Application logs need durable storage, and a separate KMS permission must govern which employees can decrypt them.

Which design meets all requirements?

options.text: Use a TCP Network Load Balancer and copy the TLS private key from an encrypted S3 bucket to each web server during startup. Store application logs in S3 with SSE-KMS and restricted policies.

Use a TCP Network Load Balancer and configure the web servers to perform TLS private-key operations in CloudHSM with a non-extractable key. Spread adequately sized HSM capacity across AZs. Store logs in S3 with a customer-managed KMS key and policies restricting object reads and decryption.
Terminate TLS on an Application Load Balancer using an imported certificate and private key. Store logs on encrypted instance-store volumes and keep the decryption keys only on the instances.
Use a TCP Network Load Balancer and a single CloudHSM in one AZ for TLS operations. Store logs in a private S3 bucket using SSE-S3 and grant authorized employees GetObject access.

explanation.text:
Correct: <<2>>. A TCP listener passes the encrypted TLS connection to the web server, whose supported cryptographic integration invokes the HSM for private-key operations. Generate the key as non-extractable and maintain enough HSM and application capacity in surviving AZs. S3 supplies durable log storage; SSE-KMS adds a separate decrypt authorization requirement.

<<1>> creates server-side copies of the private key, violating the custody requirement even if the S3 source is encrypted.

<<3>> moves TLS key custody to the load balancer, and instance-store logs are not durable across instance loss.

<<4>> leaves a single-AZ cryptographic dependency. SSE-S3 does not supply the separately controlled KMS permission requested here.

HSM storage alone does not make a key non-extractable: set the key attribute explicitly. For logs, both S3 read authorization and KMS decrypt authorization matter. Configure TLS clients for HSM redundancy and retry transient failures; merely creating additional HSMs does not prove sufficient surviving capacity.

Official AWS references (checked 2026-09-18):
[CloudHSM TLS integration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cloudhsm/latest/userguide/ssl-offload.html)
[CloudHSM key management](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cloudhsm/latest/userguide/bp-hsm-key-management.html)
[CloudHSM availability](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cloudhsm/latest/userguide/bp-cluster-management.html)
[S3 SSE-KMS permissions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingKMSEncryption.html)

question:
A company runs an increasing number of ECS tasks on Fargate On-Demand in one AWS account and Region. Task sizes vary. Operations needs an SNS notification when concurrently running Fargate vCPUs exceed 75% of the applicable quota. The team wants to avoid custom metric publishers and manual updates when the quota changes.

Which solution is the most operationally efficient?

options.text: Use the SampleCount statistic for ECS CPUUtilization as the number of running vCPUs. Divide it by the Fargate quota and create a CloudWatch alarm.
Select the AWS/Usage ResourceCount metric with Service=Fargate, Type=Resource, Resource=vCPU, and Class=Standard/OnDemand. Alarm on 100*m1/SERVICE_QUOTA(m1) greater than 75 and notify an SNS topic.
Request a larger Fargate quota and configure an AWS Health event rule to publish an SNS notification whenever consumption reaches 75% of the new quota.
Publish a custom count of running ECS tasks, divide it by a manually configured task limit, and alarm when that percentage exceeds 75.

explanation.text:
Correct: <<2>>. Fargate publishes account usage as ResourceCount in AWS/Usage. The dimensions select On-Demand vCPU consumption, and SERVICE_QUOTA returns the associated quota for the usage metric. A metric-math alarm can notify SNS without maintaining a separate publisher or hard-coded quota value.

<<1>> is incorrect because SampleCount counts samples included in a metric statistic; it is not the number of allocated vCPUs. CPUUtilization also measures utilization rather than quota consumption.

<<3>> changes the ceiling but does not create the requested usage-threshold monitor. AWS Health is not a replacement for this CloudWatch usage alarm.

<<4>> uses task count, which diverges from vCPU usage when task sizes differ, and adds custom maintenance.

Match the metric dimensions and quota scope. Fargate Spot uses a separate class and quota, so monitor it separately if introduced. Set the alarm period and evaluation policy deliberately; crossing 75% does not guarantee enough capacity remains until someone responds.

Official AWS references (checked 2026-09-18):
[Fargate usage metrics](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/monitoring-fargate-usage.html)
[CloudWatch quota alarms](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/CloudWatch-Quotas-Visualize-Alarms.html)

question:
A company runs a Linux application in an EC2 Auto Scaling group. Each new instance must access a shared 500 GB read-only dataset before serving traffic, without downloading a complete local copy. Developers release application updates several times each day. All running instances must receive available OS security patches within 48 hours.

Which solution meets these requirements with the least operational overhead?

options.text: Automate patching and testing of a base AMI with AWS Systems Manager. Update the launch template and replace instances within the patch deadline. Use CodeDeploy for application releases and mount an EFS file system during startup.

Automate patching and testing of a base AMI with AWS Systems Manager. Replace instances within the patch deadline. Deploy all application releases in one nightly batch and mount an EFS file system during startup.

Use CodeDeploy for application releases and Systems Manager for timely OS patching. Download the complete dataset from S3 to an EBS volume on every new instance before registering it with the load balancer.

Use CodeDeploy for application releases and mount an EFS file system during startup. Replace instances only when AWS publishes a new base AMI, without a separate patch evaluation or deployment schedule.

explanation.text:
Choose <<1>>. Separate the three lifecycles: maintain a tested OS image, deploy application revisions independently, and mount shared data. Systems Manager Automation can create a patched AMI, but the rollout must also update the launch template and replace existing instances before the 48-hour deadline. Gate application readiness on a successful EFS mount. CodeDeploy can deploy revisions to both existing and newly launched Auto Scaling instances.

<<2>> restricts releases to a nightly window, which cannot satisfy several deployments during the day. <<3>> can patch and deploy software, but a full 500 GB copy on every launch violates the stated startup constraint and adds duplicated storage. <<4>> delegates timing to the base-image publisher; it does not establish that every running instance receives each applicable patch within 48 hours.

A shared file system avoids mandatory full-dataset transfer during scale-out. Its total cost still depends on storage class, throughput and access patterns; EFS is not universally cheaper than S3 plus EBS.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Linux AMI maintenance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/automation-tutorial-update-patch-linux-ami.html), [EFS automatic mounting](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/mount-fs-auto-mount-onreboot.html), [CodeDeploy and Auto Scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/integrations-aws-auto-scaling.html).

question:
A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled. All established member accounts are in a Production OU. A custom SCP attached to the organization root explicitly denies changes to AWS Config. A newly invited account needs its Config rules updated before joining Production. The administrators already have the necessary IAM permissions.

How should the company enable a repeatable onboarding process while keeping the established accounts continuously protected?

options.text: Remove the Config deny from the root SCP and publish approved Config templates in AWS Service Catalog for all accounts to use.
Leave the root SCP unchanged. Move the new account to an Onboarding OU and attach an SCP that explicitly allows Config changes.
Leave the root SCP unchanged. Attach an IAM policy allowing Config changes to the new account administrators for the onboarding period.

Attach the Config restriction to the Production OU before removing that restriction from the root. Retain the required SCP allows and other guardrails. Make the changes in a separate Onboarding OU, then move the account to Production.

explanation.text:
Choose <<4>>. Scope the Config deny to the accounts that have completed onboarding. Attaching the deny to Production first preserves its protection while the root policy is changed. The new account can then use its existing IAM permissions in the separate Onboarding OU, provided the SCP path allows the actions and no other deny applies. Moving it to Production activates the Config restriction.

<<1>> removes the enforcement boundary for established accounts. An approved Service Catalog product does not prevent administrators from calling Config APIs directly. <<2>> cannot override the inherited root deny with a lower-level allow. <<3>> also fails because an IAM allow cannot override an applicable SCP deny.

SCPs set permission boundaries; they do not grant permissions. Keep appropriate allows at the root, every OU and the account. Root-level denies are valid for restrictions that truly must apply everywhere; the problem here is the scope of this particular deny.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [SCP evaluation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps_evaluation.html).

question:
A manufacturer has 500 sensors that each publish a small telemetry record every 10 seconds. Records require a short stateless enrichment before delivery to an S3 data lake. No device or application needs to subscribe to the telemetry topics. Under normal operation, records should arrive in S3 within 20 minutes.

Which design minimizes ingestion overhead and avoids managing processing servers?

options.text: Publish through the AWS IoT Core message broker. Start a Step Functions Standard workflow for every record to invoke a Lambda enrichment function and write one S3 object.
Publish to AWS IoT Core Basic Ingest topics. Route records to Amazon Data Firehose, use a Lambda transformation, and configure short transformation buffering with a 300-second S3 delivery buffer.
Route each record from AWS IoT Core into a Timestream database. Schedule Lambda queries to read unprocessed records, enrich them, track progress and write batches to S3.
Route records from AWS IoT Core Basic Ingest to Kinesis Data Streams. Run an EC2 Auto Scaling group to enrich records, manage stream checkpoints and upload S3 objects.

explanation.text:
Choose <<2>>. Basic Ingest routes published messages directly to the rules engine, bypassing broker messaging charges when publish/subscribe fan-out is unnecessary. It still uses authenticated IoT connections. Firehose manages buffering and S3 delivery, and invokes Lambda on batches for enrichment. Transformation buffering, function time and destination buffering all contribute to arrival latency; a 300-second delivery interval leaves room within the stated 20-minute normal-operation target.

<<1>> is technically possible, but per-record Standard workflows and individual S3 writes add avoidable orchestration and request overhead for this simple task. <<3>> introduces a staging database plus checkpoint and polling logic without a time-series query requirement. <<4>> adds servers and stream-consumer management that the question explicitly seeks to avoid.

Buffer intervals are delivery hints, not a hard end-to-end deadline during failures or retries. Monitor delivery freshness and transformation errors. Use the IoT broker instead when other subscribers need the messages.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [IoT Basic Ingest](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/iot/latest/developerguide/iot-basic-ingest.html), [Firehose transformation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/firehose/latest/dev/data-transformation.html).

question:
A company is building a stateless REST API with brief requests and long idle periods between unpredictable traffic bursts. Users need standard sign-up and sign-in features. Metadata must remain durable, and authorized users must download large private objects without sending the object bytes through the application.

Which design meets these requirements with the least infrastructure and authentication code to operate?

options.text: Run the API on Fargate behind an ALB with a custom authentication service. Store metadata in DynamoDB and private objects in S3. Proxy each authorized object download through the containers.
Run an always-on Fargate service behind an ALB with Cognito authentication. Store metadata in DynamoDB and private objects in S3. Return short-lived presigned URLs after checking object access.

Use API Gateway REST APIs with Lambda integrations and a Cognito user pool authorizer. Store metadata in DynamoDB and private objects in S3. Return short-lived presigned URLs after checking object access.

Use API Gateway REST APIs with Lambda integrations and a custom Lambda authorizer. Store the only copy of metadata in an ElastiCache Memcached cluster and private objects in S3. Return presigned URLs after checking object access.

explanation.text:
Choose <<3>>. API Gateway and Lambda fit brief, intermittent API work without an always-running application fleet. Cognito supplies the required identity features and a built-in REST API authorizer. DynamoDB stores durable metadata. After application-level authorization, a presigned S3 URL lets the client transfer an object directly using the signer's delegated permission.

<<1>> requires custom identity code and proxies large transfers through the compute tier, violating the download requirement. <<2>> can satisfy the functional requirements, but its continuously running service and ALB add infrastructure to operate during idle periods. It is not the best fit for the stated operating model; Fargate is not universally more expensive than Lambda. <<4>> adds unnecessary authorizer code and uses an evictable Memcached cache as the sole metadata store.

A valid identity token does not establish permission to every object. Check ownership or other resource authorization before signing. Presigned URLs are bearer credentials: anyone who receives one can use its allowed operation until it expires or the signing credentials cease to be valid.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Cognito API authorizers](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/apigateway-integrate-with-cognito.html), [S3 presigned URLs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html).

question:
An insurer runs web servers behind a load balancer. Its security policy requires the TLS private key to be generated and used inside company-controlled dedicated HSMs, with key extraction disabled. Application logs must survive instance termination, and only an audit role may read and decrypt the archived logs.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Pass TCP traffic through a Network Load Balancer. Store the TLS private key on encrypted EBS volumes attached to the web servers. Archive logs in S3 with SSE-KMS and restrict access to the audit role.

Pass TCP traffic through a Network Load Balancer. Download the TLS private key from a restricted S3 bucket at server startup. Archive logs in S3 with SSE-S3 and allow all server administrators to read them.
Pass TCP traffic through a Network Load Balancer. Use a non-extractable key in CloudHSM for TLS private-key operations. Store logs only on encrypted EC2 instance-store volumes.

Pass TCP traffic through a Network Load Balancer. Use a non-extractable key in a multi-AZ CloudHSM cluster for TLS private-key operations. Archive logs in S3 with SSE-KMS and restrict object reads and key decryption to the audit role.

explanation.text:
Choose <<4>>. The web servers terminate TLS while delegating supported private-key operations to CloudHSM. The Network Load Balancer uses a TCP listener so it passes the TLS session through. Generating the key inside the HSM and marking it non-extractable establishes the required key boundary. S3 provides durable log storage, and S3 authorization plus the KMS key policy restrict who can obtain plaintext archives.

<<1>> places usable private-key material on the servers, even though the disks are encrypted. <<2>> likewise copies the key out of an HSM boundary; SSE-S3 does not prevent permitted S3 readers from receiving decrypted logs. <<3>> protects the TLS key but instance store is not durable across termination.

Key custody and data-read authorization are separate controls. An HSM can protect a key from extraction while an authorized application still invokes it. Configure HSM client access, resilient HSM placement and least-privilege log-writer permissions; do not grant the writers log-read access merely because they upload logs.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [CloudHSM TLS offload](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cloudhsm/latest/userguide/ssl-offload.html), [CloudHSM key attributes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cloudhsm/latest/userguide/key-attribute-table.html), [S3 SSE-KMS permissions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingKMSEncryption.html). [CloudHSM availability](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cloudhsm/latest/userguide/cluster-high-availability-load-balancing.html).

question:
A service provider exposes an EC2 logging service through an AWS PrivateLink endpoint service backed by a Network Load Balancer. The NLB was created with a security group and enforces its inbound rules for PrivateLink traffic. Consumer endpoint connections are accepted, and consumer-side networking is verified. Provider-side flow logs show rejected traffic between the NLB and its targets, and some NLB listener traffic is blocked.

Which changes address the provider-side network controls? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Update the NACLs on the NLB and target subnets to allow the relevant application and health-check traffic between those subnets, including response traffic on ephemeral ports.
Update the provider target-subnet NACLs to permit only the consumer interface-endpoint subnet CIDRs as sources of application and health-check traffic.
Allow client private-IP ranges on the NLB listener port. Permit NLB outbound target and health-check traffic, and reference the NLB security group in the target security group.
Allow only the consumer client-IP ranges in the target security group. Use those same ranges as the sources for the NLB health-check port.
Update the Auto Scaling launch template to use the latest AMI and larger EC2 instances so that the NLB bypasses the rejected flows.

explanation.text:
Select <<1>> and <<3>>. NACLs are stateless, so the provider subnet rules must permit both the forward traffic and the return path. Target security groups can reference the NLB security group for the target and health-check ports. The NLB must also be able to send those requests through its outbound rules.

When NLB inbound-rule enforcement is enabled for PrivateLink, the source evaluated at that boundary is the client's private IP address, not the endpoint ENI address. <<2>> therefore uses the wrong peer for the provider NLB-to-target path. <<4>> applies the consumer source ranges at the wrong target boundary and fails to authorize NLB health checks. <<5>> changes compute capacity, which cannot override a network deny.

Treat the consumer endpoint, NLB listener and NLB-to-target connection as distinct enforcement points. Some designs deliberately disable NLB inbound-rule enforcement for PrivateLink, but this question keeps it enabled. The NLB was explicitly created with a security group because one cannot be added later to an NLB created without any.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [NLB security groups](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/network/load-balancer-security-groups.html). [NLB target networking](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/network/target-group-register-targets.html).

question:
A utility ingests meter readings through API Gateway and invokes Lambda once per request. As usage grows, Lambda reports TooManyRequestsException, and DynamoDB PutItem calls report provisioned write-capacity throttling. Profiling shows most of the longer execution time is spent retrying database writes; CPU and memory are not saturated. Readings may be processed asynchronously, but every accepted reading must be retained.

Which combination addresses both bottlenecks? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Increase the provisioned write capacity of the affected DynamoDB table and indexes to cover sustained demand, with appropriate Auto Scaling bounds and retry handling.
Increase Lambda memory while leaving the invocation pattern, database write capacity and retry configuration unchanged.
Have meters combine more readings into larger requests while leaving database capacity and the backend processing architecture unchanged.

Integrate the ingestion API with Kinesis Data Streams and return after durable ingestion. Process records with a Lambda event-source mapping using tuned batches and shard parallelism that fit the available concurrency.
Increase API Gateway rate and burst limits so that more requests can invoke the existing Lambda functions simultaneously.

explanation.text:
Select <<1>> and <<4>>. Sufficient DynamoDB write capacity addresses sustained storage demand. A durable stream separates accepting readings from processing them, so transient bursts wait in Kinesis instead of requiring one simultaneous long-running Lambda invocation per request. Tune batch size, shard count and parallelization against Lambda concurrency and downstream write capacity.

<<2>> can benefit CPU-bound code, but the measured delay is database retry time; more memory does not increase DynamoDB WCUs. <<3>> alone neither fixes sustained write demand nor creates a durable server-side backlog. <<5>> admits more work into already-throttled components and can worsen the problem.

Batching does not reduce the write capacity needed for the same set of item writes. Use backoff for throttled operations and idempotent processing because stream records can be delivered more than once. Monitor iterator age and retention so the backlog drains before records expire. A buffer absorbs bursts; it cannot compensate indefinitely for a consumer slower than sustained ingestion.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Lambda stream processing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/with-kinesis.html), [DynamoDB capacity throttling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/throttling-provisioned-capacity-exceeded-mitigation.html).

question:
An online retailer must recover its three-tier application in a second AWS Region more than 250 miles from the primary site. The recovery time objective is 5 minutes and the recovery point objective is 1 hour. Recovery exercises show that restoring the database or provisioning the complete application tier takes longer than 5 minutes. A running reduced-capacity stack can promote its replica, scale out and switch traffic within the target.

Which strategy meets the objectives at the lowest ongoing cost among these options?

options.text: Copy hourly backups to the recovery Region. After a disaster, provision the stack with CloudFormation and restore the latest backup.
Keep only a small database replica running in the recovery Region. After a disaster, resize it and provision the web tier, application tier and load balancers.
Keep a complete reduced-capacity application stack and a continuously replicated database in the recovery Region. Automate and regularly test promotion, scale-out and traffic switching.
Keep a complete application stack with full production capacity running idle in the recovery Region, with a continuously replicated standby database.

explanation.text:
Choose <<3>>. Warm standby keeps all required tiers deployed and running at reduced capacity. The stated recovery tests establish that promotion, scaling and traffic switching fit the five-minute objective. Monitor replication lag to verify the one-hour data-loss objective as well.

<<1>> requires infrastructure creation and database restore, which the measured recovery times exclude. <<2>> is a pilot-light approach; its missing application infrastructure and database resizing also exceed the measured budget. <<4>> is full-capacity hot standby and can meet the objectives, but pays for capacity that the validated warm-standby design does not need to keep running. It is not active-active because the second Region is idle.

RTO measures time to restore the required service level. RPO measures acceptable lost data, not restart time. Strategy names do not guarantee numerical objectives: include detection, promotion, DNS or traffic propagation, scaling and application validation in recovery exercises. Select a Region pair that independently satisfies the geographic requirement.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Recovery strategy selection](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reliability-pillar/rel_planning_for_recovery_disaster_recovery.html).

question:
A news publisher is migrating its Oracle database to Amazon RDS for Oracle. Readers and editors use the application at all hours. The database must automatically resume read and write service after a DB instance or Availability Zone failure, with minimal database administration.

Which configuration meets this requirement?

options.text: Use a Single-AZ RDS for Oracle instance and schedule RMAN backups with the RDS administrative procedures.
Use an RDS for Oracle Multi-AZ DB instance deployment with a synchronous standby in another Availability Zone.
Enable Oracle Real Application Clusters as the availability option for the RDS for Oracle database.
Use a Single-AZ RDS for Oracle instance with an asynchronous read replica and direct readers to the replica.

explanation.text:
Choose <<2>>. An RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment maintains a synchronous standby in a different Availability Zone and provides managed failover. Applications retain the database endpoint name but must retry and reconnect during recovery. The standby is for availability, not for serving normal read traffic.

<<1>> provides backups, not a running failover target. RDS for Oracle does support RMAN backup tasks through its administrative package; claiming that RMAN is entirely unsupported would be incorrect. <<3>> is unavailable because RDS for Oracle does not support Oracle RAC. <<4>> can offload reads, but an asynchronous read replica does not by itself provide automatic writable failover through the primary endpoint. Promotion and connection changes would require a separate recovery design, and replication lag can affect data loss.

Choose an availability mechanism for failure recovery and a read-scaling mechanism for query throughput. Backups remain necessary even when a standby protects against infrastructure failure.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [RDS Multi-AZ DB instances](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Concepts.MultiAZSingleStandby.html), [RDS Oracle RMAN tasks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Appendix.Oracle.CommonDBATasks.RMAN.html), [RDS Oracle FAQs](https://aws.amazon.com/rds/oracle/faqs/), [RDS failover and DNS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Concepts.MultiAZ.Failover.html).

question:
An online retailer expects a sharp burst of checkout requests during a sale. Users sign in with Google or Facebook. The checkout service must durably accept orders even when payment and fulfillment workers are temporarily at capacity. The UI may show a pending order and later display the completed result. Repeated requests must not create duplicate orders.

Which design best supports these requirements?

options.text: Use CloudFront and an ALB with an EC2 Auto Scaling group. Authenticate users through Amazon Cognito and complete payment processing synchronously before inserting each order into a Multi-AZ RDS database.
Use CloudFront and an ALB with an EC2 Auto Scaling group and Cognito sign-in. Send orders to SQS using an EC2 role. Scale separate idempotent workers to process orders and persist status in DynamoDB.
Host the frontend on an S3 website endpoint and add that endpoint to Global Accelerator. Use Cognito sign-in and have the browser write completed orders directly to DynamoDB.
Use CloudFront and an ALB with a fixed-size EC2 fleet and Cognito sign-in. Complete each payment request synchronously in the web tier before writing the order to DynamoDB.

explanation.text:
Choose <<2>>. The queue provides a durable boundary between request acceptance and downstream work. Web capacity and worker capacity can scale independently, while order status in DynamoDB supports the pending-to-completed user flow. Use role credentials and enforce authorization before accepting an order.

<<1>> retains a synchronous dependency on payment processing. It cannot durably accept checkout work while those workers are at capacity; adding database redundancy does not create a backlog. <<3>> uses an unsupported Global Accelerator endpoint type; S3 content delivery belongs behind a service such as CloudFront. Writing a record also does not establish that payment and fulfillment succeeded. <<4>> has no durable backlog and couples checkout acceptance to the fixed web fleet and downstream response time. DynamoDB itself is not the scalability defect.

SQS standard queues can deliver a message more than once. Store a stable order or idempotency key and make payment and status transitions safe to retry. A successful enqueue means accepted for processing, not payment completed; report those states accurately to the customer.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [SQS standard queues](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/standard-queues.html), [Global Accelerator endpoints](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/global-accelerator/latest/dg/about-endpoints.html). [Cognito social sign-in](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-user-pools-social-idp.html).

question:
A software company is deploying an issue-tracking application with a steady baseline of traffic and periodic growth. The existing application uses relational joins, constraints and multi-statement SQL transactions; redesigning its data model is outside the project scope. It must continue operating after an Availability Zone failure and replace failed application instances automatically. Static assets should load quickly for global users.

Which architecture best meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy an EC2 Auto Scaling group across multiple AZs behind an ALB, use CloudFront for static assets, and use an RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment. Manage the resources with CloudFormation.
Deploy the application on one Dedicated EC2 instance, use Redshift as the transactional database, and add ElastiCache for frequently requested records.
Deploy an EC2 Spot Auto Scaling group behind an ALB, use CloudFront for static assets, and use a Single-AZ RDS primary with an asynchronous read replica and manual promotion.
Deploy a fixed set of On-Demand EC2 instances in one AZ, use DynamoDB for the existing database without changing application queries, and add ElastiCache for read performance.

explanation.text:
Choose <<1>>. The application tier spans failure domains, and Auto Scaling can replace unhealthy instances while the load balancer sends requests to healthy targets. RDS Multi-AZ provides managed database failover for the existing relational workload. CloudFront caches eligible static assets near users, and CloudFormation makes provisioning repeatable.

<<2>> leaves one application instance as a single point of failure. Dedicated tenancy does not provide redundancy, and a warehouse is not a drop-in operational SQL database. <<3>> lacks automatic database failover: an asynchronous read replica with manual promotion does not satisfy the stated recovery model. Spot can be useful in resilient fleets, but a Spot-only fleet also requires interruption and capacity planning. <<4>> places all compute in one AZ and assumes DynamoDB can run unchanged relational queries. A cache does not repair those design gaps.

Evaluate availability at every tier. Several application servers do not remove a single database failure point, and a managed database does not fix application servers placed in only one AZ. Plan enough surviving capacity to support the required service level after a failure.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Auto Scaling across AZs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-add-az-console.html), [RDS Multi-AZ DB instances](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Concepts.MultiAZSingleStandby.html), [CloudFront content delivery](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/Introduction.html), [CloudFormation templates](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/Welcome.html).

question:
A property-search mobile app sends location updates in bursts. Each accepted update must be retained for processing, even when offer-lookup workers are briefly at capacity. An existing lookup service uses a tested geographic-cell index in DynamoDB. The app needs iOS and Android operating-system push notifications, including when it has no active API connection. The company targets notifications within a minute under normal conditions.

Which design best meets these requirements?

options.text: Send location updates to an authenticated API and EC2 workers. Query the existing DynamoDB index and deliver alerts only through AppSync subscriptions.

Send location updates to API Gateway and invoke Lambda synchronously for each request. Query the existing index and publish through SNS, without retaining work when the worker concurrency limit is reached.
Send location updates through an authenticated API to SQS. Use independently scaled workers to query the existing DynamoDB index and publish to registered SNS mobile endpoints through APNs and FCM.
Send location updates through an authenticated API to SQS. Use workers to query the existing DynamoDB index and send alerts only through API Gateway WebSocket connections.

explanation.text:
Choose <<3>>. SQS retains accepted work while workers catch up, and the workers can scale independently of the ingestion API. The existing geographic-cell index supplies the required lookup path. SNS mobile push uses platform endpoints and services such as APNs and FCM to deliver operating-system notifications.

<<1>> provides application subscription updates, but does not by itself deliver an OS push notification when the app has no active connection. <<2>> has an appropriate push channel but lacks the durable buffer required when processing concurrency is exhausted. <<4>> buffers work, yet WebSocket delivery depends on an active client connection and is not a substitute for APNs or FCM.

A queue and push service do not guarantee a one-minute arrival on every device. Scale for queue age, monitor processing latency and provider responses, and account for offline devices and platform delivery policies. Use event IDs and timestamps to handle duplicate or stale location updates. DynamoDB does not infer proximity from arbitrary coordinates; the explicitly supplied index makes the location queries valid.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [SQS standard queues](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/standard-queues.html), [SNS mobile push](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sns-mobile-application-as-subscriber.html).

question:
A company has configured direct IAM SAML 2.0 federation with its corporate identity provider. A custom federation client exchanges SAML assertions for AWS STS credentials. One administrator can assume a role successfully, but other employees authenticate at the IdP and fail when requesting AWS credentials. No IAM users are provisioned for these employees.

Which configuration checks directly address this failure? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Create an IAM user for each employee and attach a policy allowing sts:AssumeRoleWithSAML to that user.
Confirm that each target role trusts the correct IAM SAML provider and permits sts:AssumeRoleWithSAML with conditions that match the assertion.
Confirm that the employees belong to an IAM group named AWSFederatedUser, which AWS automatically creates for the SAML provider.
Confirm that the STS request includes the correct RoleArn, PrincipalArn for the SAML provider, and valid SAMLAssertion from the IdP.
Confirm that every workload subnet in the VPC has a route to the corporate IdP so that the workloads can authenticate each STS request.
Confirm that the IdP maps the affected users or groups to the appropriate AWS role and provider ARN pairs in the assertion.

explanation.text:
Select <<2>>, <<4>> and <<6>>. The target role must trust the intended SAML provider and accept the assertion conditions. The client must pass the matching role ARN, provider ARN and assertion to AssumeRoleWithSAML. The IdP must include the role mapping for each affected user; one administrator succeeding does not prove that other groups receive the same mappings.

<<1>> is unnecessary: this federation flow is specifically designed to obtain temporary credentials without a separate IAM user for each employee. <<3>> names a nonexistent automatically provisioned IAM group. Role mappings are configured in the IdP, rather than inherited from such a group. <<5>> confuses workload networking with federation. The federation client needs connectivity to the relevant endpoints; each application subnet does not have to contact the IdP to validate an STS request.

Separate trust from permissions. Role trust controls whether the identity can obtain a session; the role permission policies control what a successful session may do. Also inspect assertion validity, audience, signature and time conditions when troubleshooting. This is direct IAM federation, not an IAM Identity Center role flow.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [IAM SAML federation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_providers_saml.html), [AssumeRoleWithSAML](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/STS/latest/APIReference/API_AssumeRoleWithSAML.html).

question:
An application connects to an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment through its database endpoint hostname. During maintenance, an OS update triggers failover from the primary to the standby in another Availability Zone.

Which behavior should the application be designed to handle?

options.text: The original primary private IP address moves to the standby, and all established database connections continue without interruption.
The primary database only reboots in place, while the standby remains unavailable to application connections throughout the maintenance event.
RDS creates a new replacement database from a snapshot, and the application must be reconfigured with a new endpoint hostname.
RDS promotes the standby and updates the existing endpoint DNS record. The application resolves that hostname again and re-establishes its database connections.

explanation.text:
Choose <<4>>. For an RDS Multi-AZ DB instance failover, RDS changes the endpoint DNS mapping to the promoted standby. The application keeps using the same hostname, but existing connections must be re-established. Connection pools should detect failures, retry appropriately and avoid caching an old address indefinitely.

<<1>> incorrectly describes a private-IP move and uninterrupted sessions. <<2>> omits the standby promotion that the stem explicitly says occurs. A reboot is not a complete description of failover. <<3>> describes a restore-based recovery workflow rather than promotion of the existing synchronized standby.

A stable endpoint name abstracts a changing database host; it does not preserve established TCP sessions or guarantee zero interruption. Re-resolve DNS and reconnect, then apply transaction-aware retry logic so a lost response does not cause a duplicate business operation. These details refer to the Multi-AZ DB instance deployment type, not every RDS or Aurora topology.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [RDS failover and DNS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Concepts.MultiAZ.Failover.html).

question:
A software company wants to version and repeatedly deploy its AWS networking, application and database infrastructure across development and production. Shared network and data resources must have lifecycles independent of application releases. Engineers need to review infrastructure changes and identify the deployed template revision. Public applications also require a CDN that caches static content near global users.

Which approach best meets these requirements?

options.text: Use Elastic Beanstalk application versions as the record of all infrastructure changes and Global Accelerator for content caching. Configure shared network resources manually.

Use Elastic Beanstalk application versions and CloudFront distributions. Keep shared networking and databases outside the versioned infrastructure definition and recreate them manually for each environment.
Use version-controlled CloudFormation templates for the resource stacks and Global Accelerator as the service that caches static objects at edge locations.

Use version-controlled CloudFormation templates with separate stacks for shared and application resources. Review change sets, record the template revision on deployments, and define CloudFront distributions for content delivery.

explanation.text:
Choose <<4>>. CloudFormation templates describe resources and their dependencies, making consistent environments reproducible. Separate stacks allow shared resources and applications to evolve independently. Version control and deployment metadata identify the intended configuration, while change sets support review before updates. CloudFront supplies the required edge caching.

<<1>> leaves shared infrastructure outside version control and treats Global Accelerator as a cache. <<2>> uses a suitable CDN but still requires manual reconstruction of resources that the company wants to reproduce from code. <<3>> models infrastructure correctly, but Global Accelerator routes network traffic to regional endpoints; it does not provide CloudFront-style object caching.

Elastic Beanstalk can use versioned configuration files and CloudFormation resources, so it is incorrect to claim that it cannot express infrastructure as code. The proposed Beanstalk choices fail because of their incomplete resource definitions. Reapplying an older template is also not a database-data rollback: review resource replacements, retention policies and state migration before reversing an infrastructure change.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [CloudFormation templates](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/Welcome.html), [CloudFront content delivery](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/Introduction.html), [Beanstalk configuration files](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/ebextensions.html), [Global Accelerator endpoints](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/global-accelerator/latest/dg/about-endpoints.html).

question:
A bank runs a public portal on EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. DevOps engineers need operating-system administrator access to the instances. A separate cybersecurity team must control the public TLS certificate and its private key, and the key must not become available to the EC2 administrators. The teams use separate IAM roles and DevOps cannot modify security-role policies.

Which design meets this separation-of-duties requirement?

options.text: Have the cybersecurity team create an exportable ACM certificate, install it and its private key on every EC2 instance, and restrict the key file to the operating-system root user.

Terminate public TLS on the ALB with a non-exportable ACM certificate. Grant certificate and listener-certificate administration only to the cybersecurity role, while limiting the DevOps role to its required instance operations.
Store an exportable certificate and private key in a private S3 bucket. Allow only the EC2 instance role to download them and terminate public TLS on the instances.
Terminate public TLS on the ALB with an ACM certificate. Use only an SCP Allow statement to grant the cybersecurity role certificate-management access, without granting corresponding IAM permissions.

explanation.text:
Choose <<2>>. The ALB performs TLS termination through its ACM integration, so the public-facing private key does not need to be installed on the application hosts. Selecting a non-exportable certificate and controlling certificate, listener and IAM administration preserves the intended separation.

<<1>> exposes the private key to the operating-system administrators who control the root account. File permissions do not isolate secrets from those administrators. <<3>> likewise delivers key material to the EC2 environment; restricting the S3 download to the instance role does not prevent an administrator of that instance from obtaining it. <<4>> mistakes an SCP for a permission grant. SCPs constrain the available permissions and cannot replace the IAM allow needed by the cybersecurity role.

A certificate contains a public key; its associated private key is the secret material. ACM now offers exportable public certificates, so key non-exportability is a selected property rather than a universal ACM guarantee. If the ALB-to-target connection also uses TLS, it is a separate TLS session with its own certificate and key controls.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [ALB HTTPS certificates](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/https-listener-certificates.html), [ACM exportable certificates](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/acm/latest/userguide/acm-exportable-certificates.html), [SCP evaluation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps_evaluation.html).

question:
A university runs a public learning website on EC2 instances behind an existing Application Load Balancer. Students use ordinary web browsers on unmanaged devices. The university owns the domain and needs HTTPS with the lowest additional certificate cost and renewal effort.

Which solution should the solutions architect implement?

options.text: Request and validate a non-exportable ACM public certificate in the ALB Region. Attach it to an HTTPS listener and retain the configuration required for managed renewal.
Create an AWS Private CA, issue a private certificate for the website through ACM, and attach it to the ALB HTTPS listener.
Request an exportable ACM public certificate, replace the ALB with a TCP Network Load Balancer, and deploy the certificate and renewed private-key material to the EC2 web servers.
Create an AWS Private CA, export a private certificate to each EC2 web server, and replace the ALB with a TCP Network Load Balancer.

explanation.text:
Choose <<1>>. An ACM public certificate supplies a browser-trusted chain for the validated domain. The ALB integrates with ACM so the certificate can be managed without distributing private keys to each server. Non-exportable public certificates for integrated AWS services have no additional certificate charge; the existing infrastructure still has its normal charges.

<<2>> can secure traffic for clients configured to trust the private CA, but ordinary unmanaged browsers do not automatically trust that CA. <<3>> is possible: exportable ACM public certificates can be installed on EC2. It adds certificate charges, a load-balancer change and responsibility for deploying renewals, none of which is needed here. <<4>> combines private-CA trust distribution with host-level certificate deployment and does not meet the stated operating model.

Choose the trust model first, then the termination point. Public users need a chain their browsers trust. Use the existing ACM-integrated endpoint when it satisfies the requirements, and validate that the certificate covers the website hostname and can continue renewing.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [ALB HTTPS certificates](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/https-listener-certificates.html), [ACM certificate pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/certificate-manager/pricing/), [ACM exportable certificates](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/acm/latest/userguide/acm-exportable-certificates.html), [Certificate trust](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/acm/latest/userguide/acm-concepts.html).

question:
A company stores application objects in Amazon S3 and uses HTTPS for uploads and downloads. It wants AWS to manage encryption at rest without administering a customer-managed KMS key or performing encryption in the application.

Which description correctly explains server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3)?

options.text: The application supplies its own encryption key in each upload and download request, and S3 uses that key without retaining it after the request.
S3 encrypts each object with a unique data key and encrypts that key with S3-managed key material. S3 manages the encryption and key rotation.
The customer creates a KMS key and grants callers permission to decrypt it, while S3 uses the key for server-side object encryption.
The application obtains a plaintext data key, encrypts the object locally, and uploads the ciphertext and encrypted data key to S3.

explanation.text:
Choose <<2>>. SSE-S3 performs encryption inside the S3 service. Object data is encrypted with a unique key, and that key is itself protected by S3-managed key material. The customer does not manage a KMS key or receive the plaintext data key for this operation.

<<1>> describes the customer-provided-key model associated with SSE-C, not SSE-S3. <<3>> describes SSE-KMS using a customer-managed KMS key, which provides a separate key-policy and decryption authorization boundary. <<4>> describes client-side envelope encryption: the application encrypts the bytes before uploading them.

S3 already applies baseline server-side encryption to new uploads. Choosing a different mode changes key control and authorization capabilities. Encryption at rest does not replace S3 access policies: an authorized read of an SSE-S3 object returns decrypted data. HTTPS protects the transport connection separately. The general principle is to distinguish where encryption occurs from who owns and authorizes use of the keys.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [S3 managed encryption](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingServerSideEncryption.html), [S3 SSE-KMS permissions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingKMSEncryption.html).

question:
A weather agency publishes sensor readings to AWS IoT Core. An IoT rule writes the readings to DynamoDB. Monitoring shows that no new rows have arrived, but the cause is unknown. Fleet connectivity indexing and AWS IoT logging are enabled. The agency also runs Device Defender security audits.

Which investigation is most likely to identify where the data path is failing?

options.text: Rerun the Device Defender policy audit and treat a successful audit as proof that all devices are connected and all DynamoDB writes are succeeding.
Migrate the sensors to AWS IoT SiteWise and use its asset hierarchy to replace the existing ingestion path before examining connection or rule logs.

Query fleet connectivity status and correlate device, authentication and publish events with IoT rule logs. For connected publishers, inspect rule matching, action IAM permissions and DynamoDB errors.
Increase DynamoDB write capacity immediately and restart every sensor, assuming that a lack of rows proves that the table is throttling writes.

explanation.text:
Choose <<3>>. Trace the path in stages: device connectivity, authentication and authorization, message publication, rule execution, and the destination write. Configured fleet indexing helps find disconnected devices. IoT logs record message progress through the broker and rules engine. A device can be connected and publishing while its rule fails because of SQL matching, action permissions or a DynamoDB error.

<<1>> confuses a security configuration audit with proof of end-to-end delivery. <<2>> changes the architecture without establishing the fault and introduces an industrial asset service that is not required for this diagnosis. <<4>> makes an unsupported assumption: absent rows can result from many upstream failures, not only insufficient table capacity. Restarting devices can also obscure evidence.

Use the last confirmed successful stage to narrow the search. Correlate client IDs, timestamps and rule actions, and inspect the actual destination error before changing capacity or permissions. Connectivity status can lag and is not proof of data delivery; current logs and service metrics provide the supporting evidence.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [IoT connectivity indexing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/iot/latest/developerguide/managing-index.html), [IoT message logs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/iot/latest/developerguide/cloud-watch-logs.html).

question:
A company runs batch applications in private IPv4 subnets across two Availability Zones. They use public NAT instances to reach internet APIs. Instance failures and bandwidth limits repeatedly interrupt jobs. The company wants resilient outbound IPv4 access without maintaining NAT operating systems or custom failover automation.

Which design best meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a public zonal NAT gateway with an Elastic IP address in a public subnet in each AZ. Route each private subnet default IPv4 route to its same-AZ gateway, and route the public subnets to an internet gateway.
Replace the existing NAT instances with larger EC2 instances that support enhanced networking. Keep the current routes and perform operating-system patching during maintenance windows.
Run a NAT instance in each AZ and build monitoring and Lambda automation to replace failed instances and update private-subnet routes during outages.
Attach an egress-only internet gateway to the VPC and replace the private subnet default IPv4 routes with routes to that gateway.

explanation.text:
Choose <<1>>. Public NAT gateways provide managed outbound translation for the private IPv4 workloads. A zonal gateway is redundant within its AZ; placing one in each AZ and routing workloads to the local gateway avoids making both AZs depend on one gateway AZ. Internet access also requires a public-subnet route to an internet gateway and an Elastic IP for each public NAT gateway.

<<2>> may increase bandwidth, but retains customer maintenance and the instance-failure problem. <<3>> can form a resilient NAT-instance design, but explicitly requires the maintenance and custom failover automation the company wants to remove. <<4>> cannot carry the required IPv4 traffic because an egress-only internet gateway is for IPv6.

Managed NAT does not make every topology resilient: a shared zonal gateway still introduces an AZ dependency. Size and monitor connection and throughput limits, and verify route tables and NACLs. NAT permits response traffic for connections initiated from inside; it does not expose private instances for unsolicited internet connections.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [NAT gateway resilience](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/nat-gateway-basics.html), [NAT gateway comparison](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-nat-comparison.html), [Egress-only IPv6 gateway](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/egress-only-internet-gateway.html).

question:
A company uses AWS Organizations to manage thousands of accounts. Each application team must retain ownership of its VPC and route tables. The network team must centrally inspect outbound internet traffic with third-party stateful appliances. Organization guardrails prevent application accounts from creating alternative internet egress paths.

Which design meets these requirements with the least network management overhead?

options.text: Build an EC2 transit VPC with a VPN connection from every application VPC. Operate the routing and firewall appliances in the transit VPC.
Share subnets from a central VPC with the application accounts through AWS RAM. Allow each participant account to manage its subnet route tables and use central proxy servers.
Peer every application VPC with an inspection VPC. Route internet-bound packets through the peering connections to the inspection VPC internet gateway.

Share an AWS Transit Gateway through AWS RAM. Attach the application VPCs and a central egress VPC. Route outbound traffic through Gateway Load Balancer endpoints and a fleet of inspection appliances before NAT and internet egress.

explanation.text:
<<4>> separates application VPC ownership from centrally managed transit and inspection. Transit Gateway aggregates the VPC attachments, and Gateway Load Balancer endpoints insert the appliance fleet into the packet path. Configure the return path consistently, use Transit Gateway appliance mode where required for flow symmetry, and deploy the egress components across Availability Zones.

<<1>> can implement transit, but managing a VPN overlay and EC2 routing fleet adds overhead at this scale. <<2>> fails the ownership requirement: shared-subnet participants cannot manage the owner’s route tables. <<3>> cannot provide internet-gateway transit through VPC peering. Peering connectivity to a proxy application is a different design from transparent gateway transit.

Central routing is only effective if account permissions and guardrails prevent workloads from bypassing inspection.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/building-scalable-secure-multi-vpc-network-infrastructure/using-nat-gateway-and-gwlb-with-ec2.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/en_en/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-share-limitations.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/peering/vpc-peering-basics.html

question:
A hospital runs a three-tier web application with unpredictable demand. Users must retain their sessions when an application instance is replaced. Most database traffic consists of read-only reports that can tolerate brief replication lag, and peak report traffic exceeds the capacity of one database instance. The application must also recover automatically from a database Availability Zone failure.

Which architecture meets these requirements?

options.text: Use Auto Scaling groups for web and application instances, keep sessions on each instance, and deploy an RDS Multi-AZ DB instance without read replicas.
Use Auto Scaling groups for web and application instances, keep sessions on each instance, and use an RDS Single-AZ primary with read replicas.

Use stateless web and application instances in Auto Scaling groups with CloudWatch-based scaling policies. Store shared sessions in a resilient ElastiCache deployment. Use an RDS Multi-AZ DB instance and direct reporting queries to read replicas.

Use stateless web and application instances in Auto Scaling groups with CloudWatch-based scaling policies. Store shared sessions in a resilient ElastiCache deployment. Direct all queries to an RDS Multi-AZ DB instance without read replicas.

explanation.text:
<<3>> addresses three separate scaling and availability concerns. External session storage lets requests move between application instances. RDS read replicas offload lag-tolerant reads, while a Multi-AZ DB instance provides a synchronous standby for automatic failover. Size and configure the session store for its own availability and recovery needs.

<<1>> retains instance-local sessions and does not offload reports. <<2>> still loses local sessions when instances are replaced and lacks the requested Multi-AZ primary/standby failover design. <<4>> solves session placement and database failover but sends the excessive read workload to the primary.

A standby in an RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment does not serve reads. This differs from an RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster, whose reader instances can serve queries. Monitoring alone also does not scale instances; configure scaling policies and route read traffic explicitly.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Concepts.MultiAZSingleStandby.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReadRepl.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-scaling-target-tracking.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/rel_mitigate_interaction_failure_stateless.html

question:
A company must retain an Oracle RAC database while migrating it to Amazon EC2. The company has already validated the licensing, cluster interconnect, storage design, and Oracle support requirements. Its database team has tested application-consistent backup scripts for the EBS-backed database volumes. The team wants scheduled backups and controlled operating system patching with the least custom orchestration.

Which solution should a solutions architect recommend?

options.text: Run the validated RAC design on EC2. Use an Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager snapshot policy with the tested pre- and post-snapshot scripts, and use Systems Manager Patch Manager in maintenance windows that respect the cluster maintenance procedure.
Migrate the RAC database to an Amazon RDS for Oracle Multi-AZ DB instance. Use its managed standby as the second RAC node and rely on RDS backups and maintenance.
Migrate the RAC database to Amazon Aurora. Preserve the Oracle RAC engine configuration and use Aurora automated backups and managed patching.
Run the validated RAC design on EC2. Build scheduled Lambda functions to create snapshots, and build CodePipeline and CodeDeploy workflows to coordinate operating system patches.

explanation.text:
<<1>> preserves the required database architecture and uses managed scheduling for the operational tasks. Data Lifecycle Manager can invoke Systems Manager pre- and post-snapshot scripts to coordinate application-consistent snapshots. Patch Manager can run in maintenance windows, with the database team controlling safe node order, draining and reboot behavior. Verify script success and restoreability rather than assuming every EBS snapshot is application-consistent.

<<2>> is unsuitable because RDS for Oracle does not support Oracle RAC; a Multi-AZ standby is not a RAC node. <<3>> changes the database engine and cannot preserve an Oracle RAC configuration. <<4>> can be engineered to work, but duplicates snapshot and patch orchestration available in the managed services and therefore adds operational work.

This choice does not establish that an arbitrary EC2/EBS arrangement supports RAC. The validated cluster and storage design is an explicit prerequisite.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Oracle.Concepts.FeatureSupport.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/automate-app-consistent-backups.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/patch-manager.html

question:
VPC A (172.16.0.0/16) has separate peering connections to VPC B and VPC C, as shown. Both peer VPCs use 10.0.0.0/16. Instances in VPC A must initiate connections to 10.0.0.77 in VPC B and to every other required address in VPC C, including 10.0.0.88. Address 10.0.0.77 is not used in VPC C. Security groups and network ACLs already permit the required traffic.

Which route configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Add two routes for 10.0.0.0/16 to the VPC A subnet route table, one for each peering connection. Use network ACLs to choose which peer receives each destination.
Enable automatic route propagation on both VPC peering connections so VPC A learns which addresses belong to each peer.
Add a 10.0.0.0/24 route through the peering connection to VPC B and a 10.0.0.0/16 route through the connection to VPC C. Add return routes to VPC A in both peers.

Add a 10.0.0.77/32 route through the peering connection to VPC B and a 10.0.0.0/16 route through the connection to VPC C. Add return routes to 172.16.0.0/16 in the relevant subnet route tables of both peers.

explanation.text:
<<4>> uses longest-prefix matching. Traffic to 10.0.0.77 matches both routes, but the /32 route is more specific and selects VPC B. Traffic to 10.0.0.88 matches only the /16 route and selects VPC C. Each peer also needs a return route through its own peering connection to VPC A.

<<1>> cannot use duplicate destination routes and network ACLs as a peer-selection mechanism. ACLs allow or deny packets; they do not select route targets. <<2>> assumes a route-propagation feature that VPC peering does not provide. <<3>> sends the entire 10.0.0.0/24 subnet, including 10.0.0.88, to VPC B.

The overlapping networks are in two separate peers of A, not two endpoints of one B-to-C peering connection. The narrow exception works because A needs a disjoint set of destination addresses; it cannot distinguish two different hosts with the same destination IP.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/peering/peering-configurations-partial-access.html

question:
A photo-sharing service stores photos and associated JSON metadata in Amazon S3 Standard. Objects are larger than 128 KB, remain frequently accessed for 30 days, and then are retained for at least a year with infrequent access. All objects must remain immediately retrievable. The service uses an RDS Single-AZ DB instance. The company also wants to detect personal information in the JSON files and automatically fail over after a database Availability Zone failure.

Which combination best meets these requirements?
