options.text: Use Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery jobs for the JSON files, transition eligible S3 objects to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 30 days, and convert the database to an RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment.
Use Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery jobs for the JSON files, transition eligible S3 objects to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days, and convert the database to an RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment.

Use Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery jobs for the JSON files, transition eligible S3 objects to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days, and create a read replica of the Single-AZ database in another Availability Zone.
Use Amazon Inspector to discover personal information in S3, transition eligible S3 objects to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days, and convert the database to an RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment.

explanation.text:
<<2>> matches all three requirements. Macie can inspect supported JSON object contents for sensitive data. S3 Standard-IA retains millisecond access for long-lived objects whose reads become infrequent. An RDS Multi-AZ DB instance adds a synchronous standby and automatic failover. Evaluate transition, retrieval and minimum-storage charges against the observed access pattern.

<<1>> uses an archive class that requires a restore before ordinary object retrieval, so it fails the immediate-access requirement. <<3>> provides an asynchronous read replica that requires a separate promotion procedure; it does not provide the requested automatic Multi-AZ failover. <<4>> uses a vulnerability-management service for a sensitive-data discovery task; Macie is the appropriate service for supported JSON objects in S3.

Macie creates findings; protection or remediation requires a response workflow. It does not inspect the visual content of photographs. The JSON metadata is the supported sensitive-data discovery target in this scenario.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/macie/latest/user/discovery-supported-storage.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/macie/latest/user/what-is-macie.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Concepts.MultiAZSingleStandby.html

question:
A company deploys an application with AWS CloudFormation. Each release creates a new AMI and updates the version of the EC2 launch template used by an existing Auto Scaling group. The deployment must replace the group’s running instances in controlled batches while keeping enough healthy instances behind the load balancer. The group has capacity headroom for replacements, and new instances can signal application readiness.

Which template change enables this behavior during a stack update?

options.text: Create a CloudFormation change set for the new launch template version. Rely on the change set to replace every running instance after execution.
Add a DeletionPolicy to the launch template and set MinSuccessfulInstancesPercent to 50 on that policy.
Add an UpdatePolicy with AutoScalingRollingUpdate to the Auto Scaling group. Configure batch size, minimum instances in service, and readiness signals with an appropriate timeout.
Create a second CloudFormation stack for every release and switch DNS to its load balancer after deployment.

explanation.text:
<<3>> directs CloudFormation to roll the existing Auto Scaling group’s instances when the referenced launch template version changes. MinInstancesInService and MaxBatchSize control capacity during replacement. WaitOnResourceSignals and PauseTime allow the deployment to wait for an application-level readiness signal. Configure that signal only after initialization and relevant health checks pass.

<<1>> previews and applies resource changes but does not itself define how existing instances are replaced. <<2>> confuses deletion behavior with update behavior; DeletionPolicy is not a rolling-deployment policy. <<4>> describes a possible blue/green architecture, but does not enable rolling replacement in the existing group as required.

A rolling policy is not an unconditional zero-downtime guarantee. Adequate spare capacity, load-balancer health checks, connection draining, and meaningful readiness signals remain necessary.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/TemplateReference/aws-attribute-updatepolicy.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/quickref-ec2-auto-scaling.html

question:
A company hosts an internal application on EC2 instances with private IP addresses. Employees need access from both the corporate office and home internet connections. Access must require the corporate identity provider, and the application must not expose a public endpoint.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a Site-to-Site VPN from the office router to the VPC and allow application traffic only from the office network.
Create an AWS Direct Connect connection from the office to the VPC and configure office workstations to use it.

Create an AWS Client VPN endpoint with federated authentication. Associate target subnets, configure application network routes and group authorization rules, and allow the Client VPN security group to access the private application.
Create an internet-facing Application Load Balancer with a public TLS certificate and forward requests to the application without configuring user authentication.

explanation.text:
<<3>> provides authenticated remote access from individual employee devices. Client VPN authentication establishes identity; authorization rules, routes and security groups then restrict access to the private application. Users at home and in the office can use the client connection.

<<1>> connects the office network but provides no access path for employees on home internet. <<2>> has the same location limitation and does not authenticate remote employees. <<4>> exposes a public application endpoint, and a server TLS certificate alone does not establish employee identity.

Authentication and network reachability are separate checks. A successful VPN connection is insufficient unless authorization rules, endpoint routes and application security groups also allow the requested destination.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/client-authorization.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/cvpn-getting-started.html

question:
A company has two interconnected data centers. Applications in an AWS VPC depend on systems reachable through either data center. A single Site-to-Site VPN connection currently terminates on one customer gateway device in the first data center and uses a virtual private gateway attached to the VPC. Both VPN tunnels are configured.

Which change removes the customer gateway device and first data center as single points of connectivity failure?

options.text: Deploy a separate customer gateway device with an independent internet connection in the second data center. Create another Site-to-Site VPN connection to the existing virtual private gateway and configure routing through both connections.
Deploy a NAT gateway in the second data center and use it as the termination point for an additional AWS VPN tunnel.
Create another virtual private gateway in a second Availability Zone and attach it to the same VPC while retaining the existing customer gateway device.
Create a second virtual private gateway, attach it concurrently to the same VPC, and connect a second customer gateway device to it.

explanation.text:
<<1>> adds an independent on-premises failure domain while reusing the managed virtual private gateway. Each VPN connection has two tunnels, and routing must advertise the necessary prefixes through both customer gateways. The data-center network must also maintain access to the dependencies through the surviving location.

<<2>> treats a NAT gateway as a VPN customer gateway device; these are different functions, and an AWS NAT gateway is a VPC resource. <<3>> retains the failing on-premises device and incorrectly treats a virtual private gateway as a customer-selected zonal resource. <<4>> assumes that two virtual private gateways can be attached concurrently to one VPC.

Two tunnels protect against AWS-side tunnel endpoint failures, but both can fail together if they share one customer gateway device, internet connection or data center.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpn/latest/s2svpn/vpn-redundant-connection.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpn/latest/s2svpn/vpn-limits.html

question:
A company uses a versioned S3 general purpose bucket and wants its application to upload and retrieve new object versions with server-side encryption using customer-provided keys (SSE-C). The bucket is already configured to allow SSE-C writes, and the company will retain a secure mapping of object versions to keys.

Which implementation requirements apply? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use the secure WebSocket protocol to send the encryption key to Amazon S3 before uploading an object.
Set x-amz-server-side-encryption-customer-key-MD5 to AES256 to select the encryption algorithm.
Include the SSE-C algorithm header set to AES256, the base64-encoded 256-bit key, and the base64-encoded MD5 digest of that key in the applicable upload and retrieval requests.
Upload and retrieve SSE-C objects only through the Amazon S3 console so that the console can retain the encryption keys.
Use HTTPS for SSE-C requests. When using a presigned URL, include the required SSE-C headers in the signed request and supply the matching headers when making the request.

explanation.text:
<<3>> supplies the three SSE-C header values: the algorithm, the key, and a digest that checks key transmission integrity. <<5>> provides the required HTTPS transport and the headers needed when invoking a presigned request. A bare presigned URL in a browser is insufficient for SSE-C.

<<1>> substitutes WebSockets for the S3 HTTPS API. <<2>> confuses the algorithm field with the key-MD5 field. <<4>> is incorrect because the S3 console does not support SSE-C operations and S3 does not retain the supplied encryption key.

Keep each version’s key independently recoverable; losing it makes that version unreadable. Enabling SSE-C does not convert older SSE-S3 versions. Also distinguish permission to use SSE-C from a bucket default: affected new and existing buckets block SSE-C writes by default from April 2026, and applications must explicitly unblock them when required.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/ServerSideEncryptionCustomerKeys.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/specifying-s3-c-encryption.html

question:
A company maintains custom Linux AMIs for EC2 applications. A candidate AMI must pass application tests and a vulnerability review before production use. Approved images must be rebuilt at least every 30 days, and running instances must receive approved operating system patches. The operating system and installed packages are supported by Amazon Inspector.

Which actions should the company take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Install SSM Agent in the image and treat its presence as proof that the image has passed a CVE scan.

Build an automated image pipeline that evaluates application tests and Inspector findings before publishing an approved AMI ID to a protected Parameter Store parameter. Schedule image rebuilds every 30 days and use Patch Manager for approved patching of the running fleet.

Enable current Amazon Inspector EC2 scanning and launch candidate AMIs as isolated test instances with the required scan coverage. Confirm scanning completed and evaluate findings before approving each image.
Use AWS Config configuration history as the source of operating system package vulnerability findings and approve images with no configuration changes.
Use CloudTrail API event logs to identify all installed packages and approve images that have no recorded security-related API calls.

explanation.text:
<<2>> implements the approval, publication and recurring maintenance workflow. <<3>> supplies actual vulnerability evidence from eligible EC2 instances launched from the candidate image. The pipeline must verify scan coverage and completion; an empty findings list alone could mean scanning never succeeded.

<<1>> confuses an inventory/management agent with a completed vulnerability assessment. Inspector can use SSM-managed inventory, but the agent’s presence is not approval. <<4>> records resource configuration, not the package-to-CVE assessment required here. <<5>> records API activity, not a complete software inventory or package vulnerability assessment.

An AMI is immutable. Patch a build instance and create a new AMI, then retest and republish it. Patching already running instances is a separate fleet operation. Restrict production launches to the controlled approved-image path and protect permission to change approval metadata.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/inspector/latest/user/scanning-ec2.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/patch-manager.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html

question:
A company hosts several HTTPS applications for unrelated domain names. Each domain already has a valid certificate, and the company must retain those certificates without reissuing them as a combined certificate. All supported clients send Server Name Indication (SNI). The company wants to serve the applications through one load balancer.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Attach a wildcard certificate for one of the domains and use it to authenticate all unrelated domain names.
Edit the Subject Alternative Name entries of one existing certificate to include the other domains without requesting a new certificate.
Create one CloudFront distribution and attach each existing certificate as a separate viewer certificate for that distribution.

Import the certificates into ACM as needed and add them to the HTTPS listener certificate list of an Application Load Balancer. Use SNI certificate selection and host-based listener rules for the applications.
Attach the existing certificates to a Gateway Load Balancer and configure hostname-based TLS termination.

explanation.text:
<<4>> lets one ALB HTTPS listener present different certificates for different SNI hostnames. After TLS is established, host-based listener rules can route HTTP requests to the corresponding target groups. Certificate selection and application routing are related but distinct steps.

<<1>> fails because a wildcard covers a defined domain namespace, not unrelated domains. <<2>> would invalidate the certificate’s signature; changing its covered names requires a newly issued certificate. <<3>> incorrectly assumes that one CloudFront distribution accepts multiple viewer certificates. <<5>> assigns application TLS termination and hostname routing to Gateway Load Balancer, whose purpose is transparent network appliance insertion.

Keep imported certificates renewed and ensure every certificate covers its intended hostname. A default ALB certificate handles clients without a matching SNI certificate; it does not make an unrelated hostname valid.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/https-listener-certificates.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cloudfront/latest/APIReference/API_ViewerCertificate.html

question:
A company serves static content through the default domain name of an Amazon CloudFront distribution, such as d123example.cloudfront.net. It does not use an alternate domain name. Every applicable cache behavior must deliver content to viewers only over HTTPS.

Which settings provide the required viewer connection? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Set the Viewer Protocol Policy on each applicable cache behavior to HTTPS Only or Redirect HTTP to HTTPS.
Install a self-signed certificate on the S3 origin and leave the Viewer Protocol Policy set to allow HTTP and HTTPS.
Use the default CloudFront certificate for the distribution’s cloudfront.net domain name.
Install a self-signed certificate on an origin load balancer and rely on it to authenticate the viewer-to-CloudFront connection.
Use the origin load balancer’s default DNS name as the viewer certificate for the CloudFront distribution.

explanation.text:
<<1>> controls whether a viewer request can receive content over HTTP. HTTPS Only rejects HTTP requests, while Redirect HTTP to HTTPS directs supported requests to the secure URL. <<3>> supplies the AWS-managed certificate appropriate for the default cloudfront.net hostname. Together they cover protocol enforcement and server authentication.

<<2>> leaves viewers able to use HTTP and proposes an origin setting instead of a viewer control. <<4>> also confuses the origin TLS connection with the viewer connection. <<5>> treats a DNS name as a certificate and uses the wrong hostname for the viewer endpoint.

Viewer and origin transport are separate connections. Requiring viewer HTTPS does not itself establish HTTPS from CloudFront to a custom origin. An alternate viewer domain would also require a certificate covering that domain instead of the default CloudFront certificate.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/using-https-viewers-to-cloudfront.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cloudfront/latest/APIReference/API_ViewerCertificate.html

question:
A company uses a Storage Gateway stored volume to expose a 5 TB filesystem to an on-premises application through iSCSI. Scheduled snapshots have completed successfully in AWS. After a data-center outage, both the application server and gateway are unavailable. The company wants to recover the filesystem on an EC2 instance from the latest completed snapshot.

Which recovery procedure should it use?

options.text: Locate the gateway’s internal S3 objects and mount their bucket directly as the EC2 instance’s original filesystem.
Attach the unavailable on-premises gateway’s iSCSI volume directly to the EC2 instance without restoring a snapshot.
Restore the gateway snapshot directly into an EFS filesystem and mount that filesystem on the EC2 instance.
Create an EBS volume from the completed gateway snapshot in the EC2 instance’s Availability Zone. Attach the volume and mount the recovered filesystem.

explanation.text:
<<4>> uses the supported block-storage recovery path. Stored Volume Gateway keeps primary data on premises and asynchronously creates EBS snapshots in AWS. A completed snapshot can create an EBS volume that an EC2 recovery instance can attach and mount. Validate filesystem compatibility and application recovery steps.

<<1>> assumes the service’s internal storage is an ordinary, directly readable S3 file bucket. <<2>> depends on the failed gateway and local disks remaining available. <<3>> assumes EFS can directly restore an EBS-format volume snapshot.

The recoverable point is the latest successfully completed snapshot. The outage does not make unsent local writes available in AWS, and recovery cannot depend on creating a new snapshot from the unavailable site.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/storagegateway/latest/vgw/StorageGatewayConcepts.html

question:
A research team runs a tightly coupled MPI workload on 200 EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones. The workload reads and writes large shared files on Amazon EFS. Tests at 1,000 instances show excessive time spent on inter-instance communication and parallel file I/O. The team prioritizes job performance and can restart jobs from checkpoints after an Availability Zone failure.

Which changes should the team make? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Place the compute instances in a cluster placement group within one Availability Zone, with capacity planning for the required fleet.
Attach extra standard network interfaces to the existing instances and assume their aggregate bandwidth increases without changing instance limits.
Use supported EFA-enabled instances and an MPI/libfabric software stack configured to use Elastic Fabric Adapter.
Stripe EBS volumes from different Availability Zones into one RAID 0 device attached to every compute instance.
Replace EFS with a single st1 EBS volume and mount it concurrently from all compute instances as the shared filesystem.
Use an appropriately sized Amazon FSx for Lustre filesystem for the shared parallel file workload, and validate throughput and metadata settings with representative tests.

explanation.text:
<<1>> reduces network distance for a tightly coupled cluster. <<3>> enables a lower-overhead communication path for supported MPI workloads. <<6>> provides a parallel filesystem designed for concurrent high-performance file access. These address the measured communication and storage bottlenecks.

<<2>> does not remove the instance’s networking limits merely by adding interfaces. <<4>> assumes cross-AZ EBS attachment and universal shared RAID access that this design does not provide. <<5>> treats an st1 block volume as a shared multi-client filesystem.

EFS is not categorically unable to support 1,000 clients; the evidence is the workload’s measured I/O bottleneck. FSx throughput, striping, client configuration and available compute capacity still need validation. Concentrating the compute fleet in one AZ trades fault isolation for performance, so checkpoint and restart procedures remain necessary.

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/placement-strategies.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fsx/latest/LustreGuide/performance.html

question:
A company is moving large analytical files to managed storage in AWS. It must control the encryption key policy and automatic rotation schedule, enforce encrypted uploads, and query the files directly with Amazon Redshift Spectrum. The company does not want to operate storage servers.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use S3 File Gateway to write the files to a bucket encrypted only with SSE-S3. Rely on the S3-managed key for the company’s rotation controls.

Store the files in S3 with SSE-KMS using a customer managed symmetric KMS key with automatic rotation enabled. Require HTTPS and the designated key for uploads, and grant the Spectrum role the required S3 and KMS permissions.
Store the large files as DynamoDB items encrypted with a customer managed KMS key, and configure Spectrum to read the items directly.
Store the files on encrypted EBS volumes attached to an EC2 storage server, and point Spectrum external tables at those volumes.

explanation.text:
<<2>> combines a Spectrum-compatible object store with customer control over KMS permissions and rotation. Enforce TLS and the approved encryption configuration at the S3 access boundary. The query role also needs access to the objects and permission to decrypt with the KMS key.

<<1>> uses S3-managed encryption keys, which do not provide the requested customer KMS policy and rotation controls. <<3>> is not a suitable large-file object store and is not a direct Spectrum data source. <<4>> adds server management and does not make EBS volumes a Spectrum external data source.

Automatic KMS rotation changes key material while retaining the logical key and older material needed for decryption. It does not rewrite existing S3 objects or rotate their data keys. Transport encryption and encryption at rest require separate controls.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/redshift/latest/dg/c-spectrum-data-files.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/rotate-keys.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingKMSEncryption.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingEncryptionInTransit.html

question:
A company runs MySQL on EC2 in us-east-1 and has a prepared application fleet in us-west-2. It wants a managed database design for Regional disaster recovery with a target RPO below 1 minute and target application RTO below 5 minutes. The company can migrate to a MySQL-compatible engine. The recovery procedure must make a secondary database writable and reconnect the application.

Which design provides the strongest fit for these objectives?

options.text: Migrate to RDS for MySQL and create a cross-Region read replica. During an outage, change application DNS to the replica endpoint without promoting the replica.

Migrate to Aurora MySQL Global Database with a provisioned secondary cluster in us-west-2. Monitor replication lag and automate a tested cross-Region failover procedure, application reconnection, and traffic redirection.
Migrate to an RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB instance in us-east-1 and rely on its standby for a complete us-east-1 outage.
Copy daily database snapshots to us-west-2. During an outage, restore the newest snapshot and manually reconfigure the application.

explanation.text:
<<2>> maintains a cross-Region database through Aurora Global Database storage-level replication and includes the steps needed to resume writes. AWS describes typical unplanned-failover RPO in seconds and recovery time in minutes, making this a strong design candidate. Validate the complete application recovery time, including detection, failover, connections and traffic switching, against the stated targets.

<<1>> leaves the RDS replica read-only; DNS alone does not promote it. A properly promoted and tested RDS replica can support other DR designs, but this procedure is incomplete. <<3>> provides AZ resilience inside one Region, not a secondary Region. <<4>> can lose up to the snapshot interval of changes and adds restore and manual reconfiguration time.

Cross-Region replication is asynchronous. Actual data loss depends on lag at failure, and neither a service name nor a nominal failover duration guarantees the application’s RPO or RTO.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/aurora-global-database-disaster-recovery.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/AuroraMySQL.Replication.CrossRegion.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReadRepl.html

question:
A company runs stateless web and application tiers on EC2 and stores 40 TB in Aurora MySQL. Its cross-Region disaster recovery objectives are an RPO of 5 minutes and an RTO of 30 minutes. Tests show that copied AMIs and infrastructure templates can rebuild both stateless tiers in 10 minutes. Tests also show that an Aurora MySQL cross-Region read replica stays within the required lag and that promotion plus application reconnection keeps total recovery below 30 minutes. The company wants to minimize steady-state DR compute cost.

Which actions should it combine? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Copy the approved AMIs and deployment artifacts to the recovery Region for every release, and keep the infrastructure templates ready. Launch the stateless web and application tiers when recovery is required.
Keep a full production-sized copy of both EC2 application tiers running continuously in the recovery Region.
Replace database replication with a snapshot every 5 minutes and assume a 40 TB snapshot restore will always finish within the 30-minute RTO.
Maintain the tested Aurora MySQL cross-Region read replica. Monitor lag and automate promotion, application reconnection, and traffic switching through the validated recovery procedure.
Remove the database replica and rely on nightly AWS Backup recovery points copied to a vault in the recovery Region.

explanation.text:
<<1>> avoids continuously running recoverable stateless capacity, using the measured 10-minute rebuild time. <<4>> keeps the large stateful database close to current and uses a recovery procedure already shown to meet the objectives. Together they minimize the proposed application-tier standby cost without replacing the tested database recovery path.

<<2>> increases steady-state cost even though the measured rebuild time fits the objective. <<3>> assumes an unverified restore duration and that a snapshot schedule alone establishes both RPO and RTO. <<5>> introduces a nightly recovery-point interval that cannot meet a 5-minute RPO.

The 30-minute outcome is workload-specific evidence, not a universal restore or promotion guarantee. Aurora MySQL cross-Region read replicas use binary-log replication, unlike Aurora Global Database storage replication. Keep measuring lag and rehearsing the entire recovery path as the workload grows.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/AuroraMySQL.Replication.CrossRegion.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/aurora-global-database-disaster-recovery.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/CopyingAMIs.html

question:
A company runs a CRM application on RDS for MySQL. Scheduled reporting queries cause latency spikes on the transactional primary. The reports tolerate short replication delays and produce small status summaries for an external operations system. That system accepts standard Amazon SNS email notifications and can confirm the subscription. The company wants minimal changes to its transactional data model.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Run the reporting queries against RDS read replicas. Publish each status summary to an SNS standard topic with a confirmed email subscription for the operations system.
Move the transactional CRM database to Redshift, run reports through Spectrum, and publish each summary to an SNS email subscription.
Move the transactional CRM database to Redshift and send each summary to an SQS queue with the operations system’s email address as the queue consumer.
Run the reporting queries against RDS read replicas and configure an SQS queue to deliver the summaries directly to the operations system’s email address.

explanation.text:
<<1>> offloads lag-tolerant reporting from the RDS primary and uses SNS’s supported email subscription protocol. The subscription must be confirmed before delivery. This is suitable for the small operational notifications explicitly accepted by the receiving system.

<<2>> changes the transactional database architecture unnecessarily; Redshift is an analytical warehouse, and Spectrum queries external S3 data rather than serving as a drop-in CRM engine. <<3>> adds that migration and assumes SQS can deliver directly to an email address. <<4>> chooses the correct read-scaling mechanism but still lacks an email-delivery consumer for SQS.

Read replicas are asynchronous, so reports must tolerate lag and use the replica endpoint. SNS email is not a general-purpose customized email or attachment service; the scenario’s receiving system and message format must support its notification behavior.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReadRepl.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sns-email-notifications.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/redshift/latest/dg/c-spectrum-data-files.html

question:
A promotions service writes customer submissions to RDS for PostgreSQL. Short, unpredictable bursts overwhelm the database. Each submission must eventually be committed without duplicate business effects, but the API may return an acceptance receipt before the database transaction completes. The company must preserve its relational data model and limit database write concurrency.

Which architecture best meets these requirements?

options.text: Increase the database instance size before expected promotions and continue writing synchronously from every incoming request.

Persist accepted submissions in SQS and process them with a Lambda event source mapping. Bound consumer concurrency, use idempotent database transactions, and configure retries, failure monitoring and dead-letter recovery.
Replace the PostgreSQL schema with DynamoDB tables and modify all transactional access patterns to use DynamoDB.
Buffer accepted submissions only in ElastiCache for Memcached and write them to PostgreSQL when the traffic burst ends.

explanation.text:
<<2>> decouples acceptance rate from database commit rate. A durable queue absorbs a temporary burst while bounded consumers drain work at a rate the database can support. Idempotency prevents repeated deliveries from duplicating business effects. Acknowledge successful processing only after the database transaction commits, and recover failed messages before retention expires.

<<1>> requires predicting the burst and provides no durable buffer if capacity is exceeded. <<3>> violates the requirement to preserve the relational model. <<4>> uses an evictable cache as the only record of accepted work and therefore risks losing submissions.

SQS and Lambda event source mappings can deliver a message more than once. A crash after database commit but before acknowledgment must therefore be safe to retry. An acceptance receipt means durable intake, not that the business transaction has already committed; expose processing status separately when needed.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/with-sqs.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/standard-queues.html

question:
A company processes independent image jobs on one EC2 instance. Images and results are stored on its EBS volume, and a daily run now takes 20 hours. Arrival rates vary sharply, and the company wants more workers during backlogs and fewer workers when demand falls. Jobs can be retried safely after a worker failure.

Which design provides the most effective elastic processing?

options.text: Keep the images on the existing EBS volume, publish job notifications to SNS, and scale worker instances from the number of SNS notifications sent.

Store source images and results in S3. Place image object keys in SQS and use an Auto Scaling group of workers to process the queue. Scale from backlog per in-service worker, with a target based on acceptable queue delay and average processing time.
Keep the images on the existing EBS volume and publish jobs only to SNS. Scale worker instances from an SQS queue metric without routing jobs to a queue.
Store source images and results in S3 and send jobs to SQS, but scale worker instances only from the count of SNS notifications sent.

explanation.text:
<<2>> separates shared durable objects from the workers and uses SQS to track unfinished work. A backlog-per-worker metric relates pending work to processing capacity. For target tracking, a useful target is acceptable queue delay divided by average processing time per job. Workers use the queued object key to read and write S3 data.

<<1>> retains a storage dependency on the original instance and measures notifications rather than pending work. <<3>> adds no queue that corresponds to its proposed scaling metric. <<4>> has a suitable data and work path but scales from an unrelated metric that cannot show the remaining backlog.

Choose visibility timeouts for actual processing duration, make output writes idempotent, and manage repeated failures through a dead-letter and redrive process. Use instance scale-in protection or safe shutdown behavior for active jobs. Local EBS can still serve as scratch space; shared authoritative inputs and outputs belong in S3.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-using-sqs-queue.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/standard-queues.html

question:
A company deploys a web application to an EC2 Auto Scaling group through AWS CodePipeline. AWS CloudFormation manages the infrastructure, and instance user data downloads application artifacts from Amazon S3. A recent template update replaced instances before the new application was ready, causing an outage.

The company wants automated validation before production changes, visibility into resource replacements, and a quick way to return application traffic to the previous release. Which deployment approach best meets these requirements?

options.text: Add cfn-init and cfn-signal to instance user data. Have a tester inspect the application after each in-place production stack update.

Run automated tests in CodeBuild against a nonproduction environment. Review a CloudFormation change set, then use a CodeDeploy blue/green deployment with health validation and rollback alarms before retiring the previous environment.
Validate the template syntax in the developer IDE and with the CloudFormation CLI. Continue replacing the production Auto Scaling group directly after validation succeeds.
Use CodeDeploy blue/green deployment to switch production traffic immediately after installation. Run the functional tests after the previous environment has been terminated.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. Automated tests exercise the release before production, a change set exposes infrastructure changes such as replacement, and a blue/green deployment keeps a known release available while the replacement is validated. Health checks and rollback alarms provide a controlled traffic cutover. Infrastructure changes must also remain compatible with both application releases.

<<1>> improves bootstrap coordination only when the signals are wired to the relevant CloudFormation policies. It does not provide the required preproduction application tests or a separate rollback environment.

<<3>> checks template validity but does not prove that the application starts correctly or that replacing production instances is safe. Even a valid change set can fail during execution.

<<4>> uses a suitable deployment mechanism but places the test gate too late and discards the previous environment before validation.

Traffic rollback does not automatically undo destructive database migrations or every infrastructure update. Design those changes for backward compatibility and recovery.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [CloudFormation change sets](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/using-cfn-updating-stacks-changesets.html); [CodeDeploy EC2 blue/green deployments](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/deployment-steps-server.html).

question:
A company serves https://www.example.com through Amazon CloudFront. The distribution uses an Application Load Balancer in eu-west-1 as its custom origin. The company requires trusted TLS for both the viewer connection and the connection from CloudFront to the ALB, and wants HTTP viewer requests redirected to HTTPS.

Which configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Install trusted third-party certificates on CloudFront and the ALB. Redirect viewers to HTTPS, and configure the CloudFront origin protocol policy as HTTP Only.
Request ACM certificates for both CloudFront and the ALB in eu-west-1. Redirect viewers to HTTPS, and configure the origin protocol policy as HTTPS Only.

Request the viewer ACM certificate in us-east-1 and an ALB ACM certificate in eu-west-1, with names matching the respective TLS hostnames. Configure the ALB HTTPS listener, redirect viewers to HTTPS, and use HTTPS Only for the origin.
Use the default CloudFront certificate for www.example.com and an ACM certificate on the ALB. Redirect viewers to HTTPS, and configure the origin protocol policy as HTTPS Only.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. There are two independent TLS connections. CloudFront uses an ACM viewer certificate from us-east-1 for the custom viewer hostname. The ALB uses a certificate in its own Region. The origin certificate must match the hostname CloudFront uses for TLS validation, and the origin protocol policy must require HTTPS.

<<1>> can use valid third-party certificates, but HTTP Only leaves the CloudFront-to-origin connection unencrypted.

<<2>> places the viewer ACM certificate in the wrong Region. The ALB certificate belongs in eu-west-1, but the CloudFront viewer certificate belongs in us-east-1.

<<4>> does not provide a certificate for the custom viewer hostname. The default CloudFront certificate covers the distribution's cloudfront.net hostname.

A secure viewer connection alone does not establish secure transport to the origin.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [CloudFront HTTPS certificate requirements](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/cnames-and-https-requirements.html).

question:
A stateless application runs on identical EC2 instances distributed evenly across three Availability Zones. During scheduled sales events, average CPU utilization reaches 90%. Load tests show that CPU demand is proportional to traffic and that the remaining instances must stay at or below 90% CPU after an Availability Zone fails. New instances take several minutes to become ready.

Which capacity strategy meets the failure requirement while avoiding year-round provisioning for the largest sales event?

options.text: Use scheduled scaling to make sufficient capacity healthy before each event. Size the three-AZ fleet for at most 60% CPU at the forecast peak, and use target tracking and suitable capacity limits as demand changes.
Keep the fleet at 90% CPU during each event. Increase the Auto Scaling maximum so that replacement instances can be launched after an Availability Zone fails.
Keep the fleet sized for 60% CPU at the largest annual event throughout the year. Disable scale-in to ensure that this capacity remains available.
Use scheduled scaling to make sufficient capacity healthy for 75% CPU at the forecast peak. Rely on equal distribution across three Availability Zones for failure headroom.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. Losing one of three equally sized AZs leaves two-thirds of the capacity. At unchanged demand, utilization increases by a factor of 3/2: 60% becomes 90%. Scheduling capacity ahead of the event accommodates launch and warmup time, while scaling back afterward avoids carrying the annual peak all year. Real deployments should include additional margin for forecast error and imperfect balancing.

<<2>> allows future recovery but lacks capacity during the replacement interval. A fleet already at 90% would require 135% of the surviving capacity immediately after the failure.

<<3>> meets the failure-headroom requirement, but retaining peak-event capacity all year violates the cost objective.

<<4>> leaves insufficient headroom: 75% becomes 112.5% after one AZ is lost.

An Auto Scaling maximum is permission to grow, not preexisting healthy capacity.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Auto Scaling target tracking](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-scaling-target-tracking.html); [Scheduled scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/ec2-auto-scaling-scheduled-scaling.html).

question:
A mobile application uploads each user's photos to Amazon S3 and stores captions in Amazon DynamoDB. Users already authenticate with an OpenID Connect identity provider. The company is removing a custom API tier and wants the mobile application to call AWS APIs directly. It will configure IAM trust and permissions for the existing identity provider, and must not embed long-term AWS credentials in the application.

Which authentication flow meets these requirements?

options.text: Exchange the identity provider token with AWS STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. Use the returned access key ID, secret access key, and session token to sign requests with permissions scoped to the authenticated user.
Embed an IAM user's access key in the application. Use that key to call STS AssumeRole and obtain temporary credentials for each signed-in user.
Submit the OpenID Connect identity token to STS AssumeRoleWithSAML. Use the returned credentials for the user's S3 objects and DynamoDB items.
Exchange the identity provider token with STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. Sign AWS requests with the returned access key ID and secret access key, and discard the session token.
Create an Amazon Cognito user pool and use its ID token directly as the AWS credential for S3 and DynamoDB API requests, without a credential exchange.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity accepts a token from a trusted, configured identity provider without requiring an AWS access key in the client. STS returns temporary credentials, including the session token, for the role session. The trust policy and permissions must enforce the intended identity and user-specific access boundary.

<<2>> obtains temporary role credentials but exposes a reusable IAM user credential in every application installation, violating the stated constraint.

<<3>> uses the wrong federation protocol. AssumeRoleWithSAML expects a SAML assertion, not an OIDC identity token.

<<4>> omits a required part of the temporary credential set. A temporary access key pair must be accompanied by its session token.

<<5>> confuses authentication tokens with AWS signing credentials. Cognito identity pools can exchange supported identity tokens for temporary AWS credentials, but a user pool token alone is not an S3 or DynamoDB signing credential.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/STS/latest/APIReference/API_AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity.html).

question:
An application writes records to a provisioned-capacity DynamoDB table. Short traffic bursts cause throttling, although average write demand is below the table's provisioned capacity and the keys are well distributed. Records can be committed asynchronously within several minutes. The company wants to accept every record durably without permanently provisioning for the burst peak.

Which solution best meets these requirements?

options.text: Convert the table to a DynamoDB global table and continue sending all writes to the existing Region.
Increase provisioned write capacity to the maximum burst rate and keep that setting throughout the day.
Distribute incoming records across multiple manually sharded tables, each provisioned for its share of peak traffic, and update application queries to combine the shards.
Accept records into an Amazon SQS queue. Use workers with controlled concurrency and retry backoff to write to DynamoDB, deleting each message only after its write succeeds.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. A durable queue separates the arrival rate from the commit rate. Workers can drain a short backlog at a rate the table can sustain, so capacity need not match a brief ingestion peak. Standard SQS delivery can repeat messages, so writes must be idempotent. Monitor backlog age, configure retention and failed-message handling, and keep average processing capacity above average arrivals.

<<1>> adds regional replicas and replication work. It does not split the write demand sent to the existing Region across independent regional write quotas.

<<2>> avoids throttling but pays for unused peak capacity between bursts.

<<3>> adds routing and query complexity and still provisions each shard for its peak. The scenario has no hot-key problem that requires a new partitioning design.

Buffering changes when writes occur, not the total write work. It cannot indefinitely compensate for sustained demand above the database's processing capacity.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [SQS standard queues](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/standard-queues.html).

question:
A company must encrypt objects in an S3 bucket with SSE-KMS. Its security policy requires the KMS key material to be generated in the company's existing on-premises HSM. The policy permits securely importing a copy into AWS KMS, and routine S3 reads and writes must not depend on connectivity to the on-premises HSM.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an AWS CloudHSM cluster and generate a new KMS key in a CloudHSM custom key store. Configure the bucket to use that key.
Create a KMS external key store connected to the on-premises key manager. Keep the key material exclusively on premises and use that key for SSE-KMS.
Create a symmetric KMS key with EXTERNAL origin, obtain its import parameters, wrap the on-premises-generated key material as required, and import it. Configure S3 to use that KMS key ARN.
Create a symmetric KMS key with AWS_KMS origin. Replace its AWS-generated material with the on-premises-generated material, and configure S3 to use its key ARN.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. Importing key material preserves its external generation provenance while allowing KMS to perform cryptographic operations using the imported copy. S3 can use the resulting customer managed key for SSE-KMS without contacting the original HSM during every request.

<<1>> generates new material in a different HSM environment and therefore fails the required origin of the material.

<<2>> retains an operational dependency on the external key manager and its connectivity, which the scenario explicitly excludes.

<<4>> uses the wrong immutable key origin. The import workflow requires a KMS key created for externally supplied material, not replacement of material in an AWS_KMS-origin key.

Protect a recoverable copy of imported material and manage its expiration. If required imported material is deleted or expires, the key becomes unusable until the appropriate material is restored. Automatic rotation is not supported for EXTERNAL keys, although current KMS supports on-demand rotation for symmetric keys with imported material.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Importing KMS key material](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/importing-keys.html); [S3 SSE-KMS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingKMSEncryption.html); [KMS key rotation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/rotate-keys.html); [KMS external key stores](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/keystore-external.html).

question:
A company uses AWS Organizations for its workload accounts. Finance requires CostCenter and ProjectID tags on existing and future RDS DB instances and DynamoDB tables, and needs costs grouped by those tags. Teams create resources through CloudFormation or approved API calls that support tags on creation. Workload administrators must be unable to create an untagged resource or remove either required tag.

Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Use Tag Editor to tag existing resources and activate both cost allocation tag keys in the management account. Ask teams to include the tags in new templates.
Activate both cost allocation tag keys and use an hourly AWS Config remediation workflow to apply missing tags after resources have been created.

Tag existing resources and activate both cost allocation tag keys. Require tags in CloudFormation and apply scoped SCP denies for supported creation requests missing either required tag and for removal of the required tags.
Attach a required-tag policy to the federated developer role and activate both cost allocation tag keys. Leave other workload roles and existing resources unchanged.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. Three separate controls are needed: repair existing resources, prevent future violations, and activate the keys for cost reporting. The SCPs must be scoped to supported service actions and tested against the actual creation and tagging APIs. A separate deny for each missing request tag ensures that absence of either tag is rejected. Empty or invalid values also need an explicit policy if prohibited. Resource creation still requires normal IAM permissions, including required tagging permissions.

<<1>> performs cleanup and billing setup but relies on a convention for future resources.

<<2>> is detective and corrective. An hourly repair window does not meet the requirement to prevent untagged creation, and automation may not know the correct business values.

<<4>> restricts only one role and leaves existing resources and other creation paths uncovered.

Activating a cost allocation key does not add tags to resources. SCPs limit affected member-account principals rather than granting access, and service support for request-tag conditions must be verified for each covered action.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Activate cost allocation tags](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awsaccountbilling/latest/aboutv2/activating-tags.html); [RDS tags on creation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/security_iam_id-based-policy-examples-grant-permissions-tags-on-create.html); [DynamoDB request-tag conditions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/us_en/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/abac-example-use-cases.html); [SCP evaluation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps_evaluation.html).

question:
A development organization maintains an approved list of AMI IDs. Its automated build pipeline must remain able to launch EC2 test instances without manual approval or a new launch-time authorization restriction. Security accepts a short detection window but requires unapproved instances to be terminated automatically and the security team notified. The approved list is maintained centrally.

Which TWO designs can independently provide the required post-launch control? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add a manual approval action to the deployment pipeline before each EC2 launch and notify security when approval is rejected.

Enable AWS Config recording and the approved-amis-by-id rule with the approved AMI list. Route noncompliance events through EventBridge to a Lambda function that rechecks the current AMI, terminates unapproved instances, and publishes an SNS notification.

Use EventBridge Scheduler to invoke a Lambda function frequently. Have the function inventory running instances, compare their AMI IDs with the approved list, terminate unapproved instances, and publish an SNS notification.
Apply an IAM deny to RunInstances for AMIs outside the approved list, and publish an SNS notification when a launch is denied.
Enable the approved-amis-by-id AWS Config rule and send its noncompliance events to an SNS topic for the security team to investigate manually.

explanation.text:
<<2>> and <<3>> are correct. Both evaluate instances after launch, compare their AMI IDs with the centrally maintained allowlist, perform automated remediation, and notify security. The Config managed rule evaluates running instances on configuration changes. A scheduled inventory implements the same control through polling. Update the rule parameters or polling configuration when the approved list changes, and make termination logic idempotent and resistant to stale events.

<<1>> introduces the manual launch gate that the pipeline cannot accept.

<<4>> is a valid preventive pattern when properly scoped, but it introduces the launch-time restriction excluded by the scenario.

<<5>> detects and reports violations but leaves remediation manual.

Post-launch controls permit a detection and remediation window. If the requirement were that an unapproved AMI must never run, neither selected design would satisfy it by itself.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Approved AMIs Config rule](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/approved-amis-by-id.html).

question:
A news application runs its web tier on AWS but must retain its on-premises database for the next six months. Readers repeatedly request the same articles, which change infrequently. Tracing shows that repeated database round trips across the hybrid connection dominate response time. Users also submit comments that must continue to be stored in the database.

Which change most directly reduces read latency with the least application redesign?

options.text: Migrate the database to Amazon Aurora and redirect all application reads and comment writes to the new database.
Copy the articles and comments into Amazon OpenSearch Service and redesign the application to use it as the authoritative store.

Add an ElastiCache for Redis OSS cache with a cross-AZ replica and Multi-AZ automatic failover near the web tier. Use cache-aside reads for article content, with expiration and invalidation when content changes, while retaining the on-premises database as the source of record.
Add CloudFront caching for the site's images, style sheets, and JavaScript files while leaving article reads unchanged.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. A cache hit returns article content close to the AWS web tier and avoids the slow on-premises read. On a miss, the application retrieves the article from the database and fills the cache. Expiration and invalidation limit stale content, while authoritative comment writes continue to reach the database. Cross-AZ replicas with Multi-AZ automatic failover reduce cache downtime. Cache loss must still be recoverable from the source of record.

<<1>> could remove the hybrid database round trip but violates the six-month database-location constraint.

<<2>> changes the authoritative storage model and query/write paths instead of adding a focused read cache.

<<4>> improves static asset delivery but leaves the measured article-read bottleneck unchanged.

Choose cache keys, freshness rules, and failure behavior deliberately. Caching is effective when repeated reads and an acceptable freshness policy justify reusing prior results.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Cache-aside and expiration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonElastiCache/latest/dg/Strategies.html); [ElastiCache replication and failover](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonElastiCache/latest/dg/Replication.Redis.Groups.html).

question:
A Lambda function processes records from DynamoDB Streams and calls downstream AWS services. The team wants each new release to receive approximately 10% of invocations for five minutes, then receive the remaining traffic if alarms remain healthy. The team also needs sampled execution traces with downstream call timing and enough correlation data to identify the source stream.

Which implementation meets these requirements?

options.text: Publish function versions and use CodeDeployDefault.LambdaAllAtOnce on an alias targeted by the event source mapping. Enable active tracing and record the source stream ARN.

Publish function versions and point the event source mapping to a deployment alias. Use CodeDeployDefault.LambdaCanary10Percent5Minutes with rollback alarms, enable active tracing, instrument downstream calls, and record source-stream correlation data.
Publish function versions and point the event source mapping to an alias. Use CodeDeployDefault.LambdaLinear10PercentEvery1Minute, enable active tracing, and record the source stream ARN.

Publish function versions and configure an alias with CodeDeployDefault.LambdaCanary10Percent5Minutes. Keep the event source mapping pinned to the original version, and enable active tracing and downstream instrumentation.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. CodeDeploy changes the alias weights from an initial 10% allocation to the new version to 100% after five minutes, subject to deployment success and configured rollback behavior. The event source mapping must invoke that alias for the routing change to affect stream processing. Active tracing and downstream instrumentation provide sampled timing data, while source ARN and record identifiers support correlation.

<<1>> shifts all traffic immediately, eliminating the required observation interval.

<<3>> uses a linear rollout, adding 10 percentage points each minute instead of holding at 10% for five minutes and then shifting the rest.

<<4>> updates an alias that the event source mapping does not invoke, so it leaves the stream workload on the original version.

Alias routing is probabilistic per invocation. For a batched stream consumer, it does not promise exactly 10% of individual records. Tracing also does not automatically provide an unsampled, continuous trace back through every DynamoDB writer.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [CodeDeploy deployment configurations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/deployment-configurations.html); [Lambda weighted aliases](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuring-alias-routing.html); [Lambda with X-Ray](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/services-xray.html).

question:
A company stores confidential documents in an S3 bucket used only by authorized applications and employees. The bucket has legacy ACLs, and a recent policy change accidentally exposed some objects publicly. The company needs a managed preventive control against public access through both ACLs and bucket policies, with minimal custom automation.

Which solution best meets these requirements?

options.text: Require the private canned ACL on every PutObject request, and leave bucket-policy and ACL modification permissions unchanged.
Enable AWS Config rules for public S3 access and notify the security team whenever the bucket becomes noncompliant.
Apply an SCP that denies PutObjectAcl when a public canned ACL is requested, and leave bucket-policy changes unrestricted.
Enable all four S3 Block Public Access settings for the bucket and restrict who can change them. Apply an account-level baseline where compatible with the other buckets.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. The four settings cover both new public grants and access derived from existing public ACLs or policies. BlockPublicAcls rejects public ACL operations, IgnorePublicAcls ignores public ACL grants, BlockPublicPolicy rejects public policies, and RestrictPublicBuckets restricts access when a resource policy is public. Protecting the settings prevents workload users from removing the control.

<<1>> constrains an upload path but leaves later ACL changes and public bucket policies uncovered.

<<2>> detects an exposure after it occurs and depends on a response. It does not provide the requested preventive control.

<<3>> covers one ACL modification operation, not public bucket policies or every public ACL creation path.

Block Public Access does not rewrite existing ACLs or policies, so audit and repair them as well. It also does not replace least-privilege authorization for named IAM principals or control every way an authorized user might share data.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [S3 Block Public Access](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/access-control-block-public-access.html).

question:
A company has a desktop application that makes many synchronous HTTP calls to application servers backed by MySQL. Remote users experience high latency. The company wants to migrate the system to AWS, retain the existing desktop application with minimal changes, and keep its application and database tiers available after an Availability Zone failure. Users need access to this application, not a managed personal desktop.

Which architecture best meets these requirements?

options.text: Keep the desktop application on users' computers. Put CloudFront in front of the uncacheable HTTP API, run the servers across two AZs, and use Aurora MySQL with a reader in another AZ.
Rewrite the desktop application as a browser application. Replace the server and database tiers with Lambda and DynamoDB.

Run the desktop application through Amazon WorkSpaces Applications (formerly AppStream 2.0) near an ALB and an EC2 Auto Scaling group spanning AZs. Use Aurora MySQL with a writer and at least one reader in another AZ.
Provide each user with a WorkSpaces Personal desktop. Run the application servers in one AZ and retain MySQL on a single EC2 instance in that AZ.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. Application streaming moves the chatty client-to-server interactions into AWS while users receive the application display and send input over the remote connection. WorkSpaces Applications supports existing desktop applications without requiring a browser rewrite. Multi-AZ application servers and an Aurora reader outside the writer's AZ provide recovery capacity for the backend tiers.

<<1>> improves backend availability but leaves the chatty desktop client remote. The specified uncacheable API still requires repeated WAN round trips, and CloudFront caching cannot remove them.

<<2>> can produce a different cloud architecture but requires a substantial client and data-model rewrite, violating the migration constraint.

<<4>> hosts full desktops that users do not need and, decisively, retains single-AZ application and database failure points.

Aurora's replicated storage and its DB instance placement are separate considerations. Include a reader in another AZ for an existing compute failover target rather than assuming that a writer-only cluster provides the same recovery behavior.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Amazon WorkSpaces Applications](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/appstream2/latest/developerguide/what-is-appstream.html); [Aurora high availability](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/Concepts.AuroraHighAvailability.html).

question:
EC2 instances in private subnets call an external service through a NAT gateway. The application reuses TCP connections that can remain idle for several minutes. Logs show that an idle connection is reset when it is reused after more than 350 seconds. NAT gateway metrics show no port-allocation errors or packet-rate exhaustion.

Which change most directly addresses the cause?

options.text: Enable TCP keepalive so the first probe occurs before 350 seconds of inactivity and subsequent probes maintain the connection. Also handle resets with connection reestablishment and appropriate retries.
Change the NAT gateway idle timeout from 350 seconds to 30 minutes so idle connections remain in its connection table.
Add more NAT gateways and distribute outbound traffic across them without changing the application's connection behavior.
Replace the NAT gateway route with a direct route to an internet gateway while leaving the instances with private IPv4 addresses only.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. A NAT gateway expires a connection that is idle for 350 seconds. When the client subsequently sends traffic on that connection, the gateway returns a TCP reset. Timely TCP keepalive traffic prevents that idle interval. The application should still tolerate broken connections and retry only operations that can safely be retried.

<<2>> assumes a configurable timeout that the NAT gateway does not expose.

<<3>> can help other scaling or port-allocation problems, but every new gateway has the same idle-connection behavior. The metrics exclude the relevant capacity symptoms here.

<<4>> removes the required IPv4 source translation. A private-only instance cannot obtain direct internet connectivity merely by adding an internet gateway route.

Match the remedy to the observed failure mode: connection lifetime and gateway capacity are different causes.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [NAT gateway troubleshooting](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/nat-gateway-troubleshooting.html).

question:
A flight-information website serves users worldwide from one AWS Region. Static assets are in S3, the web tier uses an EC2 Auto Scaling group, and flight data is stored in Amazon RDS. The scale-out threshold is 90% CPU, and a new flight-data version is published every 10 minutes. The application may reuse results within a version but must show the new version after publication.

Page loads average 7 seconds. Measurements attribute most delay to distant static-asset downloads and repeated identical database queries, while web-tier CPU remains low. The company wants to move toward a 3-second page-load target with limited additional cost. Which TWO changes most directly address the measured delays? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Cache repeated database-query results in ElastiCache. Include the flight-data version in cache keys or invalidate entries when a new version is published.
Lower the web-tier CPU target so that the Auto Scaling group adds more EC2 instances even though the existing instances have spare CPU.
Use CloudFront to cache and deliver versioned static assets from S3 at edge locations near users.
Deploy a complete application and database stack in every Region where the company has users, and operate global replication and traffic routing.
Move RDS to a larger instance class while continuing to execute every identical flight-data query for every request.

explanation.text:
<<1>> and <<3>> are correct. Reusing query results removes repeated database work, while version-aware keys or invalidation preserve the publication boundary. CloudFront addresses the separate delay caused by distant static-content delivery. These focused changes target the two measured bottlenecks without multiplying the entire stack.

<<2>> adds web compute to a tier that is not CPU constrained, leaving the costly downloads and repeated queries largely unchanged.

<<4>> could reduce distance to regional backends but introduces substantially more infrastructure, replication, and operational cost than the targeted optimizations.

<<5>> may improve individual database operations, but continues doing redundant work and does not address static-asset distance. The measurements support caching before a broad capacity upgrade.

A cache TTL alone can allow an old result to survive a data publication. Align invalidation or cache versioning with the actual freshness requirement, then measure end-to-end page loads to verify the target rather than assuming a guaranteed latency.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Cache-aside and expiration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonElastiCache/latest/dg/Strategies.html); [CloudFront content delivery](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/Introduction.html).

question:
A public web application runs behind an ALB and serves static objects from S3. It is experiencing SQL injection attempts, HTTP floods, and abusive bots. The company wants managed request filtering, enhanced DDoS protection for its public entry points, and controls that prevent users from bypassing those entry points to reach the origins directly.

Which solution best meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy the application in a second Region and use Route 53 failover routing. Keep the existing public ALB and S3 access paths without request inspection.
Add network ACL rules that deny the source IP addresses observed in recent attacks. Keep S3 publicly readable so legitimate users can bypass blocked paths.

Place CloudFront in front of the ALB and a private S3 origin. Apply WAF SQL injection, rate-based, and appropriate bot rules, enroll eligible public resources in Shield Advanced, use S3 origin access control, and restrict ALB access to the intended CloudFront path.
Place CloudFront in front of both origins and restrict origin access. Enroll the public resources in Shield Advanced, but omit WAF request-inspection rules for SQL injection and bots.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. WAF can inspect HTTP request contents and rates at CloudFront or an ALB. SQL injection rules address payload patterns, and rate-based and bot controls address abusive request behavior. Shield Advanced adds DDoS protections for enrolled eligible resources. CloudFront origin access control and an appropriately restricted S3 bucket policy prevent public S3 bypass, while the ALB needs its own origin-access restriction.

<<1>> adds recovery capacity but does not filter the attack traffic or close direct-origin paths.

<<2>> relies on a changing IP list and network-layer matching rather than inspecting application requests. It also deliberately retains a bypass path.

<<4>> addresses origin bypass and DDoS protection but omits the requested application-specific SQL injection and bot filtering. DDoS protection alone is not an application input-validation policy.

Test and tune WAF rules against legitimate traffic, retain application-side validation, and protect every reachable origin. WAF does not attach directly to an S3 bucket.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [AWS WAF protected resources](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/waf-chapter.html); [WAF SQL injection matching](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/waf-rule-statement-type-sqli-match.html); [WAF rate limiting and Bot Control](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/waf-rate-limiting-options.html); [Shield Advanced overview](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/ddos-advanced-summary.html); [CloudFront origin access control](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.html).

question:
A company operates an internet-facing application in two AWS Regions. Each Region has an ALB, an Auto Scaling group, and a local ElastiCache cache. Persistent data is available in either Region, caches can be rebuilt, and either application stack can handle the full workload. The company wants new DNS responses to prefer a low-latency healthy Region and to avoid an ALB whose application targets are unhealthy.

Which Route 53 configuration best meets these requirements?

options.text: Create latency-based alias records for the regional ALBs in the public hosted zone and set EvaluateTargetHealth to true. Configure the ALB target health checks to reflect application readiness.
Create latency-based alias records for the regional ALBs only in a private hosted zone associated with the application VPCs, and remove the public application records.
Create latency-based alias records in the public hosted zone with EvaluateTargetHealth set to false. Enable DNSSEC signing to detect an unhealthy regional application.
Create equally weighted alias records in the public hosted zone with EvaluateTargetHealth set to true, so both Regions receive the same configured traffic weight.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. Latency-based routing selects a regional endpoint using Route 53 latency measurements, and evaluated alias target health excludes an unhealthy ALB while a healthy alternative is available. Meaningful ALB target checks are necessary because routing can only respond to the health signal it receives.

<<2>> makes the records available through the associated private DNS context instead of publishing the required internet-facing name.

<<3>> disables the health evaluation needed for this design. DNSSEC authenticates DNS data; it does not monitor application availability.

<<4>> provides health-aware distribution but selects by configured weights rather than the required latency preference.

DNS failover affects answers to subsequent queries. Existing connections and cached answers may continue to use the previous endpoint until clients reconnect or caches expire. Routing also cannot repair missing data or insufficient capacity in the surviving Region; those prerequisites are explicit in this scenario.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Route 53 latency routing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/routing-policy-latency.html); [Route 53 alias target health](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/APIReference/API_AliasTarget.html); [Route 53 healthy record selection](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/health-checks-how-route-53-chooses-records.html).

question:
A security team must identify S3 objects containing personally identifiable information and determine which identities retrieved those objects during the previous month. The objects have not changed during the audit period, use supported text and document formats, and can be read and decrypted by the team. An organization trail has already retained S3 GetObject data events for all relevant buckets throughout the audit period.

Which approach best meets these requirements?

options.text: Use Athena to search the S3 object-key inventory for names associated with PII, and use CloudWatch request-count metrics to identify the users who downloaded matching objects.

Run Amazon Macie sensitive-data discovery jobs with suitable managed and custom identifiers over the relevant objects. Correlate the identified bucket and object keys with retained CloudTrail GetObject data events to investigate access identities and times.
Use GuardDuty threat findings to classify all PII in the objects, and use the findings as a complete record of every object retrieval.
Run Amazon Macie sensitive-data discovery jobs, and use only CloudTrail management-event history to find each GetObject request.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. Macie discovers sensitive content in eligible S3 objects, while CloudTrail data events provide the object-level API audit evidence. Correlating bucket and key information joins the content finding to recorded retrievals, including the request identity and time. Review discovery coverage and failed analyses rather than assuming every object was successfully inspected.

<<1>> infers content from filenames, which cannot establish whether an object contains PII. Aggregate request metrics do not supply a per-request identity history.

<<3>> treats threat detection as both content classification and a complete audit ledger. GuardDuty findings do not replace either Macie discovery or retained object-level events.

<<4>> selects the wrong CloudTrail event category. GetObject is an S3 data event, not a management event available through standard management-event history.

Enabling data-event logging today cannot reconstruct last month's unrecorded requests. The retained logging prerequisite is therefore essential. Discovery is also subject to Macie's supported formats, storage classes, object coverage, and analysis limits.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Macie discovery coverage](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/macie/latest/user/discovery-supported-storage.html); [CloudTrail data events](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/logging-data-events-with-cloudtrail.html).

question:
A company uses a provisioned Amazon Redshift cluster encrypted with AWS KMS. Its disaster recovery policy requires encrypted snapshot copies in a second AWS Region more than 500 miles away. The destination must use a customer managed KMS key, and the team will configure the workflow through the CLI. The recovery objective permits restoring a new cluster from the latest copied snapshot.

Which solution meets these requirements with the least ongoing operational effort?

options.text: Locate the Redshift-managed snapshot objects in an S3 bucket and enable S3 Cross-Region Replication to a bucket encrypted with the destination KMS key.

Create a snapshot copy grant in the destination Region for its customer managed KMS key. Enable Redshift cross-Region snapshot copy on the source cluster with that grant and configure snapshot retention.

Keep cross-Region snapshot copy disabled. Schedule a Lambda function to call CopyClusterSnapshot on each new automated snapshot, and retain the resulting manual snapshots as the disaster recovery copies.
Enable cross-Region snapshot copy and specify the destination customer managed KMS key, but omit the destination snapshot copy grant because the source cluster is already encrypted.

explanation.text:
