<<2>> is correct. Redshift's managed cross-Region snapshot-copy feature continuously handles eligible snapshot copies after configuration. For a destination customer managed KMS key, the snapshot copy grant authorizes use of that key. The copied snapshot is encrypted in the destination Region and can be used to restore a new cluster.

<<1>> assumes that Redshift-managed snapshots are customer-controlled S3 objects to which an ordinary bucket replication rule can be attached. Use the Redshift snapshot-copy feature instead.

<<3>> preserves automated snapshots as manual snapshots in the same Region. CopyClusterSnapshot does not perform the required cross-Region copy, so those copies do not meet the geographic separation requirement.

<<4>> omits the grant required by the specified destination key choice. Source encryption does not grant permission to use a separate destination customer managed key.

Snapshot copying is a backup-and-restore DR strategy, not an already running failover cluster. Set retention, monitor copy completion, and test restore times against the recovery objectives. A snapshot copy grant is not required when the destination uses a Region-owned key, which is why this scenario explicitly specifies a customer managed key.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Redshift encrypted snapshot copies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/redshift/latest/mgmt/working-with-db-encryption.html); [Redshift cross-Region snapshot copy](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/redshift/latest/mgmt/cross-region-snapshot-copy.html). [CopyClusterSnapshot API](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/redshift/latest/APIReference/API_CopyClusterSnapshot.html).

question:
A startup is launching a React single-page application. The browser runs the application logic, users upload photos to S3, and captions are stored in DynamoDB. Users authenticate with an existing supported OIDC provider. The startup expects low initial usage and wants HTTPS delivery, direct user-scoped data access, and minimal server administration without embedding long-term AWS credentials.

Which architecture best meets these requirements?

options.text: Host the static application in S3 behind CloudFront. Operate a single EC2 credential broker that authenticates users and issues temporary AWS credentials for direct data access.

Host the static application in a private S3 bucket behind CloudFront using origin access control. Configure web identity federation to exchange OIDC tokens for temporary, user-scoped AWS credentials that the browser uses for S3 and DynamoDB.
Host the static application on an EC2 Auto Scaling group behind an ALB, and operate an EC2 credential-broker fleet that issues temporary AWS credentials after OIDC authentication.
Host the static application on an EC2 instance with an IAM role. Have the downloaded browser application use the instance role automatically for its direct S3 and DynamoDB requests.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. A React application that executes in the browser can be distributed as static files. CloudFront provides HTTPS delivery from the private S3 origin, and OAC authorizes origin reads. A configured web identity exchange supplies short-lived AWS credentials for the signed-in user, with IAM permissions restricting the user's object prefixes and database access.

<<1>> can issue temporary credentials, but introduces a server to operate and a single availability dependency for sign-in. The supported identity provider already permits a managed credential exchange.

<<3>> can be made resilient, but allocates server fleets to static hosting and credential brokering that the stated design does not require.

<<4>> confuses the web server's identity with the browser's identity. Downloading JavaScript from an EC2 instance does not give that JavaScript the instance role credentials.

Keep static delivery permissions separate from user-data permissions. The browser must obtain its own scoped credential session, refresh it on expiration, and sign data requests correctly. Configure the required S3 browser CORS behavior in addition to authorization.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [CloudFront origin access control](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.html); [AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/STS/latest/APIReference/API_AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity.html).

question:
An HPC application uses a controller and many EC2 worker instances. The workers are in one cluster placement group, but the controller is outside the group. All instances are in the same Availability Zone, use a supported EBS-backed instance type, and communicate by private IP address. The team has measured excessive latency between the controller and workers.

The controller can be stopped briefly, but the workers must remain running. Which action most directly improves network locality while meeting this constraint?

options.text: Stop the controller, change its placement to the workers' existing cluster placement group, and restart it when capacity is available.
Stop all workers and the controller, create a new cluster placement group, and restart every instance in the new group.
Associate an Elastic IP address with the controller and switch controller-to-worker traffic from private addresses to public addresses.
Move the controller into a spread placement group while leaving the workers in their existing cluster placement group.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. Cluster placement groups place supported instances close together within an AZ to improve latency and inter-instance network performance. An existing instance must be stopped before its placement group can be changed. Moving only the controller into the workers' group preserves the requirement that workers remain running.

<<2>> can colocate the instances but violates the worker-availability constraint.

<<3>> changes addressing rather than placement. An Elastic IP address does not move the controller closer to the workers or establish the cluster placement relationship.

<<4>> uses a strategy intended to separate instances across distinct hardware, not to colocate the controller with the existing worker group.

Placement depends on available capacity, so a stopped instance may not be able to restart immediately in the requested group. Plan the change and capacity ahead of time. Achievable throughput also depends on instance type and networking features; group membership is not a universal bandwidth guarantee.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Change EC2 instance placement](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/change-instance-placement-group.html); [EC2 placement strategies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/placement-strategies.html).

question:
A governance team finds that several AWS Lambda execution roles allow all actions on all Amazon S3 buckets and DynamoDB tables. The team must replace these policies with permissions based on each function's actual needs, including infrequently used recovery paths. It wants to use AWS tooling to reduce manual analysis without treating observed activity as a complete specification.

Which actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use Amazon GuardDuty findings as the complete list of API actions required by each function. Remove every permission that does not appear in a finding.
Use service last-accessed timestamps to retain full access to each recently used service and remove all other services.

Use IAM Access Analyzer policy generation for each role. Review the generated template, add required permissions not inferred by the tool using logs and application requirements, scope resources, and test the replacement policy.

Configure a CloudTrail trail with relevant management events and S3 object and DynamoDB data events. Collect representative function activity, including recovery paths, for policy generation and supplemental review.
Attach the same AWS managed full-access policies for S3 and DynamoDB to every execution role so that AWS maintains the permissions.

explanation.text:
<<3>> and <<4>> are correct. CloudTrail supplies usage evidence, and IAM Access Analyzer turns supported activity into a policy starting point. Representative execution and a tested review are still necessary: an operation absent from the observation window might be required later.

Access Analyzer does not infer action-level permissions from data events. Capturing S3 object and DynamoDB data events supports supplemental analysis; it does not remove that limitation. Review required data-plane actions, resource ARNs, conditions, and other omissions such as `iam:PassRole` where applicable before replacing the policy.

<<1>> confuses threat detection with a required-permissions inventory. Legitimate activity need not produce GuardDuty findings.

<<2>> identifies used services but retains excessive actions and resources within them.

<<5>> retains broad permissions and does not distinguish what individual functions require.

The transferable rule is to use observed access as evidence for least privilege, then reconcile it with required behavior and test it.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [IAM Access Analyzer policy generation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access-analyzer-policy-generation.html).

question:
A company is moving a stateful web application to AWS. It will use an Application Load Balancer (ALB), Amazon EC2, and an Aurora MySQL DB cluster. Session data has been moved to a shared durable store so any web instance can serve a request. Most database traffic consists of read-only queries, and load testing confirms that one appropriately sized writer can handle peak writes.

Which design lets the web tier and database read capacity scale with demand?

options.text: Place the web instances in an Auto Scaling group behind the ALB. Enable Aurora Auto Scaling and send all reads and writes to the cluster writer endpoint.
Place the web instances in an Auto Scaling group behind the ALB. Add Aurora Replicas and configure Aurora Auto Scaling to increase the number of writer instances as write traffic rises.

Place the web instances in an Auto Scaling group behind the ALB. Configure Aurora Auto Scaling for Aurora Replicas, route read-only connections to the reader endpoint, and route writes to the writer endpoint.
Place a fixed number of web instances behind the ALB with sticky sessions. Configure Aurora Auto Scaling for Aurora Replicas and route read-only connections to the reader endpoint.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. EC2 Auto Scaling adjusts web capacity, while Aurora Auto Scaling adjusts the number of Aurora Replicas. The application must direct read-only work to the reader endpoint to use that capacity and keep writes on the writer endpoint. Shared session storage allows requests to move between web instances safely.

<<1>> creates readers but bypasses them by directing all traffic to the writer.

<<2>> misidentifies the scaling target. Aurora Auto Scaling adds or removes reader instances; it does not add writers to this Aurora MySQL cluster.

<<4>> scales database reads but leaves web capacity fixed. ALB stickiness provides routing affinity, not additional capacity or durable session storage.

Reader scaling also depends on connection behavior: the reader endpoint balances new connections, not individual SQL queries. Pools and scaling policies need to be tested against the workload.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Aurora Auto Scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/Aurora.Integrating.AutoScaling.html).

question:
A company has an on-premises data center in Texas and nonoverlapping VPCs in us-east-1 and us-west-2. It already has an AWS Direct Connect connection with sufficient bandwidth and wants both VPCs reachable over that dedicated connection. Connection redundancy is handled by a separate project. The company does not require routing between the VPCs.

Which solution meets the requirement with the least additional connectivity infrastructure?

options.text: Provision a separate Direct Connect connection for each AWS Region and attach each connection to that Region's virtual private gateway.

Create a private virtual interface on the existing connection to a Direct Connect gateway. Associate a virtual private gateway from each VPC with the Direct Connect gateway and configure the required routes.
Connect the existing private virtual interface directly to the us-east-1 VPC. Peer that VPC with the us-west-2 VPC and use the peering connection to forward on-premises traffic.
Create an internet-based Site-to-Site VPN from the data center to each VPC and use these tunnels for all application traffic.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. A Direct Connect gateway can associate with virtual private gateways for VPCs in different Regions. A private virtual interface connects the existing Direct Connect connection to that gateway, allowing reuse of the dedicated connection. Route advertisements, allowed prefixes, and VPC routes must agree.

<<1>> can provide connectivity, but requires additional connections when the existing connection has sufficient capacity.

<<3>> relies on edge-to-edge routing that VPC peering does not provide. Peering does not let the second VPC transit the first VPC's Direct Connect attachment.

<<4>> provides encrypted connectivity but uses the internet rather than the required dedicated path.

A Direct Connect gateway is a routing construct, not a physical circuit. It does not itself add connection redundancy, encrypt traffic, or enable transit between its associated VPCs.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Direct Connect gateway associations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/virtualgateways.html). [VPC peering limitations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/peering/vpc-peering-basics.html).

question:
A retailer is migrating a LAMP application to AWS after DDoS, SQL injection, and SSH password attacks. The team has fixed vulnerable SQL code and prepared patched EC2 images with the Systems Manager Agent. The new design must tolerate an Availability Zone failure, filter malicious HTTP requests, and provide administrative access without inbound SSH ports. The company has approved AWS Shield Advanced and an eligible support plan for specialist DDoS response assistance.

Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy an ALB and an EC2 Auto Scaling group across Availability Zones with an RDS Multi-AZ database. Use CloudFront with AWS WAF rules and Shield Advanced protection. Configure Session Manager permissions and endpoint connectivity, and remove inbound SSH access.

Deploy an ALB and an EC2 Auto Scaling group across Availability Zones with an RDS Multi-AZ database. Use CloudFront, AWS WAF, and Shield Advanced, and administer the instances through an internet-facing SSH bastion.
Deploy an ALB and an EC2 Auto Scaling group across Availability Zones with an RDS Multi-AZ database. Use CloudFront and Shield Standard without AWS WAF, and use Session Manager for administration.
Deploy an ALB and an EC2 Auto Scaling group across Availability Zones with a Single-AZ RDS database. Use CloudFront, AWS WAF, Shield Advanced, and Session Manager.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. The design addresses independent failure and attack surfaces: multiple Availability Zones protect the web tier, RDS Multi-AZ provides database failover, WAF filters HTTP requests, and Shield Advanced supplies the approved DDoS protection and response capabilities. Session Manager removes the need to expose inbound SSH ports when its agent, IAM, and network prerequisites are configured.

<<2>> retains an inbound SSH administration path, contrary to the requirement.

<<3>> omits the application-layer request filtering and the explicitly required Shield Advanced response assistance. Shield Standard does not replace a WAF web ACL.

<<4>> leaves the database vulnerable to an Availability Zone outage.

These controls complement secure code and patching. WAF does not prove an application free of SQL injection, and Multi-AZ failover still requires application reconnection and retry handling.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Session Manager](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/session-manager.html). [Layered DDoS mitigation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-best-practices-ddos-resiliency/mitigation-techniques.html). [RDS Multi-AZ DB instances](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Concepts.MultiAZSingleStandby.html).

question:
A supermarket is launching an online store on EC2 and Amazon RDS for MySQL. The application must restore service automatically after the loss of one Availability Zone, without waiting for that zone to recover or for an operator to promote a database replica. Web instances are interchangeable, and clients can retry connections during a database failover.

Which architecture meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy an ALB and an EC2 Auto Scaling group across three Availability Zones. Use a Single-AZ RDS primary and an asynchronous read replica in another Availability Zone.
Deploy an ALB across two Availability Zones and restrict its EC2 Auto Scaling group to one Availability Zone. Use an RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment.
Deploy an ALB and an EC2 Auto Scaling group across three Availability Zones. Use a Single-AZ RDS DB instance covered by a Reserved DB Instance reservation.
Deploy an ALB and an EC2 Auto Scaling group across three Availability Zones. Use an RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment with a synchronous standby in another Availability Zone.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. Distributing the ALB and web group across Availability Zones protects the web tier. An RDS Multi-AZ DB instance maintains a synchronous standby in another Availability Zone and provides managed failover for supported failures.

<<1>> uses a read replica for read scaling or recovery, but an ordinary RDS MySQL read replica is not the managed automatic failover standby of a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment.

<<2>> protects the database but places all web capacity in one failure domain.

<<3>> changes billing. A reservation does not create a standby or improve the deployment's availability.

Multi-AZ does not mean uninterrupted connections: applications must reconnect to the database endpoint after failover. The standby in this DB instance deployment does not serve read queries; RDS Multi-AZ DB clusters have different reader capabilities.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [RDS Multi-AZ DB instances](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Concepts.MultiAZSingleStandby.html). [RDS read replicas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReadRepl.html).

question:
A media company wants to reduce operating effort and processing cost for its video service. Its server-rendered web application already runs in containers and must be retained. A custom normalization step can run for 30 minutes per video and supports checkpoints and retries. Amazon Rekognition supports the required video-label analysis. The company can retain EC2 workers for normalization but wants to stop managing web-server hosts and replace third-party categorization software.

Which design best meets these requirements?

options.text: Run the web containers on Amazon ECS with Fargate. Store videos and static assets in S3 and deliver cacheable content through CloudFront. Queue normalization jobs in SQS for diversified EC2 Spot workers, then start asynchronous Rekognition analysis and retrieve results after completion.
Run the web containers on Amazon ECS with Fargate. Store videos in S3 and process each complete normalization job in one Lambda invocation before starting asynchronous Rekognition analysis.
Host the existing server-rendered application entirely as an S3 static website. Use SQS and EC2 Spot workers for normalization and Rekognition for analysis.
Run the web containers on a self-managed EC2 fleet. Store videos in S3, process normalization on an On-Demand-only EC2 fleet, and retain the third-party categorization software.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. Fargate removes web-host management, S3 separates durable content from worker lifetimes, and interruption-tolerant normalization can use Spot capacity. Rekognition's stored-video workflow is asynchronous: start a supported analysis job, consume its completion notification, and retrieve the results.

<<2>> exceeds Lambda's 15-minute maximum invocation duration for the stated 30-minute task. Lambda could orchestrate the job, but cannot execute that entire task in one invocation.

<<3>> removes the compute required by the retained server-rendered application. S3 can host static assets, but this proposal provides no server-side runtime.

<<4>> retains both web-host operations and the third-party software, and forgoes the stated opportunity to use interruption-tolerant capacity.

Spot workers need durable checkpoints, suitable SQS visibility handling, and idempotent retries. A lower Spot price is useful only when the workload tolerates interruption and available capacity.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Fargate and Lambda](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/decision-guides/latest/decision-guides/fargate-or-lambda.html). [Lambda timeout](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html). [Rekognition stored-video analysis](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/rekognition/latest/dg/video.html). [EC2 Spot Instances](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/using-spot-instances.html).

question:
A company uses AWS CloudFormation to deploy EC2 application instances and a DynamoDB table in the same account. The application must call DynamoDB without storing long-lived AWS access keys in the template, image, or instance configuration.

Which template design meets the requirement?

options.text: Give the CloudFormation execution role access to DynamoDB and allow the EC2 instances to inherit that role automatically after deployment.
Create an IAM user for the application, pass its access keys as NoEcho template parameters, and write the keys into the instances' user data.

Create an IAM role trusted by the EC2 service with the required table permissions. Add the role to an AWS::IAM::InstanceProfile, assign the profile through the instances' IamInstanceProfile property, and use the SDK credential provider chain.
Create an IAM role with the required table permissions and store credentials obtained during stack creation in a configuration file on each instance.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. The role defines EC2 trust and application permissions; the instance profile attaches that role to the instance. The SDK can obtain and refresh temporary role credentials through the instance metadata credential provider. Scope the role to required DynamoDB actions and table resources.

<<1>> confuses deployment permissions with runtime permissions. CloudFormation's execution role is used by CloudFormation to manage resources, not inherited by the EC2 application.

<<2>> still distributes long-lived credentials. `NoEcho` masks some parameter displays but does not turn access keys into a managed credential mechanism or secure their use in user data.

<<4>> snapshots credentials rather than arranging automatic credential refresh. Temporary credentials expire, and copying them at deployment is unnecessary when the instance profile provides them at runtime.

Infrastructure permissions and application permissions are separate identities. Creating the role alone is insufficient: the instance profile must be associated with the EC2 instance.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [CloudFormation instance profiles](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/TemplateReference/aws-resource-iam-instanceprofile.html). [IAM roles for EC2 applications](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_use_switch-role-ec2.html).

question:
A retailer uses an ALB in eu-west-1 as a custom origin for CloudFront. Viewers use shop.example.com. The origin hostname is origin.example.com, which resolves to the ALB. The company must reject HTTP viewer requests and encrypt traffic on both the viewer-to-CloudFront and CloudFront-to-ALB connections.

Which configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Request or import a viewer certificate covering shop.example.com in ACM in us-east-1 and attach it to CloudFront. Attach a certificate covering origin.example.com to the ALB in eu-west-1. Configure HTTPS Only for both the viewer protocol policy and origin protocol policy.

Attach a certificate covering shop.example.com to CloudFront and set the viewer protocol policy to HTTPS Only. Configure HTTP Only for the origin protocol policy because CloudFront already encrypted the viewer connection.
Use CloudFront's default *.cloudfront.net certificate for shop.example.com. Attach a valid certificate to the ALB and configure HTTPS Only for both protocol policies.
Configure HTTPS Only for both protocol policies. Attach the viewer certificate from us-east-1 to CloudFront and use a self-signed certificate on the ALB for origin.example.com.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. CloudFront terminates viewer TLS and establishes a separate TLS connection to the origin. An ACM viewer certificate for CloudFront must be in us-east-1. The ALB uses a certificate in its own Region. Certificate names and the configured hostnames must match, and the origin certificate must have a trusted chain.

<<2>> encrypts only the viewer leg. Viewer HTTPS does not force origin HTTPS.

<<3>> presents a certificate that does not cover the custom viewer hostname. The default CloudFront certificate covers CloudFront's assigned domain name.

<<4>> fails CloudFront's origin trust requirements. CloudFront does not accept a self-signed origin certificate.

Both protocol policies are necessary controls for this requirement. Two encrypted connections are not a single TLS tunnel through CloudFront to the ALB.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [CloudFront certificate requirements](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/cnames-and-https-requirements.html). [CloudFront origin HTTPS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/using-https-cloudfront-to-custom-origin.html). [Viewer HTTPS policy](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/using-https-viewers-to-cloudfront.html).

question:
A company uses AWS Organizations to manage development accounts. Its security team maintains a list of approved AMI IDs for each Region. Developers must be allowed to launch instances from other AMIs, but security must receive a notification when a running instance is evaluated as noncompliant. No automatic blocking or termination is required.

Which solution meets these requirements with the least custom code?

options.text: Attach an SCP that denies ec2:RunInstances unless the requested AMI is approved, and send notifications for denied API requests.
Enable Amazon Inspector and treat every instance without a vulnerability finding as compliant with the approved AMI list.
Create an AWS Config aggregator in the security account and supply the approved AMI IDs to the aggregator without deploying evaluation rules in source accounts.

Enable AWS Config recording and deploy the approved-amis-by-id managed rule in each relevant account and Region. Match noncompliant rule-evaluation events with EventBridge and send notifications through SNS.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. The `approved-amis-by-id` managed rule evaluates running EC2 instances against its configured AMI IDs. Config compliance events can be matched by EventBridge and delivered to SNS. This is a detective control applied after the resource exists, so it does not block development deployments.

<<1>> is preventive and violates the requirement to permit launches.

<<2>> checks a different property. A vulnerability assessment does not establish that an instance uses an approved image ID.

<<3>> aggregates existing configuration and compliance data but does not replace source-account recording and rule evaluation.

Deploy the rule with the appropriate regional list and verify the event and notification configuration. Config events use best-effort delivery, so a compliance dashboard or reconciliation process can complement operational alerts.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Approved AMI managed rule](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/approved-amis-by-id.html). [Config events with EventBridge](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/monitor-config-with-cloudwatchevents.html).

question:
A broadcaster expects a short burst of millions of visits to a voting website. Viewers sign in with supported social identity providers and may cast one vote per contest. The company will retain its dynamic EC2 web application. It can acknowledge a vote as accepted for processing before the vote is tallied, but acknowledged votes must be durably queued and repeated delivery must not count a vote twice. Final totals are published after all accepted work has been reconciled.

Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Use Cognito social sign-in, CloudFront, an ALB, and web Auto Scaling. Write each vote synchronously to a fixed-capacity database, and acknowledge the vote even when the write times out to avoid slow responses.
Use Cognito social sign-in, CloudFront, an ALB, and web Auto Scaling. Acknowledge votes after storing them in web-instance memory, then periodically flush the votes to DynamoDB.
Use Cognito social sign-in, CloudFront, an ALB, and web Auto Scaling. Place votes in an SQS standard queue and have workers increment a DynamoDB counter unconditionally for every delivered message.

Use Cognito social sign-in, CloudFront, an ALB, and web Auto Scaling. Acknowledge votes only after successful SQS submission. Have workers conditionally create a DynamoDB vote record keyed by contest and voter, and tally accepted records after processing completes.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. Cognito supports social identity federation, while SQS decouples bursty acceptance from processing. A condition that prevents replacing an existing contest-and-voter record makes retries and repeated votes harmless to the count. The tally is derived from accepted unique records after processing and failed-message reconciliation.

<<1>> can acknowledge a vote that was never committed. Synchronous persistence can be valid when sized and handled correctly, but acknowledging failed writes violates this requirement.

<<2>> loses acknowledged votes if an instance fails before flushing memory.

<<3>> ignores SQS standard queues' at-least-once delivery. Unconditional increments can count a retry twice.

The queue does not enforce the business rule of one vote per person or contest. Authenticate and authorize submissions, derive voter identity on the server, design DynamoDB keys to distribute load, and load-test queue consumers and service quotas before the event.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Cognito identity providers](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-user-pools-identity-provider.html). [SQS delivery semantics](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/standard-queues-at-least-once-delivery.html). [DynamoDB conditional writes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/Expressions.ConditionExpressions.html).

question:
A company builds a searchable photo catalog with several Lambda functions that extract different kinds of metadata. Photos are independent, and the extraction rules for a photo can run independently. Each function completes within five minutes, but processing photos and rules sequentially makes the overall batch take 45 minutes. The company must collect all rule results for each photo before updating its ElastiCache catalog. It wants to reuse the functions and minimize custom orchestration code.

Which change will reduce batch duration?

options.text: Use a Step Functions workflow with a Map state to process photos concurrently. For each photo, use a Parallel state to invoke independent extraction functions, combine their results, and then update the catalog.
Use a Step Functions workflow with a Map state whose maximum concurrency is one. Run each photo's extraction functions sequentially and update the catalog after the last function.
Create one SQS queue per batch and configure each extraction function as a competing consumer of that queue so that every function receives every photo.
Port all extraction functions to containers and build a custom AWS Batch scheduler that submits and polls each rule job before updating the catalog.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. Map expresses concurrency across photos, and Parallel expresses concurrency across independent rules for one photo. A Parallel state waits for its branches to complete before passing their collected outputs to the next state, which provides the required join before the catalog update.

<<2>> preserves both forms of serialization and therefore does not address the stated bottleneck.

<<3>> treats a work queue as a broadcast mechanism. Competing consumers distribute messages; they do not ensure that every rule processes every photo or provide a per-photo result join.

<<4>> could support parallel processing, but requires a container migration and custom coordination when Step Functions can orchestrate the existing functions directly.

The 45 minutes describes the whole batch, not one Lambda invocation. Select Map concurrency and workflow mode to fit the dataset, Lambda concurrency quotas, downstream capacity, and retry behavior.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Step Functions Map](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/state-map.html). [Step Functions Parallel](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/state-parallel.html).

question:
Each EC2 application instance has a separate 120 GiB io1 EBS data volume provisioned for 3,000 IOPS. The application needs persistent block storage, not a shared network file system. Production-workload tests on a 120 GiB gp3 volume at 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s meet the application's latency, throughput, and durability requirements. The EC2 instances have sufficient EBS bandwidth.

Which change removes unnecessary storage and provisioned-performance expense while preserving the tested requirements?

options.text: Replace each data volume with an Amazon EFS file system and access it through NFS.
Change each data volume to 120 GiB gp3 with its included baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s.
Change each data volume to a 1 TiB gp2 volume to obtain slightly more than 3,000 baseline IOPS.
Move the data to EC2 instance store volumes and recreate them whenever an instance is replaced.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. gp3 includes 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s independently of volume size. The stated test establishes that this baseline meets the workload's needs, so additional performance provisioning and extra capacity are unnecessary.

<<1>> changes the required storage interface from block storage to a network file system.

<<3>> couples performance to unnecessary capacity. gp2 baseline IOPS scale at 3 IOPS per GiB, so 1,024 GiB provides 3,072 baseline IOPS, but the application needs only 120 GiB.

<<4>> does not preserve the required data lifecycle. Instance store data does not persist through instance stop or termination.

IOPS and throughput are different constraints: IOPS counts operations per second, while MiB/s measures bytes transferred. The conclusion depends on measured latency, throughput, durability needs, and instance limits, not matching an IOPS number alone.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [General Purpose SSD volumes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/general-purpose.html). [EC2 instance store persistence](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/instance-store-lifetime.html).

question:
A travel company's website uses an ALB and an EC2 Auto Scaling group. The company wants HTTPS for public visitors. Developers need operating-system administrator access to the EC2 instances, but only the security team may administer the website's TLS configuration. Developers must not be able to retrieve the TLS private key. The company can terminate visitor TLS at the ALB.

Which solution meets these requirements with the least key-management effort?

options.text: Have the security team request an ACM public certificate with export disabled and attach it to an ALB HTTPS listener. Restrict certificate and listener administration to the security team, and keep the private key off the EC2 instances.
Have the security team install the private key on each EC2 instance and make the key file readable only by the root user. Terminate visitor TLS on those instances.
Have each EC2 instance download an encrypted private key from S3 and decrypt it locally with its instance role. Restrict direct S3 access to that role.
Have the security team store the private key in Secrets Manager and allow the EC2 instance role to retrieve it for local TLS termination. Deny developers direct access to the secret.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. ALB TLS termination keeps the key out of developer-administered hosts. Selecting export disabled prevents export of that ACM certificate's private key, and IAM separation protects certificate and listener administration. Public certificate contents are not the secret; the private key and administration privileges are the protected assets.

<<2>> does not isolate a secret from an operating-system administrator. Developers with root access can read or change the file's permissions.

<<3>> delivers the usable key to a host the developers administer. Encryption at rest and a bucket restriction do not prevent a host administrator from observing the decrypted key or using the host's role.

<<4>> has the same boundary problem: denying a developer's own IAM identity does not isolate a key deliberately exposed to that developer's host.

ACM now supports exportable public certificates, so a blanket claim that all ACM public certificates have non-exportable private keys would be incorrect. This design explicitly selects a non-exportable private key.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [ACM certificate export controls](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/aws-certificate-manager-now-supports-exporting-public-certificates/). [ALB HTTPS listeners](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/create-https-listener.html). [EC2 role access boundary](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_use_switch-role-ec2.html).

question:
A company is building an API-driven document service. Its application already authenticates customers and authorizes access to each tenant's documents. Every committed document version must remain retrievable. A rollback must make an older version current without deleting intervening versions. Customers must not receive long-lived AWS credentials or plaintext encryption master keys.

Which storage and access design meets these requirements?

options.text: Store documents in an unversioned private S3 bucket with SSE-KMS. Enable S3 server access logging and use the access logs to reconstruct overwritten document contents during a rollback.

Store documents in a private versioned S3 bucket with SSE-KMS. After authorization, issue short-lived presigned URLs from a scoped application role. Roll back by copying a selected older version to the same key to create a new current version, and retain noncurrent versions.
Store documents in a private versioned S3 bucket with SSE-KMS. Issue short-lived presigned URLs. Roll back by permanently deleting every version newer than the requested version.

Store documents in a private versioned S3 bucket with client-side encryption. Distribute the shared plaintext master key and long-lived IAM access keys to authorized customers so they can perform uploads and rollbacks directly.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. Versioning preserves successive object versions, while copying a selected version to the same object key creates a new current version without erasing later historical versions. SSE-KMS keeps master-key material within the managed encryption boundary, and presigned URLs provide scoped, expiring access using the application role's permissions.

<<1>> confuses request logs with content history. Access logs do not contain the complete overwritten document bodies.

<<3>> makes the old content current by destroying required history.

<<4>> violates the explicit credential and key-distribution restrictions.

Authorize the tenant, object, operation, and any requested version before signing. Presigned URLs are bearer access and can expire earlier when the signing credentials expire. Use retention controls that prevent required versions from being deleted, and do not configure lifecycle expiration of history that must remain retrievable.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Restore an earlier S3 version](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/RestoringPreviousVersions.html). [S3 presigned URLs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/ShareObjectPreSignedURL.html). [S3 SSE-KMS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingKMSEncryption.html).

question:
A serverless discussion application uses API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB. Clients currently retrieve comments with repeated GET requests. The company wants authorized clients viewing a topic to receive new comments as they are posted, without polling. The team can adopt GraphQL and change the comment-write API, and it wants managed connection handling.

Which solution best meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable API Gateway caching for GET requests and shorten the cache time-to-live so clients receive newer comments on their next request.
Increase Lambda reserved concurrency and have clients poll the existing GET endpoint every second.
Use AWS AppSync GraphQL mutations to create comments and subscriptions to deliver matching updates over WebSocket connections. Authenticate subscribers and authorize access to the requested topics.
Write comments directly to DynamoDB and enable an AppSync subscription, without connecting a comment mutation or event-publishing path to those writes.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. AppSync manages WebSocket connections for GraphQL subscriptions, and configured mutations trigger subscription updates. The write path must execute the relevant mutation, with authorization and filters that ensure a client receives only permitted topic data.

<<1>> changes read caching but still requires the client to request updates. Caching can also return stale comments during the cache lifetime.

<<2>> adds execution capacity but retains polling and its repeated requests.

<<4>> omits the event path. Writing to a DynamoDB table does not by itself trigger a GraphQL subscription merely because AppSync can read that table.

Push delivery and data retrieval solve different needs: use a query for initial state and a subscription for subsequent updates. A custom API Gateway WebSocket solution can also provide push, but the proposed AppSync design supplies managed GraphQL subscription integration.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [AppSync GraphQL subscriptions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/appsync/latest/devguide/aws-appsync-real-time-data.html).

question:
An application on EC2 downloads objects whose keys it already knows from an S3 bucket in the same account. The bucket uses SSE-S3, and no bucket policy, permissions boundary, SCP, or endpoint policy adds permissions or denies the requests. An instance profile will be associated with the instance.

Which two policy components should the architect configure on the application's IAM role to allow this access? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A permissions policy allowing s3:ListBucket on the bucket ARN, without any object actions.
A trust policy allowing only the company's administrator role to assume the application role.
A trust policy allowing the ec2.amazonaws.com service principal to perform sts:AssumeRole.
A trust policy allowing only the s3.amazonaws.com service principal to assume the application role.
A permissions policy allowing s3:GetObject on the required object ARNs in the bucket.

explanation.text:
<<3>> and <<5>> are correct. The trust policy identifies who can assume the role: the EC2 service in this design. The permissions policy authorizes what the resulting role session can do: retrieve the required S3 objects. The associated instance profile makes temporary role credentials available to the application.

<<1>> authorizes listing object keys, not downloading their contents. Known-key downloads require `s3:GetObject`, and object actions use object ARNs rather than the bucket ARN alone.

<<2>> authorizes a different principal to assume the role, so it does not establish EC2 service trust.

<<4>> trusts S3 rather than EC2. S3 is the target service here, not the compute service obtaining the application's credentials.

Trust and permissions answer separate questions. Resource-based policies can also participate in S3 authorization in other designs, and SSE-KMS would introduce relevant KMS permissions; the stem excludes those additional policy paths.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [EC2 role trust and permissions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_use_switch-role-ec2.html). [S3 identity policies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/example-policies-s3.html).

question:
A company repeatedly loses access to EC2 instances because of guest operating-system network, firewall, or RDP misconfigurations. Monitoring already identifies eligible instances and can start Systems Manager Automation. The affected Linux and Windows instances use supported, non-Marketplace AMIs with unencrypted EBS root volumes. Stopping and restarting an instance is approved, and no required data exists only on instance store volumes.

Which repair action requires the least custom automation?

options.text: Trigger EC2 automatic recovery for a failed system status check and rely on replacement hardware to correct guest firewall and RDP configuration.
Invoke the AWSSupport-ExecuteEC2Rescue Automation runbook with the required IAM permissions and a helper-instance subnet in the same Availability Zone that can reach Systems Manager endpoints.
Open a Session Manager session to every impaired instance and run repair commands, even when its guest network configuration prevents the agent from reaching Systems Manager.
Write a Lambda-based workflow that stops the instance, creates a backup, attaches its root volume to a helper instance, performs offline repairs, and restores the volume.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. `AWSSupport-ExecuteEC2Rescue` uses the AWS-maintained rescue workflow to diagnose and, where supported, repair common guest connectivity problems. It stops the instance, creates a backup AMI, and uses an offline helper workflow rather than requiring a working session to the impaired guest.

<<1>> addresses underlying infrastructure failures detected by system status checks. Moving the instance to healthy hardware does not fix its persistent guest configuration.

<<3>> depends on the connectivity that the failure can remove. Session Manager is useful when the agent remains connected, but is not a general offline-repair mechanism.

<<4>> can implement the mechanism but requires substantially more custom maintenance than the existing runbook.

This runbook is not a guarantee that every failure is repairable. Its documented restrictions include unsupported encrypted root volumes; stop/start can lose instance-store data and change an automatically assigned public IPv4 address. Validate eligibility, backups, permissions, and helper networking before execution.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [ExecuteEC2Rescue runbook](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager-automation-runbooks/latest/userguide/automation-awssupport-executeec2rescue.html). [EC2Rescue helper workflow](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager-automation-runbooks/latest/userguide/automation-awssupport-startec2rescueworkflow.html).

question:
An EC2 application accepts write requests for an on-premises database over a 10 Gbps Direct Connect connection. Measurements show that database write capacity, not network bandwidth, is the bottleneck during short bursts. The database has spare capacity between bursts. The application can report that a request is queued before the database applies it, and updates are idempotent and do not require ordering. Expected outages and backlogs fit within the configured queue retention period.

Which change absorbs bursts without losing acknowledged requests when an application instance fails?

options.text: Increase Direct Connect bandwidth and continue sending every write synchronously to the database.

Place each request with a unique identifier in an SQS standard queue and acknowledge it after successful submission. Use rate-controlled consumers to apply the update idempotently and delete the message only after the database confirms completion.
Increase the web Auto Scaling group's maximum size so that more instances can issue concurrent database writes.
Acknowledge requests after buffering them in each application instance's memory, then flush the buffer when database latency decreases.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. SQS decouples the request-arrival rate from the database's processing rate. Durable queue acceptance allows a prompt acknowledgment, and consumers can drain the backlog at a sustainable rate. Deleting only after a confirmed database update avoids discarding work prematurely.

<<1>> increases capacity in a component that is not the measured bottleneck.

<<3>> can increase pressure on the already saturated database rather than absorb it.

<<4>> can lose acknowledged requests when an instance fails before flushing its buffer.

SQS standard queues can deliver a message more than once, including after a consumer commits but fails before deletion. Use the unique request identifier to make the database operation idempotent. Monitor message age, retries, and dead-letter queues, and choose retention long enough for recovery and draining. Buffering does not increase sustained database capacity or by itself establish a cross-Region disaster-recovery RPO.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [SQS delivery and redundancy](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/standard-queues-at-least-once-delivery.html). [SQS queue parameters](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-configure-queue-parameters.html). [SQS message deletion](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/sqs/delete-message.html).

question:
A law firm wants employees to use existing Active Directory credentials to access legal documents in S3. The firm already operates a trusted SAML 2.0 identity provider. Each employee must be able to list and access only that employee's assigned object prefix. The solution must avoid creating long-lived AWS credentials for employees. No other policies grant access to the bucket.

Which actions should the architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Configure SAML federation to an IAM role so employees obtain temporary AWS credentials. Have the trusted identity provider supply a protected, unique employee identifier as a session tag.

Use the trusted employee session tag in the role's S3 policy. Restrict ListBucket with an s3:prefix condition and restrict object actions to that employee's prefix ARN. Prevent employees from choosing or overriding another employee's identifier.
Grant the federated role access to every object in the bucket and hide other employees' folders in the client interface.
Create an IAM user and access key for every employee, and synchronize their IAM console passwords with Active Directory.
Create one shared IAM user for the application and distribute its access keys to all employees, using separate S3 folder names for organization.

explanation.text:
<<1>> and <<2>> are correct. Federation exchanges trusted SAML authentication for temporary role credentials. The role can use a trusted session tag to scope each employee's S3 requests without creating a separate IAM user or long-lived access key.

Two policy scopes are required: `s3:ListBucket` applies to the bucket ARN with an allowed-prefix condition, while object actions such as `s3:GetObject` and `s3:PutObject` apply to object ARNs under that prefix. Configure the role's SAML trust and required `sts:TagSession` permission, and ensure the identity provider controls the employee identifier. A user-selectable prefix tag would defeat isolation.

<<3>> provides interface filtering, not authorization; direct API calls would retain broad access.

<<4>> introduces long-lived AWS identities and credentials instead of federation.

<<5>> loses per-user isolation and distributes a shared long-lived secret.

Do not copy a policy using `${aws:username}` into this federated-role design: that variable is not available for IAM role sessions. Use an appropriate trusted identity attribute.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [STS session tags](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_session-tags.html). [S3 home-prefix policies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_examples_s3_home-directory-console.html).

question:
A company deploys EC2 Auto Scaling groups with CloudFormation. Its image pipeline validates a new regional AMI before approving it for production. Engineers currently edit hardcoded AMI IDs in every template. The company wants reusable templates and an automated, controlled replacement of existing instances after each approved image release.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a Systems Manager State Manager association that patches packages on running instances, and leave the templates' hardcoded AMI IDs unchanged.
Create an AWS Config rule that reports instances using an old AMI, and rely on the compliance result to change their launch templates and replace the instances.
Store the approved AMI ID in Parameter Store and reference it from CloudFormation, but update only the parameter after each release and wait for existing instances to adopt the new AMI automatically.

Store each Region's approved AMI ID in Parameter Store and reference its key with an AWS::SSM::Parameter::Value<AWS::EC2::Image::Id> template parameter. Have the pipeline update the parameter, create and execute a stack change set, and roll the Auto Scaling group to the new launch-template version using a configured update policy.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. A CloudFormation Systems Manager parameter type lets the template retain a stable key while CloudFormation resolves the current AMI ID during stack creation or update. The pipeline must still initiate the stack operation and replace existing instances through an appropriate Auto Scaling update policy. Review the AMI resolved into the change set before execution.

<<1>> changes installed software but leaves the image used for newly launched instances stale. It does not implement the requested image-release process.

<<2>> detects a configuration condition; a compliance finding alone does not mutate launch templates or roll instances.

<<3>> omits the deployment trigger and rollout. Changing Parameter Store does not automatically update a CloudFormation stack or replace an instance's running image.

Separate image approval, parameter publication, stack update, and instance rollout. A latest-value reference selects configuration at deployment time; it is not a subscription that continuously reconciles running hosts.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [CloudFormation SSM parameter types](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/cloudformation-supplied-parameter-types.html). [CloudFormation update policies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/TemplateReference/aws-attribute-updatepolicy.html).

question:
A media company runs a private RDS for MySQL database in a VPC. An on-premises analytics system needs a continuously updated MySQL copy with read-only access for analysts. The selected tables and engine versions have passed AWS DMS compatibility testing. Database endpoints must remain private, and replication traffic must be encrypted.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Make the RDS instance publicly accessible and configure ongoing replication to the on-premises server using TLS over the public internet.
Replicate changes through a self-managed MySQL server on EC2, then replicate to the on-premises database through public endpoints protected by TLS and source-IP restrictions.
Export the database nightly to S3 and download the export over HTTPS to refresh the on-premises MySQL server.

Establish Site-to-Site VPN connectivity and run a DMS full-load-and-CDC task from RDS to the on-premises MySQL target. Configure the required source binary logs, retention, endpoint TLS and restricted database accounts. Grant analysts read-only target permissions.

explanation.text:
<<4>> separates secure connectivity from ongoing replication. The VPN provides a private IPsec path, while DMS first loads existing rows and then applies captured changes. Configure RDS binary logging for CDC, retain logs through expected interruptions, validate endpoint TLS and monitor replication lag. The DMS target account needs write privileges even though analyst accounts are read-only.

<<1>> encrypts traffic but violates the private-endpoint requirement. <<2>> adds an intermediary but still exposes public endpoints, violating the private-endpoint requirement. TLS and IP restrictions do not make an endpoint private. <<3>> provides periodic copies rather than continuous updates.

DMS CDC is asynchronous and requires supported schema and datatype behavior. The documented native RDS-to-external MySQL export procedure is limited to the export period and instructs operators to stop replication afterward; it should not be presented as an indefinitely supported analytics replica procedure.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/dms/latest/userguide/CHAP_Task.CDC.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/dms/latest/userguide/CHAP_Source.MySQL.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/dms/latest/userguide/CHAP_Target.MySQL.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/MySQL.Procedural.Exporting.NonRDSRepl.html

question:
A company hires a third-party auditing SaaS provider that operates from its own AWS account and serves many customers. The provider needs a defined set of read-only API operations in the company’s account. The company prohibits shared long-term credentials and wants to prevent the provider from accidentally using its role for another customer.

Which access configuration should the company use?

options.text: Create a cross-account role trusted by the provider and require its customer-specific external ID. Attach AdministratorAccess to cover any audit request.
Create a least-privilege IAM user and give its access key and secret key to the provider for recurring audits.
Create a least-privilege audit role that trusts the provider’s designated AWS principal and requires the provider-generated external ID for this customer. Have the provider call STS AssumeRole.
Create a least-privilege role with a wildcard principal and require the external ID as the sole condition for assuming it.

explanation.text:
<<3>> combines temporary credentials, narrowly scoped permissions and a trust condition binding the request to the correct customer. The provider must also authorize its calling principal to assume the role. The external ID addresses the confused-deputy risk when one service operates for multiple customers.

<<1>> grants far more access than the audit requires. <<2>> distributes persistent credentials and violates the stated constraint. <<4>> treats the external ID as a secret password while leaving the trusted principal unrestricted. External IDs are not secrets and do not replace principal restrictions.

Keep the trust policy and permissions policy conceptually separate: trust controls who can obtain a session, while permissions control what that session may do.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_common-scenarios_third-party.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/STS/latest/APIReference/API_AssumeRole.html

question:
An external audit team uses an established IAM role in its own AWS account. It needs read-only configuration access to selected resources in each of 30 company accounts for a six-week review. The company wants to reuse the auditor’s existing identity and avoid creating local users or long-term access keys.

Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Provide the auditor with the sign-in credentials of existing company administrators and ask the auditor to perform only read operations.
Create a company directory account for every auditor and build a new federation integration for the review.
Create one IAM user with read-only permissions in the company management account and give its access keys to the auditor as access to all member accounts.

Create an audit role in each target account with scoped read-only permissions and a trust policy for the auditor’s designated role. Authorize the auditor to assume those roles and remove access when the review ends.

explanation.text:
<<4>> places the authorization in the accounts that own the resources. The auditor retains its existing identity and assumes a separate temporary role session for each target account. Scope permissions to the necessary configuration APIs and use identifiable sessions for auditability.

<<1>> shares privileged identities and grants write capabilities even if the auditor promises not to use them. <<2>> can be a valid federation approach, but it duplicates an identity integration and does not meet the requirement to reuse the existing external role. <<3>> introduces long-term keys and assumes that a management-account user automatically gains resource access in member accounts.

Cross-account trust does not grant the caller permission to assume a role by itself; both accounts must authorize the relationship. At the end of an engagement, prevent new sessions and address already issued sessions according to the required revocation timing.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/STS/latest/APIReference/API_AssumeRole.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_common-scenarios_third-party.html

question:
A company uses AWS Organizations and must retain an audit record of management API activity across all organization accounts and enabled Regions. Delivered log object versions must resist deletion for 365 days, including deletion attempts by account administrators. The security team also needs evidence of whether delivered log files have been altered.

Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a multi-Region trail only in the management account. Store logs in a versioned S3 bucket and enable MFA Delete.

Create a multi-Region organization trail and enable log-file integrity validation. Deliver logs to an encrypted, restricted S3 bucket in the logging account with Object Lock compliance-mode retention for 365 days. Run integrity validation and monitor trail delivery.
Create a single-Region organization trail. Send SNS delivery notifications and encrypt the destination bucket, relying on notifications to establish complete coverage and immutable retention.

Create a multi-Region organization trail with integrity validation. Use an encrypted, versioned S3 bucket with a lifecycle rule that expires logs after 365 days, relying on that schedule to prevent earlier administrator deletion.

explanation.text:
<<2>> covers account scope, Region scope, retention and integrity as separate controls. The organization trail includes member accounts. Object Lock compliance mode protects each retained object version from deletion or overwrite during its retention period. Signed CloudTrail digest files enable validation of delivered log files; enabling digest delivery is not the same as actually running validation.

<<1>> does not include member-account events merely because the trail is multi-Region, and MFA Delete is not the specified fixed retention mechanism. <<3>> omits activity outside one Region; notifications and encryption do not enforce retention or prove integrity. <<4>> schedules object expiration but does not prevent an authorized administrator from deleting retained versions earlier.

Configure the required event selectors: management events cover control-plane activity, while selected data events are needed for object or item access. Protect logging and KMS administration separately and monitor delivery failures.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/creating-trail-organization.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-log-file-validation-intro.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/security-reference-architecture/log-archive.html

question:
A city is deploying a MySQL-compatible web portal at the zone apex example.com in a Route 53 public hosted zone. The application must continue operating after a single Availability Zone failure, and the database needs a ready failover instance in another AZ. Application instances are stateless. The team must avoid maintaining DNS records containing individual load-balancer IP addresses.

Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Use an ALB and an Auto Scaling group across two AZs with an RDS Multi-AZ DB instance. Create a non-alias A record at example.com containing the ALB’s current IP addresses.
Use an ALB and an Auto Scaling group across three AZs. Use Aurora MySQL with a writer and replicas in other AZs, and create an A alias record at example.com targeting the ALB.
Use an ALB and an Auto Scaling group across three AZs with an RDS Multi-AZ DB instance and read replicas. Create a CNAME record at example.com targeting the ALB DNS name.
Use an ALB and an Auto Scaling group across three AZs. Use one Aurora MySQL writer without any replica instances, and create an A alias record at example.com targeting the ALB.

explanation.text:
<<2>> combines compute capacity across AZs, database failover compute in another AZ and a Route 53 alias that tracks the ALB endpoint. Aurora’s distributed storage and separately placed replica instances provide different parts of database resilience.

<<1>> has a suitable availability foundation but pins DNS to changing ALB addresses. <<3>> uses a CNAME at the hosted-zone apex, where CNAME records are not permitted. A CNAME can be valid for a subdomain, so it is the apex requirement that eliminates this choice. <<4>> has durable multi-AZ Aurora storage but lacks the requested ready replica instance for failover.

An alias can be an A record: “alias” describes Route 53 target resolution, while A is the DNS record type. Size surviving application capacity for the AZ failure and test connection recovery; a multi-AZ diagram does not itself guarantee a numerical RTO.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/routing-to-elb-load-balancer.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/Aurora.Overview.Reliability.html

question:
A document-sharing application runs on EC2 and stores PDFs in a private S3 bucket. After checking the signed-in user's authorization, the application checks whether a requested download exists and generates a presigned URL. Uploads also use presigned URLs. Long-term AWS access keys must not be stored on the instance.

Which configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an IAM user with GetObject and PutObject permissions and store its access keys in an encrypted configuration file on the instance.
Create an IAM user with GetObject and PutObject permissions and associate the user with the instance so that its credentials appear in instance metadata.
Attach a role with ListBucket permission to the instance and read its temporary credentials from EC2 user data before signing URLs.

Attach an instance profile containing a role with GetObject and PutObject permissions on the permitted prefixes. Add ListBucket only if needed. Use the SDK's instance-profile credential provider with IMDSv2 to sign URLs.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. The instance profile supplies a role to EC2, and the SDK obtains rotating temporary credentials from instance metadata. GetObject authorizes downloads and HeadObject checks, while PutObject authorizes uploads. Presigning runs locally with the credentials; S3 evaluates the resulting request against the signer's permissions. The application must authorize the user before issuing the URL.

<<1>> encrypts stored keys but still retains long-term credentials. <<2>> confuses an IAM user with an instance profile: EC2 metadata does not expose an attached IAM user's credentials. <<3>> lacks object read/write permissions and uses the wrong credential location; user data is not the instance-profile credential endpoint.

ListBucket is not needed simply to issue HeadObject, but it affects a missing object's response: 404 with ListBucket and 403 without it. A presigned URL is a bearer token and cannot remain valid beyond the signing credentials' lifetime. SSE-KMS objects can require additional KMS permissions.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/iam-roles-for-amazon-ec2.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/API/API_HeadObject.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html

question:
An Auto Scaling group runs EC2 application instances in three Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer. The instances in one zone receive no requests. They are registered in the correct target group, the listener forwards to that group, and their processes and network rules pass independent checks. The affected targets show the state unused with reason Target.NotInUse.

Which configuration should the solutions architect check first?

options.text: Whether the affected Availability Zone is enabled through a subnet mapping on the Application Load Balancer.
Whether cross-zone load balancing is disabled on the target group, even though the affected Availability Zone is enabled on the load balancer.
Whether the Auto Scaling group uses EC2 health checks instead of Elastic Load Balancing health checks.
Whether target-group stickiness is causing established clients to continue using instances in other Availability Zones.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. Registering a target is insufficient when its Availability Zone is not enabled on the ALB. Target.NotInUse can also mean that no listener uses the target group, but the stem rules out that case. Check the ALB subnet mappings for the missing zone.

<<2>> can change which healthy, eligible targets a load balancer node reaches; it does not explain why an enabled-zone target is marked unused with this reason. <<3>> affects how Auto Scaling detects unhealthy instances for replacement, not whether the ALB enables an Availability Zone. <<4>> can influence request distribution but does not place targets in the unused state.

Diagnose target eligibility separately from traffic balance. An ALB spans enabled zones in a VPC, and an Auto Scaling group can span multiple zones. EC2-Classic guidance does not apply.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/en_en/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/target-group-health-checks.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/edit-target-group-attributes.html

question:
A company must expand storage for a backup application on a non-x86 on-premises server. The application needs a POSIX filesystem backed by block storage and cannot use an object API. The data set is 1,000 TiB, and users must read the active working set while backups run. The company wants to keep only that working set locally and use one supported Storage Gateway appliance. The host's iSCSI and filesystem layer has been validated to combine multiple volumes into one namespace.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Store the data in S3 Glacier Deep Archive and mount the archive directly as an iSCSI block device on the server.
Use a Volume Gateway with stored volumes and allocate up to 32 volumes of 16 TiB each.

Use a Volume Gateway with cached volumes and allocate sufficient volumes within the limit of 32 volumes of 32 TiB each. Aggregate the iSCSI devices on the host and size the local cache for the active working set.
Write directly to an S3 bucket through the S3 API and use the bucket name as the application's POSIX mount point.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. Cached volumes provide iSCSI block devices with primary storage in AWS and a local cache for frequently accessed data. A gateway supports up to 32 cached volumes of 32 TiB each: 1,024 TiB in aggregate, enough for the 1,000-TiB data set. The host supplies the filesystem and the combined namespace.

<<1>> provides archival object storage, not a directly mounted iSCSI volume with immediate working-set access. <<2>> retains the entire primary data set on premises and provides only 512 TiB per gateway, so it violates both the local-storage requirement and the capacity requirement. <<4>> requires object-API integration and does not create POSIX semantics by naming a bucket.

The 1,024-TiB limit is not the size of one volume. Gateway appliance compatibility, host filesystem limits, cache sizing and workload performance must all be validated independently.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/storagegateway/latest/vgw/resource-gateway-limits.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/storagegateway/latest/vgw/StorageGatewayConcepts.html

question:
A blogging platform stores public articles in a private S3 bucket. Articles change frequently during their first three months and become immutable after editorial approval, usually by month six. Under normal origin availability, edits to mutable articles must appear within five minutes. Approved articles should be eligible for a full day of edge caching. The platform wants one managed delivery configuration.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Duplicate each article into two buckets and create a CloudFront distribution for each bucket. Set both distributions to cache every article for 24 hours.
Use one CloudFront distribution with a minimum TTL of 0 and a default and maximum TTL of 24 hours. Omit origin cache headers because the zero minimum TTL prevents caching.
Create separate CloudFront distributions for different geographic groups. Configure both distributions with a fixed 24-hour TTL for every article.

Use one CloudFront distribution with origin access control for the private bucket. Set minimum TTL to 0 and maximum TTL to 24 hours. Publish Cache-Control: max-age=300 for mutable articles and max-age=86400 for approved articles, with versioned URLs or invalidations for urgent corrections.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. Origin cache headers express each article's freshness requirement, while the CloudFront cache policy bounds the allowed TTL. With a zero minimum and a 24-hour maximum, max-age=300 permits five minutes of caching and max-age=86400 permits a day. Origin access control restricts access to the private S3 origin.

<<1>> duplicates storage and delivery configuration but retains the wrong TTL for mutable content. <<2>> misinterprets minimum TTL: zero permits a short TTL but does not force every request to reach the origin. Without cache headers, the default TTL still applies. <<3>> changes geographic coverage without meeting the five-minute update requirement.

An upload-month prefix can organize content, but age alone does not change cache settings. The publisher must update headers when an article changes state. Changing origin metadata does not immediately purge cached responses; use invalidation or a new versioned URL when needed. TTL is a freshness limit, not a promise that an object remains resident at the edge.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/Expiration.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.html

question:
A company uses CloudFormation to deploy EC2 application instances and a DynamoDB table. The application must read and update that table using the AWS SDK. The template and instance configuration must not contain long-term AWS access keys.

Which template configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an IAM user and an access key resource with DynamoDB permissions. Pass the access key and secret access key to the instances through user data.
Create a role with DynamoDB permissions and store its ARN in Systems Manager Parameter Store. Set each instance's IamInstanceProfile property to that role ARN.
Accept an IAM user's access key and secret access key as NoEcho template parameters and write their values into the application configuration through user data.

Create an IAM role trusted by the EC2 service with permissions scoped to the table. Create an IAM instance profile containing that role and reference the profile from each instance's IamInstanceProfile property.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. The EC2 trust policy allows the service to use the role, the role policy authorizes the required DynamoDB actions, and the instance profile associates the role with the instance. The SDK retrieves and refreshes temporary role credentials through instance metadata.

<<1>> provisions long-term credentials and distributes them in user data. <<2>> creates configuration containing a role ARN but never creates the required instance profile; a role ARN is not a valid substitute for that profile. <<3>> hides parameter values in some CloudFormation displays but still stores long-term credentials on the instance.

A role, an instance profile and the SDK credential provider have separate jobs: define permissions, attach the role to compute, and obtain temporary credentials. Restrict table and index ARNs and DynamoDB actions to those the application needs.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/TemplateReference/aws-resource-iam-instanceprofile.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/iam-roles-for-amazon-ec2.html

question:
A photo-sharing mobile application will serve millions of users. An existing backend authenticates users and maintains a trusted mapping from each user to an S3 object prefix.
