Each morning, a workflow exports all required raw records to S3, verifies the export, handles late-arriving writes, and produces the users' aggregates. The retention policy permits removing a completed day's records from DynamoDB after this workflow succeeds.

The company wants to retain DynamoDB and reduce both capacity charges and unnecessary table storage. Which TWO changes meet these goals? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Replace the DynamoDB tables with a Multi-AZ RDS database and read replicas, and retain all raw records indefinitely.
Keep every completed day in DynamoDB at peak provisioned capacity, and move frequently accessed S3 aggregates to S3 One Zone-IA.
Purchase DynamoDB reserved capacity sized to the eligible provisioned baseline that will be used throughout the commitment term.
Add an ElastiCache write-back layer that acknowledges events before they reach DynamoDB, and retain every DynamoDB item indefinitely.
Use daily tables, prepare the next table before rollover, and delete a completed table only after its required export and late-write reconciliation have been verified.

explanation.text:
<<3>> and <<5>> are correct. Reserved capacity discounts eligible provisioned read and write capacity in exchange for a commitment, making a stable baseline the relevant purchase quantity. Retiring a fully archived daily table removes data that the stated retention policy no longer requires in DynamoDB.

<<1>> violates the requirement to retain DynamoDB and introduces a database migration without demonstrating a saving.

<<2>> preserves the unnecessary provisioned capacity and DynamoDB storage. A different S3 storage class does not solve either cost identified in the question, and infrequent-access storage must fit access and durability needs.

<<4>> adds another data tier and a potential durability gap before database commit while retaining all stored items. It is not a supported shortcut for reducing authoritative write requirements.

Do not delete a table merely because aggregates exist: the required raw export and late writes must be complete. Reserved capacity covers eligible provisioned capacity, not on-demand request charges. Include daily-table automation and retention checks in the operational design.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [DynamoDB reserved capacity billing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/bp-understanding-billing.html); [DynamoDB time-series tables](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/bp-time-series.html).

question:
A company uses two Direct Connect connections between its data center and AWS. It wants to reduce recurring connectivity cost while retaining a dedicated primary path. During a primary-path outage, the business accepts lower bandwidth and less predictable latency as long as connectivity remains available. An independent internet connection already exists at the data center.

Which design best meets these requirements?

options.text: Keep one Direct Connect connection as the preferred path and configure an AWS Site-to-Site VPN over the independent internet connection as backup. Set routing preferences and test failover and failback.
Keep one Direct Connect connection and configure a second private virtual interface on that same physical connection as the backup path.
Keep one Direct Connect connection and run an IPsec VPN over that connection as the only backup path.
Replace both Direct Connect connections with internet Site-to-Site VPN tunnels, and use VPN CloudHub to route through them.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. The dedicated connection remains the normal path, while the independently routed internet VPN provides a path when that connection fails. This design avoids retaining a second dedicated circuit, with the accepted tradeoff that backup performance differs from Direct Connect. Routing must prefer the intended primary and withdraw or supersede failed routes correctly.

<<2>> adds a logical interface but retains the same physical failure point.

<<3>> can add encryption to traffic carried over Direct Connect, but the VPN is unavailable if its underlying Direct Connect path fails.

<<4>> can provide internet VPN connectivity but removes the dedicated primary path required by the business. CloudHub does not create dedicated network capacity.

A VPN backup is not equivalent to diverse redundant Direct Connect circuits. Validate its throughput, tunnel redundancy, customer equipment, and failover behavior against the reduced-service requirements before removing the second circuit.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Direct Connect redundancy](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/toolkit-classic.html).

question:
An analytics company is an existing customer of the legacy Amazon Glacier vault API. It archives completed datasets containing thousands of files, and rare retrieval requests restore an entire dataset. Users must first find datasets by file ID, name, author, or tags. The retrieval workflow has been tested to finish within a 24-hour delivery objective using asynchronous archive retrieval.

Within this existing vault-based system, which design best combines low-cost archival storage with efficient metadata lookup?

options.text: Compress each completed dataset into an archive and upload it to Glacier. Store its archive ID and searchable metadata in DynamoDB, with lookup keys and indexes for the supported searches. Use the resulting archive ID to initiate retrieval and download the completed job output.
Keep all completed datasets in S3 Standard and index the object keys and searchable metadata in DynamoDB. Do not transition the data to an archival storage class.
Store compressed datasets in S3 Glacier storage classes and metadata as separate S3 objects. Use only the S3 ListObjects API to query arbitrary author and tag fields inside those metadata objects.
Upload each dataset to Glacier with a descriptive archive name. Use a vault search API to find archives by file ID, author, and tags without maintaining a separate index.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. The archival payload and the searchable catalog have different jobs. DynamoDB provides indexed lookups that return the archive ID, while Glacier stores the rarely retrieved dataset. The legacy retrieval workflow first creates a job and later downloads its output. Whole-dataset retrieval makes bundling appropriate for the stated access pattern.

<<2>> supports the catalog but retains cold data in a higher-access storage tier instead of using the existing archival workflow.

<<3>> uses valid archival storage but assumes that listing S3 objects can query arbitrary fields inside metadata documents. It needs a suitable query/index layer.

<<4>> assumes a rich metadata-search API that the vault service does not provide. Preserve the archive identifiers in an external catalog.

The legacy vault service is closed to new customers. New architectures should evaluate S3 Glacier storage classes. Retrieval time, download time, and decompression must all fit the objective; bundling can be inefficient when callers usually need only one file.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Legacy Glacier archive retrieval](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazonglacier/latest/dev/downloading-an-archive-two-steps.html); [DynamoDB key conditions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/Query.KeyConditionExpressions.html).

question:
A mobile game's backend exposes REST APIs and stores small player-session records on a central file server. Traffic varies sharply, and each backend operation is short-lived and stateless once session state is externalized. The company wants to retain the REST contract, use managed per-client API keys and usage plans for metering and throttling, and authenticate players separately. It also wants to avoid managing application servers and reduce session lookup latency.

Which architecture best meets these requirements?

options.text: Run the backend on EC2 behind a Network Load Balancer and move session records to Aurora. Implement client metering and throttling in the application.
Run the backend in Lambda behind an ALB and store sessions in DynamoDB. Use ALB listener rules as the managed per-client usage-plan system.

Expose a REST API through API Gateway with usage plans and a suitable authorizer, invoke Lambda for game logic, and store keyed session records in DynamoDB with capacity configured for the traffic profile.
Replace the REST API with an AppSync GraphQL API, invoke Lambda for game logic, and store player sessions in DynamoDB.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. API Gateway REST APIs provide the requested API-key and usage-plan features while a separate authorizer enforces player identity and access. Lambda fits the specified short-lived stateless operations, and keyed DynamoDB records replace the shared file server for session access. Size capacity and concurrency for peaks; DynamoDB on-demand mode or correctly provisioned capacity with scaling can be appropriate.

<<1>> retains application-server administration and custom implementation of the API-management features.

<<2>> correctly uses a supported ALB-to-Lambda integration, but ALB listener rules do not provide API Gateway's managed usage plans and API-key metering.

<<4>> changes the client-facing contract from REST to GraphQL, violating the compatibility requirement.

API keys identify API clients for usage management; they are not player authentication credentials. Usage-plan throttles and quotas are best effort, and they should not be treated as a strict security or spending boundary.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [API Gateway usage plans](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/api-gateway-api-usage-plans.html).

question:
A publisher runs a stateless web fleet across multiple Availability Zones. Existing EC2 reservations cover its continuously used On-Demand baseline, and peak utilization currently reaches 90%. The company will add enough healthy headroom to sustain its required service level during an AZ failure. Capacity above that protected baseline is interruption-tolerant, and the company wants to use Spot pricing for this flexible portion.

Which fleet design best meets these availability and purchasing requirements?

options.text: Use an all-Spot Auto Scaling group behind an ALB, including for the capacity that must remain available without Spot interruption.
Use an all-On-Demand Auto Scaling group behind an ALB, including for every flexible burst instance.

Use a mixed-instances Auto Scaling group behind an ALB across AZs. Maintain the required On-Demand baseline and tested headroom, and use diversified Spot pools for the interruption-tolerant capacity above it.
Use an all-Spot fleet in a single AZ behind an ALB, and request replacement Spot instances in another AZ only after an outage.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. A mixed group expresses the purchase boundary directly: sufficient On-Demand capacity for the required baseline, with Spot used where interruption is acceptable. Multiple AZs and instance pools reduce concentration, while preexisting healthy headroom addresses the time before replacements become ready. Eligible reservations discount the On-Demand usage.

<<1>> exposes the protected baseline to Spot interruption.

<<2>> can provide the required capacity but does not use the requested Spot pricing for the flexible portion.

<<4>> concentrates the fleet in one AZ and waits until failure to obtain capacity that is not guaranteed to be available.

Spot savings do not create availability headroom. A fleet at 90% utilization can overload its surviving AZs after an outage, regardless of purchase model. Reserved Instances are a billing benefit, not a separate running-instance type. AWS now recommends EC2 Fleet or Auto Scaling groups over the legacy Spot Fleet API.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Mixed-instances Auto Scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/ec2-auto-scaling-mixed-instances-groups.html); [Spot Fleet status](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/spot-fleet-automatic-scaling.html).

question:
A company ingests a reading from each of 20,000 sensors every 15 minutes into DynamoDB. A common query retrieves one sensor's readings for the previous seven days. The retention policy keeps the current calendar week and eight complete prior weeks, then retires an expired week as a unit. Older weekly data receives far less traffic than the current week.

Which table and key design most directly supports efficient queries and whole-week retirement?

options.text: Use one table with timestamp as the partition key and sensor ID as the sort key.
Use one table per calendar week with sensor ID as the partition key and timestamp as the sort key. Query each weekly table that overlaps the requested interval and merge the results.
Use one table per calendar week with sensor ID and timestamp concatenated into a single partition key, with no sort key.
Use one table for all readings with sensor ID and timestamp concatenated into a single partition key, with no sort key.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. A DynamoDB Query can select one sensor by partition-key equality and a time interval by a sort-key range. Weekly tables also allow older capacity to be reduced and a fully expired week to be deleted without issuing individual item deletes. A rolling seven-day interval can overlap two weekly tables, so query both and combine the results.

<<1>> places each timestamp in a separate partition-key value. It cannot use one sensor equality condition with a timestamp range as the primary-table Query.

<<3>> preserves weekly retirement but a concatenated partition key requires the complete key for direct lookup. It does not support a range over all timestamps for a sensor.

<<4>> has the same key-query limitation and does not support deleting a whole week by dropping its table.

The composite primary key consists of both partition and sort key. A single table with that same composite key and TTL is another valid design when its retention semantics fit; it is not one of the offered schemas.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [DynamoDB key conditions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/Query.KeyConditionExpressions.html); [DynamoDB time-series tables](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/bp-time-series.html).

question:
A financial company uses EC2, RDS, S3, CloudFront, and IAM across all enabled Regions of one AWS account. It needs a durable audit history of resource-management API activity from the console, SDKs, and CLI. The logs must be confidential, cryptographically verifiable for tampering, and retained without deletion for the company's fixed retention period.

Which solution provides the required controls?

options.text: Create a multi-Region CloudTrail trail that includes global service events and management events. Deliver logs to a restricted S3 bucket using SSE-KMS, enable log-file integrity validation and validate the digests, and apply Object Lock compliance retention to the delivered log versions.
Collect application and operating-system logs with the CloudWatch agent in every Region. Encrypt the log groups with KMS and use them as the complete history of AWS resource-management API calls.
Create a single-Region CloudTrail trail in us-east-1 with global service events. Encrypt its restricted S3 destination, validate its log digests, and apply Object Lock compliance retention.
Create a multi-Region CloudTrail trail with global service events and a restricted SSE-KMS S3 destination. Use S3 versioning alone for immutable retention, without log-file integrity validation.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. CloudTrail supplies the API audit history, including the relevant regional and global-service management activity. SSE-KMS and access policies protect confidentiality. Signed digest validation supplies evidence of modification or deletion, and Object Lock compliance mode protects retained object versions from deletion or overwrite during the configured period.

<<2>> collects useful workload telemetry but does not automatically capture every AWS control-plane API action, such as an IAM policy update made through the console.

<<3>> protects the logs it collects but misses management activity in other Regions. Global-service event inclusion is not equivalent to multi-Region coverage.

<<4>> omits cryptographic log validation and confuses recoverable versions with immutable retention. Privileged users can delete ordinary versions when authorized.

Enabling integrity validation causes digest delivery; verification must still be performed. A trail need not be split by console, SDK, or CLI. Add appropriate data-event selectors separately when object or other data-plane operations must also be audited.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [CloudTrail Region and global-service coverage](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-concepts.html); [CloudTrail log integrity validation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/en_en/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-log-file-validation-intro.html); [CloudTrail SSE-KMS encryption](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/encrypting-cloudtrail-log-files-with-aws-kms.html); [S3 Object Lock](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html).

question:
A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled. A central account owns resources that AWS Resource Access Manager supports sharing. The company wants to automate sharing with entire organizational units, including future member accounts, without ordinary invitation exchanges. RAM organization integration has not yet been enabled.

Which setup correctly enables this capability?

options.text: Create a general-purpose cross-account IAM role in each member account and configure the automation to assume those roles instead of enabling RAM integration.

From an authorized principal in the management account, run aws ram enable-sharing-with-aws-organization. Then create RAM resource shares for the supported resources and the intended OU principals with appropriate permissions.
Create the AWSServiceRoleForResourceAccessManager role manually, change its trust policy to allow the company's automation, and use it as the automation's cross-account execution role.
Run only aws organizations enable-aws-service-access for ram.amazonaws.com. Create OU resource shares without running the RAM integration operation or creating its required service-linked role.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. The RAM operation enables organization sharing and creates the service-linked role that RAM uses to read organization structure. After integration, resource shares can name the intended organization or OUs, and ordinary invitation exchange is unnecessary for those shares. Resource selection, principals, and share permissions still require configuration.

<<1>> creates a different cross-account automation pattern. It does not enable RAM organization principals or automatically establish resource shares.

<<3>> repurposes a service-linked role that only RAM is intended to assume. Use an ordinary least-privilege execution role for custom automation.

<<4>> enables only the Organizations side. AWS specifically requires the RAM console or its integration command to ensure that the RAM service-linked role is created.

The equivalent Enable sharing with AWS Organizations action in the RAM console is valid. The distinction is the RAM integration workflow versus an incomplete Organizations-only step, not console versus CLI.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Enable RAM organization sharing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ram/latest/userguide/getting-started-sharing.html); [RAM integration CLI operation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/ram/enable-sharing-with-aws-organization.html).

question:
A company uses consolidated billing in AWS Organizations. One business-unit account has purchased EC2 Reserved Instances for a workload that will launch in three months. Finance requires that the account neither share its RI discounts with other member accounts nor receive their shared discounts. The account must remain in the organization, and sharing among the other accounts must continue.

Which change meets these requirements?

options.text: Have an administrator in the business-unit member account set the purchased reservations to private visibility in the EC2 console.
Remove the business-unit account from the organization and pay its charges separately until the workload launches.

Have an authorized management-account administrator deactivate Reserved Instance and Savings Plans discount sharing for the business-unit account in Billing preferences, leaving the other accounts enabled.
Attach an SCP to the business-unit account that denies PurchaseReservedInstancesOffering and ModifyReservedInstances, while leaving the billing sharing preferences enabled.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. The management account controls reservation discount sharing in Billing preferences. Disabling sharing for the specified account isolates its discount participation while preserving sharing among the other enabled accounts.

<<1>> assumes a reservation visibility setting in a member account that is not the billing control for organization sharing.

<<2>> breaks the requirement to retain organization membership and its centralized governance.

<<4>> restricts API actions for purchasing or modifying reservations. It does not change how existing reservation discounts are allocated on the bill.

The reservation commitment remains payable while unused, so isolating discounts before the workload launches can increase the organization's effective cost. Current sharing controls also support account groups, but the requirement here is no sharing to or from this one account.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Reservation discount sharing preferences](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awsaccountbilling/latest/aboutv2/ri-turn-off.html).

question:
An administrator attaches an SCP with explicit denies for several EC2 networking actions to an OU containing a workload account. Interactive calls to those actions from the account's administrator role are denied. However, CloudTrail shows successful calls to the same actions made by Amazon ECS through AWSServiceRoleForECS while it manages application networking.

What explains the difference?

options.text: The default FullAWSAccess SCP overrides explicit denies whenever the calling principal has administrator permissions.
An allow statement on a parent OU takes precedence over a deny statement attached to a child OU.
The ECS cluster was originally created by the workload account's root user, so every later API call associated with the cluster is exempt from SCPs.
The successful calls use a service-linked role, and SCPs do not restrict permissions attached to service-linked roles.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. The relevant distinction is the caller shown in CloudTrail. AWSServiceRoleForECS is a service-linked role, and such roles are outside SCP restrictions. An ordinary administrator role in the member account remains subject to the explicit deny.

<<1>> misstates deny precedence. FullAWSAccess does not override a matching explicit deny for a principal to which SCPs apply, and SCPs do not independently grant administrator permissions.

<<2>> reverses the hierarchy's effect. An applicable explicit deny is not canceled by an allow on an ancestor.

<<3>> invents a resource-creator exemption. Member-account root activity is generally subject to SCPs, and a resource's creator does not determine the permissions of later callers.

Distinguish service-linked roles from ordinary service execution roles, such as application task roles. The exemption is not a blanket rule that all actions related to an AWS service bypass organization controls.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [SCP scope and exceptions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps.html); [SCP evaluation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps_evaluation.html).

question:
A company has separate AWS accounts for finance, engineering, and human resources. Local administrators manage IAM permissions in each account. Central security needs to prohibit selected AWS services for particular departments, and those restrictions must also apply to the root users of the member accounts. The company wants policy inheritance by department without custom enforcement scripts.

Which solution best meets these requirements?

options.text: Group accounts into Organizations OUs and distribute an IAM policy to each current administrator role. Allow local administrators to manage the role policies.
Create a cross-account administration role in every account and have central security use those roles to audit service usage after resources are created.
Federate employee sign-in through an identity provider and assign restricted permissions only to the federated employee roles.
Use AWS Organizations with all features enabled, group accounts into departmental OUs, and attach SCPs that restrict the selected services for those member accounts.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. OU-attached SCPs provide centrally inherited limits on the permissions available to affected member-account principals, including their root users for actions within SCP scope. Local administrators cannot override an applicable SCP deny by adding a broader IAM allow.

<<1>> restricts selected roles, can be changed by the described local administrators, and does not constrain the account root user through an identity policy.

<<2>> enables administration and auditing but does not itself impose the required preventive service boundary.

<<3>> controls one sign-in path while leaving other principals and root outside that role policy.

SCPs set limits; normal IAM or resource-policy permissions are still needed to grant access. They do not restrict principals in the Organizations management account or service-linked roles. Keep workloads in member accounts and test restrictions before broad OU deployment.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [SCP scope and exceptions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps.html); [SCP evaluation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps_evaluation.html).

question:
A central employee-registry application runs in a VPC in one AWS Region. Servers in three departmental VPCs need private access to it, and the VPC CIDRs do not overlap. The security team wants source addresses for traffic rejected by security groups or network ACLs, with automated notifications in its separate security account. A short log-delivery delay is acceptable.

Which design meets these requirements with the least network-appliance administration?

options.text: Deploy and maintain VPN appliances between every departmental VPC and the central VPC. Collect REJECT VPC Flow Logs and build a central SNS notification processor.

Create VPC peering connections with appropriate routes and security rules. Send REJECT VPC Flow Logs to CloudWatch Logs, forward them through a cross-account destination to Kinesis in the security account, and process matching records to publish SNS notifications.
Create VPC peering connections and collect only ALB HTTP access logs. Notify security when an ALB log entry shows a request rejected by a security group or network ACL.
Connect the VPCs through a Transit Gateway and stream REJECT VPC Flow Logs to a central Kinesis stream. Rely on the log subscription itself to send notifications to the security team.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. Peering provides direct private connectivity for this small set of nonoverlapping VPCs. Flow Logs capture network-interface traffic metadata, including recorded source addresses and REJECT actions. A supported cross-account subscription path centralizes those records, and an explicit processing and SNS step generates notifications.

<<1>> can be engineered to carry traffic and alert on logs, but adds VPN appliances, patching, and tunnel administration that peering avoids.

<<3>> relies on application-layer logs for packets rejected before reaching the ALB application path. Those logs cannot replace VPC Flow Logs for the stated network-control denials.

<<4>> supplies connectivity and transport of log records but omits the notification mechanism. A subscription delivers data to its destination, not automatically to a human recipient.

Configure return routes and security rules as well as the peering links. Flow Logs are aggregated, best-effort telemetry rather than packet capture or a guaranteed immediate alert, and REJECT is not an HTTP authorization status.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [VPC peering](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/peering/what-is-vpc-peering.html); [VPC Flow Logs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/flow-logs.html); [VPC flow record fields](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/flow-log-records.html); [Cross-account log subscriptions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/CrossAccountSubscriptions.html).

question:
A company runs EC2 and RDS workloads in several AWS Regions and manages access through IAM. Security needs durable audit records of management API activity across every enabled Region, including global-service events. Logs must be readable only by authorized auditors, encrypted with a customer managed KMS key, and independently verifiable for alteration after delivery.

Which design meets all of these requirements?

options.text: Create a single-Region trail in us-east-1 that includes global-service events. Send management events to a restricted S3 bucket with SSE-KMS, enable signed digest delivery, and schedule integrity validation.

Create a multi-Region trail with global-service management events and a restricted SSE-KMS S3 destination. Use SNS log-delivery notifications as the sole evidence that delivered files have not been altered.
Create a multi-Region trail with global-service management events. Use a restricted S3 bucket with SSE-S3 encryption, enable signed digest delivery, and schedule integrity validation.

Create a multi-Region trail that records management events and includes global-service events. Deliver to a restricted S3 bucket using the customer managed KMS key, permit CloudTrail delivery and authorized auditor decryption, and enable and regularly perform log-file integrity validation.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. Multi-Region coverage and global-service inclusion address different event sources. Restricted S3 access and the KMS key policy protect confidentiality. CloudTrail log-file integrity validation supplies signed digest files, and a separate validation process uses them to detect changes to the delivered log history.

<<1>> includes global services but omits management activity for regional resources outside the single trail Region. Including IAM events does not make a single-Region trail multi-Region.

<<2>> reports delivery, not subsequent integrity. An SNS notification cannot cryptographically establish that a log object is unchanged.

<<3>> encrypts the objects, but fails the explicit customer managed KMS key requirement. SSE-S3 and SSE-KMS are distinct encryption choices.

Enable digest delivery and actually validate it; enabling the feature does not run validation automatically. Encryption does not establish tamper evidence, and tamper detection does not itself prevent deletion. Trail event collection covers supported API activity regardless of whether the caller used the console, an SDK, or the CLI, so those interfaces do not require separate trails.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [CloudTrail Region and global-service coverage](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-concepts.html); [CloudTrail SSE-KMS encryption](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/encrypting-cloudtrail-log-files-with-aws-kms.html); [CloudTrail log integrity validation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/en_en/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-log-file-validation-intro.html).

question:
A company must connect its on-premises headquarters privately to VPCs in several US Regions. The VPC CIDRs do not overlap. Traffic must use dedicated connectivity, remain available after a Direct Connect location fails, and avoid a separate physical connection for every Region. The requirement is headquarters-to-VPC access, not transit between VPCs.

Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a LAG with two Direct Connect connections at one location. Connect private VIFs to a Direct Connect gateway and associate a virtual private gateway from each VPC.
Connect a Transit Gateway in each Region to headquarters through redundant internet-based Site-to-Site VPN tunnels, and configure routes for the VPCs.

Use redundant customer devices and Direct Connect connections at two diverse locations. Connect private VIFs to a Direct Connect gateway, associate each VPC's virtual private gateway, and configure redundant BGP routes.
Connect redundant Direct Connect circuits directly to one VPC. Peer that VPC with the other regional VPCs and route their headquarters traffic through the peered VPC's connection.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. A Direct Connect gateway can associate virtual private gateways in multiple Regions, avoiding a physical circuit per Region. Private VIFs provide the relevant VPC connectivity. Diverse physical locations and customer devices remove the single-location failure present in a one-location design, provided routing and capacity support failover.

<<1>> aggregates connections but leaves a shared location dependency. Multiple links in one LAG do not satisfy the stated location-failure requirement.

<<2>> provides a valid managed network pattern, but its internet-based VPN paths do not meet the dedicated-connectivity constraint.

<<4>> assumes unsupported edge-to-edge routing. A peered VPC cannot use its peer's Direct Connect connection to reach the corporate network.

Separate logical reachability from physical resilience. A Direct Connect gateway is global and supports the multi-Region associations, but does not make a single physical circuit redundant or establish an automatic VPC transit mesh. A Transit Gateway association would use a transit VIF, rather than this private-VIF-to-VGW design.

question:
A media company shares S3 objects, KMS cryptographic operations, and OpenSearch domain APIs with approved principals in other AWS accounts. Callers must use their existing credentials without assuming a role in the resource account. Network reachability is already configured. Security also needs ongoing evaluation of the shared resources' policy configurations against approved-account rules.

Which approach best meets these requirements?

options.text: Grant callers identity-based IAM permissions in their own accounts and leave the resource policies without cross-account permissions. Use AWS Config rules to evaluate the resource configurations.
Create cross-account roles in the resource account, grant the required service permissions, and require callers to assume those roles. Use AWS Config rules to evaluate the policies.

Configure the bucket, key, and domain resource policies to authorize approved external principals, with corresponding permissions in the caller accounts. Use appropriate AWS Config recording and managed or custom rules to evaluate the relevant policy configurations.

Attach SCP allow statements for the shared resources to the caller accounts, without adding cross-account resource permissions. Use AWS Config rules to evaluate compliance with the approved-account list.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. For supported operations, resource-based policies allow direct cross-account requests using the caller's current identity. The resource account authorizes the external principal, and the caller account supplies the corresponding identity permissions. AWS Config rules can evaluate the relevant configurations when the required resource recording and managed or custom checks are configured.

<<1>> supplies only one side of cross-account authorization. A caller-account allow does not independently authorize access to another account's resources.

<<2>> is a valid cross-account pattern, but the assumed-role session uses the target role's permissions and fails the requirement to keep the existing caller identity for these requests.

<<4>> mistakes a permissions boundary for an access grant. SCPs limit available permissions and cannot replace either the resource-side permission or the caller's identity policy.

An account principal delegates authority to that account rather than identifying one employee. Scope allowed principals and actions carefully, and honor applicable explicit denies. KMS cross-account access is limited to supported operations and needs key-policy and IAM permissions. OpenSearch network and fine-grained authorization controls remain relevant. A generic check of IAM policies alone does not audit every bucket, key, and domain policy.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Cross-account resource access](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies-cross-account-resource-access.html); [Cross-account KMS permissions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/key-policy-modifying-external-accounts.html); [AWS Config rule evaluation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/evaluate-config.html); [SCP scope and exceptions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps.html).

question:
A fitness application assigns North American DNS clients to a US Region and Asian DNS clients to an Asia Region. This geographic business rule takes precedence over distance or latency. Healthy fallback is allowed, and unmatched locations need a default route.

Both Regions need a multi-AZ application tier. The MySQL-compatible database requires one authoritative writer and permits regional reads with bounded staleness. A tested recovery runbook promotes a secondary Region during a primary failure and accounts for replication lag.

Which choices implement the routing and application/database design? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use Route 53 geoproximity routing with distance biases as the sole mechanism for enforcing the continent-to-Region assignment.
Use Route 53 latency routing as the sole mechanism for enforcing the continent-to-Region assignment.
Use Route 53 geolocation records with a default and health-aware fallback hierarchy to direct clients to the regional ALBs.
Deploy multi-AZ application tiers and independent writable Aurora clusters in both Regions. Update the same records locally in each cluster and merge database changes nightly.

Deploy an ALB and multi-AZ EC2 Auto Scaling group in each Region. Use Aurora Global Database with one primary write Region and a secondary read Region, send writes through the global writer endpoint and eligible reads to regional readers, and use the tested database recovery runbook.

explanation.text:
<<3>> and <<5>> are correct. Geolocation records implement the explicit continent mapping, while a default covers unmatched or unresolved geography. Health-aware record trees permit the stated fallback. Regional application tiers and Aurora Global Database provide regional read access while retaining one authoritative primary writer.

<<1>> chooses by geographic distance and optional bias, which does not reliably enforce the required continent assignments.

<<2>> optimizes latency, a different objective from the business rule.

<<3>> needs correctly configured endpoint health checks or alias target-health evaluation throughout the routing hierarchy. Geolocation alone is not an application-readiness check.

<<4>> creates two independent writers to the same logical data and requires conflict resolution. Nightly merging does not implement the requested single authoritative writer.

<<5>> separates database promotion from DNS routing. After the database recovery operation, the global writer endpoint follows the primary. Cross-Region replication is asynchronous, so applications must enforce acceptable read staleness and account for possible data loss during an unplanned failover.

DNS geography reflects the query's inferred source location, not a verified customer address. A routing change does not promote a database, and multi-AZ capacity inside a Region does not replace multi-Region recovery.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Route 53 geolocation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/routing-policy-geo.html); [Route 53 health-aware record trees](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/dns-failover-complex-configs.html); [Aurora Global Database](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/aurora-global-database.html).

question:
Several business units have their own AWS accounts but share EC2 instances, EKS clusters, and Aurora Serverless clusters in a central production account. Developers must be able to delete only resources owned by their business unit. A central provisioning team assigns protected ownership tags, and developers must not be able to change those tags or the access policies.

Which multi-account access design meets these requirements?

options.text: Create one production role trusted by all business units with deletion permissions for all shared resources. Record the initiating business unit in CloudTrail for later review.
Group business-unit accounts into OUs and attach SCPs that allow deletion of resources tagged for each unit. Rely on those SCPs alone to grant cross-account access to production.

Create a separate production role for each business unit. Restrict its trust to the corresponding business-unit principals, authorize those principals to assume it, and scope supported deletion actions to that unit's resource ARNs or protected ownership tags. Protect the tags and role policies from developer changes.
Create a production role for each business unit with deletion permissions scoped to that unit's resources. Permit every business unit to assume every production role for operational convenience.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. The role trust policy and the caller's permissions determine who may assume the role. The production role's permission policy determines which resources that session may delete. Restricting both boundaries and protecting ownership metadata prevents a developer from selecting another unit's role or relabeling another unit's resource.

<<1>> records misuse after it happens but gives every caller the ability to delete another unit's resources. Attribution is not a preventive authorization boundary.

<<2>> uses organization guardrails as though they grant access. OUs group accounts, and SCPs restrict permissions; neither grants a principal cross-account role access or the required resource permissions.

<<4>> scopes resources within each role but leaves role selection unrestricted. A developer can assume another unit's role and gain that unit's deletion permissions.

Use service-appropriate actions and resource conditions: EC2 termination, EKS DeleteCluster, and RDS DeleteDBCluster have their own authorization definitions. Scope related actions as needed and prevent policy or tag changes that bypass ownership checks. EKS cluster deletion through the AWS API is separate from permission to manipulate Kubernetes objects inside a cluster.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Cross-account resource access](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies-cross-account-resource-access.html); [SCP scope and exceptions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps.html); [EC2 resource-scoped permissions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ExamplePolicies_EC2.html); [EKS action authorization](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/service-authorization/latest/reference/list_eks.html); [RDS action authorization](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/service-authorization/latest/reference/list_rds.html).

question:
A software company uses separate development and test accounts in AWS Organizations with consolidated billing. Administrators authenticate centrally and must stop or delete specified resources in both accounts when budgets are exceeded. They must use temporary credentials and receive only the required resource-management permissions.

Which access design meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a role only in the management account and attach policies naming development and test resource ARNs, without configuring access in either target account.
Create scoped resource-management roles in the development and test accounts that trust the central administrators' designated principal. Permit that principal to assume the roles.
Create target-account roles with trust for central administrators but no permissions policies, relying on the administrators' management-account permissions to carry into each session.
Grant the central administrators access to consolidated billing and rely on the organization's billing relationship to authorize resource-management API calls in member accounts.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. The roles live in the accounts that own the resources. Their trust policies establish who can assume them, and their permissions policies define which local resources the resulting sessions can manage. The central principal also needs permission to make the cross-account AssumeRole calls.

<<1>> supplies a caller-side policy but no authorization in the target accounts. <<3>> mistakes trust for workload permission: a trusted session does not inherit the caller's existing management-account privileges. <<4>> confuses consolidated payment with authorization to operate resources.

Central authentication, target-account authorization and billing consolidation are separate concerns. Use identifiable sessions and narrowly scoped actions, resources and conditions rather than distributing long-term keys or granting blanket administration.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/STS/latest/APIReference/API_AssumeRole.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_accounts_access.html

question:
EC2 instances download updates over HTTPS from an approved set of vendor hostnames. The vendors change their IP addresses, and the applications support explicit proxy settings. The company must block connections to other internet hosts and prevent workloads from bypassing the restriction. Filtering encrypted URL paths is not required.

Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Move the instances to private subnets and add static routes for the vendors' current IP addresses through a NAT gateway. Leave those routes unchanged when vendor addresses change.
Create network ACL rules that permit TCP 443 to the vendors' current IP addresses and deny other traffic, using the ACL as a hostname allowlist.
Allow outbound TCP 443 to 0.0.0.0/0 in the workload security group and rely on HTTPS certificate validation to restrict traffic to approved vendors.

Configure the applications to use a restricted forward proxy that allows only the approved HTTPS destinations. Remove workload internet bypass paths and permit only the required proxy connections, while providing controlled internet egress for the proxy.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. The forward proxy evaluates the destination hostname, and the network configuration forces the workloads to use that enforcement point. Restrict who can reach the proxy, configure every relevant client, and retain the proxy's own controlled path to the internet.

<<1>> is tied to a changing IP list and does not provide hostname policy enforcement. <<2>> uses an IP/protocol/port control as if it understood hostnames. <<3>> allows any HTTPS destination; certificate validation authenticates a server's identity but does not make it an approved destination.

For supported HTTPS traffic, a proxy can restrict CONNECT destinations or inspect visible TLS server names without reading encrypted URL paths. Those capabilities must match the clients' protocol behavior. An HTTP proxy is an application endpoint, not automatically a route-table next hop. Test both allowed downloads and attempts to bypass the proxy.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/how-to-set-up-an-outbound-vpc-proxy-with-domain-whitelisting-and-content-filtering/

question:
An unversioned S3 bucket contains four configuration objects: NA, LA, EUR and ASIA. The company enables S3 Versioning and waits for the setting to propagate. It then uploads a new object named OCEANIA. Later, it replaces the contents of NA, LA and OCEANIA with one PUT request per object. EUR and ASIA are unchanged, and no versions are deleted.

Which statements describe the final object versions? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The original versions of NA and LA are assigned version ID 1 when versioning is enabled.
EUR and ASIA each receive a new opaque version ID when the bucket's versioning setting changes.
NA, LA and OCEANIA each have two versions. The original versions of NA and LA retain the null version ID.
The latest versions of NA and LA retain the null version ID because those object keys existed before versioning was enabled.
EUR and ASIA each still have one version with the null version ID.

explanation.text:
<<3>> and <<5>> are correct. Enabling versioning leaves existing objects unchanged, including their null version IDs. Each subsequent PUT creates a new version with an S3-generated opaque ID. NA and LA therefore have an old null version and a new generated-ID version. OCEANIA has two generated-ID versions because both writes occurred after versioning was enabled.

<<1>> incorrectly assumes numeric sequence IDs. <<2>> incorrectly treats a bucket setting change as a rewrite of unchanged objects. <<4>> applies the original version's null ID to later PUTs, which instead create new versions.

Version identity belongs to a particular stored version, not permanently to the key. The visible latest object can change while earlier versions remain retrievable. Tag-only changes do not create new object versions, which is why the scenario specifies PUT replacements.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/versioning-workflows.html

question:
An existing Lambda function receives S3 PUT notifications, performs a required custom transformation, and copies each result to buckets in other accounts. Processing can be delayed, and load tests show that bursts drain within the configured asynchronous event age. The Region has a concurrency quota of 1,000. Critical functions reserve 700 units, and other functions peak at 150 concurrent executions. The new function needs no more than 100 concurrent executions.

Which change limits its impact with the least development effort?

options.text: Set the transformation function's reserved concurrency to 100. Monitor throttling and asynchronous event age, and configure failure handling for events that expire or exhaust retries.
Increase the function timeout to five minutes so throttled requests can wait inside the function until concurrency becomes available.
Move the function to a separate account, add SQS event buffering there, and rebuild the cross-account event and permission configuration.
Add a loop inside the function that checks account concurrency and waits before transforming an object when the account is busy.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. Reserved concurrency caps this function at 100 and sets aside those 100 units exclusively for it. With 700 already reserved for critical functions, 200 remain unreserved, exceeding the measured 150-unit peak of the other functions.

<<2>> changes how long an invocation may run after it starts; it does not let code execute while Lambda is refusing an invocation for lack of capacity. <<3>> can isolate capacity and provide durable buffering but requires substantially more integration work. <<4>> consumes a concurrency slot while its waiting code runs and does not enforce admission before invocation.

Reservations reduce the shared pool even when their function is idle. Provisioned concurrency addresses initialization latency rather than providing this cap. Asynchronous retries and event age are finite, so monitor dropped events and preserve failed work through a destination or dead-letter queue. For sustained backlogs beyond the tested envelope, add durable buffering and revisit the design.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-concurrency.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/invocation-async-error-handling.html

question:
A company runs a web application in us-west-1 and needs a passive disaster-recovery deployment in us-east-1. Each regional deployment must scale automatically and tolerate an Availability Zone failure. The standby application, dependencies and replicated data are already tested and ready to serve the required load. Under normal conditions, the public hostname must resolve only to the primary Region.

Which configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a multi-AZ ALB in us-west-1 and one Auto Scaling group spanning subnets in both Regions, connected through inter-Region VPC peering.

Create a separate multi-AZ ALB and Auto Scaling group in each Region. Configure primary and secondary Route 53 failover alias records for the same hostname, with Evaluate Target Health enabled and ALB target health checks that reflect application readiness.
Create one ALB whose enabled subnets span both regional VPCs and one Auto Scaling group across both Regions. Point a Route 53 alias at that ALB.
Create a separate multi-AZ ALB and Auto Scaling group in each Region. Configure equal-weight Route 53 records for both ALBs and evaluate their health.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. Separate regional ALBs and Auto Scaling groups provide regional application deployments, while Route 53 failover records implement the primary/standby traffic policy. ALB target health and application readiness must represent whether each deployment can actually serve requests.

<<1>> attempts to stretch an Auto Scaling group across Regions. <<3>> also attempts to deploy one ALB across regional VPCs. Both resources have regional deployment boundaries. <<4>> makes both healthy deployments eligible during normal operation, contrary to the passive-standby requirement.

Do not confuse where an ALB is deployed with every possible reachable IP target: remote private-IP targets can be supported in suitable topologies. The failure here is the proposed cross-Region ALB or Auto Scaling group resource itself. DNS health detection, caching and client connection reuse mean failover is not instantaneous; tested standby data and capacity remain prerequisites.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/dns-failover-types.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/attach-load-balancer-asg.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/load-balancer-target-groups.html

question:
A company requires employees in member accounts to provision approved CloudFormation-based products through AWS Service Catalog. Permissions already prevent bypassing that path. All resource types in scope support the required creation-time tagging. The company needs both product-origin identifiers and business tags such as CostCenter and Owner to be applied when resources are provisioned.

Which actions provide these two types of tags? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use an AWS Config required-tags rule with remediation as the mechanism that guarantees every resource has tags at the instant it is created.
Use Service Catalog AutoTags to identify the portfolio, product, provisioning principal and other supported product-origin attributes.
Activate cost allocation tags in Billing and Cost Management to create the required tag keys and values on each new resource.
Define the required business tags in the supported resource Tags properties of the CloudFormation products and configure any required propagation settings.
Run a scheduled Systems Manager Automation document that scans for untagged resources and adds tags after provisioning.

explanation.text:
<<2>> and <<4>> are correct. Service Catalog AutoTags identify a provisioned resource's origin, while the product templates supply the organization's business tags. These serve different purposes and can coexist.

<<1>> detects and remediates a configuration after creation, so it does not guarantee creation-time tagging. <<3>> makes existing eligible tag data available for cost allocation; activation does not apply the tags to resources. <<5>> also acts after creation and leaves a period with missing tags.

Tag support and propagation vary by resource type. Verify the underlying resources, not only the stack's tags, and retain the controls that prevent users from bypassing approved products. Service Catalog AutoTags are supported for the CloudFormation products in this scenario, not Terraform Open Source products, and their original values are not automatically updated when a product's launch path changes.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/servicecatalog/latest/adminguide/autotags.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/TemplateReference/aws-properties-resource-tags.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awsaccountbilling/latest/aboutv2/cost-alloc-tags.html

question:
A company uses AWS Control Tower to govern member accounts. The security team needs one place to manage compliance findings from supported services across those accounts and selected Regions. It also requires preventive controls and automated responses to a defined set of findings.

Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Designate a security member account as Security Hub CSPM delegated administrator. Use central configuration policies for the intended accounts and OUs in the home and linked Regions, aggregate findings, enable the required Control Tower controls, and configure EventBridge response workflows.
Deploy Amazon Detective across the member accounts with StackSets and use its investigation graphs as the sole mechanism for preventive controls, compliance management and remediation.
Collect organization-wide management events in CloudTrail Lake and use SQL queries alone to enforce preventive controls and remediate all security findings.
Enable GuardDuty in each account and export its findings to a central S3 bucket, relying on the export to configure compliance standards and remediate findings.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. Security Hub CSPM supplies central posture and findings management, with explicit configuration policies defining account and Region coverage. Control Tower supplies the selected preventive and detective controls, and configured EventBridge targets perform the required responses. These are distinct responsibilities.

<<2>> provides investigation capabilities, not the full requested governance and response workflow. <<3>> centralizes audit events but does not make queries preventive enforcement or a normalized findings-management system. <<4>> supplies threat detection and exported findings but does not configure the requested compliance standards or automated remediation.

Delegating administration alone is insufficient. Central configuration applies through the associated policies to centrally managed accounts in the home and linked Regions. Findings aggregation also does not execute a corrective action by itself; define matching rules, permissions, response logic and verification.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/securityhub/latest/userguide/start-central-configuration.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/controltower/latest/controlreference/controls.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/securityhub/latest/userguide/securityhub-cwe-all-findings.html

question:
Developers need broad administration of workload services, including EC2, S3, Lambda and RDS, plus organizations:DescribeOrganization. They should not receive general IAM or Organizations administration. The company is choosing an AWS managed policy as an initial baseline and will later replace it with narrower task-specific permissions.

Which policy is the closest fit among these choices?

options.text: PowerUserAccess.
AdministratorAccess.
SystemAdministrator.
ReadOnlyAccess.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. The current PowerUserAccess policy provides broad workload permissions while excluding general IAM, Organizations and account administration from its main allow statement. Separate statements permit selected exceptions, including organizations:DescribeOrganization and DescribeEffectivePolicy.

<<2>> grants full administration, exceeding the intended baseline. <<3>> provides a different job-function action set and does not include the required Organizations description permission. <<4>> does not permit developers to create or configure the workload resources.

PowerUserAccess is broad, not exact least privilege. Its NotAction allow statement is also not an explicit deny of the excluded services. Additional policies can supply permissions unless another applicable control denies them. Review the current managed-policy document and separately scope any required role-passing access.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-managed-policy/latest/reference/PowerUserAccess.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-managed-policy/latest/reference/SystemAdministrator.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-managed-policy/latest/reference/AdministratorAccess.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-managed-policy/latest/reference/ReadOnlyAccess.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_notaction.html

question:
An existing identity broker on EC2 authenticates employees against an on-premises LDAP directory and maps each employee to an approved AWS role. The company has no SAML or OIDC provider. The broker may use only its EC2 instance-role credentials; persistent IAM user keys are prohibited. It must issue temporary AWS credentials to authenticated employees.

Which credential exchange meets these constraints?

options.text: Authorize the broker's instance role to call AssumeRole on approved roles that trust it. After validating the LDAP identity and role mapping, sign the call with instance-role credentials and return the resulting role-session credentials.
Call AssumeRole with the employee's LDAP username and password as the AWS API credentials, without signing as an AWS principal.
Call GetFederationToken with the broker's temporary instance-role credentials after the LDAP login succeeds.
Create an IAM user for each employee and configure IAM to validate that user's password directly against the existing LDAP server.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. The broker uses LDAP to authenticate the employee, then uses its own authorized AWS role session to call STS. The trusted mapping chooses an approved target role, and both caller permissions and target trust must permit the assumption.

<<2>> treats an LDAP password as an AWS request-signing credential. <<3>> selects an API that requires long-term caller credentials rather than the temporary role credentials available here. <<4>> assumes ordinary IAM users provide a direct LDAP password-validation integration.

GetFederationToken is valid in other architectures, but it does not satisfy this caller constraint. Assuming another role from an existing role session is role chaining and limits the new session to at most one hour. Return and protect all three credential components: access key, secret key and session token.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/STS/latest/APIReference/API_AssumeRole.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/STS/latest/APIReference/API_GetFederationToken.html

options.text: The account-level SCP allowlist omits S3, placing CreateBucket outside the permitted action set despite the identity-policy allow.
SCPs do not support allowlists, so every Allow statement in the attached SCP is invalid.
The identity policy's Deny with NotAction s3:* explicitly denies every S3 action.
The identity policy and SCP must contain identical action lists before any allowed action can succeed.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. The action must remain permitted by the SCPs at every level on the account's organization path. This account's only attached SCP allows CloudTrail and IAM but not S3, so the identity-policy allow cannot make CreateBucket effective.

<<2>> is incorrect because SCPs support allowlist designs. <<3>> reverses NotAction: the Deny statement excludes S3 actions from its action match. <<4>> incorrectly requires identical policies; an identity policy can grant a narrower set of permissions than the SCP ceiling.

SCPs limit permissions rather than grant them. Allows from SCPs at the same level are combined, while an applicable explicit deny wins. If FullAWSAccess were also attached at this account level, the missing-S3 conclusion would change. The stem deliberately excludes that additional allow.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps_evaluation.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_notaction.html

question:
A vendor's multi-tenant auditing application runs in the vendor's AWS account and needs a limited set of EC2 discovery API operations in a customer account. The vendor supplies its designated AWS principal and a unique identifier it generated for this customer. The customer prohibits distributing persistent access keys and wants to prevent another vendor customer from causing the vendor to assume this customer's role.

Which configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a role with only the required discovery permissions. Restrict trust to the designated vendor principal and require sts:ExternalId to match the vendor-generated customer identifier.
Create a role that trusts the vendor principal and add the customer identifier only as a role tag, without an ExternalId trust condition.
Provide an administrator's access key and secret key to the vendor, and require the vendor to include the customer identifier in its application logs.
Create a least-privilege IAM user for the vendor and give it persistent access keys, relying on the restricted permissions to prevent confused-deputy access.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. Principal restrictions identify the trusted vendor, and the ExternalId condition checks which customer the vendor is acting for when it requests a session. The role's permissions separately limit the EC2 discovery operations. The vendor must also authorize its own caller to assume the role.

<<2>> stores metadata but does not make the identifier an evaluated trust condition. <<3>> shares excessive, persistent credentials; logging a customer ID does not prevent misuse. <<4>> scopes actions but still distributes prohibited long-term keys and omits the customer-binding role-assumption check.

External IDs are not secrets or per-request restrictions attached to every later API call. They mitigate the confused-deputy problem at AssumeRole. Protect the resulting temporary credentials because possession of a valid session can still permit its authorized actions until the session expires or is otherwise restricted.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/confused-deputy.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_common-scenarios_third-party.html

question:
A company uses AWS Organizations and wants to reject EC2 instance and EBS volume creation in member accounts unless both Owner and CostCenter request tags are present with approved, nonempty values. Users already have the necessary create and tag-on-create permissions. The control must apply centrally to the relevant supported creation APIs, including launches performed directly rather than through templates.

Which approach meets the requirement?

options.text: Use only an IAM Allow condition with ForAllValues:StringEquals on aws:TagKeys containing Owner and CostCenter, treating that condition as proof that both keys and values exist.
Use an AWS Config required-tags rule and notifications to synchronously reject noncompliant resource-creation API requests.

Attach an SCP to the applicable OUs with separate Deny conditions for each missing required aws:RequestTag key and for invalid values. Scope the supported EC2 actions and resource types correctly, and test all launch paths.
Run Systems Manager Automation after resource creation to add missing tags and treat successful remediation as equivalent to rejecting untagged creation.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. A centrally applied explicit deny can reject a supported creation request when either required tag is missing or invalid. Use separate deny statements for the per-key absence checks so one missing key is sufficient to trigger rejection, and validate values separately.

<<1>> checks whether supplied keys belong to the permitted key set. A subset, and even an empty request context without another presence check, can satisfy ForAllValues; that does not prove all mandatory keys exist or their values are valid. <<2>> evaluates recorded configurations after creation rather than acting as a synchronous admission gate. <<4>> also repairs resources after the prohibited untagged state already exists.

RunInstances authorizes multiple resource types, so apply request-tag tests to the intended taggable resources without accidentally denying unrelated launch resources. Tagging during creation also needs CreateTags authorization. SCPs do not grant those permissions, and protection of tags after creation is a separate policy concern.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_condition-single-vs-multi-valued-context-keys.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/en_gb/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/supported-iam-actions-tagging.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/service-authorization/latest/reference/list_ec2.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps_evaluation.html

question:
A company is migrating an NGINX application and an Oracle RAC One Node database to AWS. It must retain the approved RAC deployment model. The database team has validated an EC2 cluster topology, storage and networking, and a cluster-consistent backup procedure using custom Systems Manager pre/post scripts plus Oracle-native log backups. It now needs scheduled EBS snapshot creation and retention with minimal custom scheduling code.

Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Run NGINX on EC2 and migrate the database to an RDS for Oracle RAC cluster with automated backups.
Run NGINX on EC2 and use RDS for Oracle Multi-AZ, assuming that its standby deployment preserves the required RAC One Node model.
Use the validated EC2 database topology and have an administrator run an unscheduled shell script to create EBS snapshots after each maintenance session.

Use the validated EC2 deployment and an instance-targeted Data Lifecycle Manager snapshot policy with the tested pre/post scripts, retention schedule and failure monitoring. Retain the required Oracle-native backup and log procedures.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. Data Lifecycle Manager supplies scheduled snapshot lifecycle management, while the validated scripts and Oracle procedures establish the required application and cluster consistency. Configure failure handling so a failed consistency step is not silently treated as a successful application-consistent backup.

<<1>> assumes an RDS RAC offering that does not exist. <<2>> substitutes RDS Multi-AZ for a different, explicitly required Oracle cluster model. <<3>> preserves the deployment but provides no unattended schedule or managed retention.

A bare EC2 instance and attached EBS volumes do not automatically reproduce RAC networking and shared-storage requirements. Likewise, independent crash-consistent volume snapshots do not prove coordinated cluster recovery. DLM pre scripts run before snapshot initiation and post scripts after initiation, so I/O can resume before snapshot completion. Verify script outcomes, log coverage and restore tests, not only snapshot existence.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Oracle.Concepts.FeatureSupport.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/oracle-database-aws-best-practices/architecting-for-high-availability.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/automate-app-consistent-backups.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/script-flow.html

question:
A company wants to reduce the operating effort of an on-premises web application. It will move the application to Elastic Beanstalk and its compatible relational database to Amazon RDS. The team will adjust deployment packaging and connection settings but preserve the core application architecture and business logic.

Which migration strategy best describes this plan?

options.text: Replatform.
Rehost.
Repurchase.
Refactor or re-architect.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. Replatforming changes selected hosting or platform components to gain cloud operational benefits while preserving the application's core architecture. Moving to managed application deployment and a managed relational database fits that scope.

<<2>> moves the workload with less platform change, commonly retaining self-managed software on cloud virtual machines. <<3>> replaces the existing application with a different product, such as a SaaS offering. <<4>> substantially changes application design or code to adopt a new architecture.

Classify the strategy by what changes, not by the amount of testing required. Rehosting still needs configuration and validation, and replatforming is not universally the cheapest choice. The stated platform changes and preserved business logic make the classification here.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/migration-microsoft-workloads-aws/cloud-paths.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/migration-microsoft-workloads-aws/migrating-net-workloads.html

question:
A company must migrate a SQL Server warehouse with a 60-TB bulk export to Amazon Redshift within 30 days. The existing connection permits 50 Mbps for migration, and new connectivity cannot be provisioned before the deadline. Changes average 50 GB per day. The company has a confirmed Data Transfer Terminal reservation and tested equipment; export, transport, upload and Redshift bulk loading can finish within eight days. Schema conversion and a consistent bulk-export/CDC start-position procedure have been validated, and source logs can be retained through catch-up.

Which migration plan meets these constraints?

options.text: Run a DMS full-load-and-CDC task for the entire 60-TB warehouse over the 50-Mbps connection and rely on the 30-day window to complete the initial load.
Use the Terminal for the bulk copy, import it into an intermediate Oracle RDS database, and then perform a second engine conversion to Redshift. Copy later changes only to the Oracle database.
Wait for a new 1-Gbps Direct Connect connection, then perform the full load from SQL Server to Redshift over that connection.

Apply the validated SCT schema conversion, transfer the consistent bulk export through the Terminal to S3, and load Redshift. Apply SQL Server changes through DMS CDC from the coordinated source position, then reconcile and cut over after catch-up.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. Physical movement of the bulk export avoids the constrained WAN for the 60-TB seed. The existing connection can then carry the much smaller change stream, with CDC aligned to the bulk copy so transactions are neither omitted nor replayed incorrectly.

<<1>> fails the bandwidth test: 60 decimal TB at 50 Mbps takes about 111 days before overhead. <<2>> introduces an unnecessary engine and leaves Redshift without the specified ongoing changes. <<3>> depends on connectivity that cannot arrive within the migration window.

At the ideal link rate, 50 GB of daily changes takes about 2.22 hours to transfer, leaving capacity to catch up after the eight-day bulk phase. Actual feasibility still depends on measured export, transfer and apply performance. Preserve the required transaction logs, validate data types and CDC support, use the correct target preparation mode, and reconcile the target before the final cutover.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/datatransferterminal/latest/userguide/tech-requirements.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/patterns/migrate-an-on-premises-microsoft-sql-server-database-to-amazon-redshift-using-aws-sct-data-extraction-agents.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/dms/latest/userguide/CHAP_Task.CDC.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/dms/latest/userguide/CHAP_Target.Redshift.html

question:
A logistics application uses EC2 web and application tiers, S3 objects and a DynamoDB database. It will run primarily in us-east-1 with a ready standby in us-west-1. The business accepts a measured, nonzero replication lag. The standby must accept new data during an outage, and automatic failback must wait until the primary application and required data are ready. The application already coordinates write ownership during regional transitions.

Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy independent regional stacks through CloudFormation StackSets. Use DynamoDB global tables with multi-Region eventual consistency and two-way S3 replication, including required existing-object and metadata replication. Configure Route 53 failover with automated readiness checks that keep the primary unhealthy until recovery and data reconciliation complete.
Deploy independent regional stacks and Route 53 failover records. Replace DynamoDB with Aurora global database and configure only one-way S3 replication from primary to standby.
Deploy both application tiers in each Region, replace DynamoDB with a cross-Region RDS MySQL read replica, and require an operator to change DNS after every outage and recovery.
Deploy both application tiers in each Region and use CloudFront origin failover. Keep independent DynamoDB tables with daily backups and one-way S3 replication from primary to standby.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. Regional stacks provide ready compute, global tables replicate the NoSQL data, and two-way S3 replication carries new objects written while either Region is active. Automated readiness checks delay the primary's healthy signal until the application and required data can safely serve traffic again.
