<<2>> changes the specified NoSQL database model and omits reverse object replication for standby writes. <<3>> also changes the database model and requires manual routing changes. <<4>> substitutes periodic backups for ongoing database replication and does not provide the required complete application and data failback process.

MREC global tables and S3 replication are asynchronous, so neither promises identical regional data at every instant. Replicate existing S3 objects separately when needed, configure replica metadata synchronization as required, and verify catch-up. Route 53 changes DNS answers; caches and existing connections delay traffic movement. A healthy server alone is insufficient evidence for safe failback.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/GlobalTables.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/replication.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/dns-failover-types.html

question:
A company is moving a virtual-machine application to private EC2 instances. The application must continue reaching on-premises services through private IP addresses over a dedicated connection that avoids internet transit. The company can arrange connectivity to an AWS Direct Connect location.

Which components are required for the proposed Direct Connect path? (Select TWO.)

options.text: An internet gateway attached to the VPC as the termination point for the dedicated private connection.
A customer-side router with the required Ethernet/VLAN capabilities and BGP support, including the configured MD5 authentication key for the virtual-interface session.
A Direct Connect connection and a private virtual interface with appropriate VPC gateway association and routes for the on-premises and VPC prefixes.
An Elastic IP address on each application instance so the on-premises servers can reach the instances over Direct Connect.
A transit VPC with VPN appliances as a substitute for the underlying dedicated circuit.

explanation.text:
<<2>> and <<3>> are correct. The physical connection and private virtual interface establish the private path into the VPC, and BGP exchanges the network prefixes between the customer router and AWS. The virtual-interface BGP configuration includes an MD5 authentication key.

<<1>> does not terminate a Direct Connect private virtual interface. <<4>> is unnecessary because this traffic uses private addressing. <<5>> can be part of a routing architecture, but it does not create the dedicated transport required by the scenario.

Provision the complete path, including customer or partner connectivity to the Direct Connect location, VLAN and BGP configuration, gateway association, routing and security rules. A dedicated path does not imply payload encryption or redundancy. Add those capabilities when the workload requires them.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/toolkit-classic.html

question:
A company is migrating an Oracle database to RDS for PostgreSQL. The source contains tables, views and stored program code that require conversion. The company wants to minimize custom migration tooling and keep the source operational until a planned cutover.

Which approach best meets these requirements?

options.text: Rehost the Oracle server with Application Migration Service, then use a DMS replication task alone to translate all Oracle stored program code into PostgreSQL code.

Use AWS SCT to assess and convert the schema and supported code, manually resolve reported conversion items, and test the target. Use DMS full load and supported CDC to migrate data and catch up before cutover.
Build custom Glue transformations for schema and stored program translation, and use Batch jobs to implement the complete bulk-copy and change-replay process.
Use a DMS replication task with target table creation enabled and assume that creating target tables also converts all views, packages, procedures and application SQL.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. Schema and code conversion prepares the target database structure and behavior, while the DMS replication task transfers rows and supported changes. SCT assessment identifies objects needing manual work, and testing verifies that converted code preserves required behavior.

<<1>> rehosts the server without solving the engine conversion; a data replication task does not translate all stored program code. <<3>> can involve extensive custom engineering and does not minimize migration tooling. <<4>> mistakes basic target table creation for complete schema and code conversion.

AWS DMS also offers a separate Schema Conversion capability, but that is distinct from the replication-only behavior in the distractors. No tool removes the need to assess unsupported features, data types, constraints, logging requirements and application SQL. Validate the load, let changes catch up, and perform a controlled final cutover.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/SchemaConversionTool/latest/userguide/
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/dms/latest/userguide/CHAP_Task.CDC.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/dms/latest/userguide/CHAP_SchemaConversion.html

question:
A VPC contains EC2 clients, an AWS Managed Microsoft AD directory for private.example.com, and a Kinesis interface endpoint with private DNS enabled. VPC DNS support and DNS hostnames are enabled. The company wants clients to keep using AmazonProvidedDNS and resolve both the AWS private endpoint name and the AD namespace through centrally managed VPC configuration, without per-client split-DNS settings.

Which actions should the solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create a Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint with reachable endpoint IPs and security rules for DNS forwarding, while retaining AmazonProvidedDNS as the client resolver.
Create a Resolver FORWARD rule for private.example.com using that outbound endpoint and the two directory DNS IPs as targets. Associate the rule with the client VPC.
Create a Resolver inbound endpoint instead of an outbound endpoint to send the clients' AD queries to the directory DNS servers.
Configure each EC2 client with separate local resolver rules that send AD queries to the directory and other queries to AmazonProvidedDNS.
Create a Directory Service conditional forwarder that sends private.example.com queries from the AD DNS servers back to AmazonProvidedDNS, without a VPC Resolver forwarding rule.

explanation.text:
<<1>> and <<2>> are correct. Clients send queries to AmazonProvidedDNS. The domain-specific Resolver rule forwards AD queries through the outbound endpoint to the directory DNS servers, while AWS private endpoint names continue to use normal VPC DNS resolution. Permit both UDP and TCP DNS traffic along the forwarding path.

<<3>> reverses the direction: inbound endpoints accept queries entering the VPC Resolver from other networks. <<4>> can implement client-side split DNS, but violates the central-management requirement. <<5>> forwards in the wrong direction and does not teach AmazonProvidedDNS where the AD namespace is authoritative; it can also create a forwarding loop in a combined configuration.

A Resolver rule references an outbound endpoint and is associated with a VPC; it is not a conditional-forwarder object stored inside that endpoint. Keep the private DNS and VPC DNS settings enabled for AWS service endpoint resolution.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resolver-forwarding-outbound-queries.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/privatelink-access-aws-services.html

question:
A company is moving a queued media-processing application to AWS. Each indivisible job averages five minutes and can run for 30 minutes. Upload traffic varies sharply during the day. The application can use S3 object storage and a standard message queue, and has no requirement for a broker-specific protocol or shared filesystem. The company wants elastic worker capacity with an initial queue-delay target of ten minutes.

Which design best meets these requirements without splitting jobs into smaller steps?

options.text: Store inputs in S3, enqueue object references in SQS, and process each complete job in one Lambda invocation with a 30-minute timeout.
Store inputs in EFS and use an Amazon MQ broker with a fixed EC2 fleet sized for peak daytime load, leaving all workers running overnight.
Store inputs in S3 and invoke Lambda from an SQS queue, extending message visibility so that each Lambda invocation can run for 30 minutes.

Store inputs and results in S3 and enqueue object references in SQS. Use EC2 workers in an Auto Scaling group, scale with backlog per worker, extend visibility while processing, and delete a message only after its result is durable.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. EC2 workers can complete the indivisible 30-minute jobs, while SQS buffers variable demand and S3 supplies durable object storage. With one job processed at a time per worker, an initial backlog target is acceptable queue delay divided by average processing time: 10 ÷ 5 = 2 waiting messages per worker. Tune this estimate using measured latency and runtime variation.

<<1>> exceeds the 15-minute maximum for a standard Lambda invocation. <<2>> keeps unnecessary broker, shared-file and peak compute capacity for a workload that needs none of those constraints. <<3>> changes SQS message visibility, not Lambda's execution-duration limit.

Make processing idempotent because standard queues can deliver duplicates. Protect active jobs during scale-in, monitor age and failures, and use a dead-letter queue for repeated failures. If scaling to zero, configure a way to start workers when backlog appears; backlog per worker needs special handling when the worker count is zero.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-using-sqs-queue.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/gettingstarted-limits.html

question:
An engineering company must migrate 1 TB of files to AWS. It can begin preparing ten days before cutover, but writes may be suspended for only six hours on Friday evening. Its existing 50-Mbps link takes about 48 hours to copy the full dataset. Measurements show that repeated file-level synchronizations can keep up with changes and leave no more than 25 GB for the final transfer. The destination application's S3 access and metadata requirements have been validated. Physical transport and a network upgrade would add avoidable cost.

Which migration plan meets the outage limit at the lowest incremental cost?

options.text: Use aws s3 sync to seed the dataset before cutover and repeat incremental synchronizations. Quiesce writes on Friday, synchronize and verify the final changes and deletions, and then switch the application to S3.
Transport a complete export to an approved Data Transfer Terminal reservation and upload it to S3, adding the required travel and facility costs.
Wait until Friday evening, deploy a stored Volume Gateway, and upload a new full copy before restoring it into EBS volumes for the application.
Wait until Friday evening and upload the full dataset to S3 using parallel multipart uploads over the existing link.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. Moving the bulk data while the source remains available leaves only the measured final changes in the outage window. The ideal transfer time for 25 GB at 50 Mbps is about 1.1 hours, leaving room for the measured overhead and validation within six hours.

<<2>> can move data quickly at the facility, but adds unnecessary logistics and expense when the staged online path meets the deadline.

<<3>> starts a full transfer too late and adds a block-storage workflow that the validated S3 destination does not need.

<<4>> cannot remove the access-link bottleneck. Parallel multipart transfers improve utilization and retry behavior, but cannot push 1 TB through a 50-Mbps link in six hours.

File synchronization copies changed files, not just changed blocks inside them. Plan using bytes in changed files, not a percentage of file count. Handle source deletions deliberately, verify data, and freeze writes before the final pass. The full decimal-terabyte transfer has a theoretical minimum of about 44.4 hours; 48 hours is the measured practical estimate, not a physical constant.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [AWS CLI synchronization](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/s3/sync.html). [Data Transfer Terminal](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/datatransferterminal/latest/userguide/what-is-dtt.html).

question:
A financial company wants to replace offsite physical tapes with durable cloud archives. Its existing backup application supports an iSCSI virtual tape library and must retain its tape catalogs, backup jobs, and restore procedures. Completed backup tapes are rarely retrieved, and retrieval delays are acceptable.

Which approach preserves the workflow while reducing long-term storage expense?

options.text: Deploy Tape Gateway, present its virtual tape library to the backup application, and eject completed tapes for archival in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive according to the restore requirement.
Deploy a stored Volume Gateway, rewrite the backup jobs to target iSCSI block volumes, and keep point-in-time EBS snapshots.
Deploy Tape Gateway and retain every completed virtual tape in its online virtual tape library indefinitely, without ejecting tapes for archival.
Deploy S3 File Gateway and rewrite the backup application to create file-based backup sets on its NFS or SMB share.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. Tape Gateway exposes virtual tape drives and a media changer through the interface the backup application already understands. Ejecting a completed virtual tape initiates upload and archival; archived tapes use the selected supported Glacier archive class.

<<2>> offers block storage and snapshots, but does not preserve the virtual-tape interface and existing jobs.

<<3>> preserves tape compatibility but omits the archive transition for tapes that rarely need to be online.

<<4>> offers a file interface and can support file backups, but requires the workflow change that the stem excludes.

The virtual tape shelf is the archive abstraction, not a separate non-Glacier alternative. An archived tape must be retrieved to a gateway before the backup application restores its contents. Select the archive pool for the required retrieval time and retention economics, configure access and encryption, and test restoration with the retained backup catalog.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Tape Gateway](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/storagegateway/latest/tgw/WhatIsStorageGateway.html). [Tape archival and restoration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/storagegateway/latest/tgw/backup_netbackup-vtl.html). [S3 File Gateway interface](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/filegateway/latest/files3/what-is-file-s3.html).

question:
A travel website runs on premises and cannot be migrated before a global campaign begins. Most projected bandwidth is for public, cacheable destination photos. Load testing shows that the existing servers can handle the remaining uncached booking requests. The company also needs HTTP rules for SQL injection and cross-site scripting. Its web servers can act as an HTTPS origin.

Which change meets these requirements before the campaign?

options.text: Place CloudFront in front of the existing origin and associate a WAF web ACL. Cache public images, forward the required dynamic request methods and session data without caching personalized responses, and restrict direct origin access.
Complete a server migration to EC2, configure an ALB and Auto Scaling, and place CloudFront with WAF in front of the new web fleet before accepting campaign traffic.
Copy the public images to an S3 bucket and serve only those images through CloudFront, leaving booking traffic on the original hostname without WAF inspection.
Put the existing website behind CloudFront, cache every response using only the URL path, and configure WAF while omitting cookies and authorization data from origin requests.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. CloudFront can use an existing HTTP server as its origin. Cache hits remove image transfers from the constrained site, and the associated WAF rules inspect viewer requests before they reach that origin. Separate cache behaviors preserve dynamic transactions and session handling.

<<2>> could provide a scalable future architecture, but requires the migration that cannot be completed by the deadline.

<<3>> offloads images but leaves the dynamic application outside the required WAF entry path.

<<4>> risks mixing personalized responses and breaking authenticated transactions by treating all content as public static data.

A CDN does not create unlimited capacity for uncached application work. The stated load test is essential, as are correct cache keys, origin forwarding, TLS, and bypass restrictions. WAF rules should be tested against normal booking traffic.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [CloudFront origins](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/DownloadDistS3AndCustomOrigins.html). [Origin load reduction](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/origin-shield.html). [WAF with CloudFront](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/cloudfront-features.html).

question:
A photography company wants to retain its queue-and-worker processing model while moving to AWS. Large photos already arrive in S3. Processing is idempotent, can resume after interruption, and should normally begin within five minutes of upload. After successful processing, the originals and outputs must be retained for seven years and are almost never read. Restore requests can wait up to 48 hours. The company wants to minimize worker and archive costs.

Which design best meets these requirements?

options.text: Put S3 object keys in SQS and process them with diversified Spot workers in an Auto Scaling group. Scale on backlog per worker, acknowledge jobs after durable output commits, and use completion tags with lifecycle rules to archive eligible objects in S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
Use SQS with an On-Demand worker fleet fixed at peak size and retain all originals and outputs in S3 Standard-IA for the full seven years.
Use SQS and autoscaled Spot workers, but immediately transition newly uploaded originals to S3 Glacier Deep Archive before workers read them.
Publish jobs directly to every worker through SNS subscriptions, have each worker process every delivered job, and keep the full worker fleet running during idle periods.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. SQS decouples arrivals from retryable workers, Spot reduces the cost of interruptible compute, and a completion condition prevents archival before processing finishes. Long retention and a 48-hour restore allowance make Deep Archive a suitable storage class to evaluate.

<<2>> can process and retain data, but pays for idle peak compute and an immediate-access storage class that the archive does not require.

<<3>> makes the processing path wait for restoration of its own inputs, conflicting with the queue-latency goal.

<<4>> uses broadcast delivery where competing workers are needed and retains idle compute. SNS can deliver job notifications, including through SQS subscriptions; it is not inherently unsuitable for processing systems.

Use object references, not large photos, in queue messages. Set visibility timeouts, retry/dead-letter handling, idempotent commits, and graceful scale-in behavior. Backlog per worker reflects processing capacity better than raw depth for target tracking. Archive transitions are asynchronous, with request, retrieval, and minimum-duration costs.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Spot worker suitability](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/spot-best-practices.html). [Archive retrieval choices](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/restoring-objects-retrieval-options.html). [SQS processing and retries](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html). [Queue-based worker scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-using-sqs-queue.html). [Archive transition behavior](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-transition-general-considerations.html).

question:
A dynamic web application stores immutable media files on a fleet of EC2 file servers and copies each file between those servers. The growing replication backlog is causing missing media after server failures. The application can use object keys and HTTPS for media access and does not need shared file locks or POSIX semantics. The company wants to remove media-serving servers, improve durability, and analyze ongoing spending.

Which redesign best meets these requirements?

options.text: Move media to S3 and serve it through CloudFront with an S3 origin and origin access control. Keep dynamic processing on an ALB-backed EC2 Auto Scaling group, and use Cost Explorer to analyze costs and usage.
Move media to S3, but retain the existing EC2 file-server fleet as the required download proxy for every media request. Use Cost Explorer to analyze spending.
Move media to EFS and mount it on a separate multi-AZ EC2 media-serving fleet behind an ALB. Keep the dynamic web tier and analyze spending with Cost Explorer.
Move media to EFS and run both media-serving processes and dynamic code in a Beanstalk environment behind CloudFront. Use Cost Explorer to analyze spending.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. Media durability no longer depends on copies managed by EC2 servers, and CloudFront can retrieve objects directly from a private S3 origin. Dynamic server-side code stays on a compute tier that can scale separately. Cost Explorer helps attribute and monitor actual usage costs.

<<2>> improves the durable backing store, but retains the media-server dependency that the requirement removes.

<<3>> can provide durable shared files, but adds a dedicated serving fleet and a file interface the application does not need.

<<4>> is a valid way to serve EFS content through an HTTP application, but still operates media-serving processes rather than using the direct managed object-delivery path.

CloudFront does not use an EFS mount target directly as an HTTP origin; a server or other supported origin must expose the content. S3 also does not execute the application's server-side code. Compare the complete workload's request, transfer, storage, and compute costs rather than assuming one storage service is universally cheaper.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Private S3 origins](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.html). [Supported CloudFront origins](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/DownloadDistS3AndCustomOrigins.html). [S3 data durability](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/DataDurability.html). [Cost Explorer](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cost-management/latest/userguide/ce-exploring-data.html).

question:
A call center is replacing an on-premises NFS archive and manual transcription process. Recordings selected for quality review must be transcribed automatically soon after upload, rather than waiting days for an offshore team. All recordings need immediate access for 90 days, followed by seven-year retention with restores allowed to take hours. The portal can be refactored to a static frontend and short-lived APIs. The company wants the least infrastructure to operate.

Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Store recordings in S3. Use an event-driven Lambda function to start asynchronous Transcribe jobs for selected recordings and persist completed transcripts in a company-owned S3 bucket. Serve the frontend through CloudFront and S3 with API Gateway and Lambda APIs, and transition eligible recordings to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 90 days.
Store recordings in S3 and archive them after 90 days. Send selected object links to the existing offshore transcription team, and continue hosting the portal on a fixed EC2 fleet.
Store recordings in EFS and host the portal on EC2. After 90 days, copy selected recordings to S3 and start Transcribe jobs as part of the archival workflow.
Store recordings in S3 and use Transcribe promptly, but transition every recording to S3 Glacier Deep Archive immediately after transcription and restore it when a reviewer requests playback.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. Transcribe performs managed speech-to-text processing on S3 media. An event handler starts the batch job and a completion workflow records its result, while S3 lifecycle separates the active review period from long-term archival. The refactor removes the always-running portal fleet.

<<2>> retains manual transcription and the infrastructure the company wants to reduce.

<<3>> delays transcription until the archive date instead of supporting prompt review. EFS can remain part of other designs, but batch Transcribe input must be made available through a supported input path such as S3.

<<4>> requires restores during the 90-day immediate-access period.

Do not keep Lambda running until a transcription completes. Track job status, handle duplicate notifications and failures, and store transcripts durably in the chosen bucket. Validate audio formats, language support, and transcription quality. Archive transitions are asynchronous; restore latency, minimum storage duration, and retrieval charges must match the retention policy.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Start a batch transcription job](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/transcribe/latest/APIReference/API_StartTranscriptionJob.html). [Transcribe inputs and outputs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/transcribe/latest/dg/how-input.html). [S3 archive lifecycle](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-transition-general-considerations.html).

question:
Data scientists need to launch SageMaker AI notebook instances only when needed, using self-service provisioning without configuring AWS infrastructure. Every notebook storage volume must use an approved KMS key, and users should choose only from approved sizes. Scientists must not need broad provisioning permissions or a locally maintained script. The company wants the least custom portal code and ongoing administration.

Which solution best meets these requirements?

options.text: Build an S3 frontend, API Gateway API, Lambda provisioning service, request database, and status polling UI that create approved notebook configurations.
Publish a raw CloudFormation template in a shared S3 bucket and grant scientists broad permissions to edit the template and create SageMaker notebook resources directly.

Publish an approved CloudFormation product in a Service Catalog portfolio. Fix KmsKeyId and the execution role, map friendly size choices to approved types, and use a least-privilege launch role and constraints. Return the notebook name or ARN and an authenticated console link.
Pre-provision the largest approved notebook instance for every scientist, leave all instances running, and distribute their console links.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. A Service Catalog product presents approved configuration choices and delegates provisioning through a launch role. The template sets the notebook volume's KMS key rather than asking each scientist to configure encryption.

<<1>> can enforce the configuration, but requires a custom self-service application and provisioning lifecycle that Service Catalog already supplies.

<<2>> exposes the infrastructure details and grants a path to bypass the approved configuration.

<<4>> avoids a portal but creates idle maximum-size capacity rather than the requested on-demand, cost-conscious provisioning.

The launch role needs the relevant provisioning, KMS, and role-passing permissions; notebook runtime access uses the configured execution role. Limit direct creation paths when the product is mandatory. `AWS::SageMaker::NotebookInstance` returns an ARN through Ref and a notebook name through documented attributes, not a `Url` attribute. Notebook access still requires authorization; a presigned access URL is temporary, not a permanent product output.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Service Catalog launch constraints](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/servicecatalog/latest/adminguide/constraints-launch.html). [Notebook resource contract](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/TemplateReference/aws-resource-sagemaker-notebookinstance.html).

question:
A warehouse application currently advances orders when employees reply to emails. Shipping an order can take several days. The company wants a serverless workflow that invokes an existing label-printing service, waits durably for an authenticated dispatch scan, and then marks the order shipped. Duplicate scan events must not repeat business side effects. The company wants the least custom orchestration code.

Which design should it use?

options.text: Run a Batch job for each shipping stage and maintain a custom DynamoDB coordinator that polls job state and scan records to decide which stage to submit next.
Use SQS and Lambda for each task, and implement a custom order-state engine in DynamoDB with scheduled polling for missing dispatch scans.

Persist each order in DynamoDB and start a Step Functions Standard execution. Invoke the label-printing integration and wait in a callback task. An authenticated scan handler returns the stored task token with SendTaskSuccess, after which an idempotent workflow task marks the order shipped.
Start a Step Functions Express execution for each order and keep it running in a polling loop until a dispatch scan appears, even when shipping takes several days.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. A Standard workflow preserves orchestration state while waiting for an external event. The callback token identifies the waiting task; the scan handler returns it, and the workflow continues to its explicit shipped-state update.

<<1>> can run compute jobs, but adds a custom coordinator for a process dominated by human waiting.

<<2>> uses valid serverless components, but requires the durable state transitions and wait logic to be built and maintained by the application.

<<4>> exceeds the Express execution limit of five minutes. Express also does not support the callback integration pattern.

Keep task tokens in protected server-side state associated with the order. Authenticate and authorize scans, configure timeouts and recovery, and make printer calls and status updates idempotent. Retrying a callback or a downstream state update must not create a second shipment. The workflow still needs a real integration with the physical printer or warehouse service.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Callback task tokens](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/connect-to-resource.html). [Workflow types](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/choosing-workflow-type.html).

question:
A company will rehost VMware virtual machines as EC2 instances. Supported guest operating systems may run migration agents. Source applications must remain available while their disks are copied, and changes must continue replicating through testing until a planned cutover. The team wants a managed agent-based migration workflow rather than repeated full image exports.

Which actions are required for this approach? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Configure AWS Transform MGN, formerly AWS Application Migration Service, with the target replication and EC2 launch settings, then use its test and cutover workflow.
Install and configure the AWS Replication Agent inside each supported source VM guest operating system, with the required permissions and connectivity.
Export each VM once, import it through VM Import/Export, and launch the resulting AMI while leaving the source VM writable until cutover.
Create a CloudFormation template for equivalent EC2 instance sizes and networking, without a process to transfer the guest operating systems and disks.
Publish new standard EC2 AMIs through Service Catalog and use those clean images as substitutes for the existing server disks.

explanation.text:
<<1>> and <<2>> are correct. MGN provides continuous server-disk replication and test/cutover launches. In the selected agent-based approach, each source guest needs its own Replication Agent; installing software only on vCenter does not capture every guest's disks through that agent workflow.

<<3>> creates a point-in-time import and leaves subsequent source changes outside the imported image.

<<4>> provisions infrastructure definitions but does not capture the existing operating system, application installation, and data.

<<5>> distributes approved new images but does not migrate the state of the source machines.

Validate supported operating systems, disk layouts, bandwidth, credentials, and target networking. Rehearse the application as a whole before freezing writes and completing the cutover. MGN is more than an AMI-generation utility; the ongoing replication and launch lifecycle are what satisfy this scenario.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Per-server Replication Agent](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/mgn/latest/ug/agent-installation.html). [MGN migration workflow](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/mgn/latest/ug/what-is-mgn.html). [VM import requirements](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vm-import/latest/userguide/prerequisites.html).

question:
A company must migrate 150 VMs containing 40 TB within three months. Its migration link is limited to 12 Mbps, and funding for a higher-capacity connection is unavailable. A tested plan shows that the critical subset and its change traffic fit that bandwidth and deadline. Noncritical VMs may be shut down from export until import and cutover, and their images meet VM Import/Export requirements. The company already has approved Data Transfer Terminal access, a suitable reservation, and secure transport within the schedule.

Which plan meets these constraints?

options.text: Order a new 1-Gbps Direct Connect circuit and replicate every VM through MGN over that connection.
Use the existing assessment inventory to refactor every application onto managed services before the deadline, without a data-transfer or cutover plan.
Export every VM and upload all 40 TB through Transfer Family over the existing 12-Mbps connection, then import the images into EC2.

Use MGN continuous replication and tested cutovers for the critical subset. Export the powered-off noncritical VMs, upload them to S3 at the reserved Data Transfer Terminal facility, and use VM Import/Export to launch and validate them.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. It assigns the limited online path to workloads needing short cutovers and moves the large, quiesced exports over the facility's connection. The explicit bandwidth, image-support, shutdown, and reservation premises make the combined plan feasible.

<<1>> violates the funding constraint even though a suitable faster connection could support another migration plan.

<<2>> treats assessment as migration execution and proposes an unvalidated redesign rather than the required transfer plan.

<<3>> changes the transfer protocol but retains the bottleneck: 40 decimal TB over 12 Mbps takes about 309 days at ideal full utilization, before overhead or new changes.

Terminal service access and transport logistics must be arranged in advance; uploading an image does not automatically convert it into a running EC2 instance. Protect and verify exports, test the imports, and keep noncritical sources quiesced unless a separate delta strategy exists. Continuous replication still needs sufficient throughput to catch up with source changes.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Data Transfer Terminal access](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/datatransferterminal/latest/userguide/what-is-dtt.html). [Supported VM images](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vm-import/latest/userguide/prerequisites.html). [MGN replication](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/mgn/latest/ug/what-is-mgn.html).

question:
A company must rehost a three-tier application from supported on-premises VMs to EC2. Each VM has a root disk and several terabytes of changing application data on supported local block volumes. All required volumes must remain synchronized while the team performs application tests. The final write freeze must be short, and the company wants managed migration lifecycle operations.

Which approach best meets these requirements?

options.text: Use AWS Transform MGN with a Replication Agent on each source server and include all required supported disks. Validate test launches, quiesce source writes and verify replication catch-up, then launch and validate cutover instances before switching traffic.
Export and import complete VM images repeatedly with a scheduled VM Import/Export script, including another full export after freezing writes for cutover.
Replicate only the root disks with MGN. Import the data disks once as snapshots before testing and attach those original snapshots to the final cutover instances.
Use discovery data to create clean EC2 instances and migrate application files with a custom sequence of scheduled copy scripts and manually coordinated cutover steps.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. MGN maintains block-level replication of the selected server disks and provides test and cutover launches. Including the data disks in that replication path avoids an independently stale copy of the application's state.

<<2>> recreates point-in-time imports and a large final transfer instead of maintaining the required continuous replication.

<<3>> leaves subsequent changes to the data disks behind, even if the root disk is current.

<<4>> can form a custom migration project, but adds rebuilding, synchronization, and lifecycle coordination that the managed rehosting workflow supplies.

Replication catch-up is not a substitute for application-consistent quiescence and validation. After a cutover instance is launched, continued source replication goes to the staging area, not into that already-running cutover instance. Freeze or redirect writers correctly, validate dependencies, and define rollback before transferring production ownership.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Managed server replication](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/mgn/latest/ug/what-is-mgn.html). [MGN cutover behavior](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/mgn/latest/ug/launch-cutover.html).

question:
Employees already authenticate to a corporate SAML 2.0 identity provider. A company wants them to access assigned AWS accounts through one managed workforce portal with centrally maintained permission assignments and no separate IAM users. It also wants CLI access without distributing long-lived access keys. The company wants the least custom federation infrastructure.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Build a custom federation broker and account-selection portal, maintain role mappings in a custom database, and use STS to generate temporary sessions after corporate sign-in.

Configure IAM Identity Center with the corporate SAML identity provider, provision users and groups, and assign permission sets to the required accounts. Use the AWS access portal and supported CLI sign-in flow.
Create an IAM user in every required AWS account for each employee, synchronize corporate passwords to those users, and issue access keys for CLI use.
Configure separate direct IAM SAML federation relationships and role assignments in every account, and maintain a custom portal and CLI credential tool to coordinate access.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. IAM Identity Center connects the existing identity provider to a managed access portal and centralized account permissions. Users and groups must be provisioned, through SCIM or an appropriate manual process, before assigning account access.

<<1>> can use temporary credentials securely, but adds a custom broker, portal, and authorization mapping service.

<<3>> creates the duplicate identities and long-lived credentials the company excludes.

<<4>> is a valid federation architecture, but requires per-account configuration and custom access tooling instead of the requested managed central experience.

Authentication and authorization are separate: the identity provider validates the employee, while account assignments and permission sets determine AWS access. Direct IAM SAML federation uses AssumeRoleWithSAML; AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity accepts web-identity tokens rather than SAML assertions. Users do not first obtain STS credentials and submit those credentials to Identity Center.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Identity Center external identities](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/manage-your-identity-source-idp.html). [Direct SAML federation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/STS/latest/APIReference/API_AssumeRoleWithSAML.html).

question:
An application runs 20 identical EC2 instances in each of three Availability Zones and requires 60 healthy instances at peak. After one zone fails, the approved recovery window allows tested automation to launch 10 instances in each surviving zone. The company requires matching launch capacity to be reserved before an incident. Quotas are approved, and finance accepts charges for unused reserved capacity but no new one-year or three-year commitment.

Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Increase the Auto Scaling maximum to 90 and purchase a Compute Savings Plan to cover the additional usage during recovery.
Configure a diversified Spot fleet for 20 replacement instances and request that capacity when a zone fails.
Create active, immediate-use On-Demand Capacity Reservations for 30 matching instances in each zone. Use 20 slots per zone during normal operation and preserve the other 10 for the recovery workflow.
Purchase new one-year zonal Reserved Instances for the additional matching capacity in every zone, and configure recovery launches to use it.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. Each surviving zone retains 20 running instances and has 10 unused matching reserved slots. Launching those replacements restores 60 instances across the two healthy zones without relying solely on capacity available at incident time.

<<1>> supplies a discount and a scaling limit, not a capacity reservation.

<<2>> diversifies capacity risk but does not reserve the recovery slots.

<<4>> can provide a zonal capacity benefit, but violates the prohibition on a new annual commitment. Regional Reserved Instances do not provide that capacity benefit.

Reservations must be active, match the required zone and instance attributes, and remain available to this workload. Immediate-use reservations have no fixed term, but unused capacity is charged. This reserves launch capacity; it does not provide already-running headroom or guarantee the full application's recovery time.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Capacity Reservation behavior](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ec2-capacity-reservations.html).

question:
A mobile application lets customers upload and download documents directly from a private S3 bucket. It needs managed sign-up and sign-in plus temporary AWS credentials, without a custom credential broker or an IAM identity per customer. Unauthenticated access is disabled. AWS permissions must limit each signed-in identity to private/<identity-id>/, using the Cognito identity-pool identity ID rather than the user-pool subject.

Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Embed one shared IAM user access key in the mobile application, grant it access to every document, and hide other customers’ prefixes in the interface.

Use a Cognito user pool for sign-in and an identity pool for temporary credentials. Restrict the authenticated role trust to the intended pool and authenticated identities. Scope object actions to private/${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub}/* and ListBucket to the matching prefix.
Use a Cognito user pool and build a custom credential broker that creates and maintains a separate IAM role for every customer before returning STS credentials.
Use Cognito user and identity pools with an authenticated role permitting private/*, and have the mobile application choose the current customer’s prefix.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. The user pool authenticates the customer, the identity pool supplies temporary role credentials, and the IAM policy scopes those credentials to that identity's object prefix. Listing uses the bucket ARN with a prefix condition; object actions use the corresponding object ARN.

<<1>> exposes a shared long-lived credential and grants cross-customer access regardless of the interface.

<<3>> can implement isolation, but requires the custom broker and per-customer IAM roles that the design excludes.

<<4>> authenticates users but grants them access to other users' documents. A client-selected prefix is not an authorization boundary.

The policy variable resolves to the identity-pool identity ID, not the `sub` in the original user-pool JWT. Trust conditions should restrict the pool's `aud` and authenticated `amr`. Keep bucket policies and any KMS permissions consistent with the same least-privilege boundary; a broader independent grant can undermine the intended isolation.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Per-identity S3 permissions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_examples_s3_cognito-bucket.html). [Identity pool roles](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/iam-roles.html).

question:
A studio is migrating a tape-based video archive while retaining its media asset management (MAM) application. The MAM can restore tape contents as ordinary files to an NFS share. A Direct Connect path is available, and supported video renditions can be produced when necessary. The studio has labeled reference photos of known performers and wants managed identification and object labels in its existing search catalog, with little custom model operation.

Which implementation best meets these requirements?

options.text: Restore video files through the MAM to an S3 File Gateway share and confirm their upload completion. Index reference face images in a Rekognition collection with person-ID mappings. Use Lambda to start asynchronous stored-video face-search and label jobs, retrieve completed results, and update the MAM catalog.
Restore files through the MAM and transfer them to S3 with DataSync, then train, deploy, and maintain custom face-recognition and object-detection models on SageMaker for the catalog.
Restore and upload the videos to S3, but use Rekognition label detection alone to assign the specific identities in the studio’s performer catalog.
Restore and upload the videos to S3 through Transfer Family, then maintain EC2 inference servers with open-source face and object models and a custom scheduling system.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. The MAM converts the tape contents into accessible files, File Gateway provides the existing file interface with S3 backing, and managed Rekognition operations supply face matching and labels. Confirming upload completion keeps analysis from starting before the intended file is ready.

<<2>> is a valid data-transfer and custom-ML design, but adds model development and operation that the stated requirements avoid.

<<3>> can identify generic objects and scenes but does not match performers against the supplied face collection.

<<4>> can perform the analysis, but requires ongoing inference-server, library, model, and scheduling maintenance.

Index reference images before calling StartFaceSearch, retain mappings from returned identifiers to MAM people, and use completion notifications followed by Get operations. Lambda orchestrates the asynchronous jobs rather than waiting through the whole analysis. Validate video formats and per-object limits, prepare compatible renditions or segments when needed, and retain source-timestamp mappings for catalog navigation.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [S3 File Gateway](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/filegateway/latest/files3/what-is-file-s3.html). [Gateway upload completion](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/filegateway/latest/files3/monitoring-file-gateway.html). [Stored-video analysis](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/rekognition/latest/dg/video.html). [Face collections](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/rekognition/latest/dg/collections.html).

question:
A studio wants to identify known performers in a 50-TB tape archive and show a still image beside each match in its media catalog. It has reference photos with internal person IDs. The existing MAM can export tape contents to NFS as supported video files and extract frames at specified timestamps. Direct Connect is available. The studio wants to retain that workflow while moving the assets to S3 and minimizing model and server management.

Which design meets all requirements?

options.text: Export videos through the MAM to S3 File Gateway and confirm upload completion. Index reference photos in a Rekognition collection, keep person-ID mappings, and orchestrate asynchronous stored-video face search. Use match timestamps with the MAM’s frame-export capability to store stills in S3 and link their keys to catalog results.
Upload videos and index reference photos in a Rekognition collection, then use the face IDs returned by face search as S3 object keys for still images, without exporting or storing any frames.
Move backups into a Tape Gateway archive and stop producing ordinary video files, then submit the virtual tape archives themselves as Rekognition stored-video inputs.
Export videos to S3, deploy an EC2 fleet running custom facial-recognition models, and build a custom frame-extraction and metadata pipeline that replaces the MAM integration.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. It preserves the existing file-export and frame-export capabilities while using managed face search. Video objects, searchable face representations, person mappings, and still images remain explicit assets with their own storage and identifiers.

<<2>> omits the still images. A face collection stores mathematical representations; a returned face ID is not an image object or an automatically inferred real-world name.

<<3>> preserves tape backups but does not expose a supported video object for analysis. The backup application must first restore the contents into ordinary media files.

<<4>> can produce the desired output, but replaces existing capabilities and introduces model and server operations that the company wants to minimize.

Index known reference faces, interpret matches with appropriate confidence thresholds, and map identifiers to the studio's catalog. GetFaceSearch returns analysis results after the asynchronous job completes; separate extraction creates the displayable still. Preserve timestamp offsets if videos are segmented, and validate accuracy on representative footage.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Face representations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/rekognition/latest/dg/collections.html). [Stored-video face search](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/rekognition/latest/dg/video.html). [File-based ingestion](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/filegateway/latest/files3/what-is-file-s3.html).

question:
An art marketplace stores large image uploads in a central S3 bucket in us-east-1. Mobile clients upload directly to S3, bypassing the EC2 web tier. European uploads are slow despite tested multipart concurrency, and measurements identify the long-distance internet path as the limiting factor. The bucket meets Transfer Acceleration requirements. The company wants a managed optimization while retaining the bucket and existing direct-upload model.

Which change should it evaluate?

options.text: Increase multipart concurrency further while retaining the same regional S3 endpoint and the already tuned upload configuration.
Create a CloudFront distribution for image downloads but continue sending uploads to the existing regional S3 endpoint.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket and update the client or signing service to use the bucket’s s3-accelerate endpoint. Compare performance and cost from the affected locations.
Put Global Accelerator in front of the EC2 web tier and add web instances, while retaining direct client-to-S3 uploads through the regional endpoint.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. Transfer Acceleration routes uploads through an AWS edge location and an optimized path to the destination bucket. Enabling the bucket feature alone is insufficient: the transfer must use the acceleration endpoint.

<<1>> repeats an optimization that has already been measured and does not change the identified long-distance path.

<<2>> improves a download path while leaving the upload route unchanged.

<<4>> changes a web tier that these upload bytes do not traverse.

Multipart upload remains useful and can be combined with acceleration. Benchmark representative clients because acceleration is not guaranteed to improve every transfer and can add charges. CloudFront can support configured write methods; the reason the listed download-only option fails is its unchanged upload path, not a blanket prohibition on uploads through CloudFront.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [S3 Transfer Acceleration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/transfer-acceleration.html). [CloudFront origin methods](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.html).

question:
A company will close three data centers and rehost about 500 physical Windows and Linux servers in AWS Regions. Their operating systems and disk layouts are supported by MGN, and the existing encrypted network paths have sufficient replication capacity. A landing-zone team has provisioned the destination accounts, regional VPCs, and isolated staging and test subnets. The migration team needs centralized visibility across accounts, continuous replication, application tests, and short planned cutovers with minimal custom tooling.

Which approach should it use?

options.text: Use AWS Transform MGN with its global view across the participating accounts. Install a Replication Agent on each source server, configure replication and launch settings, validate application waves, and perform planned cutovers into the prepared environments.
Use S3 File Gateway to copy application directories and then manually rebuild the operating systems, application installations, services, and configuration on new EC2 instances.
Install AWS Outposts in the existing data centers and move the applications onto that on-premises AWS infrastructure as their permanent destination.
Convert the physical servers into VM images and use VM Import/Export as the supported bulk path for those physical-to-virtual images, then manually coordinate testing and final changes.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. MGN supports agent-based rehosting of eligible physical servers, and global view provides cross-account visibility and migration actions. Application-wave testing and final write coordination remain part of the migration plan.

<<2>> moves files but leaves server reconstruction and state synchronization to a custom process.

<<3>> keeps AWS infrastructure on premises, conflicting with the goal of closing the data centers.

<<4>> relies on an unsupported import path: VM Import/Export does not support VMs created by physical-to-virtual conversion. This is more than a question of manual overhead.

MGN source replication and EC2 launch configuration do not, by themselves, establish the entire multi-account network architecture. The prepared accounts and regional networks are explicit prerequisites here. Verify service permissions, endpoints, quotas, disk support, and application dependencies; broad platform support does not guarantee every application will run unchanged.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [MGN global view](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/mgn/latest/ug/global-view.html). [Supported rehosting workflow](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/mgn/latest/ug/what-is-mgn.html). [VM import exclusions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vm-import/latest/userguide/prerequisites.html).

question:
A company uses AWS Organizations and must deploy the same approved regional application baseline into member accounts in Europe and Asia. It wants central updates, controlled rollout settings, and automatic deployment when new accounts join designated organizational units. The template contains resources supported in the target Regions and does not use nested stacks or macros. The company wants the least custom cross-account deployment code.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use ordinary CloudFormation stacks and maintain a custom script that assumes a role in every account and Region, tracks deployments, and detects newly added accounts.
Enroll accounts in Control Tower and apply its governance controls, without creating an application-baseline deployment mechanism.

Activate trusted access for CloudFormation StackSets and use service-managed permissions. Target the designated OUs and Regions, enable automatic deployments, and configure the removal/retention and rollout settings.
Create a root CloudFormation stack with nested stacks in one account and Region, and pass the other account IDs and Region names as ordinary parameters without a cross-account deployment mechanism.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. StackSets deploy stack instances across accounts and Regions. Service-managed permissions integrate with Organizations, and configured automatic deployments cover new accounts in the targeted organizational units.

<<1>> can implement the rollout, but requires custom account discovery, credential handling, and deployment tracking.

<<2>> establishes governance and a landing zone; enrollment alone does not deploy this arbitrary application template. Customizations or additional deployment tooling would still be needed.

<<4>> organizes resources within the root stack's deployment context. Passing account or Region names as values does not move those nested stacks into other deployment contexts.

Organizations supplies account structure and trusted integration; StackSets performs deployment. Select failure tolerance and concurrency, and decide whether stacks are retained when accounts leave scope. Service-managed StackSets do not deploy to the management account, so any required management-account baseline needs a separate path.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [StackSets deployment model](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/what-is-cfnstacksets.html). [Service-managed StackSets](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/stacksets-orgs-associate-stackset-with-org.html).

question:
A logistics company will let a third-party SaaS service access selected resources through AWS APIs. The vendor serves many unrelated customers from the same AWS account. Access must use temporary credentials and least-privilege permissions, and the company must prevent another vendor customer from causing the vendor to assume the logistics company's role on that customer's behalf.

Which configuration best addresses these requirements?

options.text: Invite vendor operators into the company’s workforce access portal and rely on interactive human sign-in for every automated SaaS task.
Create a least-privilege IAM user in the company account and provide its long-lived access keys to the vendor for all API calls.
Create a least-privilege IAM role that trusts the vendor’s designated principal, but allow AssumeRole without a customer-specific external ID condition.

Have the vendor assign a unique external ID for this customer. Create a least-privilege role that trusts the vendor’s designated principal and requires that sts:ExternalId value. The vendor includes the role ARN and matching external ID in AssumeRole requests.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. The trusted principal identifies who may assume the role, the external ID binds the vendor's request to this customer context, and the role's permissions limit what the resulting temporary credentials can do. This addresses the multi-tenant confused-deputy risk described in the stem.

<<1>> provides a workforce access pattern rather than the required unattended service integration.

<<2>> violates the temporary-credential requirement and creates a distributed long-lived secret.

<<3>> supplies temporary least-privilege access, but omits the customer-context check that prevents the trusted vendor from being misdirected by another customer. Its absence does not mean every AWS account can assume the role.

The vendor must manage uniqueness and choose the correct customer ID for each request. An external ID is not a secret or a replacement for a restricted trust principal. Test that missing and incorrect external IDs are rejected. Different Organizations do not prevent properly configured role assumption.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Third-party roles and external IDs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_common-scenarios_third-party.html).

question:
Marketing owns an S3 bucket and a customer managed KMS key used to encrypt its campaign objects. Reviewers successfully assume the mgmt_reviewer role in a separate Management account, but cannot browse or download objects under published/. No applicable explicit deny exists.

Security requires read-only access to that prefix and delegation specifically to mgmt_reviewer, rather than to the entire Management account. Which policy changes are required? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Add a Marketing bucket policy allowing the exact mgmt_reviewer role ARN to list the published/ prefix and read objects in that prefix.
Add a role policy granting mgmt_reviewer all S3 actions on the Marketing bucket and kms:Decrypt on the campaign key.
Add a Marketing KMS key-policy statement allowing kms:Decrypt for the exact mgmt_reviewer role ARN.
Add a Marketing bucket policy granting the required reads to the Marketing account principal, without authorizing the Management role.
Add a Marketing KMS key-policy statement delegating kms:Decrypt to the entire Management account so its administrators can authorize additional principals.
Add a mgmt_reviewer identity policy allowing prefix-scoped s3:ListBucket, s3:GetObject on published/*, and kms:Decrypt on the exact campaign key ARN.

explanation.text:
<<1>>, <<3>>, and <<6>> are correct. The role needs S3 permission on both sides of the account boundary and separate KMS authorization to decrypt the objects. The bucket policy names the reviewer role, its identity policy grants the required object and key operations, and the key policy authorizes that same external role.

<<2>> includes unnecessary upload, deletion, and other S3 permissions, violating read-only access.

<<4>> authorizes a principal in the resource-owning account instead of the external reviewer role.

<<5>> can work technically when combined with appropriate identity policies, but grants broader delegation than this scenario permits. Naming the exact role limits whom external administrators can authorize through this key-policy statement.

Scope s3:ListBucket to the bucket ARN with a prefix condition and s3:GetObject to the object ARNs. KMS and S3 are independent authorization checks: a successful role assumption or allowed object read does not itself establish decryption permission. Confirm that the actual objects use the expected key.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Cross-account resource authorization](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies-cross-account-resource-access.html); [Cross-account KMS authorization](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/key-policy-modifying-external-accounts.html); [S3 SSE-KMS object permissions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingKMSEncryption.html).

question:
An analytics portal currently stores uploaded files on a NAS and queues processing jobs. Each job is indivisible and can run for 30 minutes. Upload volume is high during business hours and low overnight. The application can use object storage and does not require a shared filesystem or a specific broker protocol.

Which migration design minimizes idle infrastructure while preserving reliable processing?

options.text: Store files in S3 and enqueue object keys in SQS. Invoke one Lambda function per message and perform the entire 30-minute job in that invocation.
Store files in EFS and enqueue jobs in a provisioned Amazon MQ broker. Scale EC2 workers with demand and retain the broker and filesystem overnight.
Store files in S3 and enqueue object keys in SQS. Keep a fixed EC2 worker fleet sized for the daytime peak running continuously.

Store files in S3 and enqueue object keys in SQS. Run EC2 workers in an Auto Scaling group using backlog per instance, adjust message visibility for long jobs, and protect busy workers during scale-in.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. S3 separates durable file storage from the worker lifecycle, and SQS carries job references. Queue-driven scaling adds workers for the daytime backlog and reduces idle capacity afterward. A backlog-per-instance target should reflect processing time and acceptable queue delay.

<<1>> exceeds the 15-minute limit of a single Lambda invocation. A different decomposed workflow could use Lambda, but the stated jobs cannot be split.

<<2>> can process the workload, but retains a provisioned broker and a shared filesystem without a requirement for either capability. The SQS/S3 design avoids that unnecessary baseline infrastructure.

<<3>> uses suitable storage and queuing, but pays for peak worker capacity during the quiet period.

Store object keys, not large files, in messages. Delete a message only after its output is committed, maintain a sufficient visibility timeout or heartbeat, and make retries idempotent. Scale-in protection protects work in progress; it does not eliminate the need to recover from instance failure.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Queue-driven EC2 scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-using-sqs-queue.html); [Lambda invocation timeout](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html); [SQS visibility and retries](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html).

question:
An enterprise is integrating acquired companies whose employees reside in multiple self-managed Active Directory domains and forests. It already operates AWS Managed Microsoft AD with private connectivity to those directories. Employees need one portal for AWS Organizations accounts and supported SAML business applications, using their existing credentials. The team wants to avoid operating new federation servers.

Which design meets these requirements with the least administration?

options.text: Deploy and maintain a new AD FS farm, configure SAML federation separately for the AWS accounts, and maintain application relying-party integrations.

Use IAM Identity Center with AWS Organizations, connect it to AWS Managed Microsoft AD, configure the necessary two-way trusts to the self-managed directories, and assign directory groups to permission sets and supported applications.
Connect IAM Identity Center to one AD Connector attached to a single acquired domain, and use it to discover users from all other domains and forests.
Use IAM Identity Center with AWS Managed Microsoft AD, but establish only one-way trusts that permit authentication from the self-managed directories.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. Identity Center centralizes account and application assignments. For its Managed AD integration, two-way trust supports both authentication and the directory metadata access needed to synchronize users and groups. Existing group membership can drive the assigned access.

<<1>> can provide federation, but introduces the federation-server operations and account-by-account integration work the enterprise wants to avoid. Form-based sign-in does not inherently invalidate SSO.

<<3>> exceeds AD Connector's Identity Center scope. That integration accesses users and groups in the domain to which the connector attaches, rather than discovering all trusted domains or forests. AD Connector is a valid alternative for suitable single-domain requirements.

<<4>> omits the reverse trust required by Identity Center for this integration. A trust direction that suffices for a different Windows use case does not necessarily satisfy Identity Center.

Configure DNS, network reachability, trust permissions, and group assignments. Directory authentication establishes identity; permission sets and application assignments determine the access that identity receives.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Identity Center with self-managed AD](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/connectonpremad.html); [Identity Center workforce access](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/what-is.html).

question:
An employee mobile app must use a custom authentication service backed by the company's LDAP directory. After sign-in, the app must receive temporary, restricted IAM role credentials to call AWS APIs directly. Long-lived IAM user keys must not be distributed to devices.

Which architectures can independently meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Issue custom SAML assertions and call AssumeRoleWithSAML against an IAM Identity Center-managed AWSReservedSSO role, without creating a separately trusted IAM SAML role.
Authenticate against LDAP, store opaque application session tokens in DynamoDB, and send those tokens directly to S3 as the sole authorization for object API calls.
Issue OIDC tokens from the custom authentication service and embed a shared IAM user access key in the app to sign its AWS requests.

Implement a SAML 2.0 identity provider that authenticates against LDAP. Register its metadata as an IAM SAML provider, configure a restricted trusting role, and exchange valid assertions with STS AssumeRoleWithSAML.

Implement an OIDC identity provider that authenticates against LDAP. Configure a Cognito identity pool to trust it and map authenticated users to restricted IAM roles, then exchange valid ID tokens for temporary AWS credentials.

explanation.text:
<<4>> and <<5>> are alternative complete architectures. In the SAML flow, IAM provider metadata and the role trust policy allow STS to validate the assertion and return temporary role credentials. In the OIDC flow, the configured Cognito identity pool exchanges the identity token for credentials associated with an authorized IAM role.

<<1>> uses an unsupported target: AssumeRoleWithSAML cannot assume Identity Center-managed AWSReservedSSO roles. The direct SAML design needs the appropriate IAM provider and role trust configuration.

<<2>> creates an application session, but omits the AWS credential exchange. An arbitrary token stored in DynamoDB is not an AWS request signature or an S3 authorization credential.

<<3>> authenticates users but distributes shared long-lived credentials, violating both the temporary-credential and role-based access requirements.

LDAP is the authentication backend, not a SAML assertion or OIDC token format. Validate token signatures, issuer, audience, expiration, and role selection, and enforce user-specific resource permissions. Successful authentication alone does not grant access to every AWS resource.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [STS SAML credential exchange](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/STS/latest/APIReference/API_AssumeRoleWithSAML.html); [Identity-pool credential exchange](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/authentication-flow.html).

question:
A company uses an on-premises Active Directory for employee identities. It is deploying Windows workloads that require an AD domain in AWS and wants employees to use the same corporate credentials for those workloads and a workforce AWS access portal. Private network connectivity is available. The company wants AWS to manage the cloud directory servers and does not want duplicate employee accounts.

Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a Cognito user pool with new employee accounts and use its application tokens as the domain credentials for the Windows workloads.
Create new users in the IAM Identity Center identity store and separately maintain matching user accounts and passwords in the Windows workload domain.
Deploy self-managed Active Directory domain controllers on EC2 and operate their replication, backups, patching, and availability.

Create AWS Managed Microsoft AD with the necessary two-way trust to the existing directory. Join the Windows workloads to the managed domain and connect IAM Identity Center to that directory for group-based workforce access.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. Managed Microsoft AD supplies an AD-compatible cloud domain without transferring directory-server operations to the customer. Trust lets the existing directory remain the employee identity source. Identity Center adds workforce account and application assignments and requires two-way trust for the self-managed directory integration.

<<1>> supplies application identities, not an Active Directory domain for Windows workloads, and creates duplicate employee accounts.

<<2>> requires separate identities and password administration, contrary to the existing-credential requirement.

<<3>> can extend Active Directory functionality into AWS but leaves the company responsible for directory-server operations.

Trust does not copy all employee accounts into a second directory or automatically authorize access to every workload. Configure group-based permissions, DNS resolution, and network paths for the services involved. Identity Center can use an existing directory; creating new users in its built-in store is not required for SSO.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Identity Center with self-managed AD](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/connectonpremad.html); [Managed Microsoft AD responsibilities](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directoryservice/latest/admin-guide/directory_microsoft_ad.html); [Identity Center workforce access](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/what-is.html).

question:
A WordPress site uses an RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB instance deployment. Profiling identifies repeated read-only queries as the source of database CPU pressure. Storage IOPS, writes, and the web tier have spare capacity. The team can change read routing and caching, but cannot shard the schema or increase the primary instance size. The affected reads tolerate bounded staleness.

Which changes directly reduce the primary's read-query work? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Increase provisioned storage IOPS without changing query execution or routing.
Shard the schema across independently writable databases and route requests by shard.
Create MySQL read replicas and route eligible reads to their endpoints, retaining primary routing for writes and freshness-sensitive reads.
Integrate ElastiCache with a cache-aside strategy for reusable query results, including expiration and invalidation rules.
Cache static media in CloudFront and enlarge the web-server fleet without changing database access.
Upgrade the primary database to a larger instance class while keeping all queries on it.

explanation.text:
<<3>> and <<4>> are correct. Read replicas move eligible query execution to separate database compute. A cache avoids repeated database execution when a valid cached result is available. Both require changes in the application path, as the stem permits.

<<1>> adds capacity for a resource that is not saturated and leaves the diagnosed CPU work unchanged.

<<2>> violates the explicit no-sharding constraint.

<<5>> improves media delivery and web capacity, neither of which is the diagnosed bottleneck.

<<6>> could provide more CPU in another scenario, but violates the instance-size constraint.

The standby of a conventional Multi-AZ DB instance deployment provides failover, not a read endpoint. Do not generalize this to Multi-AZ DB clusters. MySQL read replicas replicate asynchronously, and cached values can become stale, so route operations requiring current data to the writer and enforce the application's staleness policy. Merely creating replicas or a cache does not redirect existing queries.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [RDS read replicas and standbys](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReadRepl.html); [ElastiCache caching strategies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonElastiCache/latest/dg/Strategies.html).

question:
A photo-processing application runs on EC2 and writes watermarked images to a private S3 bucket. It needs only PutObject access to the processed/ prefix. The company prohibits long-lived application access keys and wants credentials to rotate without deployment changes.

Which configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Grant the application the required S3 permission through an SCP and rely on that policy to issue credentials to the instance.
Create a restricted IAM user and store its access key in encrypted instance user data for the application to load at startup.

Attach an instance profile containing an EC2-trusted IAM role with the required prefix-scoped PutObject permission. Use the AWS SDK credential provider to retrieve and refresh temporary role credentials through instance metadata.
Obtain a restricted role session during deployment and place its temporary credentials in instance user data. Have the application reuse those values for the lifetime of the instance.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. The instance profile associates the role with EC2, and the role's permission policy limits uploads to the required objects. The SDK can use temporary credentials supplied through instance metadata and refresh them before expiration without embedding keys in the application.

<<1>> confuses an organization permissions limit with a credential source. An SCP neither grants S3 permission nor attaches an identity to an EC2 instance.

<<2>> still distributes long-lived IAM user credentials. Encrypting their storage does not provide the required automatically refreshed role session.

<<4>> starts with temporary credentials but freezes them in deployment data. They expire, and user data does not automatically refresh them.
