Use IMDSv2 and a supported SDK configuration, and restrict who may pass or replace the instance role. Grant ListBucket or other actions only if the application actually needs them. Role credentials eliminate static-key distribution but do not replace application and instance security.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [EC2 application role credentials](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_use_switch-role-ec2.html); [IMDSv2 and supported SDKs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/configuring-instance-metadata-service.html).

question:
A company runs Java applications in Docker containers on self-managed virtual machines and uses a self-managed MySQL database. It wants to migrate to AWS, replace its commercial JDK with a compatible OpenJDK distribution, and stop managing container hosts and database servers. Major application or relational-schema redesign is out of scope. A full database export and import takes six hours, but the allowed cutover outage is 15 minutes.

Which migration approach best meets these requirements?

options.text: Run the containers and MySQL on EC2 instances that mirror the current servers. Replace the commercial JDK with a tested OpenJDK image and manage the hosts as before.

Test Amazon Corretto container images, publish them to ECR, and run the services on ECS with Fargate. Migrate MySQL to a supported RDS for MySQL deployment using DMS full load and change replication, then validate and perform a controlled cutover.
Rewrite the application as Lambda functions and replace MySQL with DynamoDB, redesigning the data access layer around the new key structure.
Run tested Corretto images on ECS with Fargate and migrate MySQL to RDS, but stop the source database for the entire full-data export and import without ongoing change replication.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. This replatforming approach changes the runtime and managed hosting while retaining containers, Java, and MySQL's relational model. Corretto supplies a no-cost OpenJDK distribution. Fargate removes container-host management, RDS manages the database infrastructure, and DMS can transfer existing data while replicating subsequent changes before cutover.

<<1>> can reduce JDK licensing expense but retains the server operations that the company wants to remove.

<<3>> introduces the application and data-model redesign explicitly excluded from scope.

<<4>> selects suitable runtime services but makes the entire data transfer part of the outage, failing the short-cutover requirement for the proposed migration approach.

Validate Java dependencies, container compatibility, supported database versions, schema objects, and data consistency before switching traffic. Change replication reduces the final catch-up window; it does not eliminate cutover coordination or guarantee zero downtime. Replatforming does not mean every configuration remains unchanged.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Amazon Corretto](https://aws.amazon.com/corretto/); [ECS with Fargate](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/AWS_Fargate.html); [DMS homogeneous MySQL migration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/dms/latest/userguide/dm-migrating-data-mysql.html).

question:
A loan application uses a self-managed SQL Server database on EC2. At noon, an incident leaves no recoverable transactions after 10:30 a.m. The recovery design must address both database corruption and loss of the database's Availability Zone. The target RPO is 10 minutes and the RTO is two hours within the same Region.

Which backup design provides the best basis for meeting these objectives, subject to measured recovery testing?

options.text: Keep database-consistent hourly full backups in S3 Standard and archive the complete transaction-log chain there every five minutes. Monitor durable log completion and automate restoring a valid backup and replaying logs in another AZ.
Use only synchronous replication to another AZ and immediately apply every database change to the replica, without retaining recoverable historical backups.
Keep the only full backups on EBS volumes in the database AZ, and archive transaction logs to S3 every five minutes.
Keep the only full backups in S3 Glacier Deep Archive and use Standard retrieval during recovery. Archive transaction logs to S3 Standard every five minutes.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. Recovery needs both a usable base backup and an unbroken sequence of logs. Keeping them outside the failed AZ supports restoration elsewhere, while frequent completed log archival reduces the amount of recent work exposed to loss. Replay can stop at a known good point before corruption.

<<2>> improves availability but can replicate logical corruption. A current replica alone does not supply a historical recovery point.

<<3>> leaves the required base backup in the same AZ failure boundary. Transaction logs alone do not recreate the database.

<<4>> requires archive retrieval before database restoration. Deep Archive Standard retrieval typically takes hours, conflicting with a two-hour total recovery objective.

The stated incident exposes 90 minutes of transactions, exceeding the target. A five-minute schedule does not prove a five-minute RPO: measure the last durable, usable log and transfer completion. RTO includes provisioning, retrieval, restoration, replay, validation, and application recovery. Cross-Region S3 replication can add protection, but its asynchronous lag must be budgeted separately if regional disaster recovery is later required.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Database backup and log recovery](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/sql-server-ec2-ha-dr/options-considerations.html); [Database recovery scenarios](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/sql-server-ec2-ha-dr/dr-scenarios.html); [Archive retrieval latency](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/restoring-objects-retrieval-options.html); [S3 replication behavior](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/replication.html).

question:
A retailer wants to replace its on-premises call-center platform with managed AWS services. It needs inbound calling, contact flows, queues, and agent routing. Callers should also be able to state a request naturally, supply required details, and complete supported tasks without an agent, with context available if transfer is needed.

Which services should form the core of this solution? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use Amazon Polly as the sole component for recognizing caller intent and collecting conversational details.
Use Amazon Connect to provide the contact center, telephone numbers, flows, queues, and agent routing.
Use a fixed touch-tone menu as the only automated interaction, with no speech or natural-language intent processing.
Transcribe completed call recordings and analyze the text with Amazon Comprehend after calls end, using that analysis as the self-service interaction.
Integrate an Amazon Lex V2 bot into the contact flow to recognize intent, collect slots, and invoke supported business operations or transfer with context.

explanation.text:
<<2>> and <<5>> are correct. Connect supplies the contact-center workflow and agent handling. Lex provides speech recognition, natural-language understanding, and dialog state so the flow can gather the information needed for a supported task. Fulfillment code can call the retailer's authorized backend operations.

<<1>> turns text into speech, but does not by itself understand the caller's intent or manage the required dialog.

<<3>> can implement useful menu routing, but fails the natural-language interaction requirement.

<<4>> supports retrospective analytics rather than resolving the caller's request during the live conversation.

Configure intents, slots, error handling, fulfillment authorization, and the agent-transfer path. Speech understanding is not caller identity verification, and a bot should authenticate the customer before performing sensitive operations. Use a published Lex V2 version and appropriate alias for production traffic.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Connect and Lex integration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/connect/latest/adminguide/amazon-lex.html); [Amazon Lex V2 capabilities](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lexv2/latest/dg/what-is.html); [Amazon Polly text to speech](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/polly/latest/dg/what-is.html).

question:
A bank connects ten VPCs to its data center through virtual private gateways and a single 1 Gbps Direct Connect connection. An independent Internet connection already has enough capacity for the bank's reduced backup traffic. The bank must retain Direct Connect as its primary path and add automatic failover without purchasing another leased circuit or redesigning the VPC connectivity.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Purchase a second Direct Connect connection with a public virtual interface, and carry Site-to-Site VPN connections over that circuit.
Add a second set of private virtual interfaces to the existing Direct Connect connection, and use BGP to prefer the original virtual interfaces.

Create Internet-based Site-to-Site VPN connections from the data center to each VPC virtual private gateway. Configure BGP and routing preferences so the VPN paths take over when Direct Connect fails.
Purchase a physically diverse Direct Connect connection with private virtual interfaces, and configure BGP failover between the two connections.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. The existing Internet service supplies an independent transport path, and Site-to-Site VPN provides encrypted connectivity to the current virtual private gateways. BGP and appropriate routing preferences allow the primary Direct Connect route to give way to the backup path after failure detection.

<<1>> can provide an encrypted path over a separate circuit, but requires the additional leased connection that the budget excludes.

<<2>> provides additional logical interfaces, not physical-path independence. Failure of the shared Direct Connect connection removes both sets of virtual interfaces.

<<4>> is a strong resilience design when diverse Direct Connect circuits are justified, but also violates the no-new-circuit constraint.

Test both traffic directions, route withdrawal, convergence, and the reduced-throughput workload. A VPN carried over the same Direct Connect connection would not survive failure of that connection. Backup capacity and cost depend on the actual Internet service and traffic, so this choice is based on the stated existing capacity rather than a universal claim that VPN is always cheaper.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Direct Connect redundancy and VPN backup](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/toolkit-classic.html).

question:
A trading application uses a supported RDS for MySQL DB instance with a Multi-AZ standby. The company needs recovery from accidental data corruption within the same AWS Region, with an RPO of at most 10 minutes and an RTO below 2 hours. Recovery points must remain available for 14 days, and the team will monitor recovery-point freshness and validate the complete restore procedure in drills.

Which TWO alternative managed backup approaches can support this recovery plan? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Retain hourly RDS snapshots for 14 days and disable transaction-log-based point-in-time recovery.
Enable native RDS automated backups with a 14-day retention period and use point-in-time recovery to restore to a time before corruption.
Export RDS snapshots to S3 in Parquet format every hour and treat the exports as directly restorable RDS point-in-time backups.
Rely exclusively on the synchronous Multi-AZ standby, with no historical backups or point-in-time recovery.
Assign the supported DB instance to an AWS Backup plan with continuous backups for point-in-time recovery and a 14-day retention period.

explanation.text:
<<2>> and <<5>> are correct as alternative ways to manage continuous recovery protection. Native RDS automated backups combine backups and transaction logs for point-in-time restoration. AWS Backup continuous protection provides a managed PITR option for the supported RDS DB instance. Restore to a clean time in the retention window, then validate and reconnect the application.

<<1>> can lose nearly an hour of transactions between snapshots, exceeding the 10-minute RPO.

<<3>> produces an analytics export, not a native restorable snapshot or a transaction-log recovery chain. Parquet export cannot be supplied directly to RDS point-in-time restore.

<<4>> improves availability during infrastructure failure, but replicated corruption is present on the standby too. A historical recovery point is needed.

Neither service name guarantees the numeric objectives. Monitor the latest restorable time, retain enough history to precede corruption, and measure provisioning, restoration, validation, and application cutover together. The objectives here concern an in-Region recovery. AWS Backup copies of RDS continuous recovery points become snapshot copies without the source transaction-log history, so a copied recovery point must not be assumed to preserve continuous cross-Region PITR.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [RDS point-in-time recovery](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_PIT.html); [AWS Backup continuous protection](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-backup/latest/devguide/point-in-time-recovery.html); [RDS snapshot exports](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ExportSnapshot.html).

question:
A company is moving an internal Docker application to AWS. Its team operates ECS on EC2, and the stateless front end can tolerate Spot interruptions. The MySQL database has a predictable, continuously running baseline for the next three years. Documents are larger than 1 MB, read frequently for 90 days, then rarely retrieved with up to 12 hours of retrieval delay acceptable. Each document version must be protected from deletion for five years.

Which design best matches these workload characteristics while minimizing unnecessary compute and storage spending?

options.text: Run ECS tasks on Spot Instances, use an Aurora Serverless v2 database, and store documents on EBS volumes attached to the container hosts. Delete files with a cron job after five years.

Run ECS tasks on Spot Instances with draining enabled, cover eligible baseline RDS for MySQL usage with Reserved DB Instances, and store documents in S3. Use five-year Object Lock compliance retention, transition to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 90 days, and clean up versions after retention expires.
Run ECS tasks and the RDS database entirely at On-Demand rates. Keep documents in S3 Standard with five-year Object Lock compliance retention and no storage-class transitions.

Run containers on an EKS cluster with Spot worker nodes, pay On-Demand rates for the RDS database, and store documents in S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval after 90 days with five-year Object Lock compliance retention.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. Interruption-tolerant compute can use Spot capacity, while Reserved DB Instances discount eligible steady RDS usage. The document access pattern fits an online initial period followed by archival storage. Deep Archive standard retrieval typically completes within 12 hours, and compliance-mode Object Lock protects each retained version against premature deletion.

<<1>> places durable business documents on container-host block storage and provides no immutable retention control. A scheduled deletion job does not prevent earlier deletion. Aurora Serverless v2 can suit variable demand, but does not repair this storage requirement.

<<3>> preserves the documents but pays for unused flexibility in predictable database usage and keeps rarely accessed data in the frequent-access storage class.

<<4>> can operate the application, but introduces a different orchestrator and leaves both the database commitment discount and the permitted archival retrieval delay unused.

Spot draining needs replacement capacity and does not guarantee uninterrupted tasks. A Reserved DB Instance is a billing benefit, not an availability mechanism. Object Lock remains in force across lifecycle transitions. Configure version-aware expiration and cleanup after retention, because a delete marker is not permanent deletion of a protected version. Validate total cost with actual retrieval volume, transition charges, and archive minimum-duration rules.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [ECS Spot Instance draining](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/spot-instance-draining-linux-container.html); [RDS Reserved DB Instances](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_WorkingWithReservedDBInstances.html); [Archive retrieval latency](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/restoring-objects-retrieval-options.html); [S3 Object Lock retention](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html); [Object Lock and lifecycle actions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock-managing.html).

question:
A game publisher expects millions of anonymous users worldwide to download a 5 GB release package. The existing website will continue to list the download link. The publisher wants global edge caching over HTTPS, minimal origin-server administration, and no requirement for downloaders to hold AWS credentials.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Store package copies on EBS volumes in an EC2 Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer, and publish the regional load-balancer URL directly.
Store the package on EFS mounted by EC2 web servers behind an Application Load Balancer, and use that load balancer as a CloudFront origin.

Store the package in a private S3 bucket and configure its REST endpoint as a CloudFront origin with origin access control. Permit the distribution to read the object and publish its HTTPS download URL.
Store the package in an S3 Requester Pays bucket and publish the direct S3 object URL so anonymous users pay the download charges.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. S3 supplies durable object storage without web-server administration, and CloudFront caches the release at edge locations. OAC signs origin requests so the bucket can remain private while viewer downloads remain public. A 5 GB object is below CloudFront's current 50 GB cacheable-object limit.

<<1>> provides regional origin capacity but omits the required global edge cache and retains server management.

<<2>> supplies an edge cache and can work, but adds EC2 and filesystem administration to serve a static object that S3 can provide directly.

<<4>> fails the anonymous-access requirement. Requester Pays requires an authenticated requester that accepts the charge, and a direct S3 URL does not add a CloudFront cache.

Use the S3 REST origin, not an S3 website endpoint, for OAC. Scope the bucket permission to the intended distribution. Cache misses still fetch from the origin, so choose appropriate cache headers and versioned object names for releases. CloudFront reduces repeated origin transfers but does not eliminate the first fetch at every cache location.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [CloudFront origin access control for S3](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.html); [CloudFront object-size limits](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/cloudfront-limits.html); [S3 Requester Pays requirements](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/RequesterPaysBuckets.html); [CloudFront cache hits and origin fetches](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/Introduction.html).

question:
A trading application uses RDS for MySQL with a Multi-AZ standby. A failover drill interrupted service for 40 seconds. The team wants to reduce disruption toward a 20-second target, preserve idle client connections where possible, and avoid reconnecting every client after a writer change. The application can retry failed in-flight work, and migration to a compatible Aurora MySQL database is permitted. The final timing target must be verified under representative load.

Which changes work together toward these goals? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Enable RDS Optimized Writes on the existing database as the primary mechanism for preserving client connections during failover.
Cache read results in ElastiCache and use that cache as the replacement SQL writer whenever the database fails.
Place RDS Proxy between the application and its supported database targets, and configure application retries and connection timeouts for failover.
Migrate the database to an Aurora MySQL cluster after validating application and feature compatibility.
Provision Aurora Replicas in other Availability Zones and set promotion priorities to provide ready failover targets.
Add ordinary asynchronous read replicas to the existing RDS for MySQL DB instance and assume they become automatic Multi-AZ standby promotion targets.

explanation.text:
<<3>>, <<4>>, and <<5>> are correct. Aurora Replicas provide ready compute that the cluster can promote to writer, with promotion priorities influencing target selection. RDS Proxy separates client connections from backend database connections and can redirect to the new writer while preserving idle client connections. Together these address promotion and client reconnection overhead.

<<1>> targets write throughput, not preservation or rerouting of database sessions during writer failure.

<<2>> can serve suitable cached reads, but an ElastiCache cache is not a MySQL writer and cannot safely accept arbitrary SQL transactions for later replay.

<<6>> confuses ordinary RDS asynchronous read replicas with the managed Multi-AZ standby failover mechanism. Adding them does not make them automatic standby promotion targets.

A sub-20-second outage is a test objective, not a guarantee of these services. RDS Proxy can accept new client connections and temporarily hold work awaiting an available backend, subject to timeouts. It is not a durable write queue: in-flight statements and transactions can fail and require application handling. Test failover with real transaction lengths, session behavior, retries, and timeout settings, including idempotency where retrying could duplicate a committed operation.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [RDS Proxy pooling and failover](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/rds-proxy.howitworks.html); [Aurora high availability](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/Concepts.AuroraHighAvailability.html); [RDS read replicas and standbys](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReadRepl.html).

question:
An application retrieves its RDS for MySQL application-user password from an encrypted S3 file. The next CloudFormation deployment must generate a random password, store it in a managed secret, and rotate it every 90 days. An existing database bootstrap step can create or update the least-privilege application user with the generated password.

Which design meets the requirements with the least custom rotation code and scheduling overhead?

options.text: Create a Secrets Manager secret with GenerateSecretString, apply it through the existing bootstrap step, and attach database connection metadata. Use a CloudFormation RotationSchedule with a supported hosted MySQL rotation Lambda and a rate(90 days) schedule.

Generate a password in a deployment script and store it as a Parameter Store SecureString. Implement a custom Lambda function to update both the database user and parameter, and invoke it through an EventBridge schedule every 90 days.
Create a generated Secrets Manager secret and apply it through the existing bootstrap step. Write a custom MySQL rotation Lambda and invoke it directly from an EventBridge schedule every 90 days.
Create a generated Secrets Manager secret and apply it through the existing bootstrap step. Rotate only its KMS encryption key every 90 days, leaving the database user and stored password unchanged.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. Secrets Manager owns the secret version lifecycle and rotation schedule, and a supported hosted MySQL rotation Lambda avoids implementing the database-specific rotation workflow from scratch. Use the CloudFormation Secrets Manager transform required for HostedRotationLambda and ensure the database attachment exists before creating the rotation schedule.

<<2>> can be implemented, but requires custom password generation, secret-version handling, database update logic, and scheduling. Parameter Store does not supply the named Secrets Manager rotation resource.

<<3>> can also work if implemented correctly, but unnecessarily rebuilds the supported rotation implementation and scheduling integration.

<<4>> changes encryption key material, not the database password. The application credential would remain unchanged and violate the rotation requirement.

Generating a secret does not create the MySQL user or automatically apply its password. The bootstrap step establishes that initial valid credential; SecretTargetAttachment supplies connection details rather than creating database users. Rotation then creates a pending value, applies it to the database, tests authentication, and promotes the tested version to AWSCURRENT. Configure the rotation function's database connectivity and permissions, and ensure the application refreshes credentials after rotation.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [CloudFormation secret rotation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/TemplateReference/aws-resource-secretsmanager-rotationschedule.html); [CloudFormation rotation rules](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/TemplateReference/aws-properties-secretsmanager-rotationschedule-rotationrules.html); [Secrets Manager Lambda rotation steps](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/rotate-secrets_lambda-functions.html); [KMS key rotation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/rotate-keys.html).

question:
An educational mobile application uses API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB. Short exam-submission bursts exceed the table's write capacity, although average traffic fits its existing capacity. Students can receive an acceptance receipt once a submission is durably queued and obtain the grading result asynchronously within a few minutes. Immutable exam images also load slowly for users worldwide.

Which design absorbs the bursts without maintaining peak write capacity continuously and improves static-asset delivery?

options.text: Provision DynamoDB continuously for the full burst peak and keep synchronous submission processing. Store images in S3 and have clients download them directly from the bucket.
Place S3 images behind CloudFront, but keep the existing synchronous Lambda-to-DynamoDB submission path and its current capacity unchanged.

Have the API durably enqueue submissions in SQS before acknowledging acceptance. Process them with idempotent Lambda consumers at bounded concurrency, write results to DynamoDB, and serve S3 images through CloudFront.
Migrate submissions to RDS for MySQL with a Multi-AZ standby and read replicas, keep synchronous writes without a queue, and serve S3 images through CloudFront.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. SQS separates acceptance from completion, allowing the system to absorb a short input burst and process it at a rate the database can sustain. Lambda event-source concurrency limits and batch sizing help control the drain rate. CloudFront caches the images near viewers, using S3 as the durable origin.

<<1>> spends continuously on peak database capacity and omits edge caching for the images.

<<2>> improves image delivery but leaves the documented write-burst bottleneck unchanged.

<<4>> adds a database migration without providing the required buffering. A Multi-AZ standby addresses availability, and read replicas do not distribute the application's writes across independent writers.

A queue does not increase the table's write capacity or imply immediate grading. Return an accepted submission identifier, then expose completion or failure through a status API or notification. Use stable submission IDs for idempotency because SQS/Lambda processing can repeat. Monitor queue age, retries, dead-letter handling, and the end-to-end result delay. If sustained arrivals exceed processing capacity, the backlog will keep growing and additional capacity is required.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Lambda processing of SQS queues](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/with-sqs.html); [SQS event-source concurrency limits](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/api/API_ScalingConfig.html); [CloudFront cache hits and origin fetches](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/Introduction.html); [RDS read replicas and standbys](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReadRepl.html).

question:
A retailer runs a dynamic e-commerce site in its data center. Its HTTPS origin is publicly reachable through a resolvable DNS name. Most bandwidth serves cacheable product photos and videos, while checkout and account pages are personalized. A global promotion starts in a few days, but an application migration to AWS will take three months.

Which change can reduce origin traffic quickly while retaining the existing application?

options.text: Move the site's authoritative DNS to Route 53 and keep all browser requests pointed directly at the existing data-center servers.
Copy the website files to an S3 website endpoint and retire the data-center application, relying on the static website endpoint to execute checkout and account operations.
Complete the planned application and database migration to AWS, then introduce weighted DNS routing before starting the promotion.

Configure CloudFront with the existing HTTPS server as a custom origin. Cache product media, configure personalized paths to bypass caching and forward required request data, and point the public site hostname to the distribution.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. CloudFront can use an on-premises HTTPS server as a custom origin, so cached product media can be served from edge locations before the application migration. Separate cache behaviors let dynamic requests continue to reach the existing application with the cookies, headers, and other request data it needs.

<<1>> can improve DNS operations, but DNS hosting does not cache product media or remove those HTTP requests from the data-center servers.

<<2>> can host static assets, but an S3 website endpoint cannot execute the retailer's dynamic checkout and account application.

<<3>> misses the stated deadline because it depends on finishing the three-month migration.

Use the origin DNS name rather than the public hostname that will point to CloudFront, to avoid a routing loop. Configure origin TLS, permitted methods, and caching rules for the actual paths. Personalized responses should not enter a shared cache unless the cache key and policy intentionally isolate them. CloudFront still sends cache misses and dynamic requests to the origin, so this design offloads cacheable traffic without eliminating origin capacity needs. Moving authoritative DNS to Route 53 is optional.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [CloudFront custom HTTP origins](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/DownloadDistS3AndCustomOrigins.html); [CloudFront cache hits and origin fetches](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/Introduction.html).

question:
Each new S3 photo sends an SNS notification to several Lambda processors. Every processor must receive every event and write its own metadata to the existing RDS for MySQL DB instance. During upload bursts, database CPU rises and processing fails. Profiling shows that connection creation is a major cost, while the database can sustain the average write workload if arrivals are smoothed. The company must retain this database deployment.

Which changes together address the bottlenecks and provide independent retry backlogs? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Enable SNS delivery-status logging and rely on notification-delivery retries alone to control the rate of completed database writes.
Place RDS Proxy in front of the RDS DB instance and make each Lambda processor use the proxy endpoint for database connections.
Subscribe one SQS queue per processor to the SNS topic. Have each Lambda processor consume its own queue with bounded concurrency, idempotent writes, and retry and dead-letter handling.
Use RDS Data API for the existing ordinary RDS for MySQL DB instance without changing its database deployment.
Add RDS read replicas and send all metadata INSERT and UPDATE statements to their read-only endpoints.

explanation.text:
<<2>> and <<3>> are correct. RDS Proxy reuses backend database connections to reduce the measured connection-churn overhead. A separate SQS subscription preserves a copy of each SNS event for each processor and provides an independent backlog. Bound concurrency across all consumers so their combined write rate remains within the writer's capacity.

<<1>> provides delivery visibility, but a successfully delivered notification is not proof of a committed metadata write. Delivery retries alone do not provide controlled per-processor database backlogs.

<<4>> targets the wrong database deployment. RDS Data API supports compatible Aurora clusters; it is not a feature that can be enabled on this ordinary RDS for MySQL instance.

<<5>> does not offload the write workload. Read replicas are intended for reads, while these statements must reach an appropriate writer.

Do not give all processors one shared SQS queue: competing consumers would divide the messages rather than give each processor every event. Use stable event or object-version identifiers to make retries idempotent, and acknowledge a message only after its processing succeeds. Monitor oldest-message age and dead-letter queues. Proxy pooling cannot make an underprovisioned database execute unlimited writes, and session pinning can reduce pooling efficiency.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [RDS Proxy pooling and failover](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/rds-proxy.howitworks.html); [SNS fanout to SQS subscribers](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sns-sqs-as-subscriber.html); [Lambda processing of SQS queues](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/with-sqs.html); [SQS event-source concurrency limits](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/api/API_ScalingConfig.html); [RDS Data API scope](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/data-api.html); [RDS read replicas and standbys](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReadRepl.html).

question:
A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled and one member account per project. Every EC2 instance has a Name tag, but some lack the required Project tag. AWS Config records EC2 instances in the relevant accounts and Regions. The company wants a central AWS Config compliance view and a guardrail that prevents new untagged launches by member-account users, ordinary IAM roles, and member-account root users, even when local administrators grant broad IAM permissions.

Which controls should the company implement? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Use Amazon Inspector vulnerability assessments as the required-Project-tag inventory across the organization.
Deploy the AWS Config required-tags rule in each relevant account and Region, scope it to EC2 instances, and set Project as a required tag key.
Attach an SCP to the applicable organization root or OU that denies ec2:RunInstances when the required Project tag is absent from the instance tags in the request.
Attach a tag-enforcement IAM policy only to the developer roles currently known in each project account, and allow local administrators to manage those policies.
Enable the Security Hub resource tagging standard with requiredTagKeys left at its default value, and use its EC2 tagging findings to identify missing Project tags.
Create an organization AWS Config aggregator in the central account to view the member accounts and Regions and query required-tags compliance.

explanation.text:
<<2>>, <<3>>, and <<6>> are correct. Config evaluates existing recorded EC2 instances against the specific Project requirement. The SCP denies noncompliant launch requests for covered member-account principals, regardless of broad local IAM allows. The aggregator brings the resulting resource and compliance data into a central read-only view.

<<1>> uses a vulnerability-management service as though it were the required-tag compliance rule.

<<4>> covers only selected roles and leaves the controls under local administration. It does not establish the required organization-level limit for all covered member-account principals, including root.

<<5>> is a configuration error, not a lack of tagging support in Security Hub. Its tagging controls can require specific keys, but the default checks whether any tag exists. These instances already have Name, so that setting does not detect missing Project. It also does not supply the requested Config aggregation.

Scope the launch denial to the EC2 instance resource and use tag-on-create request conditions, including exact tag-key handling where required. The caller still needs normal launch and CreateTags permissions. SCPs do not grant permissions and do not cover management-account principals or service-linked roles. Config detects existing noncompliance but does not block creation, and an aggregator does not deploy the rules. Preventing later tag removal would require an additional guardrail beyond this launch requirement.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [AWS Config required-tags rule](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/required-tags.html); [EC2 tag-on-create IAM conditions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/supported-iam-actions-tagging.html); [Organization service control policies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps.html); [AWS Config organization aggregation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/aggregate-data.html); [Security Hub resource tagging standard](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/securityhub/latest/userguide/standards-tagging.html).

question:
A company will migrate supported VMware virtual machines to EC2 during an approved maintenance window. It must retain the installed guest applications and configuration, and replace an on-premises SMB logging and backup share with a managed Windows-compatible file system. Import compatibility and software licensing have been verified.

Which migration plan addresses both the servers and the shared storage?

options.text: Copy VMware snapshot files and the SMB data to an S3 File Gateway share. Select the uploaded snapshot objects directly as EC2 AMIs.
Import supported VMware images through VM Import/Export, then copy the SMB files to S3 and have the applications mount the S3 bucket directly as an SMB share.

Import supported VMware images from S3 through VM Import/Export and launch the resulting AMIs. Use DataSync to copy the SMB files and required metadata to FSx for Windows File Server, then validate and cut over the clients.
Register the VMware guests with Systems Manager, then use that registration to create EC2 AMIs automatically with AWS Backup. Copy the SMB files to FSx for Windows File Server.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. VM Import/Export handles compatible VM images, while DataSync transfers file data to an SMB file system. They solve separate migration problems. Test the imported guests, configure Active Directory and file permissions, and perform a final consistent copy before switching clients.

<<1>> treats stored snapshot files as AMIs without an import operation. <<2>> handles the compute migration but an S3 bucket does not itself expose an SMB share. <<4>> mistakes Systems Manager enrollment for an image-conversion workflow. Registration alone does not produce an EC2 AMI.

Use a supported image format such as OVA or stream-optimized VMDK; an OVF descriptor alone is not a guest disk. Import may require platform-specific preparation and driver changes, so retaining an application does not remove the need for compatibility testing.

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vm-import/latest/userguide/prerequisites.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/datasync/latest/userguide/create-fsx-location.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/filegateway/latest/files3/what-is-file-s3.html

question:
A write application runs in ECS on Fargate and connects to Aurora MySQL in the same VPC. Its task definition currently puts a Secrets Manager ARN in environment[].value for DB_PASSWORD and uses an instance-specific DB_HOST. The database security group has no rule for the task security group. The application must reconnect to the writer after failover. Execution-role secret access, supported Fargate platform version, routes, task egress and network ACLs are already configured.

Which changes are required? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Keep DB_PASSWORD in environment[] and replace its value with the Secrets Manager secret name so ECS resolves the password.
Set DB_HOST to the current writer instance endpoint and retain it unchanged after any writer promotion.
Move DB_PASSWORD to the container definition secrets[] array with valueFrom set to the secret ARN and the password JSON-key selector, if needed.
Allow inbound TCP 3306 on the Aurora security group from the security group attached to the Fargate task ENIs.
Add an inbound TCP 3306 rule to the Fargate task security group with the Aurora security group as its source.
Set DB_HOST to the Aurora cluster writer endpoint and reconnect through that hostname after failover.

explanation.text:
<<3>>, <<4>> and <<6>> are correct. ECS resolves secrets[] references at task startup. Aurora must admit the task-initiated connection, and its cluster endpoint directs new connections to the current writer. The application still needs retry/reconnection logic and appropriate DNS caching.

<<1>> supplies a literal environment value rather than secret injection. <<2>> pins connections to a specific instance, which might become a reader after promotion of another instance. <<5>> opens the wrong direction: the task initiates the database connection, and stateful security groups permit its response traffic.

Network reachability, credentials and writer discovery are separate requirements. An instance endpoint can work while that instance is the writer; it is not inherently unusable. Secret rotation also does not refresh an existing container environment: start new tasks or implement runtime retrieval.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/secrets-envvar-secrets-manager.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/security-group-rules.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/Aurora.Overview.Endpoints.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-security-groups.html

question:
A company reaches a VPC in us-east-1 through one Direct Connect connection and a private virtual interface attached directly to its virtual private gateway. It is adding a nonoverlapping VPC in us-west-1. Both VPCs need private connectivity to the data center, and the design must tolerate failure of one Direct Connect connection or location. A second diverse circuit and customer router can be provisioned.

Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Create diverse Direct Connect connections and attach each private VIF directly to both VPC virtual private gateways.
Create a transit gateway in each Region and attach a private VIF from each diverse Direct Connect connection directly to both transit gateways.
Retain the existing private VIF and create a public VIF on the second diverse connection to route private addresses in the us-west-1 VPC.

Create a Direct Connect gateway and associate each VPC virtual private gateway with it. Create private VIFs to that gateway on connections at separate locations, validate redundant routing, and retire the old direct-to-VGW VIF after cutover.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. The Direct Connect gateway provides the association point for virtual private gateways in different Regions. Private VIFs on diverse physical connections provide redundant on-premises paths to those VPCs. Configure customer-side BGP, route preferences and failover testing as well.

<<1>> tries to attach one private VIF directly to multiple virtual private gateways. <<2>> uses the wrong VIF and attachment path: a transit-gateway design uses transit VIFs through a Direct Connect gateway. <<3>> uses a public VIF for private VPC routing.

A gateway association does not create physical redundancy. Separate locations, customer equipment and diverse paths address different failure modes. Do not infer general VPC-to-VPC transit from these gateway associations.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/virtualgateways.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/disaster-recovery-resiliency.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/WorkingWithVirtualInterfaces.html

question:
Partners upload inventory through SFTP to an EC2 server with an Elastic IP. They use SSH keys, verify the server host key, and connect only from approved source IPs. The company wants managed storage and multi-AZ endpoint availability with the least server administration. Partners will retain SFTP and accept a hostname or additional IPs for failover. The existing host key is supported for import.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Run SFTP servers behind an NLB in multiple AZs and mount the same EBS Multi-Attach volume on all servers as their shared cross-AZ filesystem.
Run an SFTP container service on Fargate across AZs with EFS behind an NLB. Maintain the SFTP image, user database, host keys and scaling configuration.

Use an internet-facing VPC-hosted Transfer Family SFTP endpoint across AZs with S3 storage. Import the host key, configure partner users and scoped S3 access, reuse the old Elastic IP in one subnet, and add IPs for other AZs with source-IP security-group restrictions.
Use a Transfer Family PUBLIC endpoint with S3 storage and attach the existing Elastic IP and a partner-restricted security group directly to that PUBLIC endpoint.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. An internet-facing VPC-hosted Transfer Family endpoint supports chosen Elastic IPs and security groups while the service manages the SFTP servers. Preserve the server identity separately from partner user authentication and grant each user only the intended S3 access.

<<1>> relies on EBS Multi-Attach as a cross-AZ shared filesystem; it is neither that nor a substitute for filesystem coordination. <<2>> can be engineered, but retains more SFTP server administration than the managed service. <<4>> confuses the PUBLIC endpoint type with the VPC-hosted type that supports these network controls.

An Elastic IP belongs to one endpoint subnet. Reusing the old address alone does not provide client failover across AZs. Partners must use the agreed hostname or alternate addresses, and existing SSH sessions may still need to reconnect.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/transfer/latest/userguide/create-server-in-vpc.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/transfer/latest/userguide/configuring-servers-change-host-key.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/ebs-volumes-multi.html

question:
Financial batches arrive in an encrypted S3 raw-data bucket. Only an approved processing role may read them, and raw records must never enter queues, job arguments, logs or the downstream bucket. A tested PySpark job masks account numbers, joins each batch to a large reference dataset and emits JSON in about 20 minutes. Catalog definitions already exist. The team must reuse this whole-batch code, meet a 60-minute target and avoid managing a compute cluster.

Which processing design meets these requirements?

options.text: Send each raw record through SQS to a Lambda consumer that masks it before writing downstream.
Run the unchanged Spark transformation in one standard Lambda invocation with a 30-minute timeout.

Start a Glue Spark job with object references when a complete batch is ready. Use the approved role and catalog metadata, validate the sanitized output in restricted staging, then publish the accepted batch downstream.
Run a Glue crawler to update the catalog and copy the raw objects downstream when the crawler succeeds.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. A Glue Spark job can execute the existing transformation without operating a cluster. The catalog describes data; the job actually masks and reshapes it. A separate validation and publication gate prevents a failed or incomplete sanitization attempt from becoming a downstream batch.

<<1>> violates the explicit prohibition on placing raw records in queues. <<2>> exceeds the 15-minute limit of a standard Lambda invocation and does not provide the requested Spark execution model. <<4>> mistakes schema discovery for transformation: a crawler does not sanitize object contents.

Pass references, restrict staging and logs, and publish a batch manifest only after all expected sanitized objects pass validation. The runtime is a workload assumption, not a claim that Glue always finishes within that duration. Test capacity, schema changes and failure recovery against the target.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/glue/latest/dg/add-crawler.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/glue/latest/dg/author-job-glue.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html

question:
Standard Lambda functions process images and write metadata to DynamoDB in the same Region. They must now issue graph queries to a private Neptune DB cluster. The functions use IPv4 and can be connected to the cluster VPC. IAM database and DynamoDB permissions are already correct.

Which network designs allow the functions to reach both services? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Connect the functions to public subnets, allow their security group into Neptune, and use only a default route to an internet gateway for DynamoDB access.
Connect the functions to private subnets and permit their security group into Neptune on the configured database port. Associate a DynamoDB gateway endpoint with the function subnet route tables.
Leave the functions without customer-VPC connectivity and create a Neptune management API interface endpoint in the database VPC, using that endpoint for graph queries.

Connect the functions to private subnets and permit their security group into Neptune. Route outbound IPv4 traffic through a public NAT gateway with internet-gateway connectivity to reach the DynamoDB service endpoint.
Leave the functions without customer-VPC connectivity and add a Neptune inbound rule for the Lambda service IP ranges.

explanation.text:
<<2>> and <<4>> are correct. VPC connectivity provides a private route to Neptune. DynamoDB can then be reached through its gateway endpoint or through a working NAT egress path to its public service endpoint. Endpoint policies, security controls and IAM permissions must also permit the operations.

<<1>> does not give a standard VPC-connected Lambda function a public IPv4 address, so an internet-gateway route alone is insufficient. <<3>> supplies a private management API endpoint, not network reachability from the function to the graph database query endpoint. <<5>> changes filtering but does not establish a route into the private VPC.

A gateway endpoint avoids a NAT dependency for DynamoDB traffic. NAT remains useful when the function needs other external destinations. Adding a VPC attachment changes the function’s outbound network path, so reassess all dependencies when making that change.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-vpc-internet.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpc-endpoints-ddb.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/neptune/latest/userguide/vpc-interface-endpoints.html

question:
A company is migrating Windows applications to AWS. An on-premises SMB share contains 1 TB and gains about 5 GB daily. It remains the sole write source until cutover. Windows consumers in AWS need an SMB file system and can accept one daily refresh plus transfer time. Direct Connect, Active Directory connectivity and transfer permissions are available.

Which migration approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Create FSx for Windows File Server. Use DataSync for the initial SMB copy and scheduled daily incremental transfers, keep AWS consumers read-only, and finish with a write freeze, final transfer and validated cutover.
Create EFS, copy the files daily with DataSync, and mount the EFS endpoint directly as the existing Windows SMB share.
Copy the files daily to S3 and replace the Windows applications' SMB mounts with a Transfer Family SFTP endpoint without changing the applications.
Replace the on-premises share with an S3 File Gateway share and treat its cached files as an independent authoritative copy that remains automatically coherent with a separately writable FSx share.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. FSx for Windows supplies SMB access and DataSync moves files and supported metadata from the authoritative source. The daily schedule matches the stated freshness tolerance, provided task duration and source write behavior are considered.

<<2>> substitutes an NFS filesystem for an SMB requirement. <<3>> substitutes SFTP for an application that still requires an SMB mount. <<4>> assumes automatic coherence between separately writable file systems; those products do not establish that relationship by themselves.

Scheduled transfer is not synchronous replication. A change just after a completed run can wait roughly a day plus the next task duration. At final cutover, stop source writes, transfer the remaining changes, verify permissions and content, and switch the authoritative write location. Coordinate reader access during transfers if a consistent batch view is required. Data volume alone does not establish migration duration.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/datasync/latest/userguide/create-fsx-location.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fsx/latest/WindowsGuide/migrate-files-to-fsx-datasync.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/datasync/latest/userguide/task-scheduling.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/datasync/latest/userguide/datasync-large-migration-running-tasks.html

question:
An organization requires every production FSx for Windows File Server deployment to have managed availability across two Availability Zones. Some file systems are Single-AZ and receive frequent writes. A full restore would exceed the allowed write-outage window, but testing shows the remaining changes can be copied and verified during a short final freeze.

Which migration plan meets the policy with the least disruption?

options.text: Create a Multi-AZ file system, use DataSync for an initial copy and repeated incremental tasks while the source remains active, then freeze writes for a final verified transfer and switch clients.
Take one backup while the source remains writable, use the console restore wizard to change its deployment type to Multi-AZ, and switch clients later without transferring post-backup writes.
Create a second Single-AZ file system in another AZ, schedule DataSync copies, and manually switch clients if the original file system fails.
Edit the existing Single-AZ file system's deployment type to Multi-AZ in place, retaining its existing file-system identifier.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. Copying most data before cutover limits the final outage to the remaining transfer, verification and client switch. The destination is an actual Multi-AZ FSx deployment with managed cross-AZ availability.

<<2>> attempts to change a deployment type that the documented console restore wizard fixes. It also omits writes made after the backup. <<3>> leaves two Single-AZ deployments and relies on scheduled copies and manual recovery, which does not meet the policy. <<4>> proposes an unsupported in-place deployment-type change.

DataSync executes transfer tasks; it is not continuous synchronous replication. Monitor incremental runs, keep one authoritative writer, and test the final copy and client reconnection. A backup protects a point in time; it does not by itself provide a continuously available, current Multi-AZ destination.

question:
An organization has hundreds of AWS accounts grouped into team OUs. Each team leader must view detailed charges for that team's accounts, without viewing other teams' costs. Finance has approved using each account's current OU for attribution and wants an interactive dashboard.

Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Use AWS RAM to generate a billing report for each OU and share the resulting reports with the team leaders.

Export consolidated CUR 2.0 data from the management account to S3. Join usage account IDs to a maintained account-to-OU map in an Athena-backed dataset, and provide QuickSight readers with enforced row-level security for their teams.
Create a consolidated QuickSight cost dataset and share it with every leader, relying on a dashboard OU filter that each reader can change to control access.
Use Systems Manager OpsCenter to generate consolidated cost line items for each OU and grant leaders access to those operational dashboards.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. Billing data supplies the charges, the account map supplies the agreed OU attribution, and dataset row-level security supplies reader-specific authorization. These are three separate functions. Keep the mapping and permissions current as accounts move or leadership changes.

<<1>> assigns billing-report generation to RAM, whose purpose is resource sharing. <<3>> uses an interactive filter as though it were an access-control boundary. <<4>> assigns billing export and cost analysis to an operations-issue service.

Use QuickSight Enterprise row-level security or separately authorized datasets, and do not make restricted readers dataset owners. The underlying S3 and query permissions must also prevent bypass. Current OU attribution can reassign historical charges after an account move; historical ownership instead requires a time-aware mapping.

question:
A company wants to rightsize a large fleet of memory-intensive EC2 database instances and attached EBS volumes. Many databases use active/passive failover pairs, and no representative utilization baseline exists. The company wants automated recommendations without committing to a support-plan upgrade.

Which action should the solutions architect take first?

options.text: Use current CPU utilization to identify lightly used instances and immediately downsize every passive database to the smallest available instance type.
Enable EC2 detailed monitoring and assume it automatically supplies guest memory and filesystem usage, then downsize instances after twelve hours.

Configure the CloudWatch agent to publish supported guest memory metrics, opt in to Compute Optimizer, and collect representative history. Review eligible EC2 and EBS recommendations against active/passive roles, peaks and tested failover capacity.
Purchase Enterprise Support, wait twelve hours for Trusted Advisor recommendations, and apply every suggested reduction without collecting additional workload history.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. Compute Optimizer uses utilization history to generate recommendations, and supported memory metrics improve the evidence for memory-intensive workloads. Configure the agent and required metric dimensions; installation alone is insufficient.

<<1>> equates idle standby utilization with low required failover capacity. <<2>> confuses finer standard EC2 metric intervals with collection of guest memory data. <<4>> adds an unnecessary prerequisite and treats a short observation period as enough evidence for every workload.

For EC2, the documented minimum is 30 hours of CloudWatch data in the usual 14-day lookback. Passing that threshold does not prove a period represents business peaks. A standby must still sustain the active workload after failure. Validate memory, I/O, licensing and recovery requirements before applying changes, and distinguish recommendation eligibility from safe operational sizing.

question:
A company publishes new MP4 training videos each month for employees around the world. Its player requires adaptive-bitrate HLS. The company wants managed transcoding and global delivery without maintaining video servers. Original masters are rarely accessed, must remain immediately retrievable, and are retained for at least a year.

Which architecture best meets these requirements?

options.text: Run transcoding jobs on a self-managed EC2 fleet and store the HLS outputs on each worker's EBS volume. Use the changing worker fleet as the CloudFront origin.
Use MediaConvert to produce only standalone MP4 outputs in S3 and distribute them with CloudFront, relying on the CDN to create HLS manifests and segments.

Submit MediaConvert jobs with an HLS output group and multiple bitrate renditions to S3. Serve the HLS objects through CloudFront, and use a lifecycle rule scoped to eligible original masters to move them to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval.
Use CodePipeline and a custom transcoder to create HLS in S3, then serve global employee playback from a single AWS Wavelength Zone.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. MediaConvert creates the manifests and renditions required for adaptive streaming, S3 stores the output objects, and CloudFront distributes them geographically. Scope archival lifecycle rules to original masters so active streaming segments remain in the intended serving class.

<<1>> adds server and per-worker storage management and requires additional origin-availability coordination. <<2>> omits HLS packaging; CloudFront distributes content but does not transcode an MP4 into HLS. <<4>> can orchestrate custom processing, but a Wavelength Zone is not a substitute for a global CDN.

Choose bitrate and codec settings supported by the player and protect private training content with appropriate origin and viewer access controls. Glacier Instant Retrieval provides immediate retrieval but has retrieval charges and a minimum storage duration, so lifecycle choices depend on actual retention and access patterns.

question:
A company will migrate a supported on-premises SQL Server Always On database to RDS for MySQL. It has approved the engine change and necessary application changes, prefers managed AWS services, and needs the source to remain writable until a short final cutover.

Which migration plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Upload a native SQL Server backup to S3 and use Glue to restore that binary backup directly as an RDS for MySQL database.
Copy a SQL Server backup to S3 with DataSync and execute SQL Server BULK INSERT on RDS for MySQL to restore all schema and data.

Assess and convert the schema with AWS SCT, resolve unsupported objects and test the application, then use DMS full load plus change data capture into RDS for MySQL. Validate and complete a controlled cutover.
Configure DataSync to replicate the live SQL Server database files directly into the RDS for MySQL instance, then promote the copied files as the MySQL database.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. Heterogeneous migration requires both engine-compatible schema and a data transfer path. SCT assists with schema conversion and identifies work that must be completed manually; DMS can load data and capture ongoing changes while the source remains in use.

<<1>> treats an engine-specific binary backup as a MySQL restore format. <<2>> combines file transfer with a SQL Server command that does not restore a SQL Server database into MySQL. <<4>> treats a managed database endpoint as a filesystem destination and omits engine conversion and database-aware change capture.

For an Always On source, configure the supported DMS source topology, listener, permissions and replication prerequisites. Test source failover, data types and application semantics. Stop writes for cutover, let changes catch up and reconcile the target. Schema conversion and CDC do not guarantee that every stored procedure or SQL behavior works unchanged.

question:
A company will deploy a stateless .NET application as Linux containers. It needs an internet-facing service that tolerates an Availability Zone failure and a highly available SQL Server database. The team wants managed infrastructure and must keep database credentials out of container images and plaintext task definitions. Startup environment injection is acceptable.

Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Run both the application and a single SQL Server container as Fargate services. Enable service scaling and put a SecureString parameter ARN in environment[].value to inject the password.

Run the application as a multi-AZ ECS Fargate service behind an ALB and use a supported RDS for SQL Server Multi-AZ deployment. Put the Secrets Manager reference in secrets[].valueFrom and authorize the task execution role to retrieve and decrypt it.

Run the application on Fargate and launch independent SQL Server EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. Put a Parameter Store ARN in environment[].value and rely on instance replacement for database failover.

Use RDS for SQL Server Multi-AZ and a self-managed Kubernetes cluster. Put a Secrets Manager ARN in a pod's ordinary environment value and mount an empty volume, relying on Kubernetes to retrieve the secret automatically.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. The application runs across AZs while RDS manages supported SQL Server database failover. ECS uses the task execution role to resolve secrets[] references when starting containers, keeping the password out of the image and ordinary task-definition values. Startup network access to Secrets Manager is also required.

<<1>> does not turn one stateful database container into a replicated database and uses a literal environment value. <<3>> confuses replacement of independent machines with coordinated database replication and repeats the secret-injection error. <<4>> lacks an actual Kubernetes-to-Secrets-Manager integration; a secret ARN and an empty volume are not sufficient.

The injected password is still available inside the container environment to the application and sufficiently privileged inspection. Rotation requires replacement tasks or runtime refresh. Database Multi-AZ and application multi-AZ deployment address different components, and clients must retry connections after failover.

question:
A team stores its application in one GitHub repository. A CodePipeline pipeline builds the main branch for production. Developers need isolated feature development, automatic unit tests, separate development and production artifacts, and a reviewed path to merge changes back into main. Feature code must run only in a separate test account before approval.

Which workflow meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a feature-branch CodePipeline workflow with CodeBuild build and test actions and artifacts in the test account. Use distinct artifact locations and scoped roles, then merge reviewed changes into main to trigger the production pipeline.
Create a feature-branch pipeline with unit tests, but write successful builds to the same S3 object key consumed automatically by the production deployment stage.
Create a feature-branch pipeline that deploys each feature to production first and runs its CodeBuild unit tests afterward, rolling back only when tests fail.
Give the feature pipeline access to the production deployment role and let developers select the production account for integration tests before their pull requests are approved.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. Branch-specific triggers separate feature and release workflows, CodeBuild executes the unit tests, and account plus artifact permissions prevent development output from replacing production releases. Reviewed merges retain a clear integration path in the original repository.

<<2>> keeps separate pipeline names but shares the artifact consumed by production. <<3>> exposes production to unapproved feature code before validation. <<4>> permits the very preapproval production execution that the requirement forbids.

A branch name is not a security boundary. Use separate roles, S3 permissions and, for cross-account encrypted artifacts, appropriate customer-managed KMS key policies. Block promotion when tests fail and preserve commit-to-artifact provenance. CodePipeline orchestrates actions; CodeBuild performs builds and tests.

question:
A QA team uses approved CloudFormation templates to create temporary EC2 and Auto Scaling test environments in several Regions. Only its manager can currently provision them. The company wants team members to launch the approved configurations themselves without receiving general EC2, Auto Scaling or CloudFormation write access.

Which approach best meets this requirement?

options.text: Allow every team member to assume the manager's existing broad provisioning role, and instruct them to use only templates stored in an approved S3 folder.

Publish the templates as Service Catalog products in authorized portfolios and Regions. Apply product launch constraints using a scoped launch role, and give QA members portfolio access plus the minimum end-user permissions.
Grant QA members broad EC2 and Systems Manager permissions and distribute an Automation runbook, relying on instructions to prevent direct use of the underlying APIs.
Grant QA members CloudFormation read-only access and distribute a CLI script that calls CreateStack, relying on the script to supply the manager's missing permissions.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. Service Catalog exposes approved products while its launch role supplies the underlying provisioning permissions. Portfolio access, end-user permissions and launch constraints work together; the role is assumed by the service for the approved product lifecycle.

<<1>> retains broad underlying access and relies on a procedural restriction. <<3>> similarly permits direct resource changes outside the governed path. <<4>> cannot make an unauthorized CreateStack call succeed merely by placing it in a script.

Enforce restrictions with IAM and service configuration, not instructions to use only a console. Users need the appropriate product lifecycle permissions and any necessary read access, while the launch role needs the permissions required by the template. Scope template parameters and lifecycle permissions, and arrange cleanup for temporary environments.

question:
A network account shares one regional transit gateway with an AWS Organization. Each attached VPC contains either development or production workloads and uses nonoverlapping CIDRs. All attachments currently use the same default transit gateway route table, so both environments can reach each other. Same-environment VPCs must remain connected, but development and production must be isolated. No alternative inter-VPC path is required.

Which configuration provides the required routing isolation?

options.text: Tag attachments by environment and rely on Transit Gateway Network Manager inventory tags to block packets between different environments.
Add explicit deny rules to the EC2 security groups for the opposite environment while leaving the shared transit gateway routes unchanged.

Disable the shared default associations and propagations. Create development and production transit gateway route tables, associate each attachment with its environment's table, and propagate its routes only into that table.
Keep every attachment associated with the default table and propagate all VPC routes into both new environment tables, using attachment tags as the packet-routing selector.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. An attachment's association selects the transit gateway route table used for traffic arriving from that attachment. Propagation determines which destination routes a table learns. Keeping both operations within each environment prevents the routing table from learning the other environment's VPC routes.

<<1>> applies descriptive metadata rather than packet-forwarding rules. <<2>> proposes security-group deny rules, which do not exist. <<4>> neither selects the new lookup tables through associations nor isolates their route contents; tags are not a route lookup key.

An attachment associates with one transit gateway route table but can propagate into multiple tables, so inspect both settings. Remove cross-environment static routes or default routes that could bypass isolation, update VPC routes as needed, and control who may change the network configuration. Security groups can provide additional filtering with allow rules.

question:
Partners upload files nightly using SFTP and SSH keys to sftp.example.com. One EC2 server accepts the uploads on local storage, and a cron job later copies them to an S3 data lake. The company wants to remove that server and copy-job failure point while preserving the SFTP client workflow and hostname. It prefers the least server administration.

Which solution should it implement?

options.text: Place multiple EC2 SFTP servers behind a TCP NLB, retain local upload directories on each server, and run independent cron jobs that copy completed files to S3.
Place multiple EC2 SFTP servers behind an HTTPS ALB and route sftp.example.com to the ALB listener.
Replace the server with an S3 File Gateway and route sftp.example.com to its SMB file-share endpoint for the existing SFTP clients.

Create a Transfer Family SFTP server backed directly by the S3 data lake. Configure partner identities, directory and IAM access, preserve or coordinate the host key, then point the existing hostname to the service endpoint.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. Transfer Family accepts SFTP while placing uploaded data directly in the configured S3 storage, eliminating the self-managed SFTP host and the later local-to-S3 copy process. Migrate users and access mappings as well as DNS.

<<1>> can be developed into a working architecture, but still requires server patching, upload-state coordination and reliable per-server copying. <<2>> uses an HTTP-oriented load balancer listener for an SSH-based protocol. <<3>> provides a different file protocol and cannot receive the unchanged SFTP clients.

Preserving a DNS name does not preserve SSH server identity by itself. Import a supported host key or coordinate a verified client change. Use a VPC-hosted endpoint if the deployment needs chosen Elastic IPs or security-group source restrictions, and validate object-completion handling before downstream processing starts.

question:
A former administrator might retain the private SSH key used for Linux EC2 instances. All affected instances remain reachable through Systems Manager, and the company must revoke that key while preserving a tested recovery path. The fleet's relevant Linux users and authorized key entries are known.

Which procedure correctly rotates access?

options.text: Create a new EC2 key pair and use Run Command to replace authorized_keys with the downloaded private PEM contents on every affected instance.
Generate a new key pair and public-key replacement script, then submit AWS-RunShellScript directly to StartAutomationExecution as though it were an Automation runbook.
Delete the old EC2 key-pair resource, create a replacement with the same name, and rely on EC2 to update authorized_keys in all running instances.

Generate a new key pair and retain its private key securely. Use Run Command with AWS-RunShellScript to install the public key for the correct users, test access, then remove the former key and verify revocation.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. SSH authorization is enforced by the guest's authorized_keys contents. Systems Manager provides an independent management path for controlled fleet updates. Keep correct file ownership and permissions, inspect each command result, and explicitly verify removal of the former key.

<<1>> installs private material where public keys belong and unnecessarily exposes the replacement secret. <<2>> uses a Command document as an Automation runbook. Automation can invoke it through an aws:runCommand step, but not by treating the document types as interchangeable. <<3>> changes the EC2 key-pair resource without replacing public keys already present in the guest.

Adding a new key alone does not revoke the old one. Check other users, launch templates, images and configuration automation that could restore it, and revoke the former administrator's other credentials through the access-removal process.

question:
EC2 application instances in one VPC initiate MySQL connections to an Aurora cluster in that VPC. All application ENIs use AppSG and database ENIs use DbSG. The relevant AppSG outbound and DbSG inbound rules are absent, including any broad allow rules. Routes and network ACLs already permit the traffic. Only members of AppSG should connect to the database on TCP 3306.

Which security-group rules are required? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add an AppSG inbound rule for TCP 3306 with DbSG as the source.
Add an AppSG outbound rule for TCP 3306 with DbSG as the destination.
Add a DbSG inbound rule for TCP 3306 with AppSG as the source.
Add a DbSG outbound rule for TCP 3306 with AppSG as the destination.
Add an outbound network ACL rule allowing TCP 3306 to the entire database subnet instead of changing the security groups.
Add an inbound network ACL rule allowing TCP 3306 from the entire application subnet instead of changing the security groups.

explanation.text:
<<2>> and <<3>> are correct. The application initiates traffic toward database port 3306, so the application group must permit egress and the database group must permit ingress. Referencing the groups follows membership as the application fleet scales.

<<1>> permits initiation in the wrong direction and to the wrong application port. <<4>> is not needed to authorize responses to an allowed inbound connection. Security groups are stateful, so the return traffic uses connection tracking. <<5>> and <<6>> change controls that already permit the path, are broader than the stated group membership, and cannot override missing security-group allows.

The database response normally targets the application's ephemeral client port, not port 3306 on the application. Network ACLs are stateless and must independently permit both directions when restrictive, but that is already satisfied here. These network rules do not replace database authentication or authorization.
