question:
A company receives multipage scanned forms in S3. Staff manually extract key-value fields and tables, identify people and organizations mentioned in free-text notes, then submit validated results to an external API. A pilot has confirmed that AWS managed document and language services support the forms' languages and required entities. The company wants less manual work and no model training, while retaining review for uncertain results.

Which design best meets these requirements?

options.text: Operate an OCR engine on EKS, maintain custom parsers for fields and tables, and build an entity-recognition model before submitting validated results.
Use Step Functions with Rekognition text detection and Transcribe to infer form fields, tables and entities from the scanned pages.
Train and host a custom OCR and entity-extraction model in SageMaker, then implement a separate workflow for validation and API submission.

Use Step Functions to coordinate Textract document analysis, Comprehend entity analysis of extracted notes, and validation. Send uncertain results for human review, store approved output in S3, and use Lambda to submit it with retry and duplicate protection.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. Textract extracts document text, forms and tables, while Comprehend supplies the required entity analysis for the free-text notes. Orchestration separates asynchronous analysis, validation, review and the downstream API action.

<<1>> can work but adds cluster, parser and model operations that the requirements seek to avoid. <<2>> combines image text detection with a speech-to-text service and does not provide the required document-structure and entity workflow. Rekognition can detect text; the issue is not a total absence of OCR capability. <<3>> introduces model development despite the validated managed-service fit.

Confidence scores are evidence for routing, not guarantees of correctness. Calibrate thresholds and business validation against representative forms, review missing or inconsistent fields, and keep source provenance. Use suitable asynchronous Textract operations for multipage documents, and make retried API submission idempotent to avoid duplicate records.

question:
A retailer runs a multi-AZ EC2 Auto Scaling group behind an ALB and uses an RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB instance. Auto Scaling uses ELB health checks. Its HTTP health endpoint queries the shared database. During a traffic surge, repeated catalog reads saturate the database while local web processes remain responsive. Health-check timeouts cause repeated replacement of otherwise functional web instances. Catalog reads can tolerate a short, defined period of staleness.

Which changes prevent this replacement cycle and reduce the identified database load while preserving end-to-end monitoring? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add ordinary RDS MySQL read replicas and direct all reads to an automatically created shared reader endpoint, without selecting individual replica endpoints.

Replace the target health check with a meaningful application-local HTTP endpoint that does not query the shared database. Separately monitor an externally reachable end-to-end endpoint with a Route 53 health check and a CloudWatch alarm that notifies operators.
Change the ALB target-group health-check protocol to TCP. Continue using the database-querying HTTP endpoint only for an external alarm.
Configure a CloudWatch EC2 recovery alarm action against the RDS instance so high database CPU automatically recovers and reboots the database.
Integrate ElastiCache into the catalog read path. Use authorization-appropriate cache keys, a defined expiration or invalidation policy, and database fallback for cache misses.

explanation.text:
<<2>> and <<5>> are correct. Instance replacement should respond to an instance-local fault. An independent end-to-end check still detects a shared dependency failure without using it to replace every web instance. Caching eligible repeated reads reduces work at the measured bottleneck.

<<1>> proposes an endpoint that ordinary RDS DB-instance read replicas do not share. The application must route to their individual endpoints or supply its own routing layer. RDS Multi-AZ DB clusters and Aurora have different endpoint models.

<<3>> selects an unsupported ALB health-check protocol: ALB target checks use HTTP or HTTPS.

<<4>> applies an EC2 recovery action to the wrong resource type. Rebooting a busy database also does not remove the source of sustained query load.

A static file alone may miss a failed application process, so use a local check that reflects the service's ability to handle requests. Keep synthetic and database alarms, and define cache freshness, eviction behavior and miss capacity. Caching does not eliminate writes or guarantee that every surge will fit.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [ALB health checks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/target-group-health-checks.html). [Route 53 health monitoring](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/dns-failover.html). [Cache-aside behavior](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonElastiCache/latest/dg/Strategies.html). [RDS instance replicas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReadRepl.html).

question:
A company runs an HTTPS application behind ALBs in US and European Regions. Its existing data layer already supports the regional deployment. Clients must connect through the Route 53 hosted-zone apex, example.com, using a stable set of public IP addresses. Traffic should enter the AWS global network and be routed to regional ALBs according to endpoint health and the accelerator configuration.

Which managed design meets these requirements with the least network-appliance administration?

options.text: Create a Transit Gateway connecting the regional VPCs and publish its attachment IP addresses as the public apex endpoint for internet clients.
Create a standard Global Accelerator with regional ALB endpoints, then create a CNAME record at example.com pointing to the accelerator DNS name.
Create a standard Global Accelerator with an endpoint group in each application Region and register the regional ALBs. Create a Route 53 A alias at example.com targeting the accelerator.
Create a standard Global Accelerator with regional ALB endpoints, then configure a Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint to publish the accelerator as the authoritative public apex record.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. A standard accelerator provides static public entry IP addresses and accepts ALBs as regional endpoints. A Route 53 alias can target the accelerator at the hosted-zone apex.

<<1>> uses a VPC routing hub as though it were a public application accelerator. Transit Gateway attachment addresses are not a replacement for this managed internet entry point.

<<2>> chooses the appropriate traffic service but an invalid record type at the zone apex. CNAME records are suitable for eligible non-apex names.

<<4>> confuses recursive DNS access with authoritative public DNS records. An inbound Resolver endpoint serves queries into VPC DNS; it does not publish this apex alias.

Configure listeners, endpoint groups, health behavior and application capacity in each Region. An accelerator does not replicate application data or guarantee zero interruption. If no healthy endpoints remain, its documented fail-open behavior matters. S3 object access and database replication remain separate design concerns.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Custom accelerator domains](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/global-accelerator/latest/dg/dns-addressing-custom-domains.mapping-your-custom-domain.html). [Standard accelerator endpoints](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/global-accelerator/latest/dg/about-endpoints.html).

question:
A device platform receives millions of small event records per minute. It needs durable storage with low-latency reads by device ID and event time, without relational joins or a custom search index. Each record is smaller than 4 KB. The application must stop returning a record 120 days after creation, but physical deletion may occur several days later. The team wants managed expiration and minimal database-maintenance code.

Which design best fits these access and retention requirements?

options.text: Retain records in an MSK topic for 120 days and use topic scanning as the sole way to retrieve records for a particular device and event time.

Use DynamoDB with a well-distributed device-oriented partition key and event-time sort key. Size capacity and quotas for the workload, set a numeric TTL expiration for each record, and exclude expired items in the read path.
Use DynamoDB with a TTL timestamp for each record and return every item found by a read. Assume the TTL service removes each item at the exact expiration second.
Store each record as an S3 object and use an S3 Lifecycle rule as the only mechanism for enforcing the exact 120-day application-visible cutoff.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. The key design supports the stated lookups, while TTL performs asynchronous cleanup. The application checks expiration separately so an item that is physically present after day 120 is not exposed to users.

<<1>> provides a retained event log, but scanning it is not the requested indexed device-and-time retrieval path.

<<3>> assumes synchronous deletion. DynamoDB TTL commonly removes expired items within a few days, not at an exact second.

<<4>> also substitutes background storage expiration for a strict read-visibility rule and does not provide the requested database query path.

Store the TTL as a Number containing Unix epoch seconds. Query results can use an expiration filter; a point-read result must be checked by the application. Filtering does not avoid the read work already performed. Validate hot-device traffic, index overhead, capacity ramp-up and actual retained bytes before estimating cost; a maximum record size alone does not establish an annual storage total.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [DynamoDB TTL](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/TTL.html). [Partition-key design](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/bp-partition-key-design.html).

question:
After an application deployment, new On-Demand instances in an EC2 Auto Scaling group fail the ALB health check and are quickly terminated by Auto Scaling. The instances remain reachable through Systems Manager Session Manager, but termination interrupts investigation. Existing central logs do not explain the failure. An incident window allows a brief suspension of automated termination while operators retain sufficient healthy serving capacity.

Which action most directly preserves the existing failing instances for immediate diagnosis?

options.text: Enable more verbose application logging for the next deployment while leaving the current termination behavior unchanged.
Enable EC2 API termination protection on the failing instances and rely on it to block Auto Scaling health-check replacement.
Create a separate instance from the application image and reproduce the problem there, allowing the original failing instances to terminate.
Temporarily suspend the Auto Scaling Terminate process, connect to a failing instance with Session Manager, and capture the evidence. Resume the process after the controlled investigation.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. Suspending `Terminate` prevents Auto Scaling from performing its instance terminations while the existing machine can be examined. Session Manager provides the already-configured management channel.

<<1>> may improve later evidence, but does not preserve the current failing machine.

<<2>> confuses EC2 API termination protection with Auto Scaling behavior. That protection does not prevent Auto Scaling from terminating an unhealthy instance.

<<3>> can help reproduce a defect, but adds setup and loses the exact instance state that operators need immediately.

This is a temporary diagnostic measure, not a repair. It also suspends normal scale-in and can affect other scaling processes. Track the suspension, preserve sufficient serving capacity, and restore automation promptly. A narrower suspension of ReplaceUnhealthy may be appropriate in another incident, but is not one of the proposed actions. Neither approach protects against every external termination cause.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Suspend Auto Scaling processes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-suspend-resume-processes.html). [EC2 termination protection](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/Using_ChangingDisableAPITermination.html).

question:
EC2 workers consume video jobs from an SQS standard queue. Jobs normally take 20–40 minutes, the visibility timeout is one hour, and the redrive policy sets maxReceiveCount to 1. The workers already delete messages only after successful completion and make repeated processing idempotent. Some messages reach the dead-letter queue without a completed processing attempt. Investigation finds transient receive/delivery failures but no jobs exceeding the visibility timeout.

Which configuration change directly gives these transient failures an opportunity to recover?

options.text: Increase the Auto Scaling group minimum while keeping maxReceiveCount at 1, so additional workers eliminate transient delivery failures.
Increase the visibility timeout to two hours while keeping maxReceiveCount at 1, so the redrive policy permits additional receives.
Increase the queue delivery delay while keeping maxReceiveCount at 1, so failed receives are excluded from the redrive policy.
Increase maxReceiveCount to a value such as 10, selected for the retry budget, and continue monitoring and investigating messages that ultimately reach the dead-letter queue.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. A receive limit of one leaves no useful tolerance for a transient failure. SQS can record a delivery even when the consumer does not receive the message. A larger receive budget allows subsequent attempts before dead-letter handling.

<<1>> changes available processing capacity rather than the message's allowed retry budget.

<<2>> changes how long a received message is hidden. It does not increase the redrive receive limit, and the observed processing duration already fits the current timeout.

<<3>> delays initial availability; it does not remove failed receives from the redrive behavior.

Ten is an example, not a universal optimum. Balance recovery opportunity against repeated processing cost, poison-message delay, and the message retention period. Increasing maxReceiveCount does not shorten the one-hour invisibility window, so the total retry latency must also fit the workload requirements. Retain idempotency, delete after success, and extend visibility if real work can run longer. Repeated ReceiveMessage API calls alone are normal polling and do not prove that one particular video was retried; correlate message receive counts with application evidence.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Delivery inconsistency](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/avoiding-inconsistent-message-processing.html). [Dead-letter redrive policy](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html).

question:
A company uses Storage Gateway Volume Gateway to expose block volumes to on-premises iSCSI initiators. It must authenticate both the initiator and the gateway target and reduce the risk of replaying a captured authentication exchange. The application must retain its iSCSI block interface. Encryption of the network transport is handled as a separate control.

Which configuration meets the authentication requirement?

options.text: Configure mutual CHAP on both the Volume Gateway target and the iSCSI initiator, using the required distinct protected secrets for each authentication direction.
Encrypt the gateway connection to AWS while leaving the local iSCSI initiator-to-target connection without authentication.
Replace Volume Gateway with Tape Gateway and expose a virtual tape library, relying on the tape interface alone to authenticate clients.
Configure a CHAP username for an NFS export while retaining the application's existing iSCSI volume connection unchanged.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. Volume Gateway supports mutual CHAP, so each side authenticates the other. Both the gateway configuration and the initiator configuration must agree on the authentication identities and secrets.

<<2>> protects a different network leg and leaves the required local initiator authentication absent.

<<3>> changes the storage interface and workload model. A virtual tape interface does not itself supply the specified authentication configuration.

<<4>> applies an iSCSI authentication mechanism to the wrong protocol and does not configure the actual connection.

CHAP challenge-response authentication should not be described as encryption of the storage payload or complete protection against every attack on an established session. Protect secrets and the local network path separately. Mutual CHAP uses different secrets for authenticating the initiator and the target.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Volume Gateway mutual CHAP](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/storagegateway/latest/vgw/ConfiguringiSCSIClientInitiatorCHAP.html).

question:
A company stores CloudFormation templates in a private GitHub repository. It needs an automated pipeline that deploys each candidate into an isolated test environment, runs integration tests against the provisioned resources, and blocks production promotion when testing fails. Temporary test stacks must be cleaned up, and the team wants native source and deployment integrations.

Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Use a GitHub connection in CodePipeline, then use a CodeDeploy action to execute a CloudFormation change set. Run CodeBuild integration tests after that action.
Use a GitHub connection in CodePipeline and run CloudFormation template validation in CodeBuild. Treat successful syntax validation as sufficient evidence and promote without deploying a test stack.

Use an authorized GitHub connection as the CodePipeline source. Use CloudFormation actions to create and execute a change set for an isolated test stack, then CodeBuild to run integration tests. Gate promotion on success and configure cleanup for both successful and failed runs.
Use a GitHub connection in CodePipeline and execute the change set against production first. Run the integration tests there and rely on a later rollback when tests fail.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. CodePipeline coordinates the stages, CloudFormation provisions the candidate resources, and CodeBuild executes tests against those resources. Passing the test stage becomes a prerequisite for production promotion.

<<1>> chooses the wrong deployment action. CloudFormation actions execute CloudFormation change sets; CodeDeploy manages supported application deployment targets.

<<2>> validates the template without testing deployed behavior, so it misses the stated integration requirement.

<<4>> exposes production to the unverified change before the test gate.

Use restricted pipeline and deployment roles, isolated test data, explicit test assertions and failure cleanup. A change set previews intended resource changes but does not prove deployment success or application correctness. A cleanup stage reachable only after success is insufficient for failed runs. The pipeline reduces avoidable errors; it does not guarantee that a passing test suite detects every production defect.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [CloudFormation pipeline actions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codepipeline/latest/userguide/action-reference-CloudFormation.html). [Test and production stacks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/continuous-delivery-codepipeline-basic-walkthrough.html). [GitHub connections](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codepipeline/latest/userguide/connections-github.html).

question:
A company has a central VPC directly peered with three application VPCs in other AWS accounts in the same Region. The CIDRs do not overlap, and private routes between these VPCs already work. Remote employees need authenticated access through AWS Client VPN, with Availability Zone redundancy. The company wants one managed remote-access endpoint and minimal changes to the existing peering topology.

Which configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a separate Client VPN endpoint in each application account, associate redundant target networks for each, and require employees to select the endpoint for the desired application.

Create one Client VPN endpoint in the central VPC's Region and associate central-VPC subnets in two Availability Zones. Configure authentication, destination authorization and equivalent endpoint routes through each association to the directly peered VPCs. Permit the traffic in the VPC routes and security rules, and configure VPN clients on employee devices.
Replace the existing VPC peering topology with a Transit Gateway hub and create a separate VPN appliance fleet before enabling remote employee access.
Create one Client VPN endpoint and associate only a single central-VPC subnet. Configure all destination routes and authorization rules but omit a second Availability Zone association.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. A Client VPN endpoint can give users access to its associated VPC and directly peered VPCs. Two target-network associations in different Availability Zones provide the required association redundancy while retaining the existing network topology.

<<1>> can provide access, but violates the one-endpoint objective and adds duplicated endpoint configuration and charges.

<<3>> introduces a network redesign and appliance operation that the existing direct peering does not require.

<<4>> supplies connectivity but omits the requested Availability Zone redundancy.

Authentication, authorization, endpoint routes and VPC security controls are separate requirements. Keep equivalent destinations reachable through every associated subnet, use nonoverlapping client addressing, and validate return traffic. A working VPC route does not itself grant Client VPN authorization. This design relies on direct peers; VPC peering does not create arbitrary transitive routing through other peers.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Client VPN peered VPC scenario](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/how-it-works.html#scenario). [Target-network requirements](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/cvpn-working-target.html). [Endpoint routes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/cvpn-working-routes.html).

options.text: The SCP permits delegation of S3 actions but does not grant them to the IAM user. The user still needs an applicable IAM permission for s3:CreateBucket.
OU-attached SCPs are not inherited by member accounts until the same policy is separately attached to every account.
The Resource value must contain the new bucket ARN; an SCP using an asterisk cannot permit bucket creation.
An SCP with S3 allow statements authorizes only the member-account root user, so ordinary IAM users cannot receive S3 permissions.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. The organization guardrail allows the action to be granted, but the described user has no identity permission that grants it. Add only the required IAM permissions within the allowed scope.

<<2>> denies the inheritance that OU policies provide. The account does not need a duplicate attachment merely to inherit the OU restriction.

<<3>> invents a requirement for a bucket-specific SCP resource. The shown wildcard does not cause the missing IAM grant.

<<4>> misstates SCP scope. SCPs can limit member-account IAM users and roles as well as root activity within their documented scope; they are not grants reserved for root.

Evaluate the organization ceiling and the actual access grant separately. The stem explicitly establishes permits at every ancestor and the account level. Leaving FullAWSAccess beside this allowlist at the same OU would broaden that level's permitted actions rather than enforcing an EC2-and-S3-only ceiling.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [SCPs do not grant access](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps.html). [SCP evaluation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps_evaluation.html).

question:
A weather service publishes a complete forecast every 15 minutes as immutable S3 tile objects. Clients fetch only the tiles they need. Each refresh must discover the current published forecast from the origin, and all tiles displayed together must belong to that forecast version. Large unchanged tiles should remain cacheable at CloudFront edges. The S3 origin must remain private.

Which publication and caching design meets these requirements?

options.text: Overwrite tiles at their existing URLs and cache every URL for 15 minutes. Treat the common TTL as a guarantee that all edge locations switch versions simultaneously.

Write and verify the complete tile set under a new versioned path before updating a small latest manifest. Disable CloudFront caching for the manifest with zero minimum, default and maximum TTLs, and send no-store for browser caches. Have clients pin the manifest version, cache its immutable tile URLs, and use OAC with a restricted S3 bucket policy.
Enable S3 Versioning, overwrite the same tile keys and retain long CloudFront TTLs. Rely on bucket versioning alone to update every CloudFront cache key.
Update the latest manifest after each tile is produced, allowing it to reference a forecast whose remaining tiles are still being generated. Cache the manifest and tiles for one day.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. An uncached manifest identifies one completed forecast version, while immutable versioned URLs allow its large tiles to remain cached. Publishing the manifest only after verification prevents clients from selecting an incomplete tile set.

<<1>> mistakes cache expiration for a coordinated publication event. Individual objects and edge caches can refresh at different times.

<<3>> confuses S3 object version history with client-visible versioned URLs. Bucket versioning does not automatically change CloudFront cache keys or invalidate old responses.

<<4>> exposes an incomplete forecast and then caches that discovery response, violating both completeness and refresh requirements.

The CachingDisabled policy uses zero for all three TTL values. A zero minimum alone does not disable caching. Ensure browsers and other intermediaries also avoid caching the manifest. Use OAC request signing and a policy scoped to the intended distribution. Retain old tiles while clients can reference them, and coordinate concurrent publishers. This pattern establishes version consistency, not a fixed end-user latency guarantee.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Managed cache policies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/using-managed-cache-policies.html). [Versioned filenames](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/UpdatingExistingObjects.html). [Private S3 origin with OAC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.html). [S3 consistency](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/Welcome.html).

question:
A serverless dashboard uses CloudFront and two ready regional origins. Personalized GET requests are slow because a viewer-request Lambda@Edge function calls a distant identity provider for every request. Clients already send short-lived signed JWTs. Security policy permits offline validation until token expiry, and the team has a trusted signing-key rotation process. The primary origin sometimes returns 503 or 504 responses while the secondary remains healthy. Login POST requests use a separate behavior.

Which changes address both problems without sharing personalized responses between users? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add Route 53 latency records pointing to the existing CloudFront distribution so DNS selects between its regional origins.
Increase the origin response timeout and retain the identity-provider call on every viewer request.
Cache all dashboard responses under a shared path-only cache key and extend their TTL to the token lifetime.
Validate JWT signatures, issuer, audience, expiry, and required claims locally in the viewer-request function using trusted keys. Keep caching disabled for personalized dashboard responses.
Use a CloudFront origin group with the two ready origins, failover on 503 and 504, and connection and response timeouts appropriate for the dashboard.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. Local verification removes the identity-provider round trip from each dashboard request. Signature verification must be accompanied by claim validation and trusted key handling. The stated policy accepts the revocation delay inherent in offline validation.

<<5>> is correct. The origin group retries eligible failed GET requests against the secondary. Timeouts influence how long the viewer waits before that attempt. Origins and their data must already be ready to serve the request.

<<1>> selects a DNS endpoint, not an origin inside one CloudFront distribution.

<<2>> preserves the authentication bottleneck and can increase the wait before an origin error or failover.

<<3>> can disclose one user's dashboard to another because the cache key omits identity.

CloudFront origin failover applies to GET, HEAD, and eligible OPTIONS requests, not POST login operations. It evaluates failures per request; it does not permanently switch all future requests to the secondary.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Authorization at the edge](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/networking-and-content-delivery/authorizationedge-how-to-use-lambdaedge-and-json-web-tokens-to-enhance-web-application-security/). [CloudFront origin failover](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/high_availability_origin_failover.html).

question:
An analytics company serves reports through CloudFront at analytics.example.com. Its existing authorization mechanism correctly restricts access. Each report is identical for all users entitled to that report, and the cache key already separates report variants. The company must require HTTPS from viewers and improve cache reuse while meeting each report's freshness limit.

Which changes should the solutions architect make? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Attach an ACM certificate covering analytics.example.com, requested or imported in us-east-1, and configure the viewer protocol policy to require HTTPS or redirect HTTP to HTTPS.
Set origin Cache-Control max-age or s-maxage values to the longest duration allowed by each report's freshness requirement, and configure the cache policy TTL bounds to permit those durations.
Move report-generation code to a Lambda@Edge origin-request function while retaining the current cache-expiration settings.
Set the cache policy minimum, default, and maximum TTL values to zero for every report.
Configure HTTPS between CloudFront and the origin while continuing to allow HTTP between viewers and CloudFront.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. CloudFront's custom hostname needs a matching viewer certificate, and ACM viewer certificates must be in us-east-1. The viewer protocol policy enforces the viewer-facing HTTPS requirement.

<<2>> is correct. A suitable freshness lifetime allows repeated requests to reuse cached content. Origin cache headers operate within the distribution's TTL settings. Use s-maxage when shared-cache and browser lifetimes should differ.

<<3>> changes where generation runs, but leaves the cache lifetime and viewer transport requirement unresolved.

<<4>> disables caching and therefore reduces reuse.

<<5>> encrypts a different connection. Origin HTTPS alone does not require viewer HTTPS.

Authorization, cache-key correctness, transport encryption, and freshness are separate controls. Longer TTLs are useful only when the content remains safe to share and fresh enough for the business.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [CloudFront certificate requirements](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/cnames-and-https-requirements.html). [Requiring viewer HTTPS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/using-https-viewers-to-cloudfront.html). [CloudFront cache expiration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/Expiration.html).

question:
A game's registration site runs on EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. Serving static images and scripts consumes most instance CPU. The build pipeline already produces mobile and desktop variants under separate object prefixes. Legacy clients request the same asset paths, so the server must select a variant from User-Agent without changing client URLs. The team has a tested Lambda@Edge device classifier.

Which design removes static-asset serving from EC2 and safely caches both variants?

options.text: Use ALB HTTP-header rules to route mobile and desktop asset requests to separate EC2 target groups.

Store the variants in a private S3 bucket behind CloudFront. Run the classifier on viewer requests and rewrite each asset URI to its device-specific prefix before cache lookup. Restrict S3 access with origin access control.
Create Route 53 geolocation records that send each geographic area to either the mobile asset origin or the desktop asset origin.
Store the variants in S3 behind CloudFront, forward User-Agent to S3, and use the unchanged asset URI as the only cache key.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. Rewriting the URI before lookup creates a distinct cache identity for each prebuilt variant. S3 supplies the selected object, removing that work from the registration instances. Normalizing many User-Agent strings into a small set of variants also avoids unnecessary cache fragmentation.

<<1>> can route HTTP headers, but EC2 still serves the assets and bears their load.

<<3>> selects by geography, which does not identify device type.

<<4>> neither selects the variant object path nor separates the cached variants. Forwarding a header does not make an S3 object dynamically change its contents.

Viewer-request Lambda@Edge runs before cache lookup. The classifier here reads the incoming User-Agent itself; it must not assume that CloudFront-generated device headers are available at that event. Keep dynamic registration endpoints on their separate application behavior.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Lambda@Edge event order](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/lambda-cloudfront-trigger-events.html). [CloudFront-generated request headers](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/lambda-at-edge-function-restrictions.html). [Restricting S3 origin access](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.html).

question:
A CloudFront distribution caches product images using query parameters for color and size. The origin treats parameter names and values as case-insensitive and parameter order as irrelevant. Parameters never repeat, and these URLs contain no signatures or case-sensitive identifiers. Logs show separate cache entries for semantically identical requests such as ?Color=Red&Size=Large and ?size=large&color=red.

Which change consolidates equivalent requests without merging different image variants?

options.text: Use a viewer-request Lambda@Edge function to parse and consistently re-encode the parameters, lowercase their names and values, and sort them before CloudFront looks up the cache entry.
Exclude all query parameters from the cache key and stop forwarding them to the origin.
Add a reverse proxy at the origin that normalizes query parameters before generating each image.
Use an origin-request Lambda@Edge function to lowercase and sort parameters after a cache miss.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. CloudFront distinguishes query-string case and order. Canonicalizing equivalent inputs before cache lookup produces a shared key while retaining color and size values that select different images.

<<2>> merges genuinely different variants, potentially returning the wrong image.

<<3>> normalizes too late to combine entries already selected by CloudFront's original keys.

<<4>> also runs after the cache lookup. It can normalize requests sent to the origin, but cannot prevent the initial fragmentation.

Canonicalization must follow the application's semantics. Lowercasing arbitrary query values could corrupt identifiers or signatures; sorting repeated parameters could change their meaning. The stated URL contract makes these transformations safe here.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Query-string cache identity](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/QueryStringParameters.html). [CloudFront trigger timing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/lambda-cloudfront-trigger-events.html).

question:
A photo service stores paid images in S3. Third-party websites embed the public object URLs, allowing visitors to retrieve images without purchasing them. The service must authorize each buyer, provide short-lived download access, and prevent direct public S3 access while retaining edge caching.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Deny requests from the IP addresses of the third-party web servers in the S3 bucket policy.
Move the images to encrypted EBS volumes on EC2 and publish their download paths through a public load balancer.
Keep S3 private, serve images through CloudFront with origin access control, and have the application issue short-lived CloudFront signed URLs only after verifying a purchase.
Replicate the images to public S3 buckets in additional Regions and route users to the nearest copy.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. The application decides entitlement, CloudFront verifies the signed URL and its time limit, and the private-origin policy prevents bypassing CloudFront through a public S3 URL. Authorized requests can still use the edge cache.

<<1>> targets the wrong source. With ordinary hotlinking, the visitor's browser requests the image; the third-party web server does not necessarily fetch it.

<<2>> protects stored bytes but leaves the public download endpoint without buyer authorization.

<<4>> improves geographic distribution without restricting access.

A signed URL is a bearer capability. A recipient can share it during its validity window, and downloaded images can be copied. Short lifetimes reduce exposure, but this design is access control rather than copy protection.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [CloudFront signed URLs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-signed-urls.html). [Private S3 origins](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.html).

question:
An online game store runs its website and Oracle database in an on-premises data center. A promotion begins next week. Load tests show that cacheable catalog pages, images, and game downloads cause most of the projected overload. The existing servers can handle the projected uncached checkout and account traffic after those requests are removed. A full migration and new private connectivity cannot be completed before the promotion.

Which change best addresses the measured bottleneck within the deadline?

options.text: Deploy additional EC2 web servers behind an ALB and wait for a new private connection to the on-premises Oracle database before accepting orders.
Migrate the entire website and Oracle database to EC2 and complete application acceptance testing before the promotion.
Configure DNS failover to an S3 static maintenance page whenever the on-premises website is overloaded.
Place CloudFront in front of the existing HTTPS origin. Cache the eligible catalog and download paths, use appropriate freshness rules, and keep checkout and account responses uncached.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. A CloudFront custom origin can be an on-premises HTTP server. Serving eligible content from edge caches removes the workload identified by the tests, while dynamic transactions continue to reach the existing application.

<<1>> depends on connectivity that will not be ready and leaves an untested hybrid transaction path.

<<2>> exceeds the stated preparation window.

<<3>> can display an outage notice, but does not keep the store accepting orders.

A CDN does not automatically make a database scalable or guarantee an outage-free promotion. This choice depends on the measured cacheable fraction and validated residual origin capacity. Test cache keys, authentication, invalidation, and cold-cache behavior before the event.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [CloudFront custom origins](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/DownloadDistS3AndCustomOrigins.html). [Cache freshness controls](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/Expiration.html).

question:
A company runs production Linux containers on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate. Developers must test the same container images on existing on-premises Linux servers while using the same ECS control plane and deployment tooling. The servers run a supported operating system, and development tasks do not require an AWS load balancer. The company does not want to buy new hardware or introduce a Kubernetes control plane.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Purchase AWS Outposts capacity and run the development ECS workloads on EC2 instances provisioned on the Outposts hardware.

Register the existing servers as ECS Anywhere external instances using the required ECS and Systems Manager agents. Use EXTERNAL task configurations for development and compatible Fargate configurations for production.
Deploy Amazon EKS on Outposts for development and migrate production orchestration to Amazon EKS on Fargate.
Deploy Amazon EKS Anywhere on the existing servers and manage development with Kubernetes manifests independently of ECS.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. ECS Anywhere registers supported customer-managed servers with ECS and runs tasks using the EXTERNAL launch type. This preserves the ECS management model and reuses existing hardware.

<<1>> adds hardware that the company explicitly wants to avoid.

<<3>> adds both Outposts hardware and a different orchestrator.

<<4>> reuses hardware, but introduces Kubernetes and does not manage those workloads through ECS.

Container-image portability does not mean task definitions can move unchanged. External tasks support bridge, host, or none networking, whereas Fargate uses awsvpc. Maintain suitable launch, networking, resource, and service settings for each environment. ECS Anywhere also leaves server operating-system and agent maintenance with the customer; it is not on-premises Fargate.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [ECS Anywhere capabilities and limits](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/ecs-anywhere.html).

question:
A company has several existing standalone AWS accounts. It wants to invite them into one AWS Organizations organization and allow a designated administration role in the management account to assume an administrative role in each member account. The solution must preserve the existing accounts and use temporary credentials.

Which procedure establishes both organization membership and the required administrative access?

options.text: Invite the accounts and accept the invitations. Rely on Organizations to create an administrative access role automatically in every invited account.
Invite the accounts, then create a role in the management account that trusts the member accounts and grants administrative access to the management account.
Invite the accounts and attach a FullAWSAccess service control policy to them to grant the management-account administration role access.

Invite the accounts from the management account and accept each invitation. In each member account, create an administrative role such as OrganizationAccountAccessRole that trusts the designated administration role, and grant the caller permission to assume those member roles.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. Invitations establish membership. Separately, the member role's trust policy allows the designated caller to assume it, the caller needs sts:AssumeRole permission, and the member role's permissions govern the resulting session.

<<1>> confuses invited accounts with accounts created through Organizations. The standard administrative role is not automatically created for an invited account.

<<2>> creates trust in the opposite direction and does not authorize administration of the member accounts.

<<3>> mistakes a permissions limit for an access grant. An SCP limits available permissions; it does not create role trust or grant IAM permissions.

OrganizationAccountAccessRole is a conventional name, not a magic requirement. Use narrowly scoped trust, appropriate administrative permissions, and the company's required controls on the caller.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Inviting existing accounts](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_accounts_invites.html). [Accessing member account roles](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_accounts_access-cross-account-role.html). [SCP permission limits](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps.html).

question:
A retailer processes large product-catalog batches. Each batch requires validation, several independent transformations, and a final load only after all transformations succeed. Workers run as container jobs and can take 20–60 minutes. The system must track progress, retry transient failures with backoff, and route exhausted failures for investigation. The team wants to minimize custom orchestration code.

Which solution best meets these requirements?

options.text: Store task status in RDS and build EC2 pollers that coordinate dependencies, detect failures, and schedule retries.
Use AWS Config rules to observe job-resource changes and implement workflow state, dependency tracking, and retries in custom Lambda functions.
Use Amazon MQ for task messages and build a coordinator that stores execution state and manages fan-out, completion, and retries.
Use an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow with Parallel or Map states, integrated container jobs, Retry policies, and Catch transitions to a failure-handling path.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. Step Functions represents dependencies and progress explicitly. Parallel or Map states coordinate independent work, Retry handles selected transient errors, and Catch directs exhausted failures to remediation. Standard workflows suit these long-running jobs.

<<1>> can work, but the team must implement the orchestration behavior in database tables and pollers.

<<2>> uses resource-configuration monitoring as an indirect signal and still requires a custom workflow engine.

<<3>> decouples workers, but messaging alone does not coordinate the whole batch or track completion of every branch.

Workers should use idempotent writes because retries can repeat external effects. Pass references to large catalog data rather than the data itself through workflow state, and use the execution history to investigate failures.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Step Functions error handling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/concepts-error-handling.html). [Choosing a workflow type](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/choosing-workflow-type.html).

question:
An engineering team retains 200 TB of files but processes only a changing subset during a 72-hour job each month. Some files are not accessed for several months, yet every file must remain available without an archive restore. The application has been certified only with Lustre and requires file locking and in-place updates. A tested FSx for Lustre SSD Persistent 2 configuration meets its performance target. Jobs may release their working file system after results have been durably exported.

Which storage design meets these requirements while avoiding an idle high-performance file system between jobs?

options.text: Keep the durable repository in S3 Intelligent-Tiering with optional asynchronous archive tiers disabled. Create the tested FSx for Lustre SSD Persistent 2 file system linked to S3 for each job, load required data, and verify result exports before deleting the file system.
Keep all data in EFS and replace the certified Lustre mount with NFS without application recertification.
Keep all data in S3 Glacier Deep Archive and create a Lustre working file system immediately when each job starts, without restoring its input objects.
Mount S3 directly with Mountpoint for Amazon S3 and assume it provides the full Lustre locking and in-place-update behavior.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. S3 retains the repository between jobs, and the tested SSD Lustre file system supplies the required active-workload interface. Verify successful export before releasing the working copy. Intelligent-Tiering can move less-used objects among its immediate-access tiers when the optional asynchronous archive tiers are disabled.

<<2>> offers a managed file system, but violates the application's certification requirement.

<<3>> requires an archive restore before the job can read its inputs, contrary to the access requirement.

<<4>> treats an object-storage mount as a complete Lustre replacement. Required file semantics must be supported, not inferred from the presence of a mount path.

FSx exports new objects using S3 Standard; apply the intended S3 lifecycle transition afterward. S3 Intelligent-Tiering and FSx for Lustre Intelligent-Tiering are different features: the latter currently does not support S3 data repository associations.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Lustre data repositories](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fsx/latest/LustreGuide/fsx-data-repositories.html). [Exporting Lustre changes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fsx/latest/LustreGuide/export-changed-data-meta-dra.html). [S3 storage classes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro.html). [Mountpoint file semantics](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mountpoint-usage.html).

question:
A company currently sends variable-schema JSON events to an on-premises PostgreSQL database. It wants managed AWS ingestion and searchable dashboards that refresh within a few minutes. Events need a small normalization transform. The pipeline must buffer records, retry destination failures, and retain failed deliveries in S3 with minimal custom delivery code. Independent stream consumers and stream replay are not required. Network access to the AWS ingestion service is already established.

Which components should the company choose? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use Amazon Data Firehose with a Lambda transformation and its built-in OpenSearch Service destination, retry settings, and S3 failure backup.
Load the events into Amazon Neptune as a graph and build a custom graph-query dashboard.
Load JSONB records into Aurora PostgreSQL and refresh reporting tables and dashboards with an hourly batch job.
Index the normalized events in Amazon OpenSearch Service and build search and aggregation views in OpenSearch Dashboards.
Use Kinesis Data Streams with a Lambda consumer that implements the OpenSearch indexing, retry, and S3 failure-backup logic.

explanation.text:
<<1>> and <<4>> are correct. Firehose supplies managed buffering and delivery to OpenSearch, with Lambda available for normalization. OpenSearch indexes the events for search and aggregation, and Dashboards presents the results. Tune buffering, index capacity, and refresh behavior to the measured freshness target.

<<2>> introduces a graph model and custom dashboard work for a search-and-aggregation use case with no graph requirement.

<<3>> can store JSON, but its hourly refresh misses the stated freshness requirement. PostgreSQL's ability to handle JSON is not the issue.

<<5>> is a valid streaming design, but requires the custom destination-handling code the team wants to minimize. It becomes more attractive when independent consumers or replay are needed.

Failure backup preserves undelivered records for later remediation; it does not automatically make every failed record searchable. Monitor the backup path and implement controlled redelivery.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Firehose to OpenSearch integration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/opensearch-service/latest/developerguide/integrations-fh.html). [Firehose destination controls](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/firehose/latest/dev/create-destination.html). [OpenSearch Service and Dashboards](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/opensearch-service/latest/developerguide/what-is.html).

question:
A company is building a JSON API with indexed key-based access and small records. Users in two AWS Regions must read and write locally, and the API must remain usable if either Region fails. The application accepts cross-Region eventual consistency and a nonzero replication RPO, and has a tested conflict-handling strategy. Load tests define the peak traffic, including all traffic moving to one Region after failure.

Which design meets these requirements with managed scaling and no container-host administration?

options.text: Run Lambda APIs and a Multi-AZ Amazon DocumentDB cluster in one Region, and route all global users to that Region.
Run APIs in both Regions backed by separate S3 buckets with one-way replication, and perform all record updates against the primary bucket.

Run ECS services on Fargate behind regional ALBs in both Regions. Use on-demand DynamoDB MREC global tables and Route 53 latency alias records with target health evaluation. Configure scaling and tested compute and database headroom for regional failover.
Run Fargate APIs in both Regions with an Aurora global database, directing writes to the primary Region and using the secondary only for reads without promotion or write forwarding.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. Regional Fargate services remove container-host management, and DynamoDB global-table replicas accept reads and writes in each Region. MREC asynchronously replicates changes and resolves concurrent item updates using last-writer-wins semantics, which the stated application contract accepts. Health-aware DNS can redirect new resolutions toward the healthy regional endpoint.

<<1>> handles an Availability Zone failure but leaves the application dependent on one Region.

<<2>> retains a single write Region and does not provide the required indexed record access and local writes in both Regions.

<<4>> provides regional read capacity, but its stated write path depends on the primary Region and lacks the failover procedure needed to restore writes.

Auto scaling is not instant spare capacity. Validate Fargate quotas, startup time, and survivor capacity, plus DynamoDB warm throughput and limits. DNS caching and client retry behavior also affect recovery. MREC does not promise zero data loss or globally strong reads.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Global table consistency modes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/V2globaltables_HowItWorks.html). [DynamoDB scaling properties](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/on-demand-capacity-mode.html). [Health-aware ALB alias records](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/routing-to-elb-load-balancer.html).

question:
Account A owns a Route 53 private hosted zone used for application database names. Account B owns a VPC containing EC2 clients and an RDS database. The clients can reach the database through its native endpoint, but cannot resolve the custom names in Account A's zone. The VPC uses the Amazon-provided resolver and has DNS support and DNS hostnames enabled. Account A must remain the sole owner of the zone and its records.

Which actions provide the VPC access to the existing zone? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create VPC peering and configure the clients to send queries directly to the Amazon-provided resolver address of Account A's VPC.
Copy the database IP addresses into hosts files on every EC2 client and update them manually when they change.
Using Account A credentials, call CreateVPCAssociationAuthorization for the private hosted zone and Account B's VPC.
Create a separate private hosted zone in Account B and manually copy the records from Account A.
Using Account B credentials, call AssociateVPCWithHostedZone for its VPC and the authorized zone. After association succeeds, have Account A delete the association authorization.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. The hosted-zone owner first authorizes the specific cross-account VPC association.

<<5>> is correct. The VPC owner then creates the association. The zone owner can remove the unused authorization afterward without removing the completed association.

<<1>> does not establish private-zone visibility. The Amazon-provided resolver in a peer VPC is not a general DNS-forwarding target; explicit zone association is the direct solution here.

<<2>> bypasses centrally maintained DNS and produces brittle mappings when database addresses change.

<<4>> creates a second independently maintained zone, contrary to the ownership and maintenance requirement.

Private DNS visibility and network connectivity are separate. This association makes the names resolvable from the VPC; it does not create routes, security-group permissions, or database authentication.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Cross-account private-zone association](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/hosted-zone-private-associate-vpcs-different-accounts.html). [VPC peering limitations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/peering/vpc-peering-basics.html).

question:
A serverless application accepts jobs through an API Gateway REST API, returns an immediate acknowledgment, and runs background Lambda workers. Workers average 4.5 minutes, mostly waiting for an on-premises MySQL database. A controlled benchmark with the same workload on RDS for MySQL in the AWS Region sharply reduces that wait. DynamoDB operations are already fast. Repeated read-only API requests are also cacheable, and a cost model shows that an appropriately sized API cache would save more than it costs.

Which change best reduces the measured latency and cost?

options.text: Provision Direct Connect for the existing database and set every Lambda function to the minimum memory allocation without further benchmarking.
Add a DynamoDB read cache and increase Lambda timeouts while leaving all MySQL calls unchanged.
Set Lambda timeouts below the observed database response time so workers stop incurring charges sooner, and retry failed jobs immediately.
Migrate MySQL to the benchmarked RDS configuration in the same Region, cache eligible REST API reads with correct cache keys, and benchmark Lambda memory settings and timeout margins after migration.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. It addresses the measured database wait with the tested placement change and avoids repeated backend work for safely cacheable reads. Retuning Lambda afterward accounts for the changed workload rather than carrying forward an obsolete configuration.

<<1>> adds connectivity expense without evidence that it removes the bottleneck. Minimum memory is not necessarily minimum cost because memory also controls CPU allocation and can affect duration.

<<2>> optimizes a component that is not slow and leaves the MySQL delay intact.

<<3>> turns successful work into repeated failures. A shorter timeout limits a failed invocation but does not make the database complete sooner.

Choose memory using measured total execution cost and performance, and set timeouts with an appropriate margin. REST API caching is billed separately and must respect response variants, authorization, and freshness. The background-job design avoids holding a synchronous API response open for the entire worker runtime.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Lambda memory and performance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-memory.html). [REST API cache settings](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/api-gateway-caching.html).

question:
A company needs a backup-and-restore disaster recovery plan for a JBoss application, an Oracle database, and 512 GB of content files. Complete Oracle RMAN backup sets are available in S3 Standard, and a stored Volume Gateway produces completed EBS snapshots of the content volume. The company has tested EC2 images, licensing, network configuration, and capacity for recovery. JBoss can read the content from an attached EBS volume. Ongoing standby replication is outside the budget.

Which recovery path uses the existing backups with the fewest additional storage recovery components?

options.text: Retain the Oracle recovery backups in S3 Glacier Deep Archive, retrieve them after disaster declaration, and restore them onto the prepared EC2 instances.

Restore Oracle from the S3 RMAN backup sets onto the prepared EC2 instances. Create an EBS content volume directly from the completed gateway snapshot and attach it to the recovered application instance.
Restore Oracle on EC2, deploy and activate a new cached Volume Gateway on EC2, restore its volume from the content snapshot, and connect JBoss through iSCSI.
Restore Oracle on EC2, recover the content snapshot to a new gateway in a replacement on-premises site, and connect the AWS application to that site over a new VPN.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. Oracle RMAN backups can restore a self-managed Oracle database on EC2. A completed Volume Gateway snapshot can also create an EBS volume directly, avoiding an extra gateway when the application already supports attached block storage.

<<1>> introduces an archive-retrieval dependency on the recovery path.

<<3>> is a supported general recovery pattern, but adds gateway provisioning, activation, and iSCSI configuration that this application does not require.

<<4>> adds replacement-site and connectivity dependencies to an otherwise cloud-based recovery.

This is a comparison of the prepared backup-and-restore paths, not a claim that backup restoration provides the best possible RTO. Measure database restore, EBS initialization, application startup, validation, and traffic cutover. The backup schedule and application-consistent recovery point determine the achievable RPO.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Volume Gateway backup and restore](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/storagegateway/latest/vgw/backing-up-volumes.html). [Oracle RMAN on EC2](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/migration-oracle-database/homogeneous-migration-tools.html).

question:
A publisher has 20 TB of scanned documents and expects the archive to reach 50 TB in three years. Readers need an interactive website with full-text search across the document contents and access to the original scans. The service must tolerate an Availability Zone failure, and the small operations team wants to avoid managing a search engine on its own servers.

Which design best meets these requirements?

options.text: Store the scans on EFS and deploy an OCR pipeline and a self-managed search cluster on EC2 instances across Availability Zones.
Store the scans and search index on EBS volumes attached to one large EC2 instance, and host the website on that instance.

Store original scans in S3, extract their text with Amazon Textract, and index text and metadata in a suitably sized Multi-AZ OpenSearch Service domain. Run the website in a load-balanced Elastic Beanstalk environment across Availability Zones.
Store scans in S3 and run the website across Availability Zones, using S3 ListObjects requests against object-name prefixes as the document-content search engine.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. S3 retains original documents, Textract turns scanned text into machine-readable data, and OpenSearch supplies the searchable index. A properly configured Multi-AZ search domain and load-balanced application environment address the Availability Zone requirement.

<<1>> can satisfy the functional requirements, but leaves search-cluster operations with the small team.

<<2>> makes one instance and its Availability Zone a dependency for the archive, index, and website. Multiple disks do not remove that failure domain.

<<4>> can find objects by key prefix, but does not search words inside scanned pages.

Object storage, text extraction, indexing, and the website are separate responsibilities. Size the search index from extracted text, mappings, replicas, and query workload rather than simply equating its size to the original scan archive. Validate OCR quality and keep index entries linked to stable source-object identifiers.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Textract document text extraction](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/textract/latest/dg/what-is.html). [Managed OpenSearch](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/opensearch-service/latest/developerguide/what-is.html). [Elastic Beanstalk environment types](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/using-features-managing-env-types.html).

question:
A legacy application runs on a supported EBS-backed EC2 instance. Licensing and external allowlists depend on its instance ID, private IPv4 address, and existing auto-assigned public IPv4 address. Those identifiers cannot change during recovery. The application can restart from its EBS data after a reboot. The team wants an AWS-managed response to an underlying host failure with configurable alarm thresholds and notifications.

Which solution best meets these requirements?

options.text: Associate a new Elastic IP address and automate stopping and starting the instance when its system status check fails.
Use Systems Manager Patch Manager to reinstall operating-system updates after any failed status check.
Create a CloudWatch alarm that reboots the instance when StatusCheckFailed_System indicates a failure.
Create a CloudWatch alarm on StatusCheckFailed_System with an EC2 recover action and the required SNS notifications.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. CloudWatch action based recovery attempts to move a supported instance away from impaired underlying infrastructure while retaining its instance ID, addresses, and attached EBS volumes. The alarm supplies the requested threshold and notification controls.

<<1>> can be automated, but assigning a new Elastic IP replaces the existing public address. A stop/start without an Elastic IP also changes an auto-assigned public IPv4 address.

<<2>> addresses guest operating-system maintenance, not recovery from a failed host.

<<3>> reboots the guest on its current host and does not provide the recover action's host-relocation behavior.

Recovery resembles an unplanned reboot: RAM state is lost, and the application must restart safely. Success depends on supported configuration and available capacity. This is single-instance recovery, not an application architecture that survives an Availability Zone outage without interruption.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [EC2 automatic instance recovery](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ec2-instance-recover.html). [CloudWatch recover actions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/cloudwatch-recovery.html).

question:
A CloudFormation stack deploys an EC2 Auto Scaling application and RDS for MySQL. An approved bootstrap process creates a dedicated application database user. Its password must rotate automatically every 60 days, and new and existing instances must obtain the current password without a stack redeployment. Passwords must not be embedded in templates, user data, or machine images.

Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Pass the password through a NoEcho CloudFormation parameter and write it into each instance's user data, replacing instances every 60 days.

Create a Secrets Manager secret for the database user, initialize that user through the approved bootstrap process, and configure supported database rotation on a 60-day schedule. Grant the instance role access to this secret and have the application retrieve and refresh its current value at runtime.
Create a Secrets Manager secret, resolve its current value only during deployment, and save that value permanently in the application image while enabling secret rotation.

Store the password in an existing Systems Manager SecureString parameter, retrieve it through the instance role, and rely on automatic rotation of the KMS encryption key to rotate the database password.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. Secrets Manager database rotation coordinates a new secret value with the database credential. Runtime retrieval through the instance role avoids static credentials in deployment artifacts, and bounded caching with refresh lets existing processes adopt the rotated password.

<<1>> uses NoEcho as if it protected every downstream destination. It does not make embedding a password in instance user data safe, and instance replacement is not database rotation.

<<3>> leaves a stale credential in the image after the database password changes.

<<4>> protects the stored parameter, but rotating its encryption key does not change the password accepted by MySQL.

Use an appropriate rotation strategy, function permissions, and network path to the database. CloudFormation dynamic references are useful in supported properties, but are resolved during resource operations; they are not a runtime refresh mechanism. Keep the application's database privileges and secret access limited to its needs.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Database secret rotation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/rotate-secrets_turn-on-for-db.html). [Rotation schedules](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/rotate-secrets_schedule.html). [CloudFormation secret references](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/dynamic-references-secretsmanager.html).

question:
A public library is migrating a 50-TB digital collection to AWS. It has machine-readable document text and metadata alongside the original files. Visitors need a dynamic website with interactive full-text search and links to the matching originals. The library wants durable object storage, a managed search engine, and repeatable infrastructure deployments.

Which design provides all three capabilities?

options.text: Use CloudFormation to deploy an RDS catalog containing titles and authors, store originals in S3, and search only the catalog metadata from the website.

Use CloudFormation to deploy S3 storage, an OpenSearch Service domain, and the website's application infrastructure. Ingest document text and metadata into OpenSearch with identifiers that link results to the original S3 objects.
Use CloudFormation to deploy S3 storage and the website, and retain the text only in Kinesis Data Streams for consumers that scan the stream whenever a visitor searches.
Use CloudFormation to deploy an S3-hosted static catalog that searches only object-name prefixes through ListObjects requests.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. S3 stores the original collection, OpenSearch supplies the document-content index, and CloudFormation describes the deployable infrastructure. The ingestion process is essential: creating a search domain does not automatically index arbitrary S3 objects.

<<1>> provides useful catalog lookup, but its stated index omits document contents. A relational database is not inherently unable to search text; this proposed implementation simply does not index that text.

<<3>> uses an event stream as a query-time corpus scan rather than maintaining an interactive search index.

<<4>> lists matching object names, not words inside documents. A static frontend can participate in a dynamic application, but it still needs an appropriate search backend.

Keep a stable identifier from each indexed document to its source object, track ingestion failures and updates, and return original-file links only after the application's applicable access checks.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [OpenSearch Service](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/opensearch-service/latest/developerguide/what-is.html). [S3 object storage](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro.html).

question:
A portal generates presigned S3 PUT URLs on EC2 using instance-role credentials. URLs work immediately, but some uploads fail when clients reuse saved URLs later. The same operation succeeds with newly generated URLs. The bucket and role policies have not changed, the signer remains authorized, and request methods and signed headers match. Local tests use a different valid credential session.

Which conditions can explain the saved URLs failing? (Select TWO.)

options.text: S3 Versioning is enabled, which invalidates a presigned upload URL after its first successful use.
The EC2 instance has no local AWS credentials file, even though its SDK successfully obtained instance-role credentials.
The expiration time specified in a saved presigned URL has passed.
The issuing EC2 instance was replaced, which by itself invalidates every previously issued URL even while its signing credentials remain valid.
The temporary credentials used to sign a saved URL have expired, even if the URL's requested expiration time is later.

explanation.text:
<<3>> and <<5>> are correct. A presigned URL cannot outlive either its configured expiration or the credentials that signed it. A longer requested URL lifetime does not extend an EC2 role session. Fresh credentials and a newly signed URL can therefore succeed while an older saved URL fails.

<<1>> is incorrect. Versioning changes how object versions are retained; it does not turn presigned PUT URLs into single-use tokens.

<<2>> is incorrect. An SDK can obtain temporary instance-role credentials without a local credentials file.

<<4>> is incorrect as stated. URL validity is tied to the signing credentials and applicable authorization, not to continued execution of the process or instance that generated it.

Generate URLs close to use with refreshed credentials and a suitably short lifetime. Treat them as bearer capabilities. Policy changes, revoked credentials, or mismatched signed request fields can also cause failures, but those alternatives are excluded by this scenario.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Presigned URL validity](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html).

question:
A retailer is migrating its web application and MySQL database from a data center to AWS. The application tier must scale across Availability Zones, the database must have managed cross-AZ failover, and frequently requested static content must be cached near global users. The retailer also wants managed HTTP-request filtering and less database administration.

Which combination meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Run the web tier in an EC2 Auto Scaling group across at least two Availability Zones behind an ALB, and migrate MySQL to an RDS Multi-AZ DB instance.
Run the web tier across two Availability Zones and operate the MySQL primary, replication, backups, patching, and failover software on EC2.
Serve static objects directly through an S3 Transfer Acceleration endpoint and rely on that feature to provide a global cache of the objects.
Place a private S3 REST origin for static assets and the ALB origin for dynamic requests behind CloudFront. Use appropriate cache behaviors, OAC for S3, and a WAF web ACL on the distribution.
Run the web tier across two Availability Zones behind an ALB with Global Accelerator, and use a Single-AZ RDS MySQL database without a standby.

explanation.text:
<<1>> and <<4>> are correct. The web fleet scales across failure domains, and RDS manages the database standby and failover. CloudFront handles global static-content caching, while its WAF web ACL filters HTTP requests before they reach the origins. OAC permits the static bucket to remain private.

<<2>> can provide database availability, but retains the database administration that the managed RDS design reduces.

<<3>> improves a transfer path to S3 rather than storing reusable edge-cache copies. It does not satisfy the explicit caching requirement.

<<5>> can improve network routing to the ALB, but leaves the database without the required cross-AZ standby and omits content caching.

These controls address different concerns: caching reduces repeated origin work, WAF applies configured request rules, and Multi-AZ protects database availability. None replaces the others. Test WAF rules before blocking production traffic, configure dynamic paths to avoid caching personalized content, and prevent direct origin access from bypassing the intended protection. The traditional RDS Multi-AZ standby is not a read-scaling target.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [RDS Multi-AZ standby deployments](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Concepts.MultiAZSingleStandby.html); [CloudFront caching](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/Introduction.html); [Private S3 origins with OAC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.html); [Resources protected by AWS WAF](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/how-aws-waf-works-resources.html); [S3 Transfer Acceleration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/transfer-acceleration.html).

question:
A gaming company is moving a custom UDP player-matching service to an EC2 Auto Scaling group across Availability Zones. The UDP application protocol cannot change. The network policy requires subnet-level filtering that permits the application's traffic and the load balancer's health checks while denying other unnecessary traffic. Shield Advanced protection is already configured.

Which actions should the architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use a Network Load Balancer with a UDP listener and a matching target group, and publish a Route 53 alias record to the NLB DNS name.
Use an Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener and send the unchanged UDP application packets to that listener.
Associate a WAF web ACL with the NLB and use it to permit UDP while rejecting other transport protocols.
