Configure network ACLs for the NLB and target subnets to permit required UDP traffic, appropriate TCP/HTTP/HTTPS health checks, and the corresponding return traffic. Deny other unnecessary traffic.
Use a CloudFront distribution in front of the load balancer to proxy the unchanged custom UDP protocol.

explanation.text:
<<1>> and <<4>> are correct. An NLB supports a UDP listener for the existing protocol. The subnet ACLs provide the requested network-layer filtering, but their rules must permit both the application path and the health-check path in the required directions.

<<2>> substitutes an HTTP application load balancer for a custom UDP endpoint. An HTTPS listener does not accept arbitrary UDP application packets.

<<3>> uses WAF outside its supported resource and protocol scope. WAF evaluates web requests and cannot be attached to an NLB as a generic UDP firewall.

<<5>> treats an HTTP content-delivery service as a transparent custom UDP proxy.

NLB health checks for a UDP service use TCP, HTTP, or HTTPS. Make the health-check endpoint reflect actual application health instead of simply proving that a TCP port is open. ACLs are stateless, so return and ephemeral-port traffic must be considered explicitly. An alias to the NLB DNS name uses its managed set of addresses rather than pinning users to one zonal IP. NLB security groups can provide additional controls, but do not replace this scenario's required subnet ACL policy.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [NLB protocol support](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/network/load-balancer-target-groups.html); [NLB health checks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/network/target-group-health-checks.html); [NLB subnet network ACL requirements](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/network/target-group-register-targets.html); [Resources protected by AWS WAF](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/how-aws-waf-works-resources.html).

question:
A public web portal receives abusive requests from a small, verified set of source CIDR ranges. Clients currently connect directly to public EC2 instances, so those source addresses are visible at the subnet boundary. The team must quickly block those ranges at that boundary while preserving HTTPS access for other Internet clients. No application or topology change is required.

Which control meets this requirement?

options.text: Add inbound network ACL deny entries for the abusive CIDR ranges with lower rule numbers than the general HTTPS allow entries, preserving the other required inbound and outbound rules.
Move the web instances into private subnets and remove all public ingress without adding an Internet-facing frontend.
Add routes for the abusive source CIDR ranges to the web-subnet route table and configure the Internet gateway to reject those source addresses.
Add explicit deny rules for the abusive CIDR ranges to the existing EC2 security group while retaining its public HTTPS allow rule.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. Network ACLs support explicit subnet-level deny entries and evaluate rules in ascending numeric order, stopping at the first match. Put the narrow deny rules before the broader HTTPS allow so the known abusive addresses are rejected while other clients retain access.

<<2>> removes legitimate public access as well as the unwanted traffic because this design adds no public frontend.

<<3>> confuses routing with source-address filtering. A route table selects a next hop for destination traffic, and an Internet gateway does not provide the proposed source-CIDR deny rules.

<<4>> requests a security-group feature that does not exist. Security groups contain allow rules, so a narrow rule cannot override a broad HTTPS allow with an explicit deny.

Preserve required outbound response rules because ACLs are stateless. Review the number and order of entries and test a blocked source alongside a legitimate client. This answer depends on direct client-source visibility at the subnet boundary. If traffic instead reaches the instances through CloudFront or an application proxy, filtering the original HTTP client may require controls at that frontend rather than matching the proxy's network address.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Network ACL rule evaluation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-network-acls.html); [Security group allow rules](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/security-group-rules.html).

question:
A company must migrate a 25 TB MySQL database to compatible Aurora MySQL within three weeks. The only data-center link to AWS is a 50 Mbps VPN, and the required baseline transfer is about 25 TB after any usable compression. Retained binary-log changes average 10 GB per day. A nearby Data Transfer Terminal reservation, compatible transport equipment, and a rehearsed S3 restore are available within the schedule.

Which approach minimizes application downtime while meeting the transfer constraint?

options.text: Copy the complete database VM image to S3 over the VPN, import it to EC2, and begin replication after the initial copy finishes.
Use DMS full load plus change data capture over the existing VPN to move the complete baseline and ongoing changes directly to Aurora.

Create a consistent supported XtraBackup baseline with its matching binlog position, upload it to S3 at the reserved Data Transfer Terminal, and restore Aurora. Apply retained binlogs over the VPN, then pause writes briefly for final catch-up, validation, and cutover.
Stop all application writes before creating the baseline, transfer it through Data Transfer Terminal, and leave the application stopped until the Aurora restore and validation are complete.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. Bulk transfer at the terminal avoids the constrained data-center uplink, while retained binlogs bring the restored baseline forward without keeping the source application offline throughout transport and restoration. The exact baseline log position connects the two phases without missing or replaying an arbitrary range of changes.

<<1>> still sends the entire baseline over the bottleneck and changes the target to a self-managed EC2 database.

<<2>> is a useful online migration pattern when bandwidth is adequate, but DMS cannot bypass the stated link capacity. At ideal decimal-unit line rate, 25 TB × 8 ÷ 50 Mbps is about 46.3 days, already longer than three weeks.

<<4>> avoids the bandwidth bottleneck but unnecessarily includes transport and restore time in the application outage.

Verify source and target versions, supported backup format and size, S3 permissions, restore duration, and objects that need separate migration. Retain binlogs throughout backup, travel, upload, restore, and catch-up, and measure actual log generation rather than equating it with database size growth. The terminal supplies network access, not database conversion or automatic replication. Cut over only after final synchronization and validation, with a tested rollback plan.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Data Transfer Terminal requirements](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/datatransferterminal/latest/userguide/tech-requirements.html); [Aurora MySQL physical import from S3](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/AuroraMySQL.Migrating.ExtMySQL.S3.html); [Aurora external binlog replication](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/AuroraMySQL.Replication.MySQL.SettingUp.html).

question:
A weather-map service uses CloudFront with an S3 origin in eu-west-1. It publishes new immutable map objects each hour. Measurements show that North American cache misses are slow because they fetch across the Atlantic, while cache-hit latency is already acceptable. The team plans a second S3 origin in us-east-1 and can publish each new map only after its replica is available.

Which changes together address the measured bottleneck? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Register the new S3 bucket directly as a Global Accelerator endpoint and use that accelerator as the CloudFront origin.
Use an origin-request Lambda@Edge function to select the us-east-1 S3 origin for North American viewers, with appropriate origin authorization and geographic cache configuration.
Keep only the European S3 origin and create Global Accelerator endpoint groups that reference that bucket in both Regions.
Extend the CloudFront TTL of all map objects indefinitely and keep fetching every new hourly object from the European origin.
Configure S3 cross-Region replication to the us-east-1 bucket, backfill existing objects, and verify replica availability before publishing new map references.

explanation.text:
<<2>> and <<5>> are correct. Replication places the data in the nearby origin, and the origin-request function selects that origin when CloudFront needs to fetch an object for the relevant viewers. Both data placement and routing are required: an empty regional bucket or an unused replica does not improve the measured miss path.

<<1>> and <<3>> use an unsupported Global Accelerator endpoint type. Standard accelerators accept supported load balancers, EC2 instances, or Elastic IP addresses, not S3 buckets.

<<4>> can retain objects longer, but cannot eliminate the first miss for each new immutable hourly object. It leaves that initial origin fetch across the Atlantic.

Live S3 replication is asynchronous and does not automatically backfill objects that existed before the rule. Use Batch Replication or another validated backfill and confirm new replicas before publishing their URLs. Configure the country header and cache policy consistently with the origin-selection logic. An origin-request function runs when an origin request is needed, not on ordinary cache hits, so the design targets the observed miss latency rather than promising that every download becomes faster.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Lambda@Edge dynamic origin selection](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/lambda-examples.html); [S3 replication scope and backfill](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/replication-what-is-isnot-replicated.html); [Global Accelerator endpoints](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/global-accelerator/latest/dg/about-endpoints.html); [CloudFront caching](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/Introduction.html).

question:
A company deploys infrastructure through CloudFormation and CodePipeline. A newly acquired team currently provisions resources with Python scripts. Its developers want to define future infrastructure using TypeScript or Python, reusable abstractions, loops, and conditionals. The company requires the resulting resources to remain managed through CloudFormation stacks in its deployment pipeline.

Which approach best meets both teams' requirements?

options.text: Continue hand-authoring CloudFormation templates and move the resource-provisioning Python scripts into EC2 user data so they execute when instances boot.
Run the existing Python SDK scripts in CodeBuild and have them create and update resources directly, bypassing CloudFormation stack management.
Continue creating every new resource with Python scripts and manually import supported resources into CloudFormation stacks after each deployment.

Define infrastructure with AWS CDK constructs in TypeScript or Python. Use a CodeBuild stage in CodePipeline to synthesize and deploy the resulting CloudFormation stacks with appropriate roles and bootstrapped environments.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. CDK supplies the requested programming-language authoring model while synthesizing the CloudFormation templates and deployment assets used by the existing governance model. The pipeline can build, validate, synthesize, review, and deploy those stacks.

<<1>> moves provisioning side effects into instance startup. It neither provides the desired infrastructure authoring model nor reliably places those side effects under stack management.

<<2>> preserves Python authoring but abandons the required CloudFormation control over resource lifecycle.

<<3>> can help adopt supported existing resources, but makes manual import a recurring deployment step and does not solve the requested ongoing authoring workflow.

CDK does not bypass CloudFormation semantics or automatically convert arbitrary SDK provisioning scripts into constructs. Refactor the infrastructure intent into CDK code, bootstrap target environments, and scope deployment roles. CloudFormation itself supports repetition with Fn::ForEach and AWS::LanguageExtensions. The reason to choose CDK is familiar general-purpose code and reusable constructs, not a claim that templates cannot express iteration.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [CDK synthesis and deployment](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/v2/guide/deploy.html); [CloudFormation Fn::ForEach](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/TemplateReference/intrinsic-function-reference-foreach.html).

question:
Every new EC2 application instance installs a stable custom framework through user data. Installation and compilation take 20 minutes, while download time is negligible. Application releases change frequently, but the framework changes only monthly. The application cannot start until the framework installation is complete.

Which change removes the repeated dependency-installation delay from instance launches?

options.text: Prepare and validate a build instance with the framework installed, create a versioned AMI with Systems Manager Automation and AWS-CreateImage, and use that AMI in the application launch template.
Compress the framework installer in S3 and continue installing and compiling the framework in user data on every application instance.
Run framework installation and application startup in parallel on each new instance, without waiting for the dependency to become available.
Move the application to Elastic Beanstalk but retain the same 20-minute framework installation in an instance initialization hook.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. Baking the stable dependency into an AMI moves its installation to the image-build stage. New instances start from that prepared image and need only the remaining application-specific deployment work.

<<2>> reduces a transfer cost that the measurements say is negligible. The dominant installation and compilation still occur on every launch.

<<3>> violates the dependency order and can start an application against a partially installed framework.

<<4>> changes the deployment service but retains the same per-instance bottleneck. Elastic Beanstalk would need a changed image or initialization design to remove it.

AWS-CreateImage captures the specified EC2 instance; it does not install the framework by itself. Build from a clean source, install and test the dependency, capture the AMI, and validate a fresh instance from it. Rebuild images for patches or framework changes and roll out a new launch-template version. Keep secrets and instance-specific identity out of the image. Baking the dependency accelerates startup but does not eliminate later image maintenance.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Systems Manager AWS-CreateImage runbook](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager-automation-runbooks/latest/userguide/automation-aws-createimage.html).

question:
A research company runs a Ruby on Rails application and a 16 TiB MySQL database on individual EC2 instances. The database continues to grow. The company needs the application to survive an Availability Zone failure, retain its current Rails runtime, and use managed database operations with automatic storage growth and a ready cross-AZ compute failover target. It wants to discount predictable application capacity while allowing demand-based expansion.

Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Place the Rails tier behind an ALB across two AZs and purchase a commitment for baseline compute. Keep MySQL on EC2 with self-managed replication, failover, backups, and LVM volume expansion.
Use RDS MySQL Multi-AZ with storage autoscaling, but put the entire Rails Auto Scaling group and its load-balancer targets in one AZ.

Run Rails in a multi-AZ EC2 Auto Scaling group behind an ALB, cover eligible baseline usage with a commitment discount, and use On-Demand capacity for bursts. Migrate to compatible Aurora MySQL with a writer and a ready replica in another AZ.

Run Rails in a multi-AZ EC2 Auto Scaling group behind an ALB with a baseline commitment discount. Use RDS MySQL Multi-AZ, disable storage autoscaling, and manually increase storage after capacity alarms.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. The application fleet spans AZs while retaining its runtime. Aurora grows its cluster storage as data grows, and a ready replica in another AZ provides a compute promotion target. A commitment discount can cover predictable eligible EC2 usage while additional instances scale with demand.

<<1>> retains database operating-system, replication, backup, and storage-management responsibilities that the scenario explicitly wants managed.

<<2>> protects the database but concentrates all application compute in one failure domain.

<<4>> provides application and database availability, but deliberately leaves storage expansion manual and fails the automatic-growth requirement.

RDS for MySQL does support storage autoscaling when enabled, so manual growth is not an inherent RDS limitation. Aurora's replicated cluster storage and its compute replicas are separate: durable copies of data do not by themselves provide an already-running replacement writer. Check engine compatibility and version-specific storage limits, size compute from measurements, and compare storage and I/O charges. Aurora is the fitting listed design here, not a universal claim that it is the least expensive MySQL service.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Aurora shared storage](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/Aurora.Overview.StorageReliability.html); [Aurora compute failover](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/Concepts.AuroraHighAvailability.html); [RDS storage autoscaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_PIOPS.Autoscaling.html).

question:
A Windows content-management application will move from one test EC2 instance to at least three production instances across Availability Zones. Its mutable content currently resides on the test instance's EBS root volume. Production instances must use the same shared files through native SMB, preserve Windows ACLs and Active Directory identities, and retain file-service availability after an AZ failure.

Which storage and deployment approach has the least file-server management overhead?

options.text: Deploy the Windows application across AZs and mount an EFS file system directly as its native SMB share with Windows ACL semantics.
Deploy the Windows application across AZs and use FSx for Lustre as the native Windows SMB share authenticated through the existing AD domain.

Deploy the Windows application across AZs, join the instances and a Multi-AZ FSx for Windows File Server file system to the appropriate AD environment, migrate the content while preserving ACLs, and mount the shared SMB path.
Deploy the Windows application across AZs and attach one io2 EBS volume to all instances with Multi-Attach, using it as the common filesystem without a file-server layer.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. FSx for Windows File Server supplies the required SMB, Windows ACL, and AD integration as a managed file service. Its Multi-AZ deployment provides a standby file server in another AZ and automatic failover. Each CMS instance accesses the same share instead of maintaining its own evolving content copy.

<<1>> substitutes an NFS-oriented file service for the required native SMB and Windows permission model.

<<2>> substitutes a Lustre filesystem for the required Windows file-server protocol and AD-backed ACL integration.

<<4>> fails the cross-AZ requirement because EBS Multi-Attach operates within one AZ. Shared block access also does not by itself implement SMB or safe concurrent filesystem coordination.

Join the AD domain and establish DNS, time, network, and file permissions before relying on the mounted share. Copy and validate existing content and ACLs, then switch the CMS content path. An AMI copies an initial disk state but does not synchronize later writes among instances. Multi-AZ improves file-service availability, but failover can briefly pause I/O, so test client and application recovery behavior.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [FSx for Windows File Server features](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fsx/latest/WindowsGuide/what-is.html); [FSx Multi-AZ availability](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fsx/latest/WindowsGuide/high-availability-multiAZ.html); [EBS Multi-Attach limits](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/ebs-volumes-multi.html); [EFS protocols and client support](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/whatisefs.html); [FSx for Lustre client model](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fsx/latest/LustreGuide/what-is.html).

question:
Remote workers cannot start new desktop sessions because the existing 10 TiB FSx for Windows File Server profile share is full. The file system supports in-place capacity increases, is below its maximum capacity, and meets the throughput requirements for scaling. The company wants to restore capacity and automatically act before future growth fills the share again, without migrating profiles to a new share.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a larger FSx file system, copy all profiles, update every client path, and send an SNS warning whenever the replacement approaches capacity.

Increase the current file system capacity now. Alarm on FreeStorageCapacity with adequate headroom, route the alarm state change through EventBridge to Lambda, and call UpdateFileSystem to increase capacity subject to growth limits and update status.
Keep storage capacity unchanged and schedule data deduplication alone as the guarantee that unique new profile data will always fit.
Enable automatic SSD IOPS provisioning on the existing file system and rely on the additional I/O capacity to expand its available storage bytes.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. FSx can grow the existing filesystem, preserving the share rather than requiring profile migration. CloudWatch evaluates free capacity; an alarm state change can invoke automation that validates current state and requests a larger StorageCapacity through the FSx API. Immediate expansion addresses today's incident, and an early threshold addresses recurring growth.

<<1>> introduces the migration and client-path changes that the scenario excludes.

<<3>> can reduce duplicate data but cannot guarantee space for continued growth, particularly when new files contain unique data.

<<4>> changes I/O performance rather than the number of provisioned storage bytes.

Expansion is one-way and is not instantaneous. Each increase must meet the minimum growth requirement, and another increase cannot proceed until the documented cooldown and storage-optimization conditions are satisfied. Use idempotent automation, an upper cost/capacity bound, sufficient lead time, and failure alerts. Recalculate absolute alarm thresholds after resizing when the intended policy is percentage-based. A persistently alarming metric is not a continuous stream of new state-change events, so monitor unsuccessful or insufficient expansions explicitly.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [FSx storage capacity changes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fsx/latest/WindowsGuide/managing-storage-configuration.html); [Automating FSx capacity growth](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fsx/latest/WindowsGuide/automate-storage-capacity-increase.html); [CloudWatch alarm events](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/Acting_Alarm_Changes.html).

question:
An education company runs application servers on EC2 and in its data center. Each server writes structured JSON logs with a level field. Operations needs an alert within minutes when an error-count metric reaches at least 20 during a five-minute period. Log delivery is prompt and monitored. The company wants centralized logs and minimal custom processing code.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Collect logs with the CloudWatch agent and run an hourly Logs Insights query that sends an SNS notification when the previous hour contains errors.
Collect host CPU metrics with the CloudWatch agent and notify an SNS topic when average CPU utilization exceeds 80 percent.
Collect logs in CloudWatch Logs and write a subscription Lambda function to parse errors, maintain counts, publish a custom metric, and trigger an SNS-backed alarm.
Collect logs in a Standard CloudWatch Logs log group with the CloudWatch agent. Use a metric filter for ERROR events and an alarm on a five-minute Sum of at least 20, with an SNS action.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. The agent centralizes both sets of logs. A filter that matches the structured level field and contributes a value of 1 converts matching events into an error-count metric. The alarm evaluates the Sum over the specified period and sends the configured SNS notification when it enters ALARM.

<<1>> retains centralized logs but its hourly schedule cannot meet the requested notification latency.

<<2>> measures resource utilization, not application errors. Error counts can rise while CPU remains low, or CPU can rise without an error.

<<3>> can implement the behavior, but adds parsing, aggregation, and publishing code that a native metric filter avoids for this simple predicate.

Use a Standard log group because metric filters are not supported in every log class. Filters apply to newly ingested events and do not backfill historical logs. Configure missing-data handling and separately monitor log-delivery health: a silent agent is not proof that the application is healthy. The alarm evaluates the reported metric over its five-minute period. Delayed log delivery affects detection, and metric filters can occasionally deliver duplicates; this operational signal is not an exactly-once event ledger. An SNS alarm action normally follows a state change rather than sending a fresh message for every additional error.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [CloudWatch agent on on-premises servers](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/install-CloudWatch-Agent-on-premise.html); [CloudWatch Logs metric filters](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/MonitoringLogData.html); [CloudWatch alarm behavior](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/CloudWatch_Alarms.html).

question:
A company replicates new satellite-image objects between S3 buckets in different Regions. Its policy requires every object to reach the destination within 30 minutes, with no exceptions. An architect proposes S3 Replication Time Control (RTC) and an EventBridge rule that directly compares a replication metric with a 30-minute threshold.

Which assessment is accurate?

options.text: Approve the design because RTC guarantees that every object replicates within 15 minutes, making the 30-minute requirement less restrictive.
Approve the design after configuring RTC with a 30-minute replication deadline and letting EventBridge poll the metric until it exceeds that deadline.
Replace RTC with S3 Transfer Acceleration because accelerated transfers impose a maximum 30-minute delay on cross-Region replicas.

Flag the absolute deadline as unmet: RTC covers 99.9 percent within 15 minutes. Use a CloudWatch replication-lag alarm and RTC missed-threshold notifications for visibility, without treating them as a guarantee.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. RTC's documented commitment is 99.9 percent of eligible new objects within 15 minutes, not a hard upper bound for every object. Monitoring can detect replication delays, but cannot establish the strict guarantee in the policy. The requirement remains unresolved and must not be silently relaxed.

<<1>> changes a percentage-based commitment into a universal deadline.

<<2>> invents a configurable 30-minute RTC deadline. It also assigns metric evaluation to the wrong component: a CloudWatch alarm evaluates the metric, and EventBridge can route the resulting alarm-state event.

<<3>> confuses accelerated client transfers with the cross-Region replication process. Transfer Acceleration does not establish the proposed replication deadline.

For operational monitoring, evaluate the rule's ReplicationLatency metric with Max and a threshold above 1,800 seconds, choosing suitable evaluation periods and missing-data handling. Subscribe to RTC events for objects that miss the fixed 15-minute threshold and those that replicate afterward. Rule-level lag and object-specific missed-threshold events answer different questions. Both help investigate delays; neither makes asynchronous replication satisfy an absolute per-object delivery deadline.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [S3 Replication Time Control](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/replication-time-control.html); [S3 replication metric definitions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/metrics-dimensions.html); [CloudWatch alarm events](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/Acting_Alarm_Changes.html); [S3 Transfer Acceleration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/transfer-acceleration.html).

question:
A company has legacy S3 buckets containing sensitive objects. Some applications previously used object ACLs, but their authorized access has now been migrated to policies. The company must prevent accidental public access, receive prompt alerts about access-control changes, and automatically restore its approved configuration after unauthorized drift.

Which design best meets these requirements?

options.text: Schedule an hourly Lambda scan of bucket and object ACLs, remove public grants when found, and notify the security team after each scan.
Invoke Lambda after every ObjectCreated notification to make the new object private, and rely on that function as the sole protection against public access.

Enable all four Block Public Access settings and Bucket owner enforced, protect those settings from unauthorized changes, and route relevant CloudTrail events through EventBridge to SNS and scoped remediation.
Encrypt objects with SSE-KMS and run Macie sensitive-data classification jobs, relying on encryption and classification alone to prevent public authorization.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. Preventive S3 controls address public authorization before a reactive workflow runs. Bucket owner enforced disables ACL authorization, while Block Public Access restricts public ACL and policy paths. Protect the configuration itself, then audit relevant changes and use narrowly scoped automation to restore the approved state and notify security.

<<1>> leaves an exposure interval between scans and omits the preventive controls.

<<2>> runs after object creation and does not cover later bucket-policy or access-control changes. Event delivery also is not synchronous with the write.

<<4>> confuses encryption and data classification with the requested authorization controls. Those are useful additional capabilities, but the proposed design does not enforce the approved public-access settings.

Enable CloudTrail management events for bucket-level changes and selected S3 data events for relevant object operations such as PutObjectAcl. Match actual CloudTrail event names and schemas in EventBridge, and test both rejected attempts and successful drift. Block Public Access does not erase existing ACL entries; Bucket owner enforced disables their authorization effect. Verify legacy compatibility before the transition. Event-driven remediation is asynchronous, so it complements prevention and protected change permissions instead of guaranteeing zero exposure on its own.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [S3 Block Public Access](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/access-control-block-public-access.html); [S3 Object Ownership](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/about-object-ownership.html); [S3 CloudTrail event coverage](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-logging-s3-info.html); [S3 events in EventBridge](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eventbridge/latest/ref/events-ref-s3.html).

question:
IoT devices upload small files to an S3 bucket every five minutes. A nightly Python job on EC2 reads the files, writes derived rows to RDS, and deletes successfully processed inputs. Each file is independent and takes seconds to process within Lambda resource limits. RDS can handle the expected processing rate with bounded concurrency.

The company wants processing to begin soon after each upload with minimal server administration and few code changes. Which approach should it use?

options.text: Keep the EC2 job running continuously and poll S3 every minute for files that have not yet been processed.
Configure CloudTrail S3 data-event logging, route matching PutObject API records through EventBridge, and invoke the Python processing code in Lambda.
Schedule a Lambda function every minute to list the entire bucket and discover inputs, then run the Python processing code for each discovered file.
Configure ObjectCreated notifications for the input prefix to invoke Lambda, and adapt the Python code to process the event object and delete it only after the RDS transaction succeeds.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. Direct S3 object-created notifications provide the needed trigger without a permanently running poller or API-audit pipeline. The existing Python processing logic can run per object in Lambda, subject to the stated runtime and resource fit.

<<1>> shortens the delay but retains instance administration and polling.

<<2>> can route audited API activity, but adds CloudTrail data-event configuration and cost for a trigger S3 can provide directly. EventBridge also supports native S3 events; CloudTrail is not required for every S3-to-EventBridge design.

<<3>> removes the EC2 host but repeatedly scans the bucket and introduces discovery and coordination work that a per-object notification avoids.

S3 notifications are delivered at least once and can be delayed or arrive out of order. Use a stable object identity and idempotent database writes so a retry cannot double-count an input. Commit the RDS transaction before deleting the source object, retain failed inputs, and monitor failed invocations. Configure Lambda network access to RDS, limit concurrency to protect database connections, and use an input prefix that excludes any output objects. These controls make event-driven processing reliable without assuming exactly-once delivery.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [S3 event notifications](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/EventNotifications.html); [S3 events in EventBridge](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eventbridge/latest/ref/events-ref-s3.html); [S3 CloudTrail event coverage](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-logging-s3-info.html).

question:
A company uses AWS Organizations. Its security team needs a durable record of who initiates account invitations, account creation, account removal, and OU moves from the management account. The team also wants prompt notifications for those operations.

Which solution meets both requirements?

options.text: Use Systems Manager Inventory to collect host metadata from member accounts and send the inventory summary to the security team.
Create a CloudWatch dashboard for organization costs and an SNS topic, and rely on the dashboard to identify and publish account-management API changes.
Record Organizations management events with CloudTrail and configure matching EventBridge rules in us-east-1 to send the operation details to an SNS topic subscribed to by security.
Use Control Tower baseline controls and Inspector vulnerability findings as the record of the caller and parameters for each Organizations API request.
Record supported resource configuration changes with AWS Config and use only configuration snapshots to identify the API caller and notify security about account-management operations.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. CloudTrail records API activity with caller identity and request details. EventBridge selects the relevant Organizations events, and SNS delivers the configured notifications. For this global service, configure the monitoring path in US East (N. Virginia) as documented by AWS.

<<1>> collects machine inventory rather than the required organization-management API audit trail.

<<2>> supplies a display and a notification destination without a mechanism that detects and routes the specified operations. Cost data does not identify the API caller.

<<4>> substitutes governance controls and workload vulnerability assessment for an API activity record.

<<5>> treats resource configuration history as a complete source of API identity and invocation details. Config complements CloudTrail but does not replace this event-audit path.

Filter for the required operations, retain logs in a protected destination, confirm SNS subscriptions, and test successful and failed requests as appropriate. A CreateAccount API response acknowledges an asynchronous request; account creation completion is a separate CreateAccountResult service event that needs its own monitoring rule if completion alerts are required. Scope event collection to the account where activity is recorded rather than assuming that every action by an external invited account appears in the management account's trail.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Monitoring Organizations changes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_tutorials_cwe.html); [Organizations CloudTrail records](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_cloudtrail-integration.html).

question:
A bank permits a limited set of legacy IAM users only after security approval. Its provisioning controls already require every new user to have a protected permissions boundary with an explicit deny of all actions. Provisioners cannot change that boundary, and credentials are withheld until approval. A multi-Region CloudTrail trail is enabled.

The bank needs an automated workflow that detects user creation, removes unintended permissions, notifies security, and preserves quarantine until an authenticated approval is recorded. Which components should it implement? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Use only CloudTrail log-file delivery notifications to SNS and treat successful delivery of a log file as approval of any users mentioned in that file.

Invoke a Step Functions Standard workflow that verifies quarantine, cleans up unintended policies and group memberships, and waits for authenticated approval before the authorized approval service enables the approved permissions.
Use periodic Audit Manager evidence collection as the sole trigger and completion record for the operational user-approval process.
Have the workflow publish an SNS notification to security with user details and a link to the protected approval application.
Create an EventBridge rule matching successful CloudTrail CreateUser events from IAM and route matching events to the approval workflow.
Run a one-off Fargate task that removes current user policies and then terminates, without retaining approval state or coordinating the later permission release.

explanation.text:
<<2>>, <<4>>, and <<5>> form the required workflow. EventBridge selects user-creation activity, Step Functions coordinates cleanup and the durable approval wait, and SNS notifies reviewers. The pre-existing explicit-deny boundary remains effective while asynchronous detection and review take place.

<<1>> confuses log-file delivery with a user-specific authorization decision. Receiving an audit artifact is not security approval.

<<3>> gathers audit evidence but does not implement the requested event-triggered cleanup and approval lifecycle.

<<6>> can remove permissions that exist at that moment, but it does not track the approval decision or control the authorized release from quarantine.

CreateUser does not itself grant service permissions; later policy attachments, group membership, credentials, or resource policies are separate concerns. This is why the protected preventive boundary is established during provisioning rather than attached only after an event arrives. Its explicit deny matters: an implicit deny in a boundary does not constrain every form of resource-based grant in the same way. Protect all ways to alter or remove the boundary. Make event handling idempotent, restrict the approval callback to authenticated reviewers, and retain quarantine on rejection, timeout, or workflow failure. An SNS notification alone must never release access.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [IAM user creation steps](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_users_create.html); [IAM permissions boundaries](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies_boundaries.html); [IAM API events in EventBridge](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eventbridge/latest/ref/events-ref-iam.html); [Step Functions integration patterns](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/connect-to-resource.html).

question:
A company runs a customer-facing application on redundant Windows EC2 instances managed by Systems Manager. The fleet has enough spare capacity to keep serving customers while individual instances are drained and rebooted. The company needs centralized compliance reporting, scheduled installation of approved security patches, and a way to deploy urgent approved patches outside the normal schedule.

Which approach best meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable automatic Windows updates on every instance at the same time and allow all instances to reboot immediately whenever updates become available.

Use Patch Manager with approved baselines and patch policies or maintenance windows, plus on-demand urgent patching. Coordinate draining, installation, required reboots, and health checks in controlled rolling batches.
Launch the fleet from one patched and hardened AMI, then rely on that original image indefinitely without subsequent patch scans, installations, or image replacements.
Run scheduled Patch Manager Scan operations and report missing approved patches, but leave all installations and required reboots disabled.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. Patch Manager provides a centrally defined approval baseline, compliance scans, and installation workflows that can run on a schedule or on demand. The redundant fleet allows required reboots to occur in controlled groups while healthy instances continue serving traffic.

<<1>> can install updates but risks taking the whole application offline during simultaneous reboots and does not implement the requested centrally controlled rollout.

<<3>> establishes only an initial patch state. An immutable-image strategy can work when images are continually rebuilt, validated, and rolled out, but the proposed one-time image does not address future patches.

<<4>> identifies noncompliance without correcting it. A Scan operation is not an Install operation.

Use approved security patches rather than interpreting the goal as immediately installing every new operating-system release. Patch Manager does not perform major OS version upgrades or guarantee application compatibility. Test patches, coordinate load-balancer draining and recovery, and stop the rollout when health checks fail. Concurrency limits and maintenance windows help control execution, but do not themselves implement application-aware draining or guarantee availability. Track pending reboots because installation alone may not complete remediation.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Systems Manager Patch Manager](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/patch-manager.html); [Quick Setup patch policies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/patch-manager-policies.html).

question:
A factory uses IP cameras to inspect parts on an assembly line. A defect-detection model has been trained in SageMaker AI. The cameras can stream images but cannot run the model. A local Linux server exposes the API that sends inspection feedback to workers, and another compatible local server is available for inference.

Inspections and feedback must continue during Internet outages. Which deployment meets this requirement?

options.text: Deploy the model to a regional SageMaker real-time endpoint and connect the factory API to that endpoint through redundant VPN connections.
Upload images to S3 and run SageMaker batch transform jobs in the Region, then deliver each completed result to the factory API.
Install Greengrass V2 on the local inference server and deploy the compatible model, runtime, and inference components in advance. Process camera images locally and invoke the local feedback API.
Use a Greengrass component to preprocess camera images locally, but invoke a regional SageMaker endpoint for every defect prediction before sending feedback.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. Both inference and feedback stay on the factory network. Greengrass components can package the application code, model artifacts, and compatible runtime so the hot path does not depend on a cloud request.

<<1>> can improve connectivity resilience but still requires a working path to the regional inference service. Redundant VPNs do not make a cloud endpoint available during a complete Internet outage.

<<2>> introduces cloud transfer and batch-processing dependencies, so it cannot continue the required local inspection loop while disconnected.

<<4>> performs only preprocessing locally. The decisive prediction still depends on the unavailable regional endpoint.

Deploy all artifacts and runtime dependencies before an outage, and avoid cloud-only authorization, model downloads, or API calls in the inspection path. Verify that local hardware supports the model and meets the required throughput. Greengrass can manage deployment when connectivity is available, but local inference code must implement the camera and feedback-API integrations. Test the full workflow with WAN access disabled; local network and server failures require their own resilience design.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Local Greengrass ML inference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/greengrass/v2/developerguide/perform-machine-learning-inference.html); [Greengrass resilience](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/greengrass/v2/developerguide/disaster-recovery-resiliency.html).

question:
Millions of temperature sensors send MQTT messages to a custom domain backed by one EC2-hosted broker. Broker overload has caused outages. The application maps each message to a DynamoDB item, and the company wants managed ingestion with less broker administration. Device firmware can support the required TLS, SNI, and authentication settings while retaining the custom domain.

Which migration best meets these requirements?

options.text: Install Greengrass on a larger EC2 instance and run the same custom broker there, retaining one server for all sensor connections and DynamoDB writes.

Use AWS IoT Core MQTT with a configured custom domain, server certificate, device authentication, and IoT policies. Point DNS to the service endpoint and use a DynamoDBv2 rule action with the required key fields and IAM role.
Operate a broker cluster behind an NLB and manage its session replication, storage, upgrades, capacity, and failover on an EC2 Auto Scaling group.
Add random publishing delays to sensor firmware and divide devices between two fixed EC2 brokers in different Regions, retaining manual capacity and failover management.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. IoT Core provides the managed MQTT ingestion layer, and the rule action can write the mapped payload directly to DynamoDB without an unnecessary processing function. The custom-domain configuration and device authorization must be completed along with the DNS change.

<<1>> relocates the bottleneck to another single broker host and retains its administration. Greengrass is not a replacement name for the managed IoT Core broker endpoint.

<<3>> can form a valid resilient architecture, but operating the broker cluster and its coordination mechanisms retains the management burden the company wants to reduce. An NLB or shared filesystem alone does not create a coherent MQTT cluster.

<<4>> smooths bursts and divides load, but does not supply managed capacity or automatic recovery for the custom brokers.

Configure the server certificate and IoT domain configuration, ensure clients send matching SNI, and grant devices only the required topic permissions. A CNAME by itself does not establish TLS identity or authorization. The DynamoDBv2 rule result must contain the table's key attributes, and its role needs write permission. Plan rule-error handling, quotas, device buffering and retries. MQTT QoS 1 can produce duplicate deliveries, so use stable message identities and an idempotent storage design; broker acknowledgement is not a guarantee that the downstream database write succeeded.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [IoT Core custom domains](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/iot/latest/developerguide/iot-custom-endpoints-configurable-custom.html); [IoT DynamoDBv2 rule action](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/iot/latest/developerguide/dynamodb-v2-rule-action.html); [IoT rule actions and failures](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/iot/latest/developerguide/iot-create-rule.html); [IoT MQTT delivery](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/iot/latest/developerguide/mqtt.html).

question:
A company is building an inbound contact center for thousands of callers. Customers must be able to describe routine requests in natural speech, answer follow-up questions, and complete actions such as balance inquiries or password resets during the call. Existing business APIs perform those actions after verifying the caller's identity and authorization.

Which architecture provides the required conversational self-service?

options.text: Use Amazon Connect flows with a Lex V2 bot for speech recognition, intent detection, and dialog. Use Lambda fulfillment to invoke the authorized business APIs and return results to the conversation.
Use Amazon Connect with touch-tone menus only, and invoke Lambda functions based on keypad selections to access the authorized business APIs.
Use Amazon Connect with Polly-generated prompts and Lambda business functions, but provide no speech-understanding or dialog component to interpret caller requests.
Record calls with Amazon Connect, transcribe and analyze the recordings after each call, and invoke business APIs from the completed post-call analysis.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. Connect handles the contact flow, Lex V2 interprets speech and gathers the information needed to fulfill an intent, and Lambda connects that intent to the authorized business operation. The result returns within the interactive conversation.

<<2>> supports a useful IVR pattern but does not meet the requirement for natural-speech requests and follow-up dialog.

<<3>> produces spoken output without the component that recognizes the request and manages the conversation. Text-to-speech is a different capability from speech recognition and intent understanding.

<<4>> can support analytics and follow-up work, but processing after the call does not fulfill the request during the live interaction.

Define supported intents and required slots, attach the fulfillment function to the appropriate Lex V2 alias and language, and test misunderstandings, missing inputs, API errors, and transfer to an agent. Intent recognition does not authenticate a caller: enforce identity and authorization before exposing a balance or changing credentials. Give the function narrowly scoped backend access and avoid logging sensitive account data unnecessarily. Text-analysis services can provide useful language insights, but do not by themselves supply the complete live voice dialog and fulfillment workflow.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Connect and Lex integration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/connect/latest/adminguide/amazon-lex.html); [Amazon Lex V2 capabilities](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lexv2/latest/dg/what-is.html); [Lex V2 Lambda integration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lexv2/latest/dg/lambda.html); [Amazon Polly text to speech](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/polly/latest/dg/what-is.html).

question:
A development team stores application code and infrastructure templates in GitHub. It wants an AWS-managed pipeline that runs unit tests and configured security scanners, notifies developers when a gate fails, and requires the lead developer to approve each production release. Feature choices must alter the infrastructure synthesized for a release; changing business features without redeployment is outside this requirement.

Which design meets these requirements with the least custom orchestration?

options.text: Connect GitHub to CodePipeline. Run tests and scanners in CodeBuild with failure propagation, notify through EventBridge and SNS, use CDK application context and conditional code during synthesis, and add a manual approval action before production deployment.

Connect GitHub to CodePipeline. Run tests and scanners in CodeBuild, put a Lambda action that publishes to SNS after the test stage, use CDK application context during synthesis, and deploy after emailing the lead developer without waiting for an approval response.

Connect GitHub to CodePipeline. Run tests and scanners in CodeBuild with failure notifications, use CDK framework feature flags as application runtime switches, and add a manual approval action after production deployment.

Connect GitHub to CodePipeline. Store build packages in CodeArtifact in place of executing tests and scanners, notify on package publication, use CDK application context during synthesis, and add manual approval before production deployment.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. CodePipeline coordinates the stages; CodeBuild executes the configured test and scanner commands and must fail when the required gates fail. An EventBridge rule can react to a failed build and publish to SNS independently of the successful pipeline path. The manual approval action pauses execution until an authorized approver responds.

<<2>> places notification on a path that a failed preceding stage does not reach. Sending an email also does not make deployment wait for approval.

<<3>> uses the wrong kind of feature flag and approves too late. CDK framework flags select CDK behavior; application context and ordinary conditional code can control synthesis-time choices.

<<4>> substitutes a package repository for executing the required tests and security checks. Publishing a package does not establish that those gates passed.

Keep release-time configuration, test results and approval tied to the same reviewed revision. A requirement for runtime feature changes would need an application configuration mechanism rather than another CDK synthesis.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Manual approval actions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codepipeline/latest/userguide/approvals.html). [Build failure notifications](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codebuild/latest/userguide/sample-build-notifications.html). [CodeBuild buildspec](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codebuild/latest/userguide/build-spec-ref.html). [CDK framework flags](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/v2/guide/featureflags.html). [CDK application context](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/v2/guide/context.html).

question:
A logistics application runs on an EC2 Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer and uses self-managed MySQL on EC2. During the last four days of each month, reporting queries saturate the database CPU. Web capacity, storage latency and write throughput remain within their targets. Reports can tolerate replication lag. The team can perform a tested one-time database migration but wants to avoid recurring interruptions to the write workload when adding reporting capacity.

Which approach best meets these requirements?

options.text: Increase the web Auto Scaling group maximum and replace the database volumes with gp3 volumes. Continue sending every report to the existing database endpoint.

Migrate to an RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB-instance deployment. Provision read replicas before month-end, validate their readiness and lag, and route reporting queries to their endpoints while keeping writes on the primary.
Configure a CPU alarm to stop the database EC2 instance, change its instance type and restart it whenever month-end reporting crosses the threshold.
Take a month-end snapshot, restore it to a larger database instance, and redirect both transactions and reports to the restored copy without replicating changes made after the snapshot.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. Read replicas add independent query capacity and can isolate reporting from transactional writes. The application must explicitly use replica endpoints for eligible reads; creating replicas alone does not reroute queries. Use a Multi-AZ source so replica creation takes its initial snapshot from the standby, avoiding the brief source I/O suspension that occurs with a Single-AZ source. Schedule provisioning early enough for creation, synchronization and validation.

<<1>> does not address the measured database CPU bottleneck. More web instances or different storage might help other bottlenecks, but those resources have headroom here.

<<3>> scales the primary vertically by stopping it, introducing the recurring write interruption the company wants to avoid.

<<4>> leaves a gap between the snapshot and the current database. Redirecting writes without a coordinated catch-up and cutover risks missing changes.

RDS MySQL read replication is asynchronous, so check replica lag and reporting freshness. RDS DB-instance read replicas do not automatically scale their count. A conventional Multi-AZ DB-instance standby serves high availability and does not accept reporting reads. The one-time migration also requires compatibility checks, replication or another transfer plan, and a validated cutover.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [RDS DB-instance read replicas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReadRepl.html). [DMS ongoing replication](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/dms/latest/userguide/CHAP_Task.CDC.html). [Creating a read replica](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReadRepl.Create.html).

question:
A payment application receives supported URL-encoded form POSTs through CloudFront. The origin supports chunked encoding. Selected sensitive fields must remain encrypted after TLS terminates so that only a designated payment component with the private key can read them. The same distribution serves public, versioned static assets whose short cache duration causes unnecessary origin requests. Payment responses must not be cached.

Which configuration meets both requirements?

options.text: Require HTTPS for viewers and origins. Add User-Agent to the static-asset cache key, and rely on the TLS certificate to keep fields encrypted after the origin terminates TLS.
Use CloudFront signed URLs for payment requests. Extend the static assets’ cache duration, and let every origin component read the submitted form fields.
Configure OAC for the S3 asset origin. Include all request headers in the asset cache key, and use the OAC signature as encryption for payment form fields.

Require HTTPS on both connections and configure field-level encryption for the selected supported form fields. Extend caching for the public versioned assets within their freshness policy, and disable caching for payment responses.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. HTTPS protects each transport connection. Field-level encryption applies additional public-key encryption to selected supported form fields at the edge, allowing those fields to pass through intermediate origin components without revealing their values. Only the designated component holds the corresponding private key.

The public assets have a separate caching requirement: longer appropriate Cache-Control lifetimes, compatible CloudFront TTL limits and stable versioned URLs allow more reuse. Disable caching on the payment response behavior instead of applying the asset policy everywhere.

<<1>> stops protecting plaintext at TLS termination, and unnecessary high-cardinality User-Agent values fragment the cache.

<<2>> supplies an access credential; signed URLs do not encrypt the submitted fields.

<<3>> authenticates origin requests to S3; it does not implement payment field encryption. Including irrelevant headers also reduces cache reuse.

Field-level encryption is format-specific, not arbitrary encryption of all request bodies. Its use does not by itself establish payment-system compliance; application access and key handling still matter.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Field-level encryption](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/field-level-encryption.html). [Cache hit ratio](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/cache-hit-ratio.html). [Cache policy TTLs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/cache-key-understand-cache-policy.html).

question:
A tutorial site uses one CloudFront distribution with a private S3 REST origin for media and an internet-facing Application Load Balancer for ECS tasks on Fargate. HTTPS is configured. For this rollout the ALB must remain internet-facing. The team must prevent viewers from bypassing the designated distribution to read either origin. Bucket owner enforced Object Ownership disables S3 ACLs, and the team can remove unintended grants and protect a secret origin header.

Which TWO changes should the solutions architect implement? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add a secret custom origin header on CloudFront requests to the ALB. Attach a web ACL to the ALB that allows the exact secret value and blocks other requests, and restrict alternate paths to the tasks.
Add a secret custom origin header on CloudFront requests to the ALB. Validate that header only in a web ACL attached to the CloudFront distribution, leaving the ALB directly accessible.
Allow only CloudFront source IP ranges in the ALB subnet network ACL, and rely on this rule to distinguish the designated distribution from every other CloudFront distribution.
Grant the CloudFront distribution ID read access through the S3 bucket ACL, and keep the bucket policy unchanged.
Associate a signing OAC with the S3 origin. Grant GetObject to the CloudFront service principal in the bucket policy with the exact distribution SourceArn, and remove other viewer read grants.

explanation.text:
<<1>> and <<5>> are correct. Each origin enforces its own access boundary. The ALB-side WAF rule must match the exact header value; the secret must remain protected and be rotated. The S3 policy authorizes the distribution’s signed origin requests.

<<2>> checks the wrong boundary. A caller reaching the ALB directly never encounters the distribution’s web ACL. CloudFront adds the custom origin header on the origin request, after viewer-side processing.

<<3>> can reduce exposed network sources but cannot identify one particular distribution: other customers also use CloudFront infrastructure.

<<4>> cannot work with disabled ACLs, and a distribution ID is not an S3 ACL grantee.

The header approach depends on secrecy; HTTPS and restrictions on who can read or modify configuration help preserve it. A CloudFront VPC origin with a private ALB is another design to consider when the rollout permits it. Origin protection remains separate from authenticating website users.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Private S3 origins](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.html). [Restrict ALB access](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/restrict-access-to-load-balancer.html). [WAF exact string matching](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/waf-rule-statement-type-string-match.html).

question:
A company shares confidential documents with partners through an existing CloudFront distribution. Viewer authentication and authorization already work. The documents are in an S3 bucket that uses bucket owner enforced Object Ownership. Partners must not read objects directly from S3, and other CloudFront distributions must not gain origin access. The company can remove unintended read grants.

Which origin configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Use a bucket policy whose Principal is the CloudFront distribution ID and whose Resource is only the bucket ARN, without an object suffix.

Use the S3 REST endpoint and an OAC that always signs origin requests. Allow s3:GetObject for cloudfront.amazonaws.com on the object ARNs, conditioned on the exact distribution AWS:SourceArn, and remove unintended read grants.
Create an IAM user with read access to the documents and attach that IAM user directly to the CloudFront distribution as its origin identity.
Allow s3:GetObject for every principal when the request Referer header contains the public CloudFront hostname, while leaving OAC disabled.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. The policy grants object reads to the CloudFront service for this distribution, and OAC supplies signed origin requests. Keep the bucket private and Block Public Access enabled. If the objects use SSE-KMS, provide the required KMS key authorization as well.

<<1>> uses the wrong principal and resource scope. A distribution ID belongs in the distribution ARN condition; GetObject needs object ARNs.

<<3>> is not how OAC is associated with a distribution. There is no attach-an-IAM-user origin identity configuration.

<<4>> trusts a request header that a caller can forge. It does not authenticate the distribution.

An S3 website endpoint is a custom origin and cannot use this S3 OAC setup. The existing viewer authorization controls who can ask CloudFront for a document; the origin policy controls whether CloudFront may fetch it.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Private S3 origins](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.html). [S3 request authorization](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html).

question:
An insurer must send an authenticated client an individual financial file through a time-limited HTTPS download link. Either direct S3 delivery or CloudFront delivery is acceptable. The business accepts that the issued link is a bearer credential and can be used by anyone who obtains it before it expires. Public access and other unintended download grants must be removed.

Which TWO designs independently meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Issue a CloudFront signed cookie after login, but keep the S3 object publicly readable so that users can choose either download endpoint.
Issue a CloudFront signed URL after login and enable field-level encryption, but keep the S3 object publicly readable for origin requests.
Keep the S3 object private. After authorizing the client, have a backend with scoped read permission issue a short-lived S3 presigned GET URL, and remove the old public and CloudFront download paths.
Keep the S3 object private and use OAC for CloudFront origin requests. Allow any viewer to download from the distribution without a signed URL, signed cookie or application authorization.
Keep the S3 object private and use a distribution-scoped OAC grant. Require CloudFront signed URLs for the file, issue one after authorizing the client, and remove direct viewer read grants.

explanation.text:
<<3>> and <<5>> are two alternative complete designs. In the S3 design, the request uses the presigner’s scoped authority for the permitted operation. In the CloudFront design, the distribution validates the viewer’s signed URL while OAC protects the separate origin connection.

<<1>> and <<2>> leave a public S3 bypass. Signed cookies can be a valid CloudFront access mechanism, but they do not revoke an independent S3 grant. Field-level encryption also does not close that bypass.

<<4>> protects the origin but leaves the viewer side unrestricted.

Both valid designs need server-side entitlement checks before issuing links and careful handling of bearer URLs. Expiration does not erase files already downloaded. An S3 URL signed with temporary credentials expires no later than those credentials. A client’s geographic location does not itself require moving the bucket or establish that client’s identity.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [CloudFront signed URLs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-signed-urls.html). [S3 presigned downloads](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/ShareObjectPreSignedURL.html). [Presigned URL boundaries](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html). [Private S3 origins](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.html).

question:
Employees upload reports through an application whose backend role has s3:PutObject permission. They download through CloudFront, where viewer authorization is already configured. Some employees can also read the objects directly from S3 because of legacy read grants. The company must remove the download bypass while preserving the backend upload workflow. The S3 origin uses its REST endpoint and has ACLs disabled.

Which change should the solutions architect make?

options.text: Attach an OAC that signs origin requests. Allow distribution-scoped CloudFront GetObject access in the bucket policy, remove the legacy employee read grants, and retain the backend’s scoped PutObject permission.
Install a custom viewer TLS certificate on CloudFront and remove every S3 permission, including the application backend’s upload permission.
Enable CloudFront field-level encryption and keep the existing S3 permissions, because field encryption forces all S3 GET requests through CloudFront.
Require CloudFront signed URLs and configure OAC, but retain the employees’ direct S3 GetObject grants to avoid changing their IAM permissions.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. Treat uploading and downloading as separate permission paths: the backend retains the object-write action it needs, while employee reads go through the authorized CloudFront distribution. Review identity policies, bucket policies and access points so no unintended direct read path remains.

<<2>> breaks uploads and does not establish the required signed CloudFront origin grant. A viewer certificate controls TLS identity, not S3 authorization.

<<3>> protects selected fields in supported requests; it does not alter S3 read grants.

<<4>> adds a CloudFront viewer gate but preserves the independent S3 bypass.

OAC authenticates CloudFront’s origin requests. Removing an Allow in one policy is insufficient if another applicable policy still grants the same direct access. Preserve the required writer deliberately instead of applying an indiscriminate deny to all S3 operations.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Private S3 origins](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.html). [S3 access controls](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/access-control-overview.html).

question:
A content management system uses CloudFront with an ALB as its only configured origin and the default cache behavior. Dynamic pages work, but requests for /assets/logo.png return 404. Application logs show those requests reaching the ALB, where the file does not exist. The object exists as assets/logo.png in a private S3 bucket. An OAC and a distribution-scoped bucket policy have already been prepared, but the S3 bucket is not an origin in the distribution.

Which TWO configuration changes correct the routing? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add the S3 bucket REST endpoint as a second origin and associate the prepared signing OAC with that origin.
Add an ALB path rule whose target group registers the S3 bucket ARN as its target.
Replace CloudFront with Global Accelerator and register the S3 bucket as a standard accelerator endpoint.
Add a cache behavior for /assets/* that selects the S3 origin, leaving the default behavior mapped to the ALB.
Add an ALB header rule that redirects /assets/* requests to unsigned direct S3 object URLs.

explanation.text:
<<1>> and <<4>> are correct. An origin defines where CloudFront can fetch content; a cache behavior selects that origin for matching requests. The /assets/* behavior sends the existing object key to S3, while the default behavior continues to serve dynamic paths through the ALB.

<<2>> is invalid because an S3 bucket ARN is not an ALB target type. The issue is not merely a missing S3 permission on an otherwise valid ALB-to-bucket target group.

<<3>> does not provide the required CDN path routing and uses an unsupported standard accelerator endpoint type.

<<5>> directs the viewer around CloudFront and fails against the private bucket.

A bucket policy or OAC resource alone does not create an origin or route requests to it. Verify behavior order and case-sensitive paths, wait for the configuration deployment, and invalidate a cached error or let its error TTL expire before retesting.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Cache behavior routing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/DownloadDistValuesCacheBehavior.html). [Private S3 origins](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.html). [ALB target types](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/load-balancer-target-groups.html). [Cached error expiry](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/custom-error-pages-expiration.html).

question:
A company is migrating a public car-registration application from one on-premises NGINX application server and a MySQL database to AWS. The application requires server-side code and a MySQL-compatible database. Its tested deployment package runs on EC2, sessions are stored outside the web instances, and the database is compatible with RDS for MySQL. The company wants a managed database, a web tier across two Availability Zones, and only a short write pause at cutover. The full data copy takes several hours. It also requires Route 53 domain registration and public DNS hosting for the apex name.

Which migration plan meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy the application across two AZs behind an ALB and migrate MySQL to RDS using full load and CDC. Register the domain in Route 53, but create an apex CNAME record pointing to the ALB.

Deploy the application in a two-AZ EC2 Auto Scaling group behind an ALB and use RDS MySQL Multi-AZ. Use DMS full load and CDC with validated catch-up and cutover. Register the domain in Route 53 and use a public hosted-zone apex A alias to the ALB.

Deploy the application across two AZs behind an ALB with RDS MySQL Multi-AZ. Stop all source database writes before starting the several-hour backup import, then publish a Route 53 apex A alias after the import.
Copy the application package into S3 website hosting and migrate MySQL to RDS. Register the domain in Route 53 and use an apex alias to the S3 website endpoint to run the server-side application.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. EC2 runs the application code, the ALB distributes requests across healthy web instances, and RDS manages MySQL. A Multi-AZ DB-instance deployment supplies a standby in another AZ. DMS loads existing data while capturing subsequent changes; source logging, connectivity and target compatibility must be configured. Freeze source writes, confirm catch-up, validate and then switch the application.

<<1>> fails at the apex DNS record: a CNAME cannot occupy the zone apex. Route 53 supports an A alias to the ALB instead.

<<3>> makes the write outage include the entire several-hour import, violating the short-pause requirement.

<<4>> cannot run this application’s server-side runtime in S3 website hosting.

Domain registration, public DNS hosting and the application endpoint are separate configuration steps. CDC reduces the amount left for cutover; it does not eliminate validation, replication lag or the need to coordinate writes. Do not generalize this example into a rule that every AWS service always uses one DNS record type.
