question:
A company is assessing migration of thousands of Linux and Windows servers across VMware, Hyper-V and externally hosted environments. The servers run Java and PHP applications with MySQL and Oracle databases, but the inventory and dependency documentation are incomplete. Before authorizing a migration wave, management needs an evidence-based inventory, a review of organizational readiness, and a cost model with explicit sizing and licensing assumptions. The discovery team can obtain approved network access and collection credentials.

Which THREE actions should the solutions architect take? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Configure the AWS Transform discovery tool for the supported hypervisors and imported servers. Collect available OS metrics, process and connection data, and reconcile missing systems and business dependencies with application owners.
Begin production cutover launches with AWS Transform MGN and treat successful instance launches as the required inventory, organizational-readiness assessment and cost estimate.
Instrument selected applications for tracing and use those traces alone as the complete inventory of all servers, storage, licensing and organizational capabilities.
Complete an AWS Cloud Readiness Assessment against the Cloud Adoption Framework with relevant stakeholders, and document gaps in skills, governance, security and operations.
Enable Amazon Inspector and treat its vulnerability findings as a complete on-premises migration inventory, dependency map and financial business case.

Create AWS Transform migration assessment scenarios from the validated inventory. Review right-sizing, target Region, pricing and infrastructure assumptions, and supplement unsupported workload or licensing details before producing the business case.

explanation.text:
<<1>>, <<4>> and <<6>> supply complementary evidence. Discovery measures the estate and observed connections. A readiness assessment evaluates the organization’s capabilities. Migration assessment scenarios translate validated inputs and assumptions into a directional cost and sizing model.

<<2>> starts execution before the requested assessment is complete. A successful server launch does not establish portfolio completeness, team readiness or total cost.

<<3>> can reveal useful behavior in instrumented applications, but it does not discover every uninstrumented server, storage dependency, license constraint or organizational gap.

<<5>> confuses vulnerability assessment with migration planning. Inspector’s managed workload scanning is not a complete on-premises inventory and financial assessment.

Discovery completeness depends on reachability, credentials, collection modules and an observation window that includes important business cycles. Imported hosts and owner interviews help fill gaps. Treat automated recommendations as estimates to review, particularly for Oracle licensing, application changes and services that lack detailed assessment support. The current readiness guidance uses Cloud Readiness Assessment; older material calls the survey the Cloud Adoption Readiness Tool.

question:
A company must migrate historical Oracle tables from its data center into an Oracle database already configured on an existing Amazon EC2 instance. The historical tables will occupy a new 4 TiB EBS data volume. They are queried infrequently by large sequential scans that require 30 MiB/s of sustained throughput. Testing confirms that HDD latency is acceptable. Transaction logs and active tables remain on separate SSD volumes, and the EC2 instance has sufficient EBS bandwidth.

Which migration and storage combination meets the requirements at the lowest storage cost?

options.text: Use AWS DMS to load the historical tables into the existing Oracle target. Store their data files on a new Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) volume.
Use AWS DMS to load the historical tables into the existing Oracle target. Store their data files on a new Cold HDD (sc1) volume.
Use AWS Transform MGN to replicate the source server to a new EC2 instance. Store the historical data on a Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) volume.
Use AWS Transform MGN to replicate the source server to a new EC2 instance. Store the historical data on a General Purpose SSD (gp3) volume.

explanation.text:
Option <<2>> matches both decisions. AWS DMS migrates the selected database data into a supported, configured Oracle target. The administrator must attach and prepare the EBS volume and place the destination tables' data files there; DMS does not choose an EBS volume or install Oracle.

At 4 TiB, sc1 has a baseline throughput of 48 MiB/s, above the specified 30 MiB/s requirement without relying on burst credits. Its cost and I/O profile fit this explicitly infrequent, sequential workload. This does not make sc1 a general recommendation for transactional Oracle databases: small random I/O and latency-sensitive work favor SSDs.

Option <<1>> supports the migration but purchases provisioned IOPS that this workload does not need. Option <<3>> uses server replication to create another server instead of loading the existing target, and st1 is intended for more frequent throughput workloads. Option <<4>> also follows the wrong server-migration path and provides SSD performance that is unnecessary under the stated tests.

question:
A company is an existing AWS Application Discovery Service customer completing an ongoing migration assessment. Its on-premises Linux and Windows servers have little documentation. The company needs an inventory, utilization history, running-process information, and network dependencies to build a total cost of ownership model before migrating workloads.

Which approach gathers the required inputs with the least custom development?

options.text: Define the applications in AWS Serverless Application Model templates. Use the templates to infer the existing servers' utilization and dependencies.
Import a spreadsheet of server names and allocated CPU and memory into AWS Migration Hub. Use this static inventory as the utilization and dependency history.
Install AWS Transform MGN replication agents and launch the servers on EC2. Collect production metrics after cutover to build the initial migration assessment.
Install AWS Application Discovery Agents on the servers. Collect utilization, process, and connection data, then export the results for dependency analysis and cost modeling.

explanation.text:
Option <<4>> collects the evidence the assessment needs before migration. Application Discovery Agents gather server configuration, performance history, running processes, and network connections. Exported observations can inform application grouping, instance sizing, and a cost model; collecting data is distinct from computing a complete business TCO.

Option <<1>> describes intended serverless resources rather than measuring existing servers. Option <<2>> supplies a useful inventory but cannot create utilization history or observed dependencies that were never collected. Option <<3>> begins server replication and delays the assessment until after migration, reversing the required sequence.

The existing-customer premise matters. AWS Application Discovery Service closed to new customers on November 7, 2025. AWS recommends AWS Transform for new discovery projects; existing customers can complete ongoing projects.

question:
A company is modernizing an application that uses IBM WebSphere, Db2 LUW, and IBM MQ on premises. It wants managed database and broker operations while retaining WebSphere on EC2. A pilot has validated conversion of the database to Aurora PostgreSQL and adaptation of the JMS clients to ActiveMQ. The company will not redesign messaging around Amazon SQS APIs. WebSphere sessions are externalized, and its deployment and licensing support a multi-AZ Auto Scaling group.

Which migration plan best meets these requirements?

options.text: Rehost WebSphere and Db2 on EC2 with AWS Transform MGN. Replace IBM MQ with Amazon SQS Standard queues and adapt the producers and consumers.

Convert the Db2 schema with AWS SCT and migrate data with AWS DMS to Aurora PostgreSQL. Run WebSphere in a multi-AZ Auto Scaling group behind an ALB and migrate the validated JMS integration to a highly available Amazon MQ for ActiveMQ broker.
Rehost WebSphere and Db2 on EC2 with AWS Transform MGN. Run WebSphere behind an ALB and migrate the validated JMS integration to Amazon MQ for ActiveMQ.
Convert the Db2 schema with AWS SCT and migrate data with AWS DMS to Aurora PostgreSQL. Run WebSphere behind an ALB and replace IBM MQ with Amazon SQS FIFO queues.

explanation.text:
Option <<2>> implements the validated modernization boundaries: managed Aurora for the database, managed Amazon MQ for messaging, and independently scalable WebSphere compute. AWS SCT assists schema and code conversion, while DMS moves data and can capture ongoing Db2 changes when prerequisites are satisfied. Validate the converted application and reconcile data before cutover.

Option <<1>> retains database administration on EC2 and requires the excluded SQS redesign. Option <<3>> preserves more of the original database deployment but fails the managed-database requirement. Option <<4>> modernizes the database but still changes messaging to SQS; FIFO ordering does not make SQS an ActiveMQ or IBM MQ replacement with identical broker semantics.

Aurora is not a drop-in Db2 engine, and Amazon MQ runs ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ, not IBM MQ. The completed compatibility pilot and planned client changes are what make this migration viable. Rehosting alone does not supply those conversions.

question:
A company runs a PHP application on EC2 with an Aurora MySQL provisioned cluster. Demand is unpredictable. Database reads are the bottleneck, while the writer has adequate capacity. The application sends reads to the reader endpoint. It requires cookie-based affinity for a local session cache, but durable session state is stored externally so instances can be replaced.

Which TWO changes automatically scale the web tier and database read capacity? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Configure Aurora Auto Scaling to adjust the number of Aurora Replicas in response to reader utilization.
Configure Aurora Auto Scaling to add writer DB instances as the write endpoint becomes busy.
Place EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind a Network Load Balancer. Enable HTTP-cookie stickiness and least-outstanding-request routing on the NLB.
Place EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group with a target tracking policy behind an Application Load Balancer. Use round robin routing with cookie-based target-group stickiness.
Place EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. Use client-port preservation as the mechanism for keeping HTTP sessions on the same target.

explanation.text:
Options <<1>> and <<4>> scale the two constrained tiers. Aurora Auto Scaling adds or removes reader instances, and the reader endpoint distributes new read connections. EC2 Auto Scaling adds or removes application instances; ALB cookie stickiness keeps subsequent eligible requests with the selected target. The initial target selection can use round robin.

Option <<2>> confuses reader scaling with writer scaling. Aurora Auto Scaling does not add writers to a conventional provisioned cluster. Option <<3>> attributes ALB HTTP routing features to an NLB: NLB affinity is not HTTP-cookie stickiness, and it does not use the ALB least-outstanding-request algorithm. Option <<5>> does not provide ALB session affinity; retaining a client port is not a cookie-based target-group feature.

Stickiness is routing behavior, not durable session storage. A failed or removed target still requires the application to recover session state. Reader scaling also cannot solve a write bottleneck, which the scenario explicitly excludes.

question:
A company runs an application on EC2 Auto Scaling, an ALB, and RDS for PostgreSQL in one Region. A second Region has an ALB, a cross-Region read replica, and an Auto Scaling group with zero running instances. The secondary group's launch configuration, quotas, and recovery capacity have been validated. The company requires a 30-minute RTO while keeping standby compute costs low. Its tested runbook can promote the replica, start the application, validate writes, and update DNS within this objective.

Which approach should automate the runbook?

options.text: Monitor a meaningful primary application endpoint with Route 53 health checks. Use a CloudWatch alarm and SNS to start a recovery workflow that fences primary writes, promotes the replica, scales the secondary group, verifies readiness, and then redirects DNS traffic.
Monitor individual ALB 502 responses. On the first error, promote the replica and update DNS immediately, then request secondary EC2 capacity.
Keep enough application instances running in the secondary Region to serve the full production load. Use weighted DNS routing and promote the replica when the primary health check fails.
Configure Route 53 failover records and health checks for both ALBs. Rely on DNS failover to promote the read replica and launch instances in the secondary Auto Scaling group.

explanation.text:
Option <<1>> automates the recovery dependencies while retaining the pilot-light compute footprint. Health checks publish metrics to CloudWatch; an alarm can notify SNS and start orchestration. The workflow must make the database writable, launch and configure application capacity, and verify the recovered service before explicitly directing clients to it. Use a durable orchestrator, such as Step Functions with Lambda tasks, for polling and retries.

Option <<2>> treats one request error as a regional failure and directs traffic to a service that is not ready. Option <<3>> can shorten recovery but pays for full standby compute, contrary to the stated cost objective. Option <<4>> changes DNS routing only; Route 53 does not perform RDS promotion or EC2 scaling.

The 30-minute RTO comes from tested end-to-end recovery, including detection, capacity acquisition, database promotion, application checks, and DNS/client caching. It is not guaranteed by these services individually. Cross-Region replication is asynchronous, so the recovery plan also needs a separate RPO and controls against competing writers.

question:
A company serves a web application through CloudFront, with an ALB forwarding requests to ECS tasks on Fargate. When the ALB returns HTTP 502, users should receive a branded error page while the HTTP response remains 502. Healthy requests must continue normally. A static HTML error page is available.

Which solution meets these requirements with the least operational overhead?

options.text: Store the page in a private S3 bucket. Add its REST endpoint as a CloudFront origin with origin access control, route an error-page path to that origin, and configure a custom 502 response using that page and status code 502.
Use an ALB error alarm to invoke Lambda. Have Lambda replace the application listener rule with a redirect to a public error-page URL, then restore the rule when the alarm clears.
Host the page on an S3 website endpoint. Configure Route 53 failover between the application and the website whenever an application health check fails.
Add a highest-priority ALB rule matching all request paths. Configure the rule to return a fixed 502 response containing the branded page.

explanation.text:
Option <<1>> handles the error on the request path that already serves the application. CloudFront can substitute a custom body for an origin's 502 response while retaining the 502 status. A separate cache behavior routes the error-page object to S3, and OAC permits CloudFront to read a private REST origin. Choose an error-caching TTL appropriate to recovery speed.

Option <<2>> changes routing globally after a metric alarm, so it redirects healthy requests too and requires custom rule-management logic. Option <<3>> performs DNS failover rather than substituting the body of a particular 502 response. An S3 website endpoint also cannot use OAC. Option <<4>> matches healthy requests as well and prevents them from reaching the application.

The custom response improves the user experience; it does not repair the underlying application. Keep the error page independently available, because a failure fetching it changes the response CloudFront can return.

question:
A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled. A network member account owns a nondefault VPC and eligible private subnets. Application teams in accounts under the Customers OU must launch their own EC2 resources in those subnets. The network team must retain control of the VPC's subnets and route tables.

Which TWO actions establish this shared network model? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Attach an SCP to Customers that denies VPC configuration changes, without creating a resource share.
From the management account, enable sharing with AWS Organizations by using AWS RAM.
Create a VPC in every application account and connect the VPCs with a transit gateway instead of sharing subnets.
From the network account, create an AWS RAM resource share containing the selected subnets and grant the share to the Customers OU.
Share the network account's managed prefix lists with Customers so that the application accounts can launch instances in the referenced networks.

explanation.text:
Options <<2>> and <<4>> establish VPC subnet sharing. The management account enables organization sharing through RAM, creating the required integration. The resource owner then shares its eligible subnets with the OU. Participant accounts can create and manage their own supported application resources inside those subnets, while the owner retains network-resource control. Participants still need appropriate IAM permissions.

Option <<1>> can restrict actions but grants no access to the owner's subnets. Option <<3>> creates separately owned networks and connectivity; it does not place resources in the centrally owned VPC. Option <<5>> shares reusable address ranges, not subnet-placement rights.

Enabling RAM trusted access only through the Organizations console is insufficient because that path does not create RAM's required service-linked role. Use the RAM console or its organization-sharing API. Sharing also does not, by itself, prohibit application accounts from creating separate VPCs elsewhere.

question:
An EC2 Auto Scaling group replaces unhealthy application instances and scales in after traffic peaks. Instances send logs to CloudWatch Logs every 5 minutes, so recent local records can be lost during termination. The instances are Systems Manager managed nodes and are normally reachable when scale-in starts. The operations team wants an automated final log upload before normal termination, in addition to continuous shipping.

Which solution best meets the requirement?

options.text: Use an EventBridge termination event to invoke a user-data script that copies local logs to S3 after the instance has entered the terminated state.
Reduce the log-shipping interval to 1 minute and increase ALB deregistration delay. Ask operators to connect by SSH and retrieve the remaining logs during scale-in.

Add an EC2_INSTANCE_TERMINATING lifecycle hook. Use EventBridge and an orchestrated Lambda workflow to run an SSM command that uploads logs to S3, monitor command success and send heartbeats, then complete the lifecycle action with CONTINUE.
Use a terminating lifecycle hook to invoke an SSM command. Immediately complete the lifecycle action with ABANDON so the instance remains paused while the command runs.

explanation.text:
Option <<3>> adds a bounded Terminating:Wait period for the final copy. The workflow must wait for the Run Command execution to succeed, not merely for SendCommand to return a command ID. Heartbeats extend the wait within the hook's limits, and CONTINUE releases the hook after the upload completes. Use idempotent handling and a defined failure policy.

Option <<1>> runs too late: a terminated instance cannot execute user data or upload its local files. Option <<2>> reduces the potential loss window but neither guarantees a final flush nor automates it; ALB draining is not a log-upload completion signal. Option <<4>> misinterprets ABANDON. For a termination hook, both ABANDON and CONTINUE allow termination; ABANDON also skips remaining hooks.

With the default termination behavior, an expired or abandoned hook does not indefinitely preserve the instance. An unreachable or abruptly failed instance may never upload its logs, so continuous remote shipping remains the primary protection.

question:
A company manages workforce identities and security-group membership in on-premises Active Directory. An existing external identity provider uses that directory and supports SAML 2.0 and SCIM. The company wants employees to use corporate sign-in to access multiple AWS accounts, with account permissions administered centrally from those groups. It wants to avoid per-account IAM users and custom synchronization scripts.

Which solution meets these requirements with the least operational overhead?

options.text: Federate the identity provider with an Amazon Cognito user pool. Use Cognito user groups as the central permission-set assignments for all AWS accounts.
Create a SAML identity provider and IAM roles separately in every AWS account. Write scripts to synchronize directory groups and each account's role mappings.

Connect the external identity provider to an organization instance of IAM Identity Center using SAML. Provision users and groups through SCIM, then assign the groups to AWS accounts with permission sets.
Export Active Directory users into a new AWS Managed Microsoft AD directory. Create directory trust relationships directly with each AWS account to grant administrative roles.

explanation.text:
Option <<3>> separates the three required functions. SAML provides federated sign-in, SCIM provisions users and groups, and IAM Identity Center account assignments associate those identities with permission sets. This centralizes access without creating an IAM user in each account.

Option <<1>> uses an application identity service as though it were the AWS Organizations workforce account-assignment system. Cognito federation does not create Identity Center permission-set assignments. Option <<2>> can implement federation, but duplicated per-account configuration and custom synchronization conflict with the low-overhead requirement. Option <<4>> introduces another directory and invents a trust between a directory and an AWS account; directory trusts do not grant AWS account roles.

Active Directory alone is not the SAML issuer in this design: the external IdP performs federation. SAML does not discover directory groups, and SCIM synchronization does not independently grant account access. Both provisioning and account assignments must be configured.

question:
An AWS Organizations management account pays the consolidated bill for hundreds of member accounts. A weekly analytics job uses tagged EC2 resources across the organization and writes results to a tagged Redshift cluster. The company applies expenseUnit=analytics to its attributable resources. Finance needs an organization-wide report of the direct charges associated with that tag; it allocates shared and untagged charges separately.

Which approach supplies the required billing data?

options.text: Activate the expenseUnit user-defined cost allocation tag in the management account. Export organization-wide Cost and Usage Report data to S3, then query line items whose expenseUnit value is analytics.
Activate the expenseUnit tag and create a Cost and Usage Report in the analytics member account. Treat that report as the consolidated organization report.
Activate the tag only in the accounting member account and export that account's Cost and Usage Report. Use the common tag value to include other accounts automatically.
Create a tag-based AWS Resource Group in the management account. Export the consolidated Cost and Usage Report without activating expenseUnit as a cost allocation tag.

explanation.text:
Option <<1>> combines organization billing scope with billing-tag activation. Activate the tag key expenseUnit, then filter its values in CUR or CUR 2.0 data. The management-account export can supply consolidated member-account costs for the applicable billing period.

Option <<2>> scopes the report to the analytics member account rather than all participating accounts. Option <<3>> has the same scope problem; a shared tag value does not expand a member account's report. Option <<4>> groups resources operationally but does not replace activation of the tag for billing reports.

Apply the tag to each relevant taggable resource and verify its appearance in the export before relying on the report. Tagging does not allocate every charge: shared resources, untagged usage, credits, and commitment discounts require the finance team's agreed cost basis and allocation rules. The requested direct-charge report is only one component of full chargeback.

question:
A company organizes its AWS member accounts into business-unit OUs. Each unit's finance readers need detailed usage and cost analysis for their own accounts, but must not see other units' costs. Accounts occasionally move between OUs, and historical costs must remain attributed to the unit that owned the account when the usage occurred.

Which reporting design meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a Cost and Usage Report in one member account per OU. Use that account's report as the source for a dashboard covering all sibling accounts in the OU.

Export consolidated Cost and Usage Report data from the management account to S3. Join usage account IDs to a dated account-to-OU mapping, then publish QuickSight dashboards with row-level security for business-unit readers.
Use Trusted Advisor recommendations from the management account as the source of billing line items. Group the recommendations by each account's current OU and publish the results to finance readers.
Export consolidated Cost and Usage Report data to S3 and publish one shared QuickSight dataset. Add an editable OU filter to the dashboard and allow each reader to select a business unit.

explanation.text:
Option <<2>> solves both attribution and authorization. Consolidated billing data identifies the usage account. A maintained mapping with effective dates associates each usage period with the correct historical OU. QuickSight row-level security then restricts finance readers to their authorized units; keep unrestricted dataset ownership with trusted reporting administrators.

Option <<1>> does not turn a member account's report into an OU-wide report. Option <<3>> substitutes optimization recommendations for detailed billing records and also rewrites history when accounts move. Option <<4>> offers a convenience filter that readers can change; it is not an access-control boundary.

An Organizations hierarchy is not automatically a complete, historical cost-allocation dimension in every billing line item. Preserve account membership history and join it deliberately. Use dataset security or separately scoped datasets to enforce who can see the resulting rows.

question:
A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled. It has a tested CloudFormation template for a standard VPC in two approved Regions. The network team must deploy the template to all member accounts and automatically deploy it when new accounts join the organization. It wants to avoid maintaining execution roles separately in every account.

Which TWO actions meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Activate trusted access between CloudFormation StackSets and AWS Organizations from the management account.
Activate trusted access for AWS Service Catalog and share a portfolio with the organization, without configuring StackSets.
Create a StackSet in the management account using service-managed permissions. Target the organization root and the two Regions, deploy the initial stack instances, and enable automatic deployment.
Create a self-managed StackSet with a fixed list of account IDs. Enable drift detection to add new organization accounts to the deployment.
Publish the VPC template as a Service Catalog product and grant all member accounts access to launch it on demand.

explanation.text:
Options <<1>> and <<3>> combine the required organization trust with the correct deployment model. Service-managed StackSets use the Organizations integration to create the necessary roles in member accounts. Deploying to the root covers its member accounts, and automatic deployment responds when accounts enter the targeted organization or OUs. Specify the Regions as part of the deployment.

Option <<2>> establishes a different service's integration and does not deploy this StackSet. Option <<4>> uses a static account list and misinterprets drift detection: drift identifies configuration differences, not newly joined accounts to provision. Option <<5>> makes a standard template available for users to request, but sharing a product does not automatically provision it everywhere.

Choose the retain-or-delete behavior for accounts that leave the target scope. Service-managed StackSets target member accounts; the organization management account is not automatically provisioned through this mechanism. A registered delegated administrator can also manage service-managed StackSets once trusted access is enabled.

question:
A company plans to migrate Windows and Ubuntu virtual machines from its data center to EC2. Before starting replication, it must identify application dependencies, group servers into migration waves, and select initial EC2 sizes based on observed usage. The team can grant a central collector access to the hypervisors and guest operating systems.

Which approach meets these requirements with the least custom tooling?

options.text: Deploy the AWS Transform discovery tool with hypervisor and OS access. Use the collected data in Transform migration planning for application groups and waves, and in a migration assessment for initial EC2 sizing and cost scenarios.

Install Systems Manager Agent and collect software inventory. Enter each server's allocated CPU and memory in AWS Pricing Calculator, and use the resulting prices as dependency and right-sizing recommendations.
Use AWS Transform MGN to start block replication immediately. After production cutover, use Compute Optimizer to select instance sizes and infer the original migration waves.

Deploy the AWS Transform discovery tool and prepare migration waves. Migrate each server using its current allocated capacity, then wait for EC2 history before using Compute Optimizer to right-size it.

explanation.text:
Option <<1>> makes discovery evidence available before execution. AWS Transform supports centralized discovery of server configuration and usage. Authorized OS access adds information about connections and their associated processes. Migration planning uses dependencies to organize application groups and waves, while migration assessments evaluate initial EC2 sizing and cost assumptions.

Option <<2>> collects useful inventory but treats a pricing calculation as if it measured runtime behavior and dependencies. Pricing Calculator prices the configuration supplied to it. Option <<3>> begins replication before the required assessment and asks post-migration optimization to retroactively plan the migration. Option <<4>> gathers planning data but delays sizing until after cutover, contrary to the requirement.

Validate collection coverage and observe a representative workload period, including peaks. A discovered dependency graph is evidence for a plan, not proof that every rare or scheduled dependency has been observed. Review the proposed groupings and sizing with application owners before migrating.

question:
A company has PROD, DEV, and UAT OUs in AWS Organizations. AWS Config detects security groups that expose ports outside an approved list to the internet and sends alerts. In PROD member accounts, designated critical security groups must remain unchanged by application teams, even when those teams have administrator IAM permissions. A protected security-team role must retain controlled maintenance access.

Which solution provides the required preventive control?

options.text: Attach an automatic Config remediation action that removes unrestricted ingress after the Config rule reports noncompliance.

Attach a tested SCP to PROD that denies application principals all relevant mutation APIs for the designated groups, including rule creation, revocation, modification and group deletion. Protect any classification tags and the security-role exception from application-team changes.
Attach an SCP to PROD that denies ec2:AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress when aws:SourceIp matches 0.0.0.0/0, using this condition to identify the CIDR being added to a rule.
Subscribe a Lambda function to the Config alert topic and have it restore the previous security-group rules after each unauthorized change.

explanation.text:
Option <<2>> places an authorization guardrail above member-account administrator permissions. A matching explicit SCP deny blocks the attempted API call. The control must cover all relevant mutation paths and use supported action, resource, and condition combinations. If protected tags identify the groups, prevent application teams from changing those tags. Protect the exception role's trust and permissions as well.

Option <<1>> detects and remediates after a change, and its port-exposure test does not cover every forbidden modification. Option <<3>> tests the API caller's public source IP, not the CIDR supplied in a security-group rule; it also omits many mutation APIs. Option <<4>> is corrective automation, leaving a period when the unauthorized configuration exists.

Keep Config as a detective supplement. The managed rule permits public ingress on configured authorized ports, so it does not classify every 0.0.0.0/0 rule as noncompliant. SCPs constrain member-account principals, including administrators, but do not grant permissions or constrain service-linked roles.

question:
A company is moving short, stateless webhook handlers from EC2 to Lambda. A social platform can send an HTTPS POST to a different URL for each event type. Each handler validates the platform's signature and processes duplicate events safely. Payloads and execution times fit Lambda function URL limits. The company does not need custom domains, API keys, request transformation, or gateway-level routing.

Which endpoint design meets the requirements with the least operational overhead?

options.text: Create a Lambda function URL for each handler with auth type NONE and the required invocation resource policy. Validate the platform signature in the handler before processing the event.
Create an AppSync GraphQL API with Lambda resolvers. Point the existing webhook POSTs at the GraphQL endpoint without changing their payload format.
Package the handlers as ECS services on Fargate behind an ALB. Add API Gateway HTTP API routes through a VPC link to the ALB.
Create an API Gateway REST API with a resource and Lambda proxy integration for every webhook. Deploy and manage stages for the REST API.

explanation.text:
Option <<1>> exposes each function through a managed HTTPS endpoint without a separate API tier. A public third-party webhook can use auth type NONE with the required resource-based permissions, while the function performs application-level signature validation before accepting the event. NONE does not itself authenticate the platform.

Option <<2>> expects the GraphQL request contract rather than the platform's existing webhook body. Option <<3>> can host an HTTP service but adds container, load-balancer, and API configuration to a workload already suited to Lambda. Option <<4>> is technically viable, but its API resources and stages add administration for capabilities this scenario does not require.

Use API Gateway when its API-management features are requirements. Function URLs are a simpler fit here, not a universal replacement. Public function URL policies must authorize both lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl and lambda:InvokeFunction under current requirements; restrict the latter to invocation through the URL where appropriate. Retain signature, replay, and duplicate-event checks in the application.

question:
A solutions architect is assessing hundreds of Windows and Linux VMs on Microsoft Hyper-V before migration. The team needs measured CPU and memory usage, server-to-server connections with process information, and initial EC2 sizing and cost recommendations. It wants a managed assessment workflow and can provide authorized hypervisor and guest OS access.

Which THREE actions form the appropriate workflow? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Export a one-time list of VM names and allocated CPU and memory. Treat this inventory as sufficient evidence of observed utilization and application dependencies.
Deploy a central AWS Transform discovery tool appliance, configure Hyper-V discovery sources, and enable remote OS collection with the required Windows and Linux credentials.
Install the CloudWatch agent for CPU and memory metrics. Use Systems Manager OpsCenter to infer and export the servers' complete process dependency graph.
Export the collected discovery data and create an AWS Transform migration assessment job. Review the imported inventory and configure target-Region, sizing, and pricing assumptions.
Build a custom Glue ETL pipeline and Athena reporting application as a mandatory prerequisite for AWS Transform to read its own supported discovery export.
Review the assessment's sizing and cost results, refine scenarios through chat, and examine collected connection and process data with application owners to validate dependency groups.

explanation.text:
Options <<2>>, <<4>>, and <<6>> cover collection, assessment, and review. The Transform discovery tool is a centralized appliance or installation that reaches Hyper-V hosts and guest operating systems remotely. Guest credentials and connectivity enable richer performance and process-connection collection. The supported export can then feed a migration assessment with explicit assumptions and human review.

Option <<1>> captures allocation rather than a representative utilization history, and it lacks observed connections. Option <<3>> combines metric collection with an unsupported OpsCenter dependency-inference role. Option <<5>> invents an ETL prerequisite: custom Glue and Athena analysis is possible when useful, but it is unnecessary for ingesting the tool's supported assessment export.

The collector does not install its own agent on every guest. Check collection failures and missing credentials; incomplete discovery can yield incomplete dependency groups. Assessment reports provide sizing and cost guidance. Migration wave planning is a separate planning activity, not something to assume every cost-assessment report automatically completes.

question:
A company manages supported Windows and Linux servers on premises and on EC2. Different teams currently use separate patch tools. All servers can reach their operating-system repositories and the required Systems Manager endpoints. The company wants one process to scan and install approved OS patches, plus a consolidated report showing compliance with its patch baselines.

Which TWO actions meet these requirements with the least custom development? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Configure the servers as Systems Manager managed nodes with the appropriate agent, registration and permissions. Use Patch Manager baselines and scheduled patch operations.
Write a custom AWS Config rule to inspect each server's installed packages. Build remediation scripts and a separate report generator around the Config findings.
Write custom patch-installation Automation documents and schedule them with EventBridge. Use OpsCenter operational items as the authoritative patch-baseline report.
Use Patch Manager compliance views and patch-compliance report exports to review missing patches and baseline status for the managed fleet.
Use Amazon Inspector vulnerability findings as the patch-baseline report and rely on those findings to install the approved updates automatically.

explanation.text:
Options <<1>> and <<4>> use the same managed-node and patch-baseline model for execution and reporting. Patch Manager can scan for missing approved patches and install them on supported EC2 and hybrid nodes. Compliance views and exported reports show the resulting baseline status. Configure the proper registration and access for on-premises nodes, and keep SSM Agent and repository connectivity healthy.

Option <<2>> rebuilds capabilities that Patch Manager already provides. Config can complement patch compliance, but custom package collection and reporting add development work. Option <<3>> can orchestrate commands, but OpsCenter operational items are not a replacement for Patch Manager's patch-compliance records. Option <<5>> confuses vulnerability assessment with baseline-based patch installation and compliance reporting.

A scan reports compliance at the time it runs; it does not install patches unless an installation operation is requested. Plan maintenance windows, reboot behavior, concurrency, and error thresholds. Patch Manager also does not perform arbitrary major operating-system upgrades.

question:
A retailer loads a new dataset into Amazon OpenSearch Service each week. Indexes are actively queried for 7 days, then queried rarely until deletion at 90 days. Older queries can wait for a cold index to be attached before searching. Complete copies of the processed datasets are also kept in a customer-owned S3 bucket for 7 years; audit retrieval is rare and can wait at least 48 hours. Each source object is large enough for archival storage to be economical.

The domain supports UltraWarm and cold storage. Capacity tests show that a smaller hot tier can handle indexing and the most recent week's searches. Which design is most cost-effective?

options.text: Reduce hot nodes to the tested capacity and retain an appropriately sized UltraWarm tier. Use ISM to move older indexes from hot to UltraWarm and then cold, deleting them at 90 days. Transition the independent S3 dataset copies to Glacier Deep Archive after 90 days.
Keep the existing hot-node count and add UltraWarm capacity. Delete both the OpenSearch indexes and the S3 dataset copies after 90 days.
Reduce hot nodes and move older indexes through UltraWarm to cold with ISM. Retain the independent S3 dataset copies in S3 Standard-IA for the full 7 years.
Replace every hot data node with UltraWarm nodes. Index new records directly into UltraWarm, query detached cold indexes directly, and archive the S3 dataset copies after 90 days.

explanation.text:
Option <<1>> separates the interactive index lifecycle from long-term data retention. Hot nodes still ingest new data. Completed indexes move through UltraWarm before cold storage; a cold index must be attached to UltraWarm for queries. Right-sizing the hot tier reduces persistent compute and attached-storage costs. The separate S3 copies remain available for the full retention period, with Deep Archive matching their rare access and tolerant restore deadline.

Option <<2>> violates the 7-year retention requirement and leaves unnecessary hot capacity. Option <<3>> preserves the data but pays for immediate-access storage that the audit workload does not require. Option <<4>> gives UltraWarm an unsupported indexing role and treats cold storage as directly queryable compute. UltraWarm indexes are read-only, and cold storage has no attached compute until reattached.

Apply S3 lifecycle rules to the company's dataset bucket, not OpenSearch's service-managed internal storage. Deep Archive requires a restore before reading and has a 180-day minimum storage duration, which the 7-year retention comfortably exceeds.

question:
A Regional API Gateway REST API invokes a Lambda function that queries Aurora MySQL. During bursts, the function opens a new database connection on every invocation, leaving many connections idle after queries finish. Queries use short transactions, and the team can avoid session features that force connection pinning. It must reduce connection setup overhead and protect the database's connection capacity.

Which TWO changes address the problem? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Configure provisioned concurrency for the Lambda function so more execution environments are initialized before the burst.
Change API Gateway to an edge-optimized endpoint and raise its request-rate limit.
Initialize and reuse the database client or bounded connection pool outside the Lambda handler, with keep-alive and recovery from stale connections.
Increase the Lambda reserved concurrency limit and memory allocation to allow more invocations to connect simultaneously.
Create an RDS Proxy for the Aurora cluster and configure the function to connect through the proxy endpoint with appropriate authentication and network access.

explanation.text:
Options <<3>> and <<5>> address different scopes of reuse. Reusing a client outside the handler avoids opening an unnecessary new connection for each invocation handled by the same execution environment. RDS Proxy pools backend database connections across clients and controls how many connections reach Aurora, reducing connection churn and idle-connection pressure during bursts.

Option <<1>> addresses initialization latency, not database connection pooling. Option <<2>> changes the API entry point and permits more incoming load without addressing database connections. Option <<4>> can increase simultaneous connection demand; more Lambda memory does not itself provide a shared database pool.

Execution-environment reuse is not guaranteed, and a cached connection can become stale, so reconnect safely. A local pool is not shared across Lambda environments. Proxy multiplexing is constrained by transactions and session pinning; configure limits, monitor pinning, and bound client-side pool sizes. Pooling does not create unlimited database processing capacity.

question:
A company uses several Lambda functions in a Step Functions transaction workflow. Each function has at most 1,792 MB of configured memory and has run at least 50 times during the past 14 days. The company wants a weekly CSV in S3 containing average observed memory use, current and recommended memory settings, and estimated monthly savings. It wants to use managed recommendations rather than build a sizing model.

Which solution requires the least development effort?

options.text: Arrange weekly AWS Support reviews of the functions. Have an engineer copy the findings and estimated savings into an S3 CSV file.
Enable CloudWatch Lambda Insights. Build a weekly Lambda job that aggregates memory metrics and implements a custom algorithm to calculate memory recommendations and savings.

Opt in to AWS Compute Optimizer and enable the required billing access for savings estimates. Use EventBridge Scheduler to invoke a weekly Lambda function that calls ExportLambdaFunctionRecommendations with the required fields and an authorized S3 destination, and monitor the export job to completion.
Extract memory and duration values from function logs. Build a SageMaker Canvas prediction workflow, derive cost comparisons, and manually export the forecasts as CSV.

explanation.text:
Option <<3>> uses a managed recommendation service and its native CSV export. Compute Optimizer's Lambda export supports average observed memory, current and recommended configuration, and estimated-savings fields. The function initiates an asynchronous export into an existing authorized bucket; monitoring the job confirms that the report was actually delivered. Schedule the export for the relevant Region and scope.

Option <<1>> makes a repeatable reporting requirement depend on manual analysis and copying. Option <<2>> collects useful diagnostics but still requires the company to build the recommendation and savings logic. Option <<4>> adds a custom forecasting workflow and manual export instead of using the available recommendation API.

The stated memory and invocation thresholds establish current Lambda recommendation eligibility. Opt-in, sufficient observation, and billing prerequisites still matter. Missing recommendations should be reported as unavailable rather than interpreted as zero savings. Recommendations and savings describe modeled alternatives based on observed behavior, so performance-test a change before applying it.

question:
A company runs a .NET REST API as a monolith on EC2. Different operations have different scaling needs, and traffic includes long quiet periods and short peaks. The company has approved refactoring. Tests confirm that the operations are stateless, finish within seconds, and fit Lambda resource and concurrency limits. A measured cost comparison favors on-demand execution for this workload. Clients must retain the existing API domain.

Which redesign minimizes ongoing compute-infrastructure administration?

options.text: Put the monolith in an EC2 Auto Scaling group behind an ALB, scale by an appropriate request metric, and point the existing Route 53 record to the ALB.
Put the monolith behind an ALB and a standard Global Accelerator, retain an EC2 Auto Scaling group, and update the domain to use the accelerator.
Containerize the monolith on EKS with EC2 Spot worker nodes, configure an ingress controller, and point the domain to the ingress endpoint.
Split the API operations into Lambda functions behind an API Gateway REST API, configure the existing custom domain and certificate, and update its Route 53 alias to the API endpoint.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. The operations can scale independently while AWS manages the execution infrastructure. API Gateway preserves the HTTP interface and custom domain. The stated tests establish workload fit and cost suitability.

<<1>> is a valid way to scale a monolith with little refactoring, but retains server and whole-application capacity management.

<<2>> improves global network entry, but also retains the EC2 operational model and does not split the operations' scaling boundaries.

<<3>> introduces Kubernetes and worker-node administration without a requirement for that control.

Lambda is not universally cheaper or suitable for every monolith. Check duration, state, dependencies, cold starts, downstream limits, and concurrency before choosing it. Route 53 multivalue responses are DNS answers, not a per-request replacement for an application load balancer.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Lambda execution limits](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/gettingstarted-limits.html). [API Gateway application interface](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/serverless-applications-lens/amazon-api-gateway.html).

question:
An S3 upload invokes a Python Lambda function that encodes a video and records the output location in DynamoDB. New clips require 30–45 minutes of uninterrupted encoding, exceeding the function's maximum timeout. The encoder cannot split or checkpoint an individual job without substantial rewriting, but it has been tested in a Linux container with resources supported by Fargate. The company wants to retain the encoder and avoid managing worker servers.

Which actions meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Package the tested encoder as a container image and push the image to Amazon ECR.
Use Step Functions Map states to invoke the unchanged encoder in Lambda, and enable provisioned concurrency for those functions.
Port the encoder to a supported SnapStart runtime and enable SnapStart while retaining a single Lambda invocation per video.
Queue jobs in SQS and process them on a fleet of EC2 instances that the team patches and scales.
Create an ECS task definition for the image and run encoding tasks on Fargate. Use a short S3-triggered Lambda dispatcher to call ECS RunTask, while the task writes its output and completion state.

explanation.text:
<<1>> and <<5>> are correct. The container packages the existing encoder, and an ECS task on Fargate runs it outside Lambda's 15-minute per-invocation limit. The dispatcher only starts work; it does not wait for the entire encoding job inside Lambda.

<<2>> does not shorten the unchanged, indivisible job. Workflow fan-out and provisioned concurrency do not extend a function invocation's execution limit.

<<3>> changes startup behavior, not the maximum duration of the encoding invocation.

<<4>> removes the Lambda duration limit but retains worker-server administration.

Use job identifiers, completion tracking, bounded retries, and idempotent output handling. A successfully accepted RunTask request is not proof that encoding completed. Fargate jobs can still fail or be interrupted, so persistent job state remains necessary.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Lambda timeout quota](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/gettingstarted-limits.html). [ECS standalone tasks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/standalone-tasks.html).

question:
A company is moving a Lambda application and Aurora MySQL database between accounts in the same organization and Region. The database supports cross-account cloning and uses a customer-managed KMS key whose sharing permissions can be configured. The team has tested a brief write freeze, clone creation, validation, and cutover within its outage window; full dump/import and snapshot restore take longer. The Lambda ZIP package is in S3, and the target network and deployment configuration are prepared.

Which actions complete the migration? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Freeze writes, export the full database with mysqldump, and import it into a new target-account Aurora cluster before reopening the application.

Share the Aurora cluster through AWS RAM with the required KMS permissions. During the tested write freeze, create the target-account clone, validate it, and redirect the application before reopening writes.
Freeze writes, create and share a database snapshot, and restore the target cluster from it before reopening the application.
Share the source Lambda function through AWS RAM and treat the share as a transfer of function ownership and configuration.

Copy the ZIP package to the target account and create the target Lambda function, reproducing its IAM, networking, triggers, dependencies, and required settings. Configure it for the target database at cutover.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. Aurora copy-on-write cloning creates a separate volume without first copying every data page. RAM permits the supported cross-account clone, and the KMS permissions authorize use of encrypted source data. The tested write freeze prevents later source writes from being missed.

<<5>> is correct. The package supplies code, while the recreated function configuration supplies the runtime permissions and integration needed in the target account.

<<1>> and <<3>> are valid database-copy approaches, but their measured full transfer or restore time exceeds this outage window.

<<4>> is not a Lambda ownership-migration mechanism.

A clone is an independent point-in-time copy, not a continuously updated replica. If writes must continue after its creation, a supported catch-up process is required before cutover. Cross-account encrypted cloning also cannot use the default RDS KMS key; check the supported configuration and quotas before migration.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Aurora copy-on-write cloning](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/Aurora.Managing.Clone.html). [Lambda ZIP deployment](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-function-zip.html). [Cross-account Aurora cloning](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/Aurora.Managing.Clone.Cross-Account.html).

question:
An organization has S3 buckets across hundreds of accounts and several Regions. Its organization-wide Storage Lens dashboard has collected advanced usage and activity metrics for more than six months. Finance needs to compare storage growth and access activity across that period and identify the accounts and buckets driving increased use.

Which approach provides the analysis with the least custom development?

options.text: Export IAM Access Analyzer findings and build a dashboard that treats access-policy findings as historical storage and request metrics.
Generate new S3 Inventory reports and combine them with Trusted Advisor recommendations to reconstruct six months of previously collected request activity.
Use the existing organization-wide S3 Storage Lens dashboard with advanced metrics, selecting the six-month period and drilling into the relevant accounts, Regions, and buckets.
Enable S3 Storage Class Analysis separately on each bucket and use its per-bucket transition recommendations as the organization-wide activity history.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. Storage Lens aggregates S3 usage and activity and provides drill-down views suited to the requested comparison. Advanced metrics are available for queries for 15 months, covering the already-collected six-month period.

<<1>> analyzes access exposure, not storage growth and request activity.

<<2>> inventories object metadata, but creating reports now does not reconstruct historical request activity. Trusted Advisor recommendations do not supply that missing time series.

<<4>> helps evaluate storage-class transitions, but does not replace the existing organization-wide usage and activity dashboard.

Historical availability depends on collection and retention. Free Storage Lens metrics have a 14-day query window, and enabling advanced metrics today does not manufacture six months of past observations. Use billing data separately when the question is actual invoiced cost rather than its storage-usage drivers.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Storage Lens metrics](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage_lens_basics_metrics_recommendations.html). [Viewing Storage Lens history](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage_lens_view_metrics_dashboard.html).

question:
A document service hosts its frontend behind CloudFront, accepts PDF uploads directly to S3, and submits asynchronous OCR jobs through a Regional API Gateway REST API. Processing and storage must remain in us-east-1. Users in Asia and the Middle East experience slow uploads and job-submission responses. Tests show that S3 Transfer Acceleration and an edge-optimized API endpoint improve those two paths enough to meet the targets at acceptable incremental cost. Backend processing time is already acceptable.

Which changes should the company make? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration and update upload requests or presigned upload URLs to use the supported acceleration endpoint.
Replace DynamoDB job metadata with Aurora Serverless and route database connections through RDS Proxy.
Introduce EC2 upload servers behind Global Accelerator, then copy uploaded PDFs from their EBS volumes into S3.
Deploy complete processing stacks and data copies in additional Regions and route users to regional deployments.
Change the REST API from a Regional endpoint to an edge-optimized endpoint, updating the deployment, custom-domain mapping, and DNS as required.

explanation.text:
<<1>> and <<5>> are correct. They address the two measured client paths while retaining the single-Region backend. Transfer Acceleration carries supported S3 transfers through AWS edge infrastructure, and an edge-optimized REST API uses a managed CloudFront distribution for API entry.

<<2>> changes a metadata store that is not the bottleneck.

<<3>> adds upload-server operation and another data-copy step when the tested managed S3 path meets the requirement.

<<4>> violates the stated single-Region processing and storage constraint.

The existing frontend distribution does not automatically accelerate separate direct-to-S3 uploads or calls to the Regional API hostname. Measure the actual client paths: acceleration benefits vary with location, network, and object size. An edge endpoint does not relocate the OCR execution or remove its regional processing time.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [S3 acceleration measurement](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/transfer-acceleration-speed-comparison.html). [API Gateway edge entry](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/serverless-applications-lens/amazon-api-gateway.html). [Changing REST API endpoint types](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/apigateway-api-migration.html).

question:
A company uses AWS Organizations with a separate member account for each of 10 departments. Finance must centrally administer a monthly cost budget for each department. Each department must receive email when its actual cost exceeds a threshold and a scheduled monthly email showing its budget and spending. Department recipients must receive only their own budget information. Finance also needs interactive cost analysis.

Which solution meets these requirements with the least custom development?

options.text: In the management account, create an AWS Budget for each department with a linked-account filter and department-specific alert recipients. Create a separate monthly AWS Budgets Report for each department. Use Cost Explorer for interactive analysis.

Create a Cost and Usage Report in every member account. Deploy Lambda functions to calculate thresholds, publish SNS alerts, and compose and email monthly departmental summaries. Use Cost Explorer for interactive analysis.

Activate department cost allocation tags, export cost data centrally, and develop Lambda functions to calculate budgets and email alerts and monthly summaries for each tag value. Use Athena for interactive analysis.
Create AWS Budgets and SNS alerts separately in each member account. Save a monthly Cost Explorer report in each account and instruct department recipients to open the saved report each month.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. A management-account budget can filter a department's linked account. Budget notifications handle threshold alerts, while a separately configured Budgets Report provides scheduled email delivery. Separate reports and recipient lists keep the departmental summaries distinct. Cost Explorer supports interactive investigation.

<<2>> can implement the requirements, but duplicates data pipelines and custom alerting and reporting code across accounts.

<<3>> can support allocation that crosses account boundaries, but account ownership already provides the required departmental boundary. The custom reporting code adds unnecessary maintenance.

<<4>> supports account-local alerts and manual analysis, but saving a Cost Explorer report does not configure the required scheduled budget email. It also distributes administration across accounts.

A budget report summarizes tracked budgets; it is not an itemized invoice. Cost data and budget alerts update periodically and are not a real-time spending cap.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Budget filters](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cost-management/latest/userguide/budgets-create-filters.html). [AWS Budgets Reports](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cost-management/latest/userguide/reporting-cost-budget.html).

question:
A legacy application on EC2 sends email through an on-premises SMTP relay. The application supports SMTP authentication and STARTTLS, but the company will not rewrite its mail-sending code. The company has verified its sending domain in Amazon SES, obtained appropriate sending access, and allowed outbound TCP port 587.

How should a solutions architect configure the application to send email through SES?

options.text: Create SES SMTP credentials for the sending Region. Configure the regional SES SMTP endpoint, port 587, and STARTTLS, and store the SMTP credentials securely.
Attach an IAM role with SES permissions to the EC2 instance. Send its temporary access key ID and secret access key directly as SMTP credentials to the regional SES endpoint over TLS.
Create a long-term IAM access key with SES permissions. Use the access key ID and the unmodified secret access key as the SMTP username and password on port 587.
Replace the SMTP mail-sending integration with an AWS SDK call to the SES API, and authorize the API calls through the EC2 instance role.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. SES exposes regional SMTP endpoints and requires an encrypted connection. Port 587 supports STARTTLS. The application must authenticate with SES SMTP credentials for that Region.

<<2>> is incorrect because temporary IAM role credentials are not supported as SES SMTP credentials. An instance role is appropriate for SES API calls, not direct SMTP authentication.

<<3>> supplies the wrong password. An SES SMTP password differs from the IAM secret access key. A supported derivation process can convert a long-term IAM secret into an SMTP password; passing the secret unchanged does not perform that conversion.

<<4>> is a valid way to send mail through the SES API without embedded long-term credentials, but requires the code change that the scenario excludes.

Choose the authentication mechanism for the interface being used: SMTP credentials for SMTP, or IAM authorization for API calls.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Connecting to SES SMTP](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/smtp-connect.html). [SES SMTP credentials](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/smtp-credentials.html).

question:
A company must move several VMware vSphere virtual machines to EC2 while retaining their installed operating systems, applications, and configuration. The applications contain undocumented settings, so rebuilding them from installation recipes is undesirable. A planned shutdown and offline export are acceptable. The guest operating systems, disk formats, boot settings, and licensing have been checked against VM Import/Export requirements.

Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Export each VM as a supported OVA or disk image, upload it to an S3 staging bucket, and use VM Import/Export with the required service role to import an AMI. Launch and validate EC2 instances from the imported AMIs.
Copy the VMware disk files to S3 through an S3 File Gateway. Use the EC2 CreateRestoreImageTask API to restore those VMware files directly as AMIs.
Use DataSync to copy the VMs' application directories to a new EC2 installation. Create an AMI from the new instance without migrating the source operating-system images.
Create EC2 Image Builder recipes using the applications' standard installers. Build new AMIs and omit settings that are not represented in the recipes.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. VM Import/Export converts supported VM images into AMIs, retaining the installed software and configuration subject to compatibility requirements. Validate the resulting instances, drivers, networking, and application behavior before cutover. An OVF descriptor alone does not contain the virtual disks needed for import.

<<2>> transports files, but CreateRestoreImageTask restores an AMI previously stored by the EC2 AMI store workflow. It does not convert an arbitrary VMware disk into an AMI.

<<3>> is useful for migrating file data. Copying selected directories to a new operating system does not capture the full installed VM stack and undocumented configuration.

<<4>> produces reproducible new images when installation and configuration are known. It does not discover and preserve the unspecified settings in this scenario.

File transfer, image conversion, and image rebuilding solve different migration problems.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Restore a stored AMI](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/APIReference/API_CreateRestoreImageTask.html). [VM Import/Export requirements](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vm-import/latest/userguide/prerequisites.html). [Import a VM as an AMI](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vm-import/latest/userguide/vmimport-image-import.html).

question:
A company has an AWS Managed Microsoft AD directory with a trust to its on-premises Active Directory. Employees need remote VPN access from their laptops to private VPC applications. The company must authenticate employees with directory credentials and require a supported RADIUS-based second factor. The network team can configure VPN routes, authorization rules, security groups, and subnet associations.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a Site-to-Site VPN connection to the corporate office and enable directory MFA for WorkSpaces desktops. Require employees to use their ordinary laptops without connecting through those desktops.

Create an AWS Client VPN endpoint with Active Directory authentication using the AWS Managed Microsoft AD directory. Enable its supported RADIUS MFA integration and configure the required Client VPN network access.

Create a VPN CloudHub topology connecting branch-office customer gateways. Keep password authentication on the private applications and use the hub for individual employees' laptop VPN authentication.

Create an AWS Client VPN endpoint with directory password authentication but no directory MFA. Add Direct Connect connectivity between the office and AWS and treat the private circuit as the second authentication factor.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. Client VPN provides remote access for individual clients and supports Active Directory authentication through AWS Managed Microsoft AD or AD Connector. When supported MFA is enabled for the connected directory, Client VPN requires it. The existing managed directory can integrate with a RADIUS server. Authentication must be combined with authorization rules and working network routes.

<<1>> connects networks and can protect WorkSpaces logins, but neither component supplies the requested MFA-protected laptop VPN sessions.

<<3>> connects branch networks through Site-to-Site VPN. It does not turn branch gateways into a managed remote-user VPN authentication service.

<<4>> supplies remote-user connectivity, but a Direct Connect circuit is a network path, not a second factor proving the employee's identity.

Successful authentication does not by itself authorize every VPC destination.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Client VPN Active Directory authentication](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/ad.html).

question:
A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled. It must centrally record CloudTrail management events from every current and future member account in all enabled AWS Regions. Account owners must not be able to alter the central logging configuration. The organization has prepared a central S3 bucket and the required permissions.

Which solution meets these requirements with the least ongoing administration?

options.text: Run a scheduled Lambda function that enumerates accounts and Regions, assumes a role in each account, and creates or updates an account-level trail when it finds a missing one.

From the management account or a CloudTrail delegated administrator, create and start a multi-Region organization trail for management events, enable the required trusted access, and deliver its logs to the central S3 bucket.
Have each account owner create a multi-Region account trail. Attach an SCP that prevents stopping those trails, and repeat the onboarding procedure when a new account joins.
Run an EC2 instance that polls Organizations for new accounts and deploys account-level CloudTrail stacks into each account and enabled Region.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. An organization trail centrally applies logging to organization members, including accounts that join later. Member accounts can view the trail but cannot change or delete it. A multi-Region trail covers enabled Regions, subject to the organization's Region enablement and trail configuration. Bucket permissions and successful delivery still need verification.

<<1>> and <<4>> can automate account-level trails, but require custom discovery, deployment, retries, and ongoing maintenance for a capability provided by an organization trail.

<<3>> can prevent selected changes after a trail exists. An SCP does not create the trail, configure delivery, or onboard future accounts automatically.

Management-event logging does not automatically enable every data-event category. Configure additional event selectors when services such as S3 object access also require auditing.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Creating an organization trail](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/creating-trail-organization.html).

question:
An e-commerce company runs MySQL transactions and a separate PostgreSQL analytics workload on EC2. The company will containerize its stateless applications and requires the Kubernetes API and deployment manifests so that the application tier can later run on another cloud. It accepts AWS-specific managed data services. Compatibility tests have validated Aurora MySQL and a redesigned Redshift analytics model and ingestion pipeline. The Linux containers require no privileged mode, DaemonSets, GPUs, or host storage.

Which design minimizes host administration and manual database-capacity management while supporting event-driven integration?

options.text: Run the containers on ECS with Fargate, use Aurora Serverless v2 for MySQL and Redshift Serverless, and route application events through EventBridge to processing workers.

Run the containers in an EC2 Auto Scaling group with a self-managed Kubernetes control plane, use provisioned Aurora MySQL and a provisioned Redshift cluster, and publish application notifications through SNS.
Run the containers on EKS with Fargate, use Aurora Serverless v2 for MySQL and Redshift Serverless, and route application events through EventBridge to processing and ingestion workers.
Run the containers on EKS with Fargate, use fixed-size provisioned Aurora MySQL instances and a provisioned Redshift cluster, and process events through Kinesis Data Streams consumers.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. EKS retains Kubernetes deployment interfaces while Fargate manages the pod compute infrastructure. Aurora Serverless v2 adjusts database compute within a configured range, and Redshift Serverless manages analytics capacity. EventBridge routes matching events to workers that perform the required processing and ingestion.

<<1>> reduces administration, but ECS does not provide the required Kubernetes API or deployment model.

<<2>> preserves Kubernetes but retains control-plane, worker-host, and provisioned database-capacity administration.

<<4>> meets the container requirement and can implement event processing, but retains the fixed provisioned database capacity the company wants to avoid managing.

Kubernetes helps application portability; it does not make AWS managed databases portable. Redshift is an analytical warehouse, not a drop-in PostgreSQL transactional server, and EventBridge does not itself migrate a database or build an ingestion pipeline. The compatibility and pipeline work in the stem is essential.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [EKS on Fargate](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/fargate.html). [Aurora serverless capacity](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/aurora-serverless-v2-administration.html). [Redshift Serverless](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/redshift/latest/gsg/getting-started.html). [EventBridge event buses](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eventbridge/latest/userguide/eb-event-bus.html).

question:
A REST API uses API Gateway and Lambda to access an RDS for MySQL DB instance. During peaks, database CPU and connection counts rise sharply. Tracing shows repeated reads of the same reference data and frequent creation of database connections. These reads can tolerate a short, defined period of staleness. Lambda memory and CPU are adequate, and individual uncached queries have already been tuned.

Which two changes address the measured bottlenecks? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Double Lambda memory and explicitly close the database connection after every query, without changing the database access pattern.
Add an ElastiCache cache-aside layer for the repeated reads. Set an appropriate TTL and invalidate or refresh affected entries when the application writes data.
Place RDS Proxy between Lambda and MySQL, configure its connection pool and authentication, and use the proxy endpoint for database access.
Increase the Lambda timeout and reserved concurrency so that more invocations can wait for or open database connections simultaneously.
Convert the database to a traditional Multi-AZ DB instance deployment with one standby and direct read queries to that standby.

explanation.text:
<<2>> reduces repeated query work: cache hits return data without executing the query in MySQL. TTL and write-handling rules must match the permitted staleness.

<<3>> reduces connection-management overhead by reusing pooled database connections across application clients. Pool limits should protect the database, and workloads that pin sessions can reduce pooling efficiency. RDS Proxy does not cache query results or create unlimited database capacity.

<<1>> addresses a Lambda resource limit that measurements do not show and increases connection churn by closing connections after every query.

<<4>> permits more outstanding database work without removing the bottleneck and can worsen overload.

<<5>> improves availability, but the standby in a traditional Multi-AZ DB instance deployment cannot serve reads. A read replica or a Multi-AZ DB cluster is a different design.

Use caching to avoid work and pooling to reuse connections; the mechanisms are complementary.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Caching strategies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonElastiCache/latest/dg/Strategies.html). [RDS Proxy connections](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/rds-proxy-connections.html). [Multi-AZ DB instances](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Concepts.MultiAZSingleStandby.html).

question:
A financial company uses WorkSpaces Personal with public streaming endpoints. Policy requires new desktop streaming sessions to originate from approved office networks. Each office has known, static public egress IP ranges. The company is opening another office and wants a central control that applies across the directory without changing individual desktops or application firewalls.

Which solution meets the requirement?

options.text: Assign a separate Elastic IP address to an EC2 jump host for each employee and record those destination addresses in the desktop inventory.
Create a Direct Connect connection from each office to the VPC while leaving the WorkSpaces streaming access policy open to all client addresses.
Update the Windows Firewall on every WorkSpace to allow access only to application servers in the offices' private address ranges.
Create a WorkSpaces IP access control group containing the approved offices' public egress CIDR ranges and associate the group with the WorkSpaces directory. Add the new office's ranges to the group.
