explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. WorkSpaces IP access control groups evaluate the source networks from which users establish streaming sessions. Associating a custom group with the directory replaces its default unrestricted group. Rules must use the public source addresses WorkSpaces sees, including any office NAT or VPN egress addresses.

<<1>> assigns addresses to infrastructure but does not restrict the source of WorkSpaces streaming connections.

<<2>> adds private network connectivity. It does not by itself restrict access through the existing public WorkSpaces streaming endpoints.

<<3>> controls traffic handled by individual desktop operating systems and changes application connectivity. It does not configure the requested directory-level streaming-origin restriction.

This control identifies a network origin, not an employee's physical location. It also does not restrict public management API operations such as restart or rebuild. Separate IAM controls govern those operations.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [WorkSpaces IP access control groups](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/workspaces/latest/adminguide/amazon-workspaces-ip-access-control-groups.html).

question:
A company owns a transit gateway in its network account. Existing production VPCs use this gateway. A staging account frequently creates and deletes VPCs and needs broad IP connectivity to approved production networks. The staging team must manage its own VPC attachments without requesting manual acceptance each time. The network team will retain control of transit-gateway route tables and has approved an automatic routing policy for staging attachments.

Which design meets these requirements with the fewest additional network components?

options.text: Share the existing transit gateway with the staging account through AWS RAM and enable automatic acceptance of shared attachments. Grant staging permission to manage its own VPC attachments and VPC routes, while the network account implements the approved transit-gateway routing policy.
Create a transit gateway in the staging account, peer it with the production transit gateway, and have the network team accept the peering and maintain routes across both gateways.
Publish each approved production application through a separate PrivateLink endpoint service and create interface endpoints in each staging VPC instead of routed connectivity.
Route staging traffic through an on-premises hub over dedicated connectivity and return it to the production VPCs through the existing transit gateway.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. RAM allows the staging account to attach its own VPCs to the existing transit gateway. Automatic acceptance removes the recurring attachment-approval step. The owner must still configure appropriate transit-gateway associations, propagation, and routes, and staging must configure its VPC routes and security controls.

<<2>> can connect the networks but adds a gateway, peering, and route-management work when one shared gateway is sufficient.

<<3>> is suitable for exposing selected services privately. It does not provide the requested broad routed IP connectivity between networks.

<<4>> can be part of a hybrid network, but adds a circuit and an on-premises dependency to an AWS-to-AWS path that the existing gateway can provide.

Sharing a transit gateway does not delegate its route tables: recipient accounts cannot modify the owner's transit-gateway route tables, associations, or propagation settings.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Shared transit gateways](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/working-with-transit-gateways.html). [Accept a shared attachment](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/acccept-tgw-attach.html).

question:
A company runs stateful third-party inspection appliances on EC2 in a security VPC. A custom script currently launches and registers replacements, but failures of that script have left too few healthy appliances. The company needs automatic replacement and demand-based scaling, plus transparent inspection of IP traffic from application VPCs. The appliances support the Gateway Load Balancer GENEVE integration. The network team can configure symmetric inspection routes.

Which two changes form the required solution? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add Direct Connect connections to the application networks and use the private circuits as the appliance replacement and load-balancing mechanism.

Put the appliances in an EC2 Auto Scaling group with a repeatable launch template. Attach a Gateway Load Balancer target group, enable suitable health checks, and configure scaling policies based on appliance load.
Peer each application VPC with the security VPC and use static routes to a single appliance IP address, retaining the existing replacement script.
Put the appliance instances behind an Application Load Balancer and forward all transparent IP traffic through an HTTP listener.

Create a Gateway Load Balancer endpoint service and consumer Gateway Load Balancer endpoints. Configure application and return routes through the endpoints so both directions of each flow traverse the inspection service.

explanation.text:
<<2>> supplies managed fleet lifecycle control. Auto Scaling launches configured appliances, registers and deregisters targets, and can replace unhealthy instances. Choose scaling signals and startup health-check settings that reflect real appliance readiness.

<<5>> supplies transparent traffic insertion across VPC boundaries. A Gateway Load Balancer endpoint is the route target for the inspection service; GWLB exchanges traffic with compatible appliances using GENEVE. Correct forward and return routing preserves the stateful inspection path.

<<1>> provides hybrid connectivity, not appliance fleet replacement or load balancing.

<<3>> supplies a network path but retains a single appliance destination and the unreliable lifecycle script.

<<4>> operates on HTTP/HTTPS requests rather than transparently distributing arbitrary IP packets to inspection appliances.

GWLB flow stickiness and symmetric routing do not replicate appliance session state. Test failure behavior and draining with the vendor; existing stateful sessions can still be disrupted when an appliance fails.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Auto Scaling load balancer integration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/autoscaling-load-balancer.html). [Gateway Load Balancer](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/gateway/introduction.html). [GWLB endpoints](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpce-gateway-load-balancer.html).

question:
A company connects an on-premises router to AWS through a 200 Mbps hosted Direct Connect connection. A transit virtual interface connects to a Direct Connect gateway associated with a transit gateway. The BGP session is established, the associations are available, and VPC and transit-gateway forwarding routes are correct. However, the on-premises router receives no advertisement for the required VPC CIDR. That CIDR is absent from the Direct Connect gateway association's allowed-prefix list.

Which change addresses the missing route advertisement?

options.text: Enable VPC attachment propagation into the transit-gateway route table and leave the Direct Connect gateway allowed-prefix list unchanged, relying on propagation to advertise the VPC CIDR over BGP.
Add the required CIDR, or an appropriate nonoverlapping aggregate, to the allowed prefixes for the Direct Connect gateway association with the transit gateway.
Upgrade the hosted connection to 500 Mbps because transit virtual interfaces require at least that bandwidth, leaving the prefix configuration unchanged.
Replace the hosted connection with a MACsec-capable dedicated connection and require encryption, leaving the gateway association and prefixes unchanged.
Rotate the BGP authentication key on both ends of the established session, leaving the gateway association and prefixes unchanged.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. For a transit-gateway association, Direct Connect advertises the prefixes explicitly configured in the allowed-prefix list. It does not automatically advertise every VPC route from the transit-gateway route table. An aggregate must be appropriate for the intended destinations and must not overlap allowed prefixes of other transit gateways on the same Direct Connect gateway.

<<1>> affects forwarding within the transit gateway but does not populate the separate advertisement list.

<<3>> relies on an obsolete bandwidth restriction. Current documentation permits transit virtual interfaces on dedicated or hosted connections of any speed.

<<4>> changes link encryption and infrastructure, not the missing BGP prefix. Direct Connect MACsec is not configured directly on a hosted connection.

<<5>> changes session authentication. The session is already established, and rekeying does not originate the missing route.

Do not apply virtual-private-gateway semantics here: with a virtual private gateway, the allowed list filters VPC CIDRs; with a transit gateway, the configured prefixes themselves are advertised.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Direct Connect allowed prefixes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/allowed-to-prefixes.html). [Direct Connect virtual interfaces](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/WorkingWithVirtualInterfaces.html). [Direct Connect MACsec](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/MACsec.html).

question:
A company stores VPC Flow Logs in S3 as gzip-compressed text and queries them with Redshift Spectrum. A dashboard reads only a few columns from recent hourly intervals, but measurements show that it scans large amounts of log data. All log records must be retained. The company wants to improve new-log storage efficiency and reduce dashboard scanning without deploying a custom conversion service. Existing retained logs can remain unchanged.

Which solution best meets these requirements?

options.text: Create replacement flow-log delivery in Parquet format with hourly partitions and suitable prefixes. Register the format and partitions in the external table catalog, and filter dashboard queries on the partition columns while selecting only required fields.
Keep text-format delivery and add a scheduled job that recompresses each gzip object with another compression algorithm, retaining the same row-oriented layout and query predicates.
Distribute new text logs among additional S3 buckets and configure the dashboard to query every bucket for each request.
Run a Glue crawler more frequently over the existing text layout, but leave the file format, partition strategy, and dashboard queries unchanged.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. Native Parquet output lets Spectrum read selected columns, while hourly partition predicates exclude unrelated time intervals. The catalog must describe the new format and expose the partitions. Coordinate the delivery transition to avoid a logging gap and retain historical records as required.

<<2>> can alter compression but adds a custom processing job and retains a row format that cannot skip unneeded columns in the same way.

<<3>> changes storage locations without giving the query a way to exclude irrelevant data; scanning all buckets retains the problem.

<<4>> updates metadata discovery, but a crawler alone does not rewrite text as Parquet or make unchanged queries prune hourly partitions.

Parquet size savings depend on the workload; very small flow-log batches can be larger because of file overhead. Verify scan bytes, partition pruning, and file sizes rather than assuming a universal performance multiplier. This change improves newly delivered data and does not retroactively convert history.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Flow log file formats](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/flow-logs-s3-path.html). [Spectrum query performance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/redshift/latest/dg/c-spectrum-external-performance.html).

question:
A company serves an application through public ALBs in two AWS Regions. Both deployments can serve live requests, and each has healthy targets that verify application readiness, including required database access. Users are distributed worldwide. The company wants DNS to select the healthy Region with the lowest estimated network latency for each user and continue using the remaining Region when one deployment is unhealthy.

Which solution meets the requirement with the least custom routing logic?

options.text: Create Route 53 geolocation alias records that map countries to the nearest Region and enable Evaluate Target Health on the aliases.
Deploy a Regional API Gateway endpoint and a custom redirect service that chooses an application Region from the client IP address country.
Create Route 53 primary and secondary failover alias records, enable Evaluate Target Health, and always prefer the primary Region while it is healthy.
Create Route 53 latency-based alias records for the two regional ALBs and enable Evaluate Target Health on each alias.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. Latency-based routing uses Route 53 latency data to select among the configured Regions. Evaluate Target Health incorporates the ALB target health into DNS selection, so an unhealthy deployment can be excluded while the other remains healthy. The application-aware target checks make this health signal meaningful.

<<1>> uses geographic rules. Geographic proximity is not the same as the lowest measured network latency.

<<2>> adds custom application routing and uses country as a proxy for latency. It does not provide the requested managed latency-based selection.

<<3>> supplies active-passive failover, but sends all users to the primary while it is healthy, regardless of which Region has lower latency.

This is DNS selection based on observed regional latency, not a new end-to-end timing probe for every request. Resolver behavior and DNS caching affect changes. If every record is unhealthy, Route 53 can return unhealthy records rather than an empty answer; health-based routing is not a guarantee of availability during total failure.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Route 53 latency routing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/routing-policy-latency.html). [Route 53 health selection](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/health-checks-how-route-53-chooses-records.html).

question:
A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled. In its member-account OU, only approved supervisory roles may perform IAM administration. Other member-account IAM users and workload roles must be blocked from IAM actions even if they receive a broad identity policy. The restriction must automatically cover future accounts placed in the OU. The supervisory roles already have appropriate identity permissions, and their creation, trust policies, and assumption permissions are centrally protected. Management-account access and service-linked roles are governed separately.

Which approach provides the required central restriction?

options.text: Attach an SCP to the member-account OU that explicitly denies IAM actions unless aws:PrincipalArn matches an approved supervisory role ARN. Retain the necessary SCP allow coverage and the supervisors' identity-based permissions.
Attach a permissions boundary that excludes IAM actions to each existing non-supervisory user and role, without enforcing boundary attachment for newly created identities.
Attach an SCP directly to each non-supervisory IAM user and role, leaving the supervisory roles without that attachment.
Create an IAM administration role and grant the supervisory team permission to assume it, without changing policies or restrictions for other principals.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. An OU-attached SCP can impose an explicit deny on affected member-account principals, including those with broad identity policies. An exception based on aws:PrincipalArn can identify the approved supervisory roles. For an assumed role, this context key contains the IAM role ARN, not its STS session ARN.

<<2>> can limit individual identities, but the described process does not cover future identities automatically and does not provide the requested OU-wide guardrail.

<<3>> uses an unsupported attachment point. SCPs attach to organization roots, OUs, or accounts, not IAM users and roles.

<<4>> grants a controlled administrative path but does not remove existing administrative paths for other principals.

An SCP sets a permission ceiling and grants nothing. Supervisors still need identity permissions and must remain allowed by all applicable controls. Protect the exempt roles from unauthorized creation, assumption, and modification. SCPs do not restrict the management account or service-linked roles, which the stem handles separately.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Service control policies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps.html). [Principal ARN condition key](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_condition-keys.html#condition-keys-principalarn).

question:
A company runs a web application with RDS for MySQL in one Region and maintains application capacity in a recovery Region. Its disaster recovery objectives are an RTO of 30 minutes and an RPO of 1 hour. Recovery exercises show that restoring this database from backup exceeds the RTO, while promoting a prebuilt replica and bringing the recovery application into service fits within 30 minutes. The company monitors replication freshness and has an approved control to stop primary writes before a replication interruption can exceed the RPO. Recovery procedures also prevent both Regions from accepting writes simultaneously.

Which two components should the solutions architect implement? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Export the database to S3 every hour and copy the exports to the recovery Region, relying on importing a complete export after a regional failure.
Copy database snapshots to the recovery Region and restore a new DB instance from the latest snapshot only after detecting a failure.

Create a cross-Region RDS read replica in advance. Use tested recovery automation, including Lambda calls to PromoteReadReplica, to promote it and configure the recovery application to use its writable RDS endpoint.
Create an RDS read replica in another Availability Zone of the primary Region and use it as the only database recovery copy for a regional outage.

Configure Route 53 failover records for the regional application endpoints. Make recovery health depend on a successfully promoted database and a functioning application, and validate DNS caching and client reconnection within the recovery procedure.

explanation.text:
<<3>> maintains a database copy in the recovery Region before failure, avoiding the measured full-restore delay. Promotion makes the replica a standalone writable DB instance. The automation must wait for readiness through a suitable orchestration mechanism rather than assume one Lambda invocation can wait indefinitely.

<<5>> directs application clients to the recovery deployment when the primary is unhealthy and the recovery application is ready. Database promotion, application configuration, and DNS failover are separate steps. Use the promoted RDS endpoint for database connections so TLS hostname verification matches the RDS certificate.

<<1>> and <<2>> are backup-and-restore designs. They retain useful recovery data, but the measured full restoration time violates this workload's RTO. An hourly schedule alone also does not bound data loss to one hour when export or copy delay is included.

<<4>> remains in the affected Region and does not supply the required regional isolation.

Cross-Region replication is asynchronous, and promotion can take several minutes or longer. The tested timing, freshness monitoring, and write controls establish this scenario's objectives; the service choice alone does not guarantee them. Route 53 moves traffic; it neither promotes RDS nor fences the former writer.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [Cross-Region read replicas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReadRepl.XRgn.html). [Read replica promotion](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReadRepl.Promote.html). [Route 53 failover selection](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/health-checks-how-route-53-chooses-records.html). [RDS MySQL TLS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/MySQL.Concepts.SSLSupport.html).

question:
An online retailer runs product browsing and checkout in one ECS service behind an ALB and CloudFront. Browsing consumes most of the capacity during sales, but the two modules currently scale together. Each module can be deployed as a separate service without changing its API. JWT authorization is already implemented with trusted signing keys.

The retailer wants independent scaling and better workload isolation while retaining ECS and minimizing application changes. Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy browsing and checkout as separate ECS services with distinct target groups and scaling policies. Route their URL paths with ALB rules, retain appropriate CloudFront behaviors, and keep JWT validation on each protected path.
Migrate both modules to EKS deployments with separate scaling policies and replace the current ECS deployment and operating processes with Kubernetes equivalents.
Add API Gateway with a JWT authorizer ahead of the existing combined ECS service, but keep one task definition and one shared scaling policy for both modules.
Rewrite both modules as Lambda functions and replace their ECS runtime with separate API Gateway integrations and concurrency settings.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. Each service has its own task count and demand metrics, so a browsing surge can add browsing capacity without forcing an equal checkout expansion. Separate target groups preserve module routing and health checks while retaining the current container platform.

<<2>> can provide independent scaling, but violates the requirement to retain ECS and introduces an unnecessary platform migration.

<<3>> improves API-level authentication controls without separating the shared compute and scaling boundary. Authorizing a request does not allocate independent module capacity.

<<4>> changes the runtime and requires the rewrite the company wants to avoid.

Choose metrics that reflect each module's bottleneck, maintain adequate checkout capacity, and ensure the underlying EC2 capacity scales if the services do not use Fargate. Shared databases and other dependencies can still couple the services. Route by the requested operation, not by treating a user role as a measure of current load. JWT claims must be accepted only after signature, issuer, audience, and expiry checks. Keep personalized checkout responses out of shared caches unless the cache configuration safely distinguishes users.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [ECS service scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/service-auto-scaling.html); [ALB listener rules](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/listener-rules.html).

question:
A consortium of healthcare organizations plans to use a permissioned Managed Blockchain network to verify the history of patient-record versions. Only specifically authorized recipients may retrieve a patient's full record. The design must avoid placing directly identifying patient data on the shared ledger and must allow off-chain retention policies to be enforced.

Which design best meets these requirements?

options.text: Store complete patient records in ledger transactions and rely on network membership alone to limit every member to the patients they are authorized to see.

Store encrypted, access-controlled records in DynamoDB. Use Lambda to publish a cryptographic commitment to each version on the ledger, with a random per-version nonce and identifying metadata kept off-chain.
Store patient names and patient identifiers on the ledger, while retaining clinical details and other sensitive attributes in DynamoDB.

Encrypt complete patient records before placing them on the ledger, retain the ciphertext there permanently, and rely solely on future decryption-key deletion to satisfy all off-chain retention requirements.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. Authorized recipients retrieve the record through the controlled off-chain path and verify its version against the ledger commitment. The ledger supplies a shared integrity reference without becoming the repository for full patient records or direct identifiers.

<<1>> distributes sensitive records through the shared ledger and equates consortium membership with patient-specific authorization.

<<3>> still puts directly identifying information on the ledger, contrary to the requirement.

<<4>> keeps the complete encrypted record on the ledger and makes retention depend entirely on key disposal. That does not implement the required off-chain record lifecycle.

Use a documented, reviewed commitment construction over a canonical record version and a sufficiently random nonce that is disclosed only to authorized verifiers. A bare hash of a name or patient ID can be guessed and linked; hashing alone is not anonymization. A matching commitment detects a changed record relative to that version, but does not prove that the original clinical information was true. Nor does the ledger make DynamoDB immutable. Define record access, key handling, versioning, audit, backups, and retention separately, including the privacy implications of the remaining ledger metadata.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Managed Blockchain permissioned networks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/managed-blockchain/latest/hyperledger-fabric-dev/what-is-managed-blockchain.html); [Verifying off-chain data](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/database/store-off-chain-data-using-amazon-managed-blockchain-and-amazon-s3-part-2/).

question:
A banking application runs on EC2 with Aurora PostgreSQL in one Region. Its disaster recovery targets are an RPO below one minute and an RTO of 15 minutes. Recovery drills have shown that its preconfigured EC2 recovery, database promotion, application checks, and routing changes finish within 12 minutes when continuous replication is healthy.

Which design minimizes idle application compute in the recovery Region while preserving this tested recovery approach?

options.text: Keep DRS replication staging and an Aurora Global Database secondary ready in the recovery Region, with networking, permissions, quotas, and recovery templates prepared. Launch application recovery instances, fail over the database, validate the stack, and then enable the Route 53 failover destination.
Run a full duplicate application fleet in the recovery Region at production capacity and keep both regional application fleets active throughout normal operation.
Keep a reduced application fleet continuously running in the recovery Region alongside the replicated database, then expand that fleet during recovery.
Copy hourly EC2 and Aurora snapshots to the recovery Region and create the complete recovery environment only after the primary Region fails.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. The pilot-light application tier avoids continuously running the recovery application fleet while keeping its replicated state and prerequisites ready. The Aurora secondary supplies the separate database recovery path. The supplied drill result establishes that this workload's launch-and-validate sequence fits the RTO; the service names alone would not establish that result.

<<2>> offers more immediately available application capacity but retains the largest idle or duplicate compute footprint for the stated objective.

<<3>> is a valid warm-standby strategy and can reduce recovery time further, but keeps application instances running when the tested pilot-light approach already meets the target.

<<4>> cannot support a sub-minute RPO with hourly recovery points and adds substantial provisioning and restore work to the outage.

Monitor both DRS replication health and Aurora replication lag. Their typical behavior supports this design but is not an absolute per-incident promise. Recover application capacity and establish a writable, healthy database before publishing the recovery destination as ready for traffic. Include secrets, certificates, KMS access, external dependencies and rollback in drills. Retest after meaningful changes to boot time, data volume or recovery capacity; CloudFormation templates are useful only when the associated prerequisites and timing have been validated.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Aurora Global Database](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/aurora-global-database.html); [Elastic Disaster Recovery objectives](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/drs/latest/userguide/CloudEndure-Concepts.html).

question:
A Java application transcodes each newly uploaded S3 video in a single CPU-based job lasting about 40 minutes. The existing EC2 host is frequently idle. The application has a durable idempotency mechanism and can run in a supported container without special hardware.

The company wants to run concurrent jobs without maintaining worker servers or paying for an always-running worker. Which design best meets these requirements?

options.text: Place upload notifications in SQS and process them with an EC2 Auto Scaling worker group that always retains at least one running instance.
Run the complete 40-minute transcoding operation inside a Lambda function invoked by the S3 upload notification.
Package the application as an ECS task on Fargate. Use the S3 event to invoke a short Lambda launcher that starts one task per accepted job, and monitor task completion and failures for retry.
Run the application container on one continuously running EC2 instance that polls the bucket and starts local transcoding processes.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. The short launcher starts the work, while a standalone Fargate task runs the long transcoding operation and exits when finished. Fargate manages the worker infrastructure and allows separate jobs to use separate task capacity.

<<1>> is a valid queued-worker design, but retains an always-running EC2 worker and its operating responsibilities. Long polling itself is not the reason to reject SQS.

<<2>> exceeds Lambda's 15-minute invocation limit. That is a runtime limit, not a memory limit, and a container image does not remove it.

<<4>> retains both the single-host bottleneck and idle worker cost.

Do not equate a successful RunTask response with successful video output. Track the task's eventual exit status, validate its output, and retry launch or execution failures through durable job state. Use the existing idempotency mechanism because upload events can be duplicated. Bound concurrent jobs to quotas and downstream capacity, configure task roles and networking, and select task CPU, memory and temporary storage to fit the workload. This design meets the stated operational and idle-worker constraints; it is not a universal claim that Fargate is cheaper than every tuned EC2 or specialized media-service alternative.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [ECS standalone tasks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/standalone-tasks.html); [Lambda function limits](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/gettingstarted-limits.html); [S3 event notifications](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/EventNotifications.html).

question:
A CloudFormation stack creates a target IAM role in Account A. An EC2 instance in Account B runs with a source role supplied by its instance profile. That source role already has an identity policy allowing sts:AssumeRole on the target role, and no applicable explicit deny blocks the request.

The target role must trust only that specific source role. Which change resolves the missing cross-account trust?

options.text: Change the source role trust policy in Account B to trust Account A, leaving the target role trust policy unchanged.
Change the target role trust policy in Account A to trust Account B as an account principal, without restricting trust to the source role.
Add CAPABILITY_IAM and CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM to the CloudFormation deployment request without changing either role policy.
Change the target role trust policy in Account A to allow sts:AssumeRole for the ARN of the specific instance-profile role in Account B.

explanation.text:
<<4>> is correct. The caller's identity policy supplies one side of cross-account authorization, and the target role's trust policy supplies the other. Naming the source role ARN in the target trust policy grants the specific trust requested by the scenario.

<<1>> changes who can assume the caller role rather than who can assume the target. The instance-profile role still needs its appropriate EC2 service trust.

<<2>> can enable cross-account assumption when Account B delegates permission to a caller, but it trusts the account more broadly than the specified-role requirement permits. An account root principal in a trust policy is not restricted to requests made with root-user credentials.

<<3>> acknowledges CloudFormation's ability to create IAM resources; it does not add runtime sts:AssumeRole authorization or change the target's trusted principal.

Use the IAM role ARN, not the instance profile ARN or an EC2 instance ARN, as the source principal. After assumption, the temporary session is governed by the target role's permissions and any applicable session restrictions and explicit denies. The trust policy determines who may enter the role, not what the resulting session can do.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [STS AssumeRole authorization](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/STS/latest/APIReference/API_AssumeRole.html); [IAM role and account principals](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_principal.html); [CloudFormation IAM capability acknowledgements](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/APIReference/API_CreateStack.html).

question:
An online retailer's single EC2 web server becomes unresponsive during traffic surges. Read-heavy queries also saturate its RDS PostgreSQL primary. The application is stateless and already supports separate read and write database connection strings. Compatibility testing has confirmed that it can use Aurora PostgreSQL.

Which listed design removes the single web-server dependency and adds database read capacity with minimal application changes?

options.text: Deploy the web tier in an EC2 Auto Scaling group across Availability Zones behind an ALB. Convert RDS to a traditional Multi-AZ DB instance and send application reads to its standby.

Deploy the web tier in an EC2 Auto Scaling group across Availability Zones behind an ALB. Migrate to Aurora PostgreSQL with replicas, using the reader endpoint for eligible reads and the writer endpoint for writes.
Upgrade the existing single web server to a larger instance. Migrate to Aurora PostgreSQL with replicas and route eligible reads through the reader endpoint.
Deploy the web tier across Availability Zones behind an ALB. Migrate to Aurora with replicas but continue routing all application reads and writes to the writer endpoint.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. Multiple web instances behind the ALB remove the single-instance dependency, while the Auto Scaling group adjusts web capacity. Routing eligible reads to Aurora Replicas supplies the independent database read capacity that the current primary lacks.

<<1>> uses a traditional RDS Multi-AZ standby as if it were a read replica. That standby is reserved for availability and cannot serve the application's reads.

<<3>> improves individual web-server capacity but leaves one server as the application availability dependency.

<<4>> creates replicas without sending the read workload to them, so it does not relieve the stated writer bottleneck.

The Aurora reader endpoint balances new connections among available replicas, not each query inside an established connection. Consider connection-pool behavior and replication lag, and keep consistency-sensitive operations on the appropriate writer path. This scenario has already validated compatibility and supports endpoint configuration changes; migration is not automatically change-free for every PostgreSQL application. Keeping RDS PostgreSQL and adding ordinary read replicas could also meet the broad need, but that complete design is not one of the choices. Do not generalize the standby restriction to readable instances in supported RDS Multi-AZ DB clusters.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Aurora reader endpoints](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/Aurora.Endpoints.Reader.html); [RDS single-standby Multi-AZ](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Concepts.MultiAZSingleStandby.html).

question:
A company hosts a proprietary TCP service in its data center. A provider VPC already reaches the service's private IP addresses through redundant Direct Connect paths with the required encryption in place. Approved partner companies need to consume only this service from their own AWS VPCs, without Internet exposure or broad network peering.

Which design should the company use?

options.text: Create an NLB in the provider VPC with the reachable on-premises private IPs as targets. Publish an endpoint service for approved partner principals, accept authorized connections, and have partners create interface endpoints.
Create an ALB in the provider VPC and associate it directly with a load-balancer-backed VPC endpoint service, without an NLB, for the unchanged TCP protocol.
Keep only the existing Direct Connect attachment and provider-VPC security groups, and assume that these automatically give every partner VPC a private service connection.
Create a public NLB for the on-premises targets and restrict its listener to approved partner public egress addresses, letting partners connect through their Internet gateways.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. The consumer interface endpoint exposes a private service connection inside each partner VPC. PrivateLink carries it to the provider's NLB, which forwards it over the existing private hybrid path to the registered on-premises targets. Endpoint-service permissions and connection acceptance control which partners can connect.

<<2>> is not the supported direct load-balancer association for this endpoint-service design and does not preserve the arbitrary TCP protocol. For HTTP use cases, an ALB can sit behind an NLB, but that is a different topology from the proposed direct ALB association.

<<3>> provides the provider's hybrid connectivity without establishing a connection for the partner VPCs.

<<4>> exposes an Internet-facing path, contrary to the stated private-access requirement, even if source addresses are restricted.

Register supported private IP ranges and configure forward and return routing, health checks, security controls, and sufficient hybrid capacity. Use multiple Availability Zones for the endpoint service and test loss of a hybrid path. Direct Connect supplies a private network path but is not, by itself, a blanket encryption guarantee; this scenario separately supplies the required encryption. Keep application authentication and tenant authorization even when the network connection is private.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [PrivateLink endpoint services](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/create-endpoint-service.html); [NLB IP targets](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/network/load-balancer-target-groups.html).

question:
A company is moving 18 Java and Node.js applications from virtual machines to AWS. Most run only for weekly reconciliation or quarter-end reporting. Tasks need up to 3 GiB of memory, and one unsplittable Java report runs for 2–4 hours. Jobs may wait a few minutes for capacity to start.

The company wants one container deployment platform, demand-based compute capacity, and no commitment to rarely used peak capacity. Which listed solution best meets these requirements?

options.text: Run the Java applications on fixed EC2 fleets and Node.js applications on App Runner, using separate deployment and scaling processes for the two platforms.

Containerize all applications on ECS with EC2 capacity. Scale services or launch report tasks as needed, and use an Auto Scaling group capacity provider with managed scaling and task-aware CPU and memory requirements.
Package each application as a Lambda container image, run the complete report in one invocation, and configure provisioned concurrency for all functions throughout the month.
Run all application containers on an EC2 fleet and purchase commitments for the full quarter-end peak capacity, retaining that capacity between reporting periods.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. ECS provides one container platform for both runtimes and supports the long report as a task. Demand creates task requirements, and the capacity provider adjusts the EC2 fleet to place those tasks. This avoids committing to the rarely used peak simply because it appears in the scaling maximum.

<<1>> retains separate platforms and operating processes, contrary to the standardization requirement.

<<3>> exceeds Lambda's 15-minute invocation limit for the unsplittable report. A container image does not remove that limit. The 3 GiB memory requirement is not the exclusion, because Lambda supports more memory than that.

<<4>> pays for or commits to peak capacity that the stated usage does not justify.

Task-count scaling and container-instance scaling are separate controls. Define resource requests that fit the selected instance types, configure capacity-provider limits, and avoid competing policies that independently change the same fleet's desired capacity. Collect memory metrics if using custom host-memory policies; memory utilization is not a default EC2 metric. A memory-only policy cannot substitute for task-aware capacity provisioning. Scale down unused capacity where startup latency permits, protect running long tasks during scale-in, and compare measured costs before choosing commitments. Fargate is also a candidate for evaluation, but is not one of the listed designs.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [ECS service scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/service-auto-scaling.html); [ECS cluster capacity scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/cluster-auto-scaling.html); [Lambda function limits](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/gettingstarted-limits.html); [Additional host metrics with the CloudWatch agent](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/Install-CloudWatch-Agent.html).

question:
A Linux web application uses PostgreSQL and shared NFS files for images and uploads. It must move to AWS without application-code changes and scale from 3 to 50 EC2 instances across Availability Zones. Compatibility with the selected Elastic Beanstalk platform and Aurora PostgreSQL has been verified. Persistent files and the database must survive replacement of the web environment.

Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Use a load-balanced Elastic Beanstalk environment with an ALB and multi-AZ Auto Scaling. Mount an independently managed Regional EFS file system during instance initialization, and use a separately managed Aurora PostgreSQL cluster with backups and a cross-AZ replica.
Use a load-balanced Elastic Beanstalk environment and attach the same EBS Multi-Attach volume directly to every web instance across Availability Zones as the shared NFS filesystem.
Use a multi-AZ EC2 Auto Scaling web tier with Regional EFS and separate Aurora, but perform the EFS mount only in a scale-in termination lifecycle hook after an instance is selected for removal.
Use a load-balanced Elastic Beanstalk environment with separate Aurora, and rewrite all file operations to use S3 object APIs instead of mounting an NFS filesystem.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. Regional EFS supplies shared NFS access across Availability Zones, and initialization mounts it before an instance serves application traffic. Managing EFS and Aurora outside the disposable web environment separates persistent data from application-environment replacement.

<<2>> substitutes shared block storage for managed NFS and tries to cross the single-AZ boundary of EBS Multi-Attach. It does not provide the required 50-instance multi-AZ shared filesystem.

<<3>> performs the initialization at the wrong lifecycle stage. A launch hook can support mount preparation, but a termination hook runs when the instance is leaving service.

<<4>> can be a useful modernization, but requires the application-code changes excluded by the scenario. S3 object APIs are not a drop-in NFS mount.

Create EFS mount targets and allow the required NFS traffic in the application AZs. Verify mount failure behavior so an instance cannot serve requests against an unintended local directory. Beanstalk configuration files can mount an existing EFS filesystem without changing application logic. Preserve data with backups and tested restore procedures: multi-AZ availability is not protection from every accidental deletion or logical corruption. Apply retention policies to persistent resources instead of assuming that environment termination always retains resources created inside it.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [EFS protocol and availability](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/whatisefs.html); [EFS with Elastic Beanstalk](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/services-efs.html); [Auto Scaling lifecycle hook timing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/lifecycle-hooks.html); [EBS Multi-Attach scope](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/ebs-volumes-multi.html).

question:
A GitHub Actions workflow deploys to S3 using a long-lived IAM-user access key. An IAM role already has the required deployment permissions. Security requires unattended access using short-lived credentials, with trust restricted to the approved repository and production branch or protected environment.

Which change meets the requirements with the least operational overhead?

options.text: Register GitHub as an IAM OIDC provider and configure the deployment role for AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity with the intended audience and approved repository subject. Let the workflow request an OIDC token and obtain temporary role credentials.
Require an engineer to complete an IAM Identity Center browser login before each deployment and copy the resulting temporary credentials into GitHub repository secrets.
Keep the IAM-user access key in a GitHub secret and rotate it daily, using that key to call AssumeRole for each deployment.
Use GitHub OIDC and the deployment role, but allow all repositories and branches in the GitHub organization to assume the role rather than restricting the approved deployment subject.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. The workflow presents a GitHub-issued identity token to STS and receives temporary credentials for the deployment role. Restricting the trust policy's audience and subject connects that authority to the intended repository and permitted branch or environment.

<<2>> introduces a human credential-distribution step instead of the required unattended workload federation.

<<3>> produces temporary role sessions but preserves the long-lived bootstrap key that security requires the company to eliminate.

<<4>> uses the correct federation mechanism with an overbroad trust boundary, allowing workflows outside the approved deployment scope.

Grant the workflow id-token: write so it can request the token, and use an appropriate credential-exchange action or equivalent STS call. That workflow permission does not itself grant S3 access: the role's permissions and trust policy still control AWS access. Protect the referenced GitHub branch or environment, test allowed and disallowed subjects, then revoke the old key after the replacement is validated. A token's audience and repository claims must be verified by the trust relationship rather than accepted from arbitrary workflow input.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [IAM OIDC trust for GitHub](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_create_for-idp_oidc.html); [GitHub workflow role federation](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/use-iam-roles-to-connect-github-actions-to-actions-in-aws/).

question:
A research pipeline reads article URLs from SQS, downloads and analyzes each article, and writes one independent JSON result. Each job takes no more than five minutes and fits Lambda's resource limits. Traffic is bursty with long idle periods. Consumers retrieve complete result files and do not require shared file locking or in-place updates.

The team can adapt its storage calls and wants to eliminate always-running worker servers and shared-filesystem administration. Which changes should it make? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use a Lambda SQS event source mapping to invoke the processing function for queued article URLs, with bounded concurrency and retry-safe processing.
Replace the existing workers with continuously running EC2 Spot instances while retaining operating-system and worker-fleet management.
Move each complete JSON result into a Neptune graph database and keep the same whole-file retrieval access pattern.
Move each complete JSON result into a continuously provisioned RDS database and keep the same whole-file retrieval access pattern.
Store each result as an S3 object with a stable key, access controls, and an appropriate lifecycle policy.

explanation.text:
<<1>> and <<5>> match the workload boundaries. The SQS event source mapping manages polling and invokes Lambda for available work, while S3 holds independently retrievable result objects. The stated duration and resource fit allow compute to run per job instead of maintaining the existing worker fleet.

<<2>> can reduce EC2 compute prices and is suitable for some retryable queue workloads, but retains the always-running servers and administration this scenario requires eliminating. Spot interruptions do not automatically make every queue workload unsuitable.

<<3>> introduces a graph database without a relationship-query requirement.

<<4>> introduces database capacity and administration without a relational-query requirement. RDS engines can store JSON; the issue is mismatch with the stated whole-object access pattern, not an inability to store the format.

Choose a batch size that fits the function timeout; one five-minute URL per invocation is a straightforward starting point. Configure the SQS visibility timeout, dead-letter handling and partial batch failures appropriately. Duplicate delivery remains possible, so use stable job identities and idempotent S3 writes, and acknowledge success only after the output is durable. Limit concurrency to respect website rate limits and downstream capacity. Compare actual request, duration and storage costs; this selection follows the explicit operational constraints rather than claiming serverless is always cheapest.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Lambda processing of SQS messages](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/with-sqs.html); [Lambda function limits](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/gettingstarted-limits.html); [S3 object storage](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/Welcome.html).

question:
A trading platform uses EC2 behind an ALB, RDS for SQL Server, and an S3 reports bucket in one Region. Read-only market analysis burdens the production database. The company wants to retain SQL Server, offload those queries, and prepare regional recovery from continuously replicated database and report data.

The source uses a supported Enterprise Edition version and instance class, and both Regions support cross-Region replicas. Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a cross-Region SQL Server read replica for analytics and configure S3 CRR with required backfill. Copy application AMIs and prepare recovery infrastructure. During disaster recovery, promote the replica, launch and validate the application, and switch its database and bucket endpoints.
Create a SQL Server read replica for analytics in the production Region and keep all application images, database replicas, and report copies only in that Region.
Copy hourly database snapshots and application AMIs to another Region and enable S3 CRR, but leave ad hoc analytics on the production writer and recover the database from the latest snapshot.
Prepare a cross-Region SQL Server replica, copied application AMIs and S3 CRR, but keep the analysis team connected to the production writer during normal operation.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. The supported cross-Region replica provides both a read-only analytics destination and a database that can be promoted for regional recovery. S3 replication and copied application artifacts cover separate state needed to restore the complete platform.

<<2>> offloads reads but leaves the recovery copies within the same regional failure domain.

<<3>> provides periodic recovery points rather than continuously replicated database state and does not offload the analytics that burdens production.

<<4>> prepares regional recovery but leaves the identified read workload on the writer.

RDS SQL Server cross-Region replicas are supported for the specified configurations; a blanket statement that SQL Server has no such replicas is outdated. Size the analytics replica so queries do not prevent it from applying changes, and monitor lag. Replication is asynchronous, so the design reduces possible data loss without promising zero loss. Validate server-level login and object synchronization, regional KMS permissions, database promotion, application configuration and traffic switching. Live S3 CRR does not automatically copy all previously existing objects, so include backfill and verify completeness. AMIs alone do not recreate networking, permissions or every runtime dependency.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [RDS SQL Server replicas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/SQLServer.ReadReplicas.html); [RDS asynchronous read replication](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReadRepl.html); [S3 replication and existing data](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/replication-what-is-isnot-replicated.html).

question:
A manufacturer is evaluating a move from on-premises Kubernetes to EKS. The cluster hosts application services and self-managed MySQL and MongoDB databases. Capacity requirements prescribe a fixed node count, and the company needs a pre-migration comparison of its current costs with the complete proposed AWS operating cost.

Which assessment approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Use Migration Evaluator with collected inventory and utilization data for the baseline business case. Supplement its results with a target-architecture estimate covering EKS, fixed worker capacity, databases, storage, backups, networking, and operating assumptions.
Begin server replication and a test migration, then treat the temporary test resources billed during that exercise as the complete steady-state TCO for the proposed EKS platform.
Use the Cloud Value Framework alone to select a generic percentage saving, then apply that percentage to the current budget without estimating the proposed service configuration.
Export only the current server inventory and use hardware counts as the complete TCO comparison, without adding service pricing, storage growth, licensing, or operating costs.

explanation.text:
<<1>> is correct. Inventory and utilization establish an evidence-based starting point, while the target-architecture estimate adds costs specific to the proposed EKS and database design. The fixed-node constraint must remain in the calculation rather than being replaced by an unsupported rightsizing assumption.

<<2>> can validate migration mechanics and reveal some real charges, but a short test does not establish steady-state usage, all target services, or the current on-premises cost baseline.

<<3>> provides a business-value perspective without the workload-specific financial model the question requires.

<<4>> supplies quantities without enough information to price either the full target architecture or the ongoing operating work.

Migration Evaluator Quick Insights specifically reports projected EC2, EBS, and operating-system license costs. It is not a complete EKS, MySQL, and MongoDB cost model by itself. Use a detailed Pricing Calculator estimate and documented assumptions for the remaining AWS services, database deployment choices, resilience, backups, transfer, support, and staff effort. Separate one-time migration costs from recurring costs and compare the same time horizon and availability level. An estimate is only as complete as its inputs; keep uncertain growth and utilization assumptions visible and test plausible alternatives.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Migration Evaluator assessments](https://aws.amazon.com/migration-evaluator/); [Migration Evaluator Quick Insights scope](https://aws.amazon.com/migration-evaluator/faqs/); [AWS Pricing Calculator estimates](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/pricing-calculator/latest/userguide/what-is-pricing-calculator.html).

question:
An energy company stores turbine data in an S3 lake cataloged with Lake Formation. Governance has approved direct S3 object reads by a research IAM role used on EC2 in two private subnets. The role already has the necessary object permissions, but its credentials must not work from unapproved networks.

Research reads must use the approved VPC without Internet routing, and direct bucket requests must not bypass this restriction. Which actions should the architect take? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Create an S3 gateway endpoint in the research VPC, associate both subnet route tables, and configure its policy for the required bucket and access point.
Create an S3 access point with network origin restricted to the approved VPC, grant the intended research access, and configure clients to use that access point.

Delegate the required bucket access through the approved access point using s3:DataAccessPointArn, and explicitly deny unintended direct or other access-point reads by the research role while aligning all relevant policies.
Enable SSE-KMS and grant the research role decryption permission, leaving the existing S3 network and request-path permissions unchanged.
Add an Allow condition checking only s3:DataAccessPointAccount for the research account, while retaining the existing direct-bucket permission.
Route both private subnets through a NAT gateway and continue using the existing direct-bucket permissions without a VPC-origin access point.

explanation.text:
<<1>>, <<2>>, and <<3>> establish the private route, approved network origin, and enforced access path. The gateway endpoint supplies S3 connectivity from both subnets. The VPC-origin access point rejects requests from other VPCs, and the bucket policy prevents the research role from avoiding that access point.

<<4>> protects stored data and governs decryption, but does not establish the required network-origin restriction.

<<5>> identifies the account that owns an access point, not the VPC from which the request originated. Keeping direct-bucket access also leaves a bypass.

<<6>> provides outbound connectivity without the requested endpoint path or network-origin authorization constraint.

An access point is not automatically the bucket's only entrance. Its policy applies only to requests made through it, and a conditional Allow does not cancel another Allow. Scope the deny to the intended research access so other approved lake services retain their required paths. The endpoint policy must allow the access point and the underlying bucket; IAM, bucket, access-point and any KMS permissions must also align. This question concerns already approved direct S3 reads, not a claim that these network controls replace Lake Formation permissions for governed query services. Test permitted VPC access, outside-VPC credentials, and direct-bucket attempts.

question:
A media service runs ECS tasks on an EC2 Auto Scaling group. Content releases have known start and end times. Measurements show that its predictive policy repeatedly launches spare capacity hours too early. Tested instance and task warm-up times are available. Frequently retrieved S3 objects remain hot throughout each month.

All traffic currently using the NAT gateway is to S3 in the same Region; other dependencies already have private paths. The company wants to remove avoidable charges without adding self-managed network servers or sacrificing required service capacity. Which actions should it take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Associate an S3 gateway endpoint with the task-subnet route tables, validate endpoint policies and access, and remove the NAT gateway after confirming it has no remaining required traffic.
Replace the NAT gateway with a single self-managed NAT instance using an On-Demand Capacity Reservation, while retaining the existing S3 routing path.
Move half the required peak capacity to Spot instances without interruption handling, replacement capacity, or an On-Demand fallback.
Move all hot S3 objects to Intelligent-Tiering and assume that objects retrieved every day will immediately enter its cheaper infrequent-access tier.

Replace the oversized predictive schedule with release-driven scheduled scaling that includes measured warm-up and safe scale-in, coordinates ECS task capacity, and retains dynamic scaling as a safety net.

explanation.text:
<<1>> and <<5>> address the two measured waste sources. A gateway endpoint removes NAT processing from the same-Region S3 path without an endpoint charge. Release-driven capacity changes can shorten unnecessary early scale-out while making instances and tasks ready before demand arrives.

<<2>> adds the self-managed network server excluded by the requirement. An On-Demand Capacity Reservation does not itself discount the instance price or supply managed NAT resilience.

<<3>> makes required capacity depend on interruptible resources without the safeguards needed to preserve availability. Spot can be part of a resilient design, but the proposed unprotected allocation does not establish one.

<<4>> assumes a tier transition that the access pattern does not support. Intelligent-Tiering keeps frequently accessed objects in its frequent-access tier; it does not immediately discount every object simply because it is enabled.

Validate that the endpoint route and policies cover every required S3 bucket before deleting NAT. For compute, schedule from measured boot, image-pull and application warm-up time, then drain safely after the release peak. Scaling EC2 instances alone does not increase the ECS service's desired task count. Keep scaling bounds and dynamic policies consistent, and verify actual savings after the change. Scheduled scaling is appropriate because the release timing is known and the current early capacity is measured as unnecessary, not because predictive scaling is inherently more expensive.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [S3 gateway endpoint routing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpc-endpoints-s3.html); [Scheduled EC2 capacity changes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/ec2-auto-scaling-scheduled-scaling.html); [ECS service scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/service-auto-scaling.html); [S3 Intelligent-Tiering access patterns](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/intelligent-tiering-overview.html); [On-Demand Capacity Reservation pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/pricing/on-demand/).

question:
A company uses AWS Organizations and publishes container images daily. Only IAM roles in its organization may access the repository; CI roles need push access and application roles need pull access. Automated cleanup must leave tagged images untouched and retain the five most recently pushed untagged images. Images are independent, are not archived, and are not referenced by manifest lists. Cleanup within 24 hours is acceptable.

Which solution meets these requirements with the least operational effort?

options.text: Use a private Amazon ECR repository. Restrict access with aws:PrincipalIsAWSService and run an AWS Glue job to delete older untagged images.
Use a public Amazon ECR repository. Add an aws:PrincipalOrgID condition to push permissions and run a Step Functions workflow to delete older untagged images.
Use a public Amazon ECR repository. Restrict access with aws:PrincipalIsAWSService and run an ECS scheduled task to delete older untagged images.

Use a private Amazon ECR repository. Grant the required role permissions, deny repository access to principals outside the organization using aws:PrincipalOrgID, and apply an untagged-image lifecycle rule with a count of five.

explanation.text:
Option <<4>> combines an organization access boundary with native retention. The repository policy's explicit deny for principals outside the expected aws:PrincipalOrgID prevents another allow from bypassing that boundary. Separate permissions still determine which internal roles may push or pull. Each caller also needs ecr:GetAuthorizationToken in an identity policy; a repository policy cannot grant that action.

Use tagStatus=untagged, countType=imageCountMoreThan, countNumber=5, and an expire action. Among matching images, ECR expires older images first. Tagged images do not match this rule. Preview the policy before applying it. Expiration is asynchronous, generally within 24 hours after an image meets the criteria, rather than an instantaneous five-image hard limit.

Option <<1>> tests whether the request is made directly by an AWS service principal, not whether an IAM role belongs to this organization, and adds custom cleanup. Options <<2>> and <<3>> use public repositories, whose public pull access cannot satisfy the private distribution requirement. Their scheduled cleanup also adds work that an ECR lifecycle policy handles.

question:
A company runs an API on API Gateway and Lambda in us-east-1, backed by Amazon RDS for MySQL. It has deployed the same API in eu-west-1 to reduce latency for European customers. Reads account for 95% of requests and tolerate replication lag. All writes must continue to use the US database, and the European functions already have secure connectivity to it. The API's Regional custom domains are configured in both Regions.

Which design reduces European read latency with the least additional database administration?

options.text: Create an independent MySQL database in Europe and maintain it with an AWS DMS full-load-and-CDC task. Use Route 53 latency records for the APIs and send European reads to the DMS target.
Create an RDS cross-Region read replica in Europe. Use Route 53 latency records for the APIs, route European reads to the replica, and route writes to the US primary.
Enable a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment for the US database. Use Route 53 failover records for the APIs and route European reads to the US standby.
Create a European MySQL database with an AWS DMS full-load-and-CDC task. Keep a simple Route 53 record pointing every customer to the US API and database.

explanation.text:
Option <<2>> uses native asynchronous replication to place a readable copy near the European API. Route 53 latency routing selects an API endpoint based on measured latency, while application code chooses the database endpoint: local replica for reads, US primary for writes. Route 53 does not route individual SQL operations or make the replica writable. Reads that require immediate visibility of a preceding write would also need the primary.

Option <<1>> can replicate data, but operating a separate target and a DMS replication task adds administration when the supported native RDS replica meets the requirements. Option <<3>> confuses high availability with read scaling: the standby of a traditional Multi-AZ DB instance deployment is neither a European replica nor a readable endpoint. Failover routing also prefers the primary endpoint until it is unhealthy rather than selecting the lower-latency healthy Region. Option <<4>> leaves European requests and reads on the US path, so the extra copy does not address their latency.

A nearby replica improves latency only when the application actually sends eligible reads to it and accepts its consistency model.

question:
An organization manages 600 AWS member accounts with all Organizations features enabled. Its existing S3 access points are compliant, and direct bucket access is governed separately. The security team must prevent IAM principals in member accounts from creating new Regional S3 access points unless those access points have a VPC network origin.

Which control enforces this requirement before creation across the member accounts?

options.text: Add a bucket policy that denies s3:CreateAccessPoint unless aws:ResourceAccount equals VPC.
Deploy an AWS Config rule and invoke Lambda to delete an access point after it is created with an Internet network origin.
Add an S3 object ACL that denies access-point creation when s3:AccessPointNetworkOrigin is Internet.
Attach an SCP at the organization root that denies s3:CreateAccessPoint when s3:AccessPointNetworkOrigin is not VPC.

explanation.text:
Option <<4>> makes the requested access point's network origin a preventive authorization condition. A deny on s3:CreateAccessPoint with StringNotEquals for s3:AccessPointNetworkOrigin=VPC blocks noncompliant requests by affected member-account principals. Other IAM permissions must still allow compliant creation; an SCP grants no permissions.

The condition describes the access point being created, not the network location from which the administrator submits the API request. A VPC-origin access point subsequently accepts data requests only through its associated VPC. The control does not convert existing access points or remove direct bucket access. SCPs do not restrict the management account or service-linked roles, so the stated member-account IAM scope matters.

Option <<1>> uses an account-ID key as though it were a network-origin key and places an organization creation guardrail in the wrong mechanism. Option <<2>> detects and remediates after creation, leaving a compliance interval. Option <<3>> misuses object ACLs: they cannot express conditional explicit denies or govern access-point creation.

question:
A company provisions resources in its member accounts only through protected CloudFormation pipelines. Existing IAM and organization controls prevent users from bypassing those pipelines or disabling governance. An enforced tag policy already restricts Project tag values, but deployments can still omit the Project tag. Every resource type in scope supports required-tag validation.

Which solution blocks deployments with missing Project tags while minimizing custom code?

options.text: Deploy an AWS Config required-tags rule to every account and notify the resource owner when Project is missing.
Deny cloudformation:CreateStack unless the request contains an aws:RequestTag/Project value, and rely on the stack tag to validate every resource.
Mark Project as required in the organization tag policy and activate the AWS-managed tagging compliance hook in WARN mode in every account and Region.

Define Project as a required key for the resource types with report_required_tag_for. Activate AWS::TagPolicies::TaggingComplianceValidator as an enabled STACK hook in FAIL mode in every deployment account and Region.

explanation.text:
Option <<4>> combines a required-key definition with preventive enforcement in the actual deployment path. The organization's effective tag policy declares which resource types require Project. The AWS-managed CloudFormation hook checks stack deployments against that policy and blocks missing required tags in FAIL mode. Activate it in every relevant account and Region, provide its execution role with the documented trust and tag:ListRequiredTags permission, and use StackSets for consistent rollout.

The existing allowed-value policy and the required-key check solve different problems: an allowed-value rule alone does not require an absent tag to exist. Required-key reporting also does not block deployments by itself; enforcement depends on the configured IaC integration. This hook operates at STACK level, not as a resource hook.

Option <<1>> detects an already-created violation. Option <<2>> checks a stack API request and cannot establish that every resource has its required tag; tag propagation varies by resource type. Option <<3>> deliberately permits a noncompliant deployment with a warning. The protected-pipeline premise closes the bypass path that a CloudFormation-only check would otherwise leave.

question:
A website uses CloudFront to cache catalog responses. Each response depends on color and size query parameters. The application treats these parameter names and values as case-insensitive, and their order has no meaning. Each parameter occurs at most once; the requests contain no signatures or case-sensitive tokens. Clients send equivalent requests with different capitalization and parameter order, fragmenting the cache.

Which change consolidates these requests into the same cache entries with the lowest edge-processing overhead?

options.text: Associate a Lambda@Edge viewer-request function that lowercases the two query parameters and sorts them before cache lookup.
Associate a CloudFront Function with the viewer-request event to lowercase the two query parameters and sort them. Include the normalized parameters in the cache policy.
Exclude both query parameters from the cache policy but continue forwarding them to the origin through an origin request policy.
Place a reverse proxy behind the origin load balancer to lowercase and sort query parameters before the application receives cache-miss requests.

explanation.text:
Option <<2>> performs a small, deterministic request transformation before CloudFront computes the cache lookup. Normalize the relevant names and values, sort the parameters, and keep them in the cache key because they change the response. For example, ?Size=M&Color=Blue and ?color=blue&size=m can both become ?color=blue&size=m under the stated application contract.

Option <<1>> can perform this transformation, but Lambda@Edge provides broader capabilities and higher execution overhead than this lightweight CloudFront Functions use case needs. Option <<3>> merges different colors and sizes into the same cache entry, potentially serving incorrect content; forwarding a value to the origin does not make it part of the cache key. Option <<4>> acts after the edge cache lookup, so it cannot prevent the original requests from creating separate CloudFront entries.

Canonicalization is safe only for transformations that preserve application meaning. Do not blindly lowercase signed values, case-sensitive identifiers, or duplicate parameters whose ordering affects processing.

question:
A company creates a VPC with primary IPv4 CIDR 10.232.18.0/24. EC2 instances must resolve records in a Route 53 private hosted zone. Instances assigned public IPv4 addresses must also receive AWS public DNS hostnames. The VPC currently uses a DHCP option set that points to an old custom DNS server with no forwarding for the private zone.

Which two changes meet these requirements using the native VPC resolver? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Associate the private hosted zone with the VPC and set both enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames to true.
Associate the private hosted zone with the VPC and change the VPC instance tenancy to dedicated.
Associate the private hosted zone with the VPC and enable Network Address Usage metrics.
Associate a DHCP option set whose domain-name-servers value is AmazonProvidedDNS and ensure the instances obtain the updated DHCP settings.
Associate a DHCP option set whose domain-name-servers value is 10.232.18.98 and ensure the instances obtain the updated DHCP settings.

explanation.text:
Options <<1>> and <<4>> configure the DNS service and direct instances to use it. Associate the private hosted zone with the VPC and enable both DNS attributes. enableDnsSupport enables Amazon DNS resolution; enableDnsHostnames, together with DNS support and a public IPv4 address, permits AWS public DNS hostnames. Private hosted-zone use also requires both attributes.

The DHCP domain-name-servers value AmazonProvidedDNS points clients at the native Route 53 Resolver. For this VPC, its VPC-relative IPv4 address is 10.232.18.2, the primary network address plus two; the link-local address 169.254.169.253 is also available. Replacing the explicitly unsuitable custom resolver is necessary here, and existing instances must obtain the changed settings.

Option <<2>> changes hardware tenancy rather than DNS behavior. Option <<3>> measures network address utilization rather than enabling DNS resolution or hostnames. Option <<5>> supplies an arbitrary address within the VPC, not the native resolver. A DHCP DNS value does not create a DNS server at that address.
